visits.text: Discover Freiburg im Breisgau, the vibrant university city known for its sunny climate and historic Old Town in Germany's Black Forest region. The magnificent Gothic Münster cathedral dominates the Marktplatz, its 116-meter spire a masterpiece of medieval architecture. The intricate stonework and stunning stained glass windows have survived centuries largely intact.

Explore the unique Bächle, small water-filled runnels that flow through the streets and alleys of the Old Town. These medieval water channels, originally used for fire-fighting and cooling, now charm visitors as they trace their path through the historic center.

The Freiburger Münster (Freiburg Cathedral) is a masterpiece of Gothic architecture, built between 1200 and 1513—one of the few cathedrals fully completed in the Middle Ages. Its 116-meter openwork tower was described in 1869 by Swiss art historian Jacob Burckhardt as the “most beautiful tower on earth.” Inside are original medieval stained-glass windows commissioned by the city's guilds, an altarpiece by Hans Baldung Grien and an Annunciation by Hans Holbein the Younger. On mornings from Monday through Saturday, the Münsterplatz market sets up directly at the foot of the facade.

The Bächle are small open-air channels that have wound through the old town streets since Freiburg's founding in 1120. Their total network reaches 15.5 km, of which 6.4 km are underground. Originally dug for water supply and firefighting, they run between the sidewalks and give the old town a unique atmosphere. According to local tradition, accidentally falling into a Bächle means you'll marry a Freiburg resident. The old town also preserves its two original medieval gates: the Martinstor (early 13th century) and the Schwabentor.

Ascent to Schlossberg, a wooded hill east of the Altstadt, accessible on foot or by funicular. Once the site of a medieval castle that has since been demolished, the hill offers a 360-degree view from its observation tower over the old town, the Rhine plain, the Vosges, and the foothills of the Black Forest.

activities.text: As the gateway to the Black Forest, Freiburg offers countless nearby hiking and cycling paths. The surrounding hills, covered in dark evergreen forests, gave the region its name and provide endless opportunities for outdoor exploration.

Wine tasting of Breisgau wines at the Münsterplatz market or in an old town cellar. The Freiburg region enjoys Germany's sunniest microclimate and produces renowned Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) and Gutedel.

days_plan.itin_title: Three-Country Tour: Switzerland, the Black Forest and Alsace
Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest
Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Black Forest & Lakes

visits.text: Experience Europa-Park in Rust, Germany's largest theme park and the second most visited in Europe after Disneyland Paris. With over 100 attractions and shows spread across 18 themed areas representing European countries, the park offers something for all ages. From high-speed roller coasters to fairy-tale worlds, each zone recreates the atmosphere of its respective nation.

The park features 13 roller coasters, some operating since 1984, demonstrating decades of innovation in theme park thrills. The Silver Star stands as one of Europe's tallest and fastest coasters, while family-friendly attractions ensure entertainment for younger visitors.

activities.text: With capacity for 60,000 guests daily, Europa-Park offers a full day of entertainment. The RailCoaster direct train from Basel makes the journey easy, with shuttle buses connecting Ringsheim station to both Europa-Park and the Rulantica water world.

days_plan.itin_title: Three-Country Tour: Switzerland, the Black Forest and Alsace

visits.text: Explore the Schluchsee, a Black Forest lake that impresses visitors with its exceptionally clear waters and the natural beauty around it. Originally a natural lake, it was dammed in 1932 and now offers an unspoilt setting for water sports and relaxing by the water. The wooded shores remain largely unspoilt, keeping their wild character.

Discover the well-maintained hiking and cycling paths that circle the lake and extend into the surrounding Black Forest. The terrain offers routes for all abilities, from gentle lakeside strolls to challenging mountain trails with rewarding views.

activities.text: Enjoy swimming, sailing, and fishing in the clean waters, or rent a boat to explore the lake's quiet coves. This idyllic area attracts nature lovers and active holidaymakers throughout the year, with winter bringing cross-country skiing and skating.

days_plan.itin_title: Three-Country Tour: Switzerland, the Black Forest and Alsace

visits.text: Visit Titisee-Neustadt in the heart of the Black Forest, famous for its crystal-clear lake and picturesque surroundings. The glacial lake, formed during the last ice age, stretches nearly two kilometers amid forested mountains. The charming lakeside promenade offers stunning views and access to boat rentals.

Discover the region's famous cuckoo clock tradition at one of the local clock factories. The Black Forest has been crafting these intricate timepieces since the 18th century, and you can watch master craftsmen create these iconic souvenirs using traditional techniques.

Relax at Titisee, one of the Black Forest's most beloved lakes nestled in a picture-perfect mountain setting. This natural glacial lake offers crystal-clear waters perfect for swimming, pedal boating or simply strolling along the scenic lakeside promenade. The surrounding forested hills and traditional Black Forest villages create postcard views in every direction.

Browse the shops along the lakefront for authentic Black Forest souvenirs, including the region's famous cuckoo clocks crafted by local clockmakers using traditional techniques. The mechanical artistry of these hand-carved timepieces represents generations of Black Forest craftsmanship passed down through families. Look for shops offering demonstrations of how these intricate clocks are assembled.

Take a boat ride across the glittering waters, either paddling yourself or aboard one of the tourist vessels that cruise the lake. The surrounding mountains are laced with hiking trails offering spectacular views of the lake and the Black Forest peaks. A visit to the Menzenschwand valley nearby reveals traditional villages and the famous Café zum Kuckuck.

activities.text: Enjoy a boat trip on the lake or simply relax by the shore. Numerous hiking and cycling routes wind through the surrounding forests, while wellness facilities offer relaxation. In winter, the area transforms into a winter sports destination with skiing, cross-country skiing, and ice skating.
Rent a pedal boat or rowboat to explore the lake at your own pace and enjoy the mountain scenery

days_plan.itin_title: Three-Country Tour: Switzerland, the Black Forest and Alsace
Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: Ten life-size wooden atlantes support the gallery of the Stiftsbibliothek in Waldsassen. Carved by Karl Stilp between 1724 and 1726, they embody human failings: the ignorant, the hypocrite, the mocker. The Rococo hall ranks among the finest monastic libraries in Central Europe. Admission €3.50, guided tours every 45 minutes.

The adjoining Stiftsbasilika dates from the 12th century and blends late Romanesque with Baroque. The ceiling frescoes by Karl Hofreiter trace the life of St. Bernard of Clairvaux. Free access outside service hours. Take a look at the carved choir stalls.

The carved figures supporting the Stiftsbibliothek gallery aren't saints, but allegories of vice: vanity, hypocrisy, ignorance. Karl Stilp carved them life-size in 1724–25. The rococo hall, with its painted ceilings, is one of Germany's most beautiful baroque libraries. Guided tours only, Tue–Sun.

The Stiftsbasilika houses reliquaries containing dressed and bejeweled skeletons, among the most remarkable in Europe. An 18th-century Cistercian goldsmith, Adalbart Eder, decked these Roman bones in silk and gemstones. The Jann organ has 103 stops.

activities.text: Wander through the monastery's botanical garden (Naturerlebnisgarten), open from May to mid-October. The Cistercian nuns cultivate medicinal plants and aromatic herbs across one hectare. Combined ticket with the library €6.

Sample the cooking at Gästehaus Sankt Joseph, attached to the monastery. The Cistercian nuns run the dining room with regional dishes that change daily. Moderate prices, monastic atmosphere. Reservations recommended on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: West Bohemia in 10 days: Spas, Castles & Beer
Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: The Centre Charlemagne, on the Katschhof between the cathedral and city hall, tells Aachen’s story through three eras: the Carolingian Empire, the coronation city, and then the Baroque spa town. It is also the first stop on the Route Charlemagne, the thread linking the city’s major sights. Start your day here when it opens at 10 a.m. to get your bearings before visiting the cathedral; the museum is closed on Mondays.

The highlight of the trip awaits beneath the octagon of Aachen Cathedral, Charlemagne’s palatine chapel, consecrated in 805, where the emperor has rested since 814. More than thirty kings were crowned here between 936 and 1531, and in 1978 the building became the first German monument inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Charlemagne’s throne and the Gothic choir can only be seen on the paid guided tour, which costs €8.50 and lasts about 45 minutes. Outside guided tours, tourists may enter from 11 a.m. on weekdays and 1 p.m. on weekends.

Around 985, goldsmiths covered the Cross of Lothair, the centerpiece of Aachen’s Domschatzkammer, with precious stones and pearls. Around it are some 130 objects on three levels, including the silver-gilt reliquary bust of Charlemagne and the Proserpina Sarcophagus, a 3rd-century marble piece believed to have served as the emperor’s first tomb. Tickets are sold only at the Dominformation, directly opposite; on Mondays, the treasury closes as early as 2 p.m.

Make your way to the coronation hall in Aachen’s Rathaus, built starting in 1330 on the walls of the great hall of Charlemagne’s palace. Coronation banquets were held here from 936 to 1531; today, Alfred Rethel’s frescoes depicting the emperor’s life surround replicas of the Imperial Regalia made around 1915. Outside, look up: the facade facing the Markt features a row of 50 statues of kings. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except during certain events.

“Aachen’s most beautiful living room”: that is how the Couven Museum describes itself, and the phrase fits. In this house on the Hühnermarkt, where the Eagle Pharmacy opened in 1662 before Jakob Couven remodeled it in 1786, the rooms range from Rococo to Biedermeier, including a historic kitchen and a music room. Two rooms display around 6,000 tin-glazed earthenware tiles. Admission is €10; open from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Thursday through Sunday.

A smell of rotten eggs drifts beneath the Elisenbrunnen’s colonnade: sulfur-rich water from the Kaiserquelle gushes from two lion mouths at 52 °C. Inaugurated in 1827 to plans revised by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, the pavilion bears marble plaques naming some famous drinkers of the waters, from Peter the Great to Casanova and Handel. Try a sip, more out of curiosity than pleasure; the tourist office is on the same square.

activities.text: Around 1806, Napoleon’s Continental Blockade deprived Aachen of cane sugar and honey: bakers switched to beet syrup, and Printen took on their modern form, hard and spicy. This fat-free gingerbread, flavored with anise, cloves, or cardamom, has protected geographical indication status. Try some in a shop or café on Münsterplatz, just steps from the cathedral.

If you still have energy, end the day at the Carolus Thermen, northeast of the center, in the thermal waters that made Aachen a spa town. Indoor and outdoor pools, around fifteen saunas, and a garden with a pond: expect to pay €18 on weekdays and €20 on weekends for 3 hours 30 minutes of thermal bathing, without sauna access. Open daily from 9 a.m. to 11 p.m., with last admission at 9:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Cologne, Bonn, and Aachen in 3 Days: Cathedrals and Treasures

visits.text: Ahlbeck's Seebrücke, with its pavilion dating from 1882, is the oldest of Germany's piers. It is listed as a historic monument. Direct views of the Polish coast.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Around 1900, painter Paul Müller-Kaempff founded Ahrenshoop's artists' colony. Thatched-roof houses, narrow lanes, galleries everywhere. The Kunstmuseum Ahrenshoop, whose buildings echo fishermen's houses, is worth the visit. Warning: high-season prices climb.

activities.text: Walk westward along the steep Hohes Ufer cliff: the coast crumbles into the sea, a wild landscape just steps from the village. Marked trail, an hour round trip.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Then head downhill along the city walls to the Albrecht-Dürer-Haus, a house built around 1420 that the painter bought in 1509 and where he died in 1528. The museum describes it as the only surviving Renaissance artist’s home outside Italy: a kitchen, living quarters, a room displaying copies of his major paintings, and a workshop where a press reconstructed from a drawing by Dürer still produces prints. Allow 1 hour. Admission is €7.50; the museum is closed on Mondays except from July through September and during the Christkindlesmarkt.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: The Alpsee, just below Hohenschwangau, is paradoxically calm despite Neuschwanstein's crowds. Crystal-clear water, alpine setting, no motors allowed. A bench and twenty minutes of silence will do.

activities.text: Rent a pedal boat on the Alpsee to see both castles from a different angle. The water is so clear you can see the bottom several meters down. Rentals at the kiosk on the north side.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Since 1516, Alsfeld’s Rathaus has stood with two half-timbered stories and three attic levels above three stone arcades, the former market hall. Around it, the Weinhaus of 1538 and the stone Hochzeitshaus, built from 1564 to 1571, form the backdrop to an old town designated a European model town for heritage preservation in 1975. Look for the ell measure attached to the left side of the Rathaus.

Excavations at the Walpurgiskirche in 1971–1972 uncovered the foundations of a small basilica with three apses, the original core of Alsfeld’s main church. Its choir was rebuilt in 1393, and its stained-glass windows by Charles Crodel date from 1963. Visit between 10:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. or in the afternoon Monday through Saturday; on Sundays, the church does not open until 2 p.m.

If you are passing through on a Saturday morning, Alsfeld’s Märchenhaus opens from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. in its half-timbered house dating from 1628. Two floors of Grimm fairy tales, a storytelling room, and a collection of 83 dollhouses from the Erzgebirge, surrounded by several hundred dolls. On Sundays and during school vacations in Hesse, it opens only in the afternoon.

activities.text: You will reach the Leonhardsturm through the lanes of the old town, among more than 400 half-timbered houses spanning seven centuries. Standing 27 meters tall and built in 1386, it is the only surviving round tower of Alsfeld’s town walls; its nickname is “Storchennest,” the stork’s nest. Ask for a map of the route at the Tourist-Center, Rittergasse 3.

days_plan.itin_title: Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel

visits.text: In 1003, the Alte Hofhaltung was simply the palace of the Duke of Bavaria, the future Emperor Henry II; in 1007, it became the bishops’ residence. Step through the Schöne Pforte, a Renaissance portal carved in 1573 by Pankraz Wagner, where Henry and Cunigunde hold a model of the cathedral. The courtyard, surrounded by Gothic half-timbered buildings with galleries, hosts the Calderón festival in summer, with performances held here since 1973. The Historisches Museum, in the Renaissance wing, opens Friday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: The Alte Nationalgalerie rises like a Roman temple, with an equestrian statue of Frederick William IV at the top of its staircase. Completed in 1876, it houses Caspar David Friedrich’s The Monk by the Sea, Adolph Menzel’s The Iron Rolling Mill, and paintings by Manet and Monet. Allow 1 hour for the highlights; if you are visiting several museums on the island, buy the day ticket covering them all. Closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: You’ll spend the afternoon facing Rubens’s Last Judgment, a canvas more than six meters tall hanging on the top floor of the Alte Pinakothek. Opened in 1836 in a building by Leo von Klenze, the museum displays more than 700 paintings, including Dürer’s self-portrait in a fur coat; a lower gallery also presents around 90 works from the Neue Pinakothek, from Goya to Klimt, while that museum undergoes renovation. Admission is €1 on Sundays, and the museum stays open until 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: To understand Altenahr’s terrain, a visit to Burg Are offers more than a glance from the road. The ruins overlook the town and serve as a landmark for routes through the vineyards and neighboring valleys. The climb contributes as much to the appeal of the stop as the walls themselves. Check local access before setting out and wear shoes suited to the steep sections.

activities.text: You can leave the vineyards behind and head to the Langfigtal, in the Ahrschleife bei Altenahr. This protected river bend brings the walk back close to the river, in surroundings more wooded than the vineyard slopes. Choose an out-and-back walk on an open trail rather than improvising a loop. Confirm access after construction work or flooding; do not cross a ford when the water is high.

If the weather stays dry, finish with a short out-and-back walk on the Rotweinwanderweg above Altenahr. The trail connects the Ahr’s wine villages, with views of the terraces and Burg Are. A selected section is enough for this four-day itinerary. Check local detours and do not start a full stage toward Dernau late in the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: No bell tower, no town around it, yet it's definitely a Dom. Altenberg Cathedral rises from deep forest in the Dhünn valley. A Cistercian church founded in 1133, rebuilt in Gothic style between 1259 and 1379, it has served both Protestant and Catholic congregations since 1857. Free admission, closed Mondays.

activities.text: Follow the short path that runs along the Dhünn downstream from the cathedral (2 km round trip, flat). The stream flows between beeches and ferns in a silence only Cistercian monks would have known. A café-restaurant sits just opposite the portal.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

activities.text: About 300 steps and no elevator: reaching the bell tower of St. Peter, known to Munich locals as “Alter Peter,” takes some legwork. This is the city’s oldest parish church, and its viewing platform at 56 m looks straight toward the Neues Rathaus; on days with foehn winds, the Alps appear on the horizon. Tickets cost €5 and cannot be reserved: check the sky before climbing, since the view depends on visibility.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: The legend is false, but more appealing than the history: Bamberg’s Altes Rathaus supposedly arose in the middle of the Regnitz because a bishop refused to grant the townspeople any land, although the boundary actually ran along the foot of the Domberg. First mentioned in 1387, the town hall was remodeled in Baroque and Rococo styles from 1744 to 1756, and its facades were painted in 1755. On the east side, look for the cherub’s leg that seems to protrude from the fresco. Walk around via the Obere Brücke and Untere Brücke, and don’t miss the half-timbered Rottmeisterhäuschen attached to the bridge tower.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Beneath the arcaded galleries of the Altes Schloss, the noise of Königstraße suddenly fades. This medieval moated castle began its transformation into a Renaissance palace in 1553, and an equestrian statue of Eberhard im Bart, who became the first Duke of Württemberg in 1495, presides over the courtyard. The Landesmuseum Württemberg occupies the upper floors: the royal crown treasury on the second floor, and the wheeled bench of the Celtic prince of Hochdorf and Aztec feather shields on the first. Closed Mondays; the Dürnitz, with its café and shop, remains free to enter.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Altötting is nicknamed “the heart of Bavaria,” and the Gnadenkapelle takes the phrase literally: silver urns here hold the hearts of members of the Wittelsbach dynasty, including Ludwig II. Beneath the octagonal structure, which may date from the 8th century, the Black Madonna draws more than a million pilgrims a year. Walk around the ambulatory and its roughly 2,000 votive offerings.

Cross Kapellplatz to the Stiftskirche St. Philippus und Jakobus, built from 1499 to 1511 to accommodate the influx of pilgrims. The tourist office describes it as the last Gothic hall church in southern Germany. On the base of the clock, look for the “Tod von Eding,” a figure of Death dating back to the plague years, then take a look at the cloister frescoes.

Altötting’s finest object is French: the Goldenes Rössl, a 62 cm enameled gold altar made in 1404 by the workshops of the Paris court as a New Year’s gift from Isabeau of Bavaria to Charles VI. It takes pride of place in the Schatzkammer on Kapellplatz. Admission is free from Easter through the end of October; afternoon opening is Monday through Thursday only.

Jerusalem surrounds you: in the Panorama’s rotunda, a canvas 12 m high and 95 m in circumference depicts the city on the day of the Crucifixion. Gebhard Fugel and his team painted it in 1902 and 1903. According to the city, it is the last surviving historical panorama in Germany. In 2026, open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., March 21 through October 31; admission €5.

Neo-Baroque and enormous, the Basilika St. Anna will not appeal to everyone, but its figures command respect: about 83 m long, with room for some 8,000 worshippers. Built from 1910 to 1912 for crowds of pilgrims, it was granted basilica status by Pius X in 1913. Step inside between services; 15 minutes is enough.

Step inside St. Konrad Church, Altötting’s second pilgrimage destination: Conrad of Parzham, a Capuchin friar, served as the friary’s porter for forty years. He died in 1894 and was canonized in 1934; he is venerated here, where his relics are kept. The meeting room is open daily from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: If you are staying in Altötting on a Saturday between May and October, linger on Kapellplatz after nightfall: a candlelight procession circles the Gnadenkapelle. A more solemn procession takes place on the eve of the Assumption, August 14. For the exact time, check the pilgrimage schedule published weekly during the season.

days_plan.itin_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach

visits.text: Hard to resist the Stadtbrille, Amberg's emblem: this 46-meter fortified passage has straddled the Vils since 1454. Its central pillar and the water create a reflection shaped like eyeglasses. Best angle: from outside the wall, south side.

Five craft breweries still supply the inns of Amberg, nicknamed “Bierstadt.” The Marktplatz, with its Gothic town hall, the four medieval gates and the nearly intact wall form one of Bavaria's finest fortified complexes.

Climb up to the Mariahilfberg for a view looking down over the old town and its tiled roofs. The Franciscan monastery and the Lorettokapelle crown the hill. Free access, 15 minutes' walk from the center.

activities.text: If the Vils is calm, try a ride in a Plätte, a flat-bottomed boat recalling the transport of iron ore in the Middle Ages. Amberg was then the "Ruhr region of the Middle Ages." Departure at the Schiffbrücke.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Gilding, a choir screen, and an organ: Amorbach’s Abteikirche contrasts sharply with the town’s restrained facades. The former Benedictine church retains its Rococo decor and an organ by the Stumm brothers. The interior details make this stop worthwhile. Check visiting conditions and book a musical session if you want to hear the instrument.

Amorbach’s Fürstliche Bibliothek is worth setting aside a time slot for rather than making a series of brief detours. This library is part of the former abbey, alongside the church and the Grüner Saal included in some tours. Ask exactly which rooms will be open. Book the appropriate tour; access to the church does not guarantee access to the library.

activities.text: If a session fits your schedule, choose a guided tour with an organ performance at Amorbach’s Abteikirche. The tour combines explanations of the decor with an organ performance, rather than leaving you looking at a silent instrument. Check the official calendar and book. This activity replaces a standard church visit; it is not a required second admission.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: At an elevation of around 700 m, with a 60 m onion-domed bell tower, Kloster Andechs crowns the Heiliger Berg above Lake Ammersee. Behind the Gothic walls of the pilgrimage church, whose construction began in 1423, Johann Baptist Zimmermann created a Rococo interior completed in 1755. Benedictine monks have lived here since 1455, and composer Carl Orff is buried in a side chapel, the Schmerzhafte Kapelle. The church opens daily from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: Prayer and hops go hand in hand here: without church tax revenue, Kloster Andechs supports itself through its brewery. At the Bräustüberl, pair a Hell or a Doppelbock Dunkel with a Schweinshaxe, out on the terrace if the weather allows. If you’re driving, leave the Doppelbock, a strong beer by definition, to your passengers.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Angermünde’s old town deserves more than a quick stop between hikes. Its streets and historic buildings form a compact ensemble, with red interpretive plaques telling the stories of former residents. Save this walk for your return from Grumsin and pick up a map at the tourist information office to give your exploration a clear direction.

Grumsin Beech Forest has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011. The Infopunkt Weltnaturerbe Grumsin in Altkünkendorf explains what this designation protects. Visits to the forest follow specific rules, and its core area is not open to unrestricted walking. Stop at the information point before hiking, choose a suitable route, and use only the designated parking areas.

The silence of St. Mary’s Church in Angermünde prepares you for the organ better than any written description. The church retains an instrument by Joachim Wagner, and demonstrations offer insight into both its sound and its mechanics. An ordinary visit, however, does not guarantee you will hear it. Check the church’s opening hours; book separately if you would like a musical demonstration.

activities.text: Follow the orange leaf markers through Grumsin Beech Forest from Altkünkendorf for a walk in tune with the woodland. The Oranges Buchenblatt loop is 10.5 kilometers long, but a variant via Luisenhof shortens the outing to about 2 hours. Fallen trees are part of the route and make some sections more difficult. Choose the short variant to leave time for Angermünde, wear sturdy shoes, and skip the hike in strong winds.

If you want to understand what grows without human intervention, book a guided hike in Grumsin Beech Forest instead of adding more kilometers. Some guided tours provide access to areas that are normally closed; departures and access permissions depend on the option you choose. This outing replaces the self-guided hike rather than adding to it. Confirm the meeting point, duration, and access conditions before booking.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeastern Brandenburg: Abbey, Forest, and Lakes in 3 Days

visits.text: Vaults that bear no weight and an altarpiece donated by miners: St. Annenkirche, completed in 1525, is Saxony’s largest hall church built entirely in the Late Gothic style. On the back of the Miners’ Altarpiece of 1521, Hans Hesse depicted work in Annaberg’s mines. On Sundays, the church opens at noon; the tower is open to visitors from May through October.

“Das macht nach Adam Riese”: Germans still invoke the name of this master, who arrived in Annaberg in 1522, to confirm a calculation. The Adam-Ries-Museum occupies the house on Johannisgasse where he ran his school; here you can try calculating on lines using the method in his 1518 textbook. Open Tuesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Saturday from noon.

At the Manufaktur der Träume, you will encounter Erika Pohl-Ströher again, the patron behind Freiberg’s terra mineralia. Her collection here comprises more than 1,000 objects of folk art from the Ore Mountains, spanning four centuries. Step-free access is through the tourist office, with an elevator; allow 1 hour in the early afternoon.

activities.text: Rediscovered during construction work in 1992, the tunnels of the Besucherbergwerk Im Gößner date to around 1500 and extend beneath the old town, opposite St. Annenkirche. The network includes 260 m of tunnels following the ore veins, with shafts reaching depths of up to 24 m. The combined ticket includes the neighboring Erzgebirgsmuseum, founded in 1887.

days_plan.itin_title: The Ore Mountains in 3 Days: Mines, Toys, and Fichtelberg

visits.text: Ansbach's Residenz surprises through its interior: more than 50 rooms in enfilade decorated in Baroque and Rococo styles, with 2,800 Delft faïence tiles in the faïence room according to the castle's count. Residence of the Margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach in the 17th-18th centuries, it's less known than Würzburg and can be explored without jostling.

Ansbach's Stiftskirche St. Gumbert houses the Ansbach Hohenzollern nobility's burial vault and the Gothic chapter stalls. Just opposite, the Johanniskirche and the Kaspar-Hauser-Denkmal recall the enigmatic wild child found in Ansbach in 1828 - one of the 19th century's unsolved cases.

activities.text: Stroll along the Promenade, a tree-lined avenue in the heart of the town, and make your way to the Hofgarten behind the Residenz. On Wednesday and Saturday mornings, the weekly market on Martin-Luther-Platz brings together the region's producers.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Pass beneath the Glockenturm, a medieval keep turned baroque bell tower after two fires (1600 and 1709). It's Arnsberg's emblem. The old town coils around the Ruhr's loop, with half-timbered houses and remnants of ramparts. The Kaiserspförtchen, the last medieval gate, deserves a detour.

The Sauerland Museum in the Landsberger Hof covers regional history from prehistory to the 20th century. The building itself is worth seeing: a palace built in 1605 by the Prince-Elector for his mistress. Admission €6, closed Mondays.

The ruins of Arnsberg Castle overlook the Ruhr loop from their wooded promontory. Only wall fragments and a tower remain, but the valley view is wide. Free access, 15 minutes on foot from Alter Markt.

activities.text: Arnsberg feels very medieval, yet its classicist quarter around Neumarkt dates from 1816, designed by architect Schinkel when the Prussians made it an administrative seat. The contrast between the two atmospheres can be walked in twenty minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: Visitors come to Arnstadt’s Schlossmuseum for the dolls, yet its most moving exhibit awaits in the attic: the console of the 1703 Wender organ, played by the young Bach. The 82 miniature rooms of Mon plaisir, created in the 18th century by Princess Augusta Dorothea, are undergoing restoration begun in January 2025, and only a selection remains on display. Take time to explore the mirrored room and its Asian and European porcelain, numbering nearly a thousand pieces.

In June 1703, an 18-year-old musician came to inspect the new organ at Arnstadt’s Neue Kirche and was hired soon afterward: Johann Sebastian Bach. Rebuilt between 1676 and 1683 after the fire of 1581, the church has been known as the Bachkirche since 1935; the Wender organ, modified several times, stands in the gallery above a 1913 Steinmeyer organ. Opening hours vary: check with the tourist office.

“Are there no more Bachs to apply for this position? I absolutely must have another Bach,” lamented the Count of Schwarzburg-Arnstadt upon the death of court musician Johann Christoph Bach. On Arnstadt’s Markt, the statue of the young Bach depicts him as he might have looked at around 18, near the Renaissance Rathaus built in 1586 after the fire of 1581. Continue to the nearby Bachkirche to follow the musician from one site to the next.

Save the Liebfrauenkirche for the end of the morning: built from the late 12th century to around 1330, it transitions from Romanesque to Gothic. Its 1498 altarpiece with double wings depicts Saints Lawrence and Boniface, and the burial chapel houses the tomb of Count Günther XXV of Schwarzburg and his wife, decorated with heraldic lions. The church is a few minutes’ walk from the Markt.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach

visits.text: Make a quick stop in this small town associated with porcelain. Arzberg long produced tableware known throughout Germany. The village retains an understated charm with its Franconian houses and hilltop church. Fifteen minutes is enough to walk around the center.

activities.text: An unassuming little town, Arzberg is mainly worth a stop between Hohenberg and Waldsassen. If a porcelain factory outlet is open, prices are significantly lower than those in Selb's stores.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Tiny on the outside, immense within: the Asamkirche, officially St. Johann Nepomuk, occupies a plot measuring 22 m by 8 m. The Asam brothers built it between 1733 and 1746 as a private church, and Egid Quirin could see the altar from a window in his neighboring house. Look up at the high altar’s four twisted columns, a nod to Bernini’s above the tomb of St. Peter in Rome. Admission is free, but visits pause during services.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Nine degrees Celsius year-round, even in August: the Atta Cave refreshes and fascinates. Discovered by chance in 1907 during a quarry blast, this grotto unfolds stalactites, stalagmites, and calcite draperies colored by iron oxide across 500 meters of developed pathways. The guided tour lasts 40 minutes. Cheese is matured in a sealed gallery.

The Biggesee lacks wild charm, but it's Westphalia's largest reservoir, and the boat ride from Attendorn to Biggedamm offers a restful panorama over the wooded hills of southern Sauerland. Embarkation at Biggedamm, sailings April to October.

activities.text: Take the Biggolino, a nostalgic glazed miniature train linking Atta Cave to Biggedamm via downtown Attendorn. The journey lasts 20 minutes, schedules sync with boat departures. Cash payment only on board.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: Augsburg, founded in 15 BCE by the Roman legions of Emperor Augustus, is one of Germany's oldest cities. During the Renaissance, it became one of Europe's financial capitals: the Fugger and Welser dynasties of merchants and bankers lent money to Emperors Maximilian I and Charles V. It was in Augsburg that the Augsburg Confession, the founding charter of Lutheranism, was read in 1530, and that the Peace of Augsburg, which formalized the coexistence of religions within the Empire, was signed in 1555. The city is also the birthplace of Leopold Mozart, the composer's father, and of the writer Bertolt Brecht. It is the only city in Germany with its own public holiday: on August 8, the Peace Festival commemorates the end of the oppression of Protestants after the Thirty Years' War.

The Fuggerei, founded in 1521 by Jakob Fugger—considered the richest man of his time—is the world's oldest social housing complex still in operation. Behind its walls and blue-and-white-striped gate, 67 ochre-fronted houses contain 142 apartments of 60 square meters each. The annual rent, set at one Rhenish guilder in 1521, has never changed: today, it is equivalent to €0.88. In return, residents must be Catholic, originally from Augsburg, in financial need, and recite three prayers each day for the founders. A 10 p.m. curfew is still in force. Mozart's great-grandfather, the mason Franz Mozart, lived here from 1681 to 1694—a commemorative plaque recalls his stay. A model apartment and a bunker dating from 1943 are open to visitors.

The Town Hall (Rathaus), designed by the architect Elias Holl and completed in 1620, is regarded as the most important secular Renaissance building north of the Alps. Everything was destroyed by the bombing in 1944 but faithfully rebuilt.

Stroll down Maximilianstraße, the city's finest avenue, laid out along the ancient Roman Via Claudia Augusta. Three monumental bronze fountains punctuate the promenade: the Augustus Fountain (1588-1594) by Dutch sculptor Hubert Gerhard, the Mercury Fountain (1596-1599), and the Hercules Fountain (1597-1600) by Adriaen de Vries. These fountains are part of Augsburg's water management system, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019—an ensemble of 22 hydraulic monuments spanning more than 700 years of history. At No. 36, the Fugger Palace features a Renaissance arcaded courtyard; at No. 46, the Schaezler Palace (1770) houses the most important gallery of German Baroque art and a Rococo ballroom.

Augsburg's Cathedral of Our Lady (Dom), whose oldest sections date back to 994, combines Romanesque and Gothic architecture. It preserves figurative stained-glass windows dating from the 11th century: the Prophets - Daniel, Jonah, Hosea, Moses, and David - set in the south windows of the nave. The Romanesque bronze door, considered the cathedral's oldest work of art, is displayed in the adjoining diocesan museum.

activities.text: Take a seat in one of the city-center beer halls to try Käsespätzle, fresh pasta baked with cheese, a Swabian specialty of Augsburg. Located on the border between Bavaria and Swabia, the city offers cuisine that draws on both traditions—round off your meal with Leberkäse (meatloaf) or Zwetschgendatschi (damson plum tart).

Attend a performance at the Augsburger Puppenkiste, the famous marionette theater founded in 1943. Housed in the former Holy Spirit Hospital, this string puppet theater stages fairy tales for children as well as adult productions, with an attention to detail that has made it renowned throughout Germany.

days_plan.itin_title: Germany's Romantic Road: Fairytale Castles and Medieval Villages in Bavaria
Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
Germany Road Trip: Castles, Medieval Villages and the Alps

visits.text: Before arriving in Bacharach, stop in Rüdesheim to visit the Drosselgasse, a 144-meter-long cobbled lane lined entirely with wine taverns and outdoor drinking venues with music and dancing. The wine served is mainly Riesling from the Rheingau.

From Bacharach, allow for a round trip to Rüdesheim, on the opposite bank of the Rhine. Cable car ride (Seilbahn) from Rüdesheim up to the Niederwald Monument, a bronze statue of Germania built between 1877 and 1883 to a design by sculptor Johann Schilling, commemorating the victory of 1870–71 and the unification of the German Empire. The monument stands 38 meters high and offers panoramic views of the Rhine and the Rheingau vineyards.

Entry into Bacharach through the old fortified gates. The 14th-century ramparts are among the best preserved in the entire Rhine Valley. A walk along the wall walk offers views from above of the slate roofs, vineyards, and Rhine below. The village is first mentioned in a document dated 923; its name evokes Bacchus, god of wine, whose cult already existed in Celtic and Roman times.

The Gothic ruins of Wernerkapelle, halfway up the slope between the village and Stahleck Castle. The chapel was begun in 1289 in memory of Werner of Oberwesel, a 16-year-old boy murdered in 1287. Its construction was never completed, interrupted by pogroms against the local Jewish community, falsely accused of the murder. A plaque today commemorates this past. The partially preserved Gothic structure remains striking despite the centuries.

Stahleck Castle dominates Bacharach from a ridge 160 meters above the Rhine. Its first mention dates to 1135. Destroyed by French troops during the War of the Palatine Succession in 1689, it was reconstructed in 1925 and now houses a youth hostel. Access to the inner courtyard is free—from the terrace, the view over the Rhine and valley meanders is one of the finest in the area.

activities.text: Riesling tasting at one of the village wine estates. Bacharach has produced wine since Roman times. Legend has it that Pope Pius II had it shipped by cart all the way to Rome.

Short Rhine cruise from Bacharach pier toward Kaub, to see Pfalzgrafenstein Castle from the water, standing on an island in the middle of the river—a former medieval customs post still intact. Round trip takes about 1 hour 15 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Germany Road Trip: Castles, Medieval Villages and the Alps
The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz

visits.text: Bavaria's smallest spa resort is tiny. Bad Alexandersbad owes its existence to a spring discovered by a farmer in 1734. The last margrave of Ansbach had a spa palace built here. Today, the village has barely 960 inhabitants and is utterly peaceful.

The Markgräfliches Schloss, built in 1783 for the margrave, dominates the Kurpark with its terraces refurbished in 2019. Queen Louise of Prussia stayed here in 1805, before lending her name to the neighboring labyrinth. Explore the park on your own.

activities.text: If your joints are creaking, the ALEXBAD offers a modern panoramic pool grafted onto the historic 1838 Kurhaus. Sauna, local peat treatments, minimalist architecture. Open from 10 a.m., admission €15–20.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Doberan Minster, from a Cistercian monastery founded in 1171, isn't a city cathedral but a country abbey church—which makes its interior even more astonishing. The Gothic red-brick construction began around 1280 and concluded with the consecration of 1386. The 76-m-long basilica houses a gilded canopy choir from the 14th century and the tombs of Mecklenburg princes. Visit in 45 min.

A small spa town since 1793, gigantic medieval heritage: Bad Doberan is this permanent contradiction. Cistercian builders shaped Baltic Backsteingotik techniques here for over a century, and their methods spread throughout the North Sea region. The Visitor Center in the Marstall explains this influence with a model of the 1550 monastery.

activities.text: Climb aboard the Molli, a narrow-gauge steam train connecting Bad Doberan to Kühlungsborn since 1886, passing through the town's shopping streets—yes, the train literally runs between the houses. The full journey takes about 45 min and hugs the Baltic coast. Ticket at Bad Doberan station.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Our favorite ruin along the Weinstraße: Kloster Limburg, a family monastery of the Salian dynasty founded beginning in 1025, overlooks the Isenach Valley above Bad Dürkheim. Count Emich IX of Leiningen-Hardenburg burned it down on August 30, 1504, and its nave has remained open to the sky. Admission is free outside events; walk up via Grethen or park on the Seebach side.

Salt tingles on your lips along the Gradierbau: brine trickles over some 250,000 bundles of thorny brushwood, filling the air with spray as if you were by the sea. Built in 1847 and measuring 333 m long—more than three soccer fields end to end—it was rebuilt in 2010 after an arson attack in 2007. Climb to the platform at the top, where the air is saltier; admission is €2.50, and it is open until 8 p.m. from April through October.

activities.text: The Dürkheimer Riesenfass is a barrel you can have lunch inside: 13.5 m in diameter, with a capacity of some 1.7 million liters, it was assembled in 1934 by cooper Fritz Keller using nearly 200 fir trees from the Black Forest. It seats close to 430 diners on two levels. Reserve on weekends; in September, the Wurstmarkt, which attracts more than 600,000 visitors, takes place right outside on the Brühlwiesen.

days_plan.itin_title: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen

visits.text: The Stiftsruine of Bad Hersfeld is the world's largest Romanesque church ruin, stretching over 100 meters in length with a transept span exceeding 50 meters. The Benedictine abbey was founded in 769 by Lullus, Archbishop of Mainz, on a site where the monk Sturmius had settled as a hermit as early as 736. Charlemagne made it an imperial abbey that served for centuries as a pillar of royal power on the eastern frontier of the Frankish kingdom. The church was destroyed by the French in 1761 during the Seven Years' War, when it was being used as a powder magazine. The Romanesque Saint Catherine's Tower, dating from 1120, still stands and houses the Lullusglocke—a bell dated 1038, Germany's oldest dated bell still in use. Since 1951, the ruins have hosted the Bad Hersfelder Festspiele theater festival, one of Germany's most important, every summer.

The historic center of Bad Hersfeld, a Hessian spa town, has preserved a network of half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries. The sacristan's house, dating from 1452, is the town's oldest. The Stadtkirche (town church) and the former buildings of the free imperial city form a cohesive ensemble around the pedestrian center.

activities.text: Attend the Bad Hersfelder Festspiele, an annual theater festival held each summer in the Stiftsruine ruins since 1951. The open-air stage, set against nine-century-old Romanesque walls, hosts large-scale productions (Shakespeare, Schiller, musicals) with up to 1,500 spectators per evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Hesse, Germany Tour: Cities and Nature Parks

visits.text: The Grosser Feldberg rises to 879 meters and is the highest point in the Taunus. The ascent through the beech and spruce forests of the Naturpark Hochtaunus offers a radical change of atmosphere after the Main plain. Several marked trails provide access from the surrounding villages.

The Naturpark Hochtaunus covers 240,000 hectares of forests, valleys, and ridges between the Main and Lahn rivers. It's one of Hesse's largest nature parks. The trail network exceeds 3,000 km. The vegetation is typically Rhenish: oak, beech, and hornbeam groves on the slopes, with some glacial relict species on the ridges.

The historic center of Bad Homburg vor der Höhe retains its 17th-century castle—one of the few residences of the landgraves of Hesse-Homburg still standing—with its medieval white tower that has become the town's emblem. The Kurpark, landscaped in English style with century-old avenues, ranks among Germany's most beautiful spa parks. In the 19th century, Bad Homburg was a popular resort among European nobility: Tsar Nicholas II, King Edward VII, and Emperor Wilhelm II were regular visitors. The first Monte Carlo casino is said to have been founded by businessmen who learned the trade here.

The Roman fort of Saalburg, in the Taunus a few kilometers from Bad Homburg, is the only fully reconstructed fort along the Germanic Limes. Built in the late 1st century to house a cohort of 500 soldiers, it was abandoned during the Alamannic raids of 258 AD. The first serious excavations began in 1853. In 1897, Wilhelm II—passionate about Roman history—ordered its complete reconstruction on the original foundations, an unprecedented project for a military installation. The site has been part of the UNESCO listing of the Germanic Limes since 2005. The archaeological museum displays weapons, tools, and everyday objects found on site.

activities.text: Spa session at the Taunus Therme in Bad Homburg, a complex featuring over 1,400 m² of pools and eight themed saunas. Bad Homburg's springs have been used therapeutically since the 17th century.

Visit the Hessenpark open-air museum in Neu-Anspach, about ten kilometers from Bad Homburg. Over 100 historic buildings—half-timbered houses, barns, mills, workshops—have been dismantled and reassembled across 70 hectares. The site offers a tangible picture of Hessian rural architecture from the 16th to 19th centuries.

Hike the Limes trail from Saalburg: portions of the fortifications (reconstructed ditch and palisade) remain visible in the Taunus landscape. A 2.4 km circular trail around the fort allows you to follow preserved sections and spot the bases of former watchtowers.

days_plan.itin_title: Hesse, Germany Tour: Cities and Nature Parks

visits.text: The Rittersaal of Schloss Iburg is one of the first baroque halls in northwestern Germany, with trompe-l'oeil frescoes considered the last of their kind north of the Alps. Sophie Charlotte, first Queen of Prussia and grandmother of Frederick the Great, was born here in 1668.

Descend to the Charlottensee for a quiet break. This lake at the castle's foot bears the princess's name. You can rent rowboats in season. The adjacent Kneipp-Erlebnispark offers water-walking basins.

activities.text: If the Baumwipfelpfad is open, the Teutoburger Wald canopy reveals itself at treetop height. Otherwise, the marked Hermannsweg trail crosses Bad Iburg with easy sections. Count on an hour for a short loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Immaculate white houses are reflected in the Baroque harbour basin — Bad Karlshafen is a planned town, drawn in a single stroke to order in 1699. Landgrave Charles I of Hesse wanted to welcome French Huguenots expelled by Louis XIV and to bypass the toll at Hann. Münden. The canal intended to reach the Rhine was never completed: only 17 kilometres were dug.

Founded in 1699 by Charles I of Hesse under the name Sieburg, Bad Karlshafen sits at the precise confluence of the Diemel and the Weser. The Hugenottenmuseum, housed in a former cigar factory, traces the exile of French Protestants from 1685 onwards. Free admission on the first Sunday of the month.

activities.text: Head up to the Weser-Skywalk, a 3 km walk from the centre: this platform on the Hannoversche Klippen offers a view across three German states simultaneously — Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia and Lower Saxony. It's also accessible by car, with a small car park nearby.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip
Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: Concert halls in the heart of a spa town: Bad Kissingen’s Regentenbau is a reminder that spa stays also involved cultural life. Max Littmann’s building is part of the historic spa district. Admire the facades, then choose an interior tour if one is offered. Check available time slots, as events may affect access.

A walk that continues under a roof: Bad Kissingen’s Wandelhalle belongs to the spa complex alongside the Brunnenhalle and arcades. These spaces bring together walking, social encounters, and the tradition of the springs, offering more than monumental architecture alone. Walk through them without trying to photograph everything. Check access conditions for the different spaces and the practices associated with serving the spring water.

Flowers, benches, and a river: Bad Kissingen’s Rosengarten brings the Fränkische Saale back into focus after the halls of the spa district. The garden forms an outdoor space in front of the Regentenbau’s north facade. It is a simple stop for viewing the complex from a distance. Plan a short visit, without expecting roses in bloom out of season.

activities.text: Follow part of Bad Kissingen’s Welterbe-Entdecken-Tour to connect gardens, spa buildings, and the history of spa treatments. The stops explain why the town is part of the UNESCO-listed Great Spa Towns of Europe. Choose the central area rather than the entire route. This walk replaces the outdoor visits already described and leaves you time to reach the train station without rushing.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhön and Fulda in 4 days: peaks and spa towns

visits.text: Kloster Pforta traded prayer for study: Cistercian monks settled here in 1137, and a state school has occupied the site since 1543. Klopstock, Fichte, and Nietzsche were students here. The Gothic church, reconsecrated in 1268, has an exceptionally long nave. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. from April through October; the audio guide is recommended.

Step into another century at the Romanisches Haus in Bad Kösen, built between 1150 and 1175 and considered one of the oldest surviving residential buildings in central Germany. In the former sheep barn next door, more than 270 dolls recall Käthe Kruse’s work here from 1912 to 1950. Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., €5.50, free for visitors under 18.

Breathing Baltic Sea air in the Saale Valley: that is the promise of Bad Kösen’s Gradierwerk, a graduation tower more than 300 m long and nearly 20 m high that has been in operation since 1779. Brine trickles over bundles of blackthorn branches while the Saale turns a waterwheel. Walk alongside it and breathe deeply.

activities.text: Tasting wine at the foot of a Cistercian abbey remains the finest way to round off a visit to Schulpforte. The Vinothek at Landesweingut Kloster Pforta opens daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The monks were already growing grapes here on a large scale: ask for a Müller-Thurgau.

“An der Saale hellem Strande”: Franz Kugler composed this song in 1826 during a stop at Rudelsburg, a ruined castle mentioned as early as 1171, perched some 85 m above the river. The path from Bad Kösen passes four monuments to student fraternities. On the neighboring hill, Burg Saaleck sheltered Walther Rathenau’s assassins in 1922. Sturdy shoes are recommended.

days_plan.itin_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra

visits.text: Stroll along the graduation wall of Bad Kösen, an impressive wooden structure where salt water flows over blackthorn bundles. This traditional spa installation creates iodine-enriched air with invigorating properties, perpetuating a centuries-old wellness tradition. Various viewpoints over the spa town reveal a hilly landscape typical of the Saale-Unstrut region.

Discover this charming spa town nestled in the Saale valley, at the gateway to Germany's northernmost wine-growing region. The Belle Époque villa architecture testifies to the golden age of German spa culture in the 19th century. The surrounding vine-planted hills offer bucolic panoramas over this preserved landscape.

activities.text: Walk through the spa park gardens and discover the spa architecture

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Built without permission, the Brückenhäuser nevertheless became the symbol of Bad Kreuznach. Between 1480 and 1600, a shortage of land led residents to build these half-timbered houses on the piers of the Alte Nahebrücke, a stone bridge erected around 1300; the bridge’s former gunpowder magazines serve as their cellars. Look for the cannonball embedded in one facade, a reminder of the sieges during the Thirty Years’ War. For a photo, head to the Geißenbrücke near the Pauluskirche.

In 1507, a certain Magister Faust became head of Kreuznach’s Latin school, then fled shortly afterward amid accusations. The Neustadt, home to the city’s oldest houses, preserves his name in Magister-Faust-Gasse and on the “Fausthaus,” although an inscription in its cellar dates the house to thirty years after his stay. Lose yourself in the winding lanes around the Eiermarkt; on Tuesdays and Fridays, from 7 a.m. to 1 p.m., the market on the Kornmarkt rounds out the walk.

Gladiators grappling with wild beasts, a sea god surrounded by ships and merchants: the mosaics at the Römerhalle teem with movement. They come from a third-century peristyle villa whose foundations are visible at ground level right beside the museum: more than 5,000 m² of interior space and over fifty ground-floor rooms, the equivalent of a small palace. Start with the Oceanus mosaic, then walk around the walls outside. On Tuesdays, the museum is open only from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., and it is closed in February.

You come to the Schlosspark-Museum for the sculptures and leave talking about the hunting room. Built in 1776 by Andreas von Recum, the house gained a wood-paneled room designed by a decorator who worked for Ludwig II of Bavaria while it belonged to the Puricelli family of industrialists. The galleries tell the story of the nineteenth-century spa town and the Cauer dynasty of sculptors, beginning with Emil Cauer the Elder (1800–1867), with glasswork by Ida Paulin as a bonus. Allow 45 minutes; the museum is closed on Mondays.

If you’re traveling with children, set aside 1 hour for the Museum für PuppentheaterKultur, nicknamed PuK. More than 2,500 figures trace the history of puppet theater, from nineteenth-century traveling theaters to permanent stages and television stars. The museum is on Hüffelsheimer Straße, the same street as the Römerhalle, so visit the two in succession. They also share the same opening schedule: Tuesday through Sunday, mornings only on Tuesdays, and closed in February.

Climb from the Neustadt to the Kauzenburg on the Kauzenberg. The counts of Sponheim built it between 1206 and 1230, despite a ban imposed by King Philip of Swabia, before Boufflers’s French troops blew it up in 1688. In 1970–1971, architect Gottfried Böhm built a structure on its ruins that now houses restaurants.

Bad Kreuznach’s Kurpark occupies the tip of an island between the Nahe and a millrace. Laid out after 1830 around the Elisabethquelle saline spring, it has 145 large trees, including a gnarled plane tree planted in 1840 and a 150-year-old copper beech. Follow the embankment lined with century-old horse chestnut trees to the Kurhaus, built in 1912–1913. Avoid the riverbanks after heavy winter rains: the park is one of the first places in the city where the Nahe overflows.

activities.text: A touch of sea air in the heart of the Nahe Valley: in the Salinental, brine trickles down graduation towers made of blackthorn branches, standing 9 meters high and stretching for 1.1 km. The tourist office describes the site as Europe’s largest open-air inhalation facility; salt was extracted from this brine for 270 years, and a waterwheel powered by the Nahe still pumps it to the top of the towers. Breathe deeply as you follow the path. Free admission year-round.

Get a taste of the Nahe in one stop at the Nahe-Vinothek, housed in the Dienheimer Hof, a former noble residence in the old town. It offers 150 wines from 50 regional winemakers at winery prices. With around 800 hectares of vineyards, Bad Kreuznach ranks among the largest winegrowing municipalities in the Naheland, with Riesling the dominant grape. Ask to compare a wine grown on porphyry with one grown on clay soil.

days_plan.itin_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern

visits.text: Bad Langensalza owes its medieval prosperity to the trade in woad—a blue dye it shared with only four other Thuringian cities—which enabled burghers to build large churches and travertine ramparts. Later, the exploitation of mineral springs made it a spa town. Today, the city is known for its ten themed parks and gardens arranged along the spa promenade. The Japanese garden “Kofuku no Niwa” (“garden of happiness”) combines two classical pavilions, a koi carp pond, a dry garden, a bamboo grove, and cherry trees that blossom in spring.

Bad Langensalza's rose garden is one of Thuringia's most significant. It showcases collections of antique and modern roses organized in themed beds, complemented by a small rose museum tracing this flower's cultural history.

The arboretum brings together trees and shrubs of rare or spectacular species, both native and exotic, planted in themed collections. Next to it, the botanical garden displays medicinal plants and plants used in pharmaceutical preparations, recalling the town's spa tradition.

Bad Langensalza's old town is one of Thuringia's best-preserved: an almost entirely preserved medieval wall, half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries restored since 1990, and several large churches testifying to the past wealth of the woad trade.

activities.text: Relaxation at the Friederiken Therme, a thermal spa fed by Bad Langensalza's sulfurous and saline springs. The complex features indoor and outdoor pools and several themed saunas.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

visits.text: Beyond the name Bad Münstereifel, the Stiftskirche recalls the town’s religious role. This Romanesque church complements the gates and houses of the historic center rather than requiring another drive. Look at its architectural forms before exploring the neighboring streets. Check interior access when you arrive and give priority to services if the church is in use.

If you want to see more than facades, the Romanisches Haus houses the Hürten-Heimatmuseum in Bad Münstereifel. This historic residential building offers a window into local history, close to the center’s other monuments. It is well suited to a short cultural stop. Check its opening hours before including it; if it is closed, spend that time at the fortified gates rather than taking a detour.

activities.text: The Erft flows between the houses of Bad Münstereifel’s Historische Altstadt. The streets combine half-timbered buildings, shops, and remnants of fortifications: the historic setting remains the backdrop to everyday life in the town. Walk up toward the gates to explore beyond the shopping streets. Park outside the historic core and keep the museum as an option depending on your schedule.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: Forget the neatly trimmed French gardens: Muskau Park plays a different tune. Prince Hermann von Pückler-Muskau designed it from 1815 onward as a living painting, with distant vistas and winding paths. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004, it sprawls across roughly 830 hectares straddling the German-Polish border. Allow at least two hours for the palace park, and arrive early in the morning: the low-angle light on the Neisse River makes the early wake-up worthwhile.

Rebuilt after the war, the Neues Schloss houses a permanent exhibition on Pückler, an unclassifiable character: writer, traveler, landscape architect, and notorious seducer. The facade regained its appearance in 2011 after a lengthy restoration. Climb the tower for a panorama over the park and town. Detail worth knowing: the tower exhibition and keep tour close occasionally, so check the dates before visiting.

activities.text: Rent a bicycle at the Schlossvorwerk or hop into a horse-drawn carriage: Pückler himself recommended touring the park by carriage, so you might as well follow the master's advice. Carriages depart from the palace forecourt. The network of paths is extensive and the park immense, so two wheels save precious time. Avoid high noon in summer—shade is scarce on the vast lawns.

If you have time, cross the Neisse via the Doppelbrücke and enter the Polish side, into Park Mużakowski. Same park, two countries: the majority of the 830 hectares lie east of the river, in Poland. This double border footbridge was erected in 2003. Bring your ID just in case, and good walking shoes, because distances stretch out quickly on the far bank.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: Vineyards outside, a nuclear shelter below: the Dokumentationsstätte Regierungsbunker brings an abrupt change of scenery. This Cold War relic preserves some of the facilities intended for the federal authorities. A guided tour makes the visit more than a procession past armored doors. Book your time slot before heading to the entrance at Silberberg, and bring a warm layer.

Beneath the remains of the Römervilla Ahrweiler, Roman comfort takes a very tangible form. The estate combined living quarters and baths: people did not come here just to work. This archaeological counterpoint complements the medieval walls of the town center. Check opening hours before making the trip, and keep this visit as an alternative if your bunker time slot takes up the morning.

activities.text: Half-timbered buildings crowd the streets around the market square: Ahrweiler’s Old Town can be explored on foot. The surrounding fortifications retain their gates, while Niederhutstraße and Ahrhutstraße run through the largely pedestrianized center. Follow the town walls instead of focusing only on storefronts. Park outside the center and allow extra time to reach Maria Laach afterward.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: The roar of water follows you into the underground passages of the Alte Saline in Bad Reichenhall. Rebuilt on the orders of King Ludwig I after the fire of 1834, the saltworks still runs waterwheels measuring 13 m in diameter, which pump brine to the surface. The underground route covers approximately 400 m and 270 steps: wear sturdy shoes, then finish with the five rooms of the Salzmuseum.

If the air feels salty in the Königlicher Kurgarten, look toward the Gradierhaus. Along this structure, 160 m long and 13 m high, brine trickles through bundles of blackthorn and evaporates into a fine mist that you breathe as you walk. From April to October, spend 30 minutes walking alongside it on the side sheltered from the wind; admission to the park, designed in 1868, is free.

The Münster St. Zeno is a reminder that Bad Reichenhall does not depend on salt alone. Consecrated in 1228, this Romanesque basilica with a nave and two side aisles is 90 m long and is considered the largest Romanesque church in southern Bavaria. Allow around 20 minutes outside service times, as the building remains an active place of worship.

activities.text: Since July 1, 1928, the Predigtstuhlbahn has linked Bad Reichenhall to Predigtstuhl with its appearance unchanged. It is considered the oldest large-cabin cable car preserved in its original condition and climbs more than 1,100 m in approximately 8 minutes 30 seconds. Have lunch on the terrace of the historic restaurant at the upper station, then walk a few minutes to the Almhütte Schlegelmulde.

days_plan.itin_title: Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits

visits.text: Designed to make salt, Bad Rothenfelde's Gradierwerke now serve as an open-air thermal cure. Salt water trickles down 412 meters of blackthorn walls, creating an iodine-rich aerosol. You'd think you were on the North Sea coast, 200 km from the shore.

In the Inhalationskammer, a salt fog so dense you can't see your hands: slip on the plastic cape sold at the entrance (€1) and breathe for ten to twenty minutes. Effective against allergies, according to regulars.

activities.text: Climb the 55 steps of the Besucherplattform on the New Gradierwerk to see the reconstructed Windkunst, the wind pump that lifted the brine. The view of the Kurpark and the rosarium of 210 varieties is a bonus. Guided tours from Easter to September.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: After all those stairs, Bad Schandau’s riverfront gives your legs a welcome break. The Marktplatz and St. Johannis Church form the heart of this small town on the Elbe. If you are leaving by train, the station is on the opposite bank, rather than behind the market square.

A waterfall controlled by a sluice gate: the Lichtenhainer Wasserfall retains the charm of old-fashioned attractions. Here in the Kirnitzsch Valley, an attendant once released the stored water when there was enough water and a large enough crowd. This brief stop is at the start of the trail to the Kuhstall; time your break for the next release, triggered automatically every 30 minutes.

activities.text: The metal ladders contrast with the moss of the Schrammsteine. Starting in Ostrau, this 9.07 km loop passes through the Lattengrund and climbs the Wildschützensteig to the Schrammsteinaussicht viewpoint. The descent follows the Mittelwinkel, which also has steps and ladders. Set out in the morning with your hands free and shoes with good traction; the exposed sections require sure footing, and this hike is unsuitable for anyone afraid of heights.

You’ll leave the Lichtenhainer Wasserfall and cross the Kirnitzsch to climb to the Kuhstall. Beneath this sandstone arch, about 11 meters high, the trail feels like a passage under a building. The Himmelsleiter continues upward through a narrow fissure, and the return route follows the Hinterer Kuhstallweg. Allow 2 hours 15 minutes for the loop, including breaks; skip the additional staircase if the passage feels intimidating.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxon Switzerland in 3 Days: Bastei and Sandstone Peaks

visits.text: The second baroque library of the trip: the Bibliothekssaal at Schussenried Abbey rivals Wiblingen's. Painter Franz Georg Hermann and sculptor Fidelis Sporer created another pinnacle of rococo art here. The great abbeys of Upper Swabia competed for prestige through their libraries.
The spa center at Bad Schussenried offers baths and a spa park. The small town provides a quiet stop between two abbeys. The Bierkrugmuseum, dedicated to beer steins, is a local curiosity.

activities.text: You're at the heart of the Upper Swabian Baroque Route, a tourist trail linking some thirty baroque churches and monasteries between Ulm and Lake Constance. Map available from the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Allow 2 hours for the Rheinland-Pfälzisches Freilichtmuseum, spread across 35 hectares in the Nachtigallental. Nearly 40 buildings dismantled throughout the state form four groups here: Hunsrück-Nahe, Middle Rhine-Westerwald, Moselle-Eifel, and Rhenish Hesse-Palatinate. Chickens roam freely, so dogs must be leashed. Admission is €9; open Tuesday through Sunday, from mid-March to early November.

activities.text: A knee-deep mud basin starts off the Barfußpfad in Bad Sobernheim, which opened in 1992 and ranks among Germany’s oldest barefoot trails. The roughly 3.5 km loop crosses the Nahe twice, once over a footbridge and once in a boat you pull across yourself. Bring a towel: lockers and foot-washing facilities are available on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern

visits.text: The painted façades along Bad Tölz's Marktstraße present a succession of façade frescoes, alpine gables, and wrought-iron signs over 500 meters. It's postcard Bavaria, lively and pedestrianized. Tölz locals call this street the “most beautiful living room in the Oberland.”

Gabriel von Seidl, a Munich architect, redesigned the Marktstraße façades between 1900 and 1910 in alpine style. The 15th-century Altes Rathaus and its onion-domed bell tower are the landmark. Thomas Mann used to vacation here.

activities.text: If you're traveling with children, the gravel banks of the Isar at Bad Tölz are a natural playground. The water is cold but crystal clear, and the ducks provide the show. The Taubenloch playground is right next door.
Tölz locals say the Isar is their municipal pool. Cross the bridge and settle on the pebbles of the right bank. Turquoise water rushes between gravel bars. Bring a towel—no changing cabins.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Bad Urach’s Marktplatz is lined with 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses around the Rathaus, built in 1440 and expanded in 1562. Since 2023, a sculpture by Peter Lenk has celebrated the Schäferlauf, the shepherds’ festival. Continue to the Amanduskirche, a Late Gothic church built between 1475 and 1499, then treat yourself to a coffee on an outdoor terrace before taking the evening drive back to Stuttgart.

activities.text: If you come after a rain shower, the Uracher Wasserfall changes its voice: its flow rises from around 70 liters per second in midsummer to 420 after heavy rain. The water plunges freely for some 37 m, then slides over 50 m of moss-covered tufa, a rock this limestone-rich stream creates itself. Start at the Maisental hiking parking lot; a trail climbs to the plateau on the right side of the falls. Allow a good hour and a half and wear shoes with good traction.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Bad Wimpfen’s Blauer Turm is a landmark even before you reach the narrow streets. This tower was part of the Kaiserpfalz, the former imperial palace; it connects the half-timbered buildings with a history of power. Save the climb for clear weather. Check access and skip the climb if stairs tire you out.

An imperial palace with no complete palace remaining: Bad Wimpfen’s Kaiserpfalz reveals itself in fragments. The Roter Turm, the chapel, and the neighborhood’s buildings outline the former complex used by the rulers. This very dispersal makes the walk interesting. Pick up the historical map and identify the buildings from outside before deciding which open interiors to visit.

Bad Wimpfen’s Steinhaus deserves a stop for its imposing shape, distinct from the neighboring half-timbered buildings. This Romanesque building in the former Kaiserpfalz houses the history museum. It adds a little depth to the tower route without requiring a long outing. Check the museum’s hours; viewing the exterior remains a separate stop from exploring the collections.

activities.text: Follow Bad Wimpfen’s Entdeckertouren using the material provided by the tourist office. These self-guided routes help connect the imperial remains with the streets where people live, rather than rushing from one tower to the next. Choose a route that fits your half-day. It replaces the exterior visits already described, so the same walk is not counted twice.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: Take the Schwarzwaldhochstrasse (B500) to reach Baden-Baden through the uplands—60 kilometers of forests and ridges, this is the scenic route through the northern Black Forest. Join it from the south when arriving from Triberg.

Next, head down into the old town to see the ruins of the Roman baths. Baden-Baden's springs rise from a depth of 2,000 meters at temperatures between 56 and 68 degrees - 800,000 liters a day flow from twelve artesian springs that are 12,000 to 17,000 years old. The Romans called the town Aquae Aureliae.

Then book a session at the Friedrichsbad, built between 1869 and 1877 by architect Karl Dernfeld. Inspired by Roman baths and Irish baths, it offers 17 bathing stations beneath a 17.5-meter dome. Mark Twain stayed there and wrote: “After 10 minutes, you forget time; after 20 minutes, the world.” The bathing tradition here is mixed-gender and without swimsuits.

End the day with a walk along the Lichtentaler Allee, which follows the Oos River for 2.3 kilometers between the town center and the Cistercian abbey of Lichtenthal founded in 1245. This avenue lined with century-old trees was Europe's open-air salon in the 19th century—Napoleon III, Queen Victoria, Dostoevsky and Brahms all stayed here.

activities.text: The modern Caracalla Therme, opened in 1985 and covering 5,000 m², allows you to enjoy the thermal waters in a swimsuit. Several pools at temperatures between 18 and 38 degrees, an outdoor pool open year-round, saunas and steam baths. More accessible than the Friedrichsbad, with or without a reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest
Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Forests & Medieval Towns

visits.text: Marvel at Bamberg, one of Germany's most beautiful cities, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This thousand-year-old city, miraculously spared by bombing, has more than 2,300 listed historic buildings. Built on seven hills like Rome, it harmoniously blends medieval, Baroque and Rococo architecture into an exceptionally cohesive whole.

Photograph the Altes Rathaus, the old town hall built on an artificial island in the middle of the Regnitz River, Bavaria's most iconic monument. Its trompe-l'oeil frescoes adorning the half-timbered facades create the illusion of three-dimensional sculptures. According to legend, when the bishop refused to cede land, the burghers created this island to build their town hall.

Visit the four-towered Imperial Cathedral, a Romanesque masterpiece housing the tomb of Emperor Henry II and the famous Bamberg Horseman, the first life-size equestrian statue of the Middle Ages. Bavaria's Little Venice, the former fishermen's quarter with colorful houses reflected in the river, completes this enchanting picture.

activities.text: Tasting Rauchbier, a smoked beer and local specialty

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps

visits.text: Bamberg Cathedral, consecrated in 1012, then rebuilt and reconsecrated in 1237, rises above the Domberg with four towers approximately 81 m tall. Inside, the Bamberger Reiter, a stone horseman carved around 1225–1237, keeps his secret: no one knows for certain whom he represents. Also see the tomb of Henry II and Cunigunde by Tilman Riemenschneider (1499–1513), the tomb of Clement II, the only pope buried north of the Alps, and the altarpiece by Veit Stoß, carved for Nuremberg. On Sundays, visits begin at 1 p.m.; sightseeing pauses during services.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO
