visits.text: The Bastei is Saxon Switzerland's iconic rock formation—sandstone columns sculpted by erosion over a million years, rising 194 meters above the Elbe from a plateau at an altitude of 305 meters. The Bastei Bridge, built in sandstone in 1851 to replace the original wooden bridge of 1826, links several of these rocky pinnacles over 76.5 meters with its seven arches. Caspar David Friedrich painted the rocks as early as 1822. In season, crowds are dense from 10 a.m.—arrive early for the best views over the Elbe's meanders.

The ruins of Neurathen Castle, on the Bastei rocks themselves, are the remains of the largest rock castle in Saxon Switzerland. Built by the Sorbs along 700 meters of the top of the ridge, it was conquered and burned in 1469. View the rocks and remains from outside, along the Bastei Bridge route: the metal walkways within the ruins have been closed since September 2023 and no longer allow access for visits.

activities.text: Hike from the village of Rathen to the Bastei Bridge and surrounding rocks. The route starts on the right bank of the Elbe after a ferry crossing (a few minutes), followed by a climb of about 40 minutes through the forest. Several trails offer different routes back.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

visits.text: On its granite spur overlooking the Spree, the Ortenburg has watched over Bautzen for centuries, the former fortress of the Slavic Milzener tribe. Today it houses the Sorbisches Museum, dedicated to the Sorbian minority, and the regional administrative court. Climb the Matthiasturm for the view, accessible on guided tour. Start the day here, before afternoon crowds arrive.

Built in 1558, the Alte Wasserkunst supplied Bautzen with water from the Spree. This tall round tower of 47 meters, now a technical museum, retains its old pumping machinery. For the price of 184 steps, the platform offers the finest panorama over the old town and river. Open year-round, with reduced hours in winter: check before climbing.

Far from Pisa, Bautzen hides its own leaning tower: the Reichenturm leans roughly 1.4 meters to the northwest, standing 56 meters tall. From its platform, the gaze plunges onto the old town's roofs and the famous tower skyline. It opens April through October, during the day. Combine it with a loop of towers and bastions that summarizes a thousand years of history.

Push open the door of Dom St. Petri, one of Germany's oldest and largest 'simultaneous' churches: Catholics and Protestants share the same building, separated by a grille. It's the only church in Saxony to function this way, with two organs, one per denomination. The calm here contrasts with the bustle of the lanes. Free entry, but respect services—the church remains an active place of worship.

activities.text: Bautzen mustard deserves the gourmet detour: at the Senfmuseum, a small shop-museum, you taste local varieties far spicier than the industrial version. It's the perfect edible souvenir to slip into your bag. Tasting takes a few minutes, perfect between tower visits. Think about a jar or two for home—they travel well.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: Wagner turned this theater down. Too gilded, too Baroque, too worldly for his dramas. Yet the Markgräfliches Opernhaus is one of the best-preserved theaters in Europe - carved, lacquered and gilded wood across three tiers of boxes, designed by Giuseppe Galli Bibiena and his son Carlo between 1744 and 1748. UNESCO-listed in 2012 after restoration.

The Festspielhaus built in 1872 on the Grüner Hügel, north of the center, was designed exclusively for Wagner's works: stage equipped with three levels of machinery beneath the platform, acoustics conceived for grand orchestrations, no decoration in the hall to avoid distraction. The laying of the first stone was marked by Wagner himself conducting Beethoven's Ninth Symphony in the Markgräfliches Opernhaus.

Bayreuth's Eremitage, the hideaway of Margravine Wilhelmine - the sister of Frederick the Great who gave the town its opera house and Baroque character - is a 50-hectare park 4 km from the center. Fountains, artificial grottos, the 17th-century Altes Schloss, and the Neues Schloss with its round temple: the ensemble is listed with the Markgräfliches Opernhaus within the same UNESCO perimeter.

activities.text: Stop by Villa Wahnfried and its Richard Wagner Museum: the composer's birthplace home, transformed into a biographical museum after post-1945 reconstruction, is the starting point of the Wagner Walk linking the town's key sites related to his stay. Wagner's and Cosima's graves lie in the villa's garden.

If you have seven years' lead time, try registering for the Bayreuther Festspiele (Wagner festival, every summer since 1876) - the waiting list is long but not impossible via direct registration at bayreuther-festspiele.de. Otherwise, the Festspielhaus offers daily guided tours outside the festival period.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Narrow lanes squeeze between the facades: Beilstein’s Marktplatz captures the village’s charm. Its historic center retains a medieval street layout, with the Zehnthaus and the former parish church around the square. Explore the narrow streets on foot from the banks of the Moselle; the steps and cobblestones call for sturdy shoes.

Burg Metternich offers expansive views after Beilstein’s narrow lanes. Its ruins stand on a spur above the village and recall the history of the family whose name they bear. Climb up only if access is open and you still have the energy: the slope adds considerably to the time needed for this short stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier

visits.text: Plan your afternoon around the guided tours of Königliches Schloss Berchtesgaden: they are the only way to see the interior. The former Augustinian monastery, later a Wittelsbach residence, opens 30 of its 214 rooms to visitors, featuring two altarpieces by Tilman Riemenschneider and three armories. Arrive a few minutes before the tour starts, then finish in the rose garden overlooking the Berchtesgaden Alps.

A 19th-century Romanesque Revival facade conceals a medieval core: the Stiftskirche St. Peter und Johannes, next to the castle, is much older than it looks. The first church on the site was consecrated in 1122, and the 14th-century Gothic choir stalls feature a lion, a pelican, a unicorn, and a stag, all Christian symbols. The Romanesque cloister is accessed from Schlossplatz rather than the nave: look for its entrance on the square.

Follow the ramp through “Vertikale Wildnis” at the Haus der Berge: the exhibition climbs from the depths of Königssee to the summits of the Watzmann, moving from water to forest, then to alpine pasture and rock. At the end, the slats of a large display window open to reveal the real Watzmann. Open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., the national park center has also reassembled the Lahner-Kaser, an alpine pasture hut dating from 1848, in its garden.

If you choose just one underground visit, make it Salzbergwerk Berchtesgaden, a mine in continuous operation since 1517. Dressed in miners’ coveralls, you ride a small train 1,400 m into the mountain, then descend a wooden slide and cross the Spiegelsee, an illuminated underground brine lake, by boat. The temperature stays at 12 °C year-round: bring a jacket and book online to avoid waiting.

activities.text: Locals call it the “Arschpfeifenrössl”: a little wooden horse with a whistle for a tail. Berchtesgadener Handwerkskunst sells it on the ground floor of the Alte Fronveste, built around 1510 between Marktplatz and Schlossplatz and once the prince-provosts’ prison. Each piece is carved and painted by hand; come on a weekday if possible, as the shop opens only in the morning on Saturdays.

Berg- und Enzianbrennerei Grassl in Unterau has distilled gentian since 1692 and describes itself as Germany’s oldest gentian distillery. The gentian roots, dug up by hand at elevations above 1,000 m, are processed in five mountain distilling huts, including the one at Priesbergalm on the Jenner. The tour and tasting of more than 40 spirits and liqueurs are free: choose a designated driver before raising a glass.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits
Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits

activities.text: The wooden cross standing in Lake Starnberg, a few meters from the shore at Berg, marks the spot where Ludwig II and his psychiatrist Bernhard von Gudden were found dead in the water on the evening of June 13, 1886. The circumstances remain unexplained. From the village, a woodland path leads to the Romanesque Revival Votivkapelle, consecrated in 1900 at the initiative of Prince Regent Luitpold, on the slope above the lake. Allow 1 hour on site, including the walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: The Brandenburg Gate was built between 1788 and 1791 on the orders of King Frederick William II of Prussia, designed by Carl Gotthard Langhans and inspired by the Propylaea of the Athens Acropolis. During Berlin's division, it stood trapped in the border strip, inaccessible to Berliners on both sides. It was here, in front of this gate, that Reagan issued his 1987 challenge to Gorbachev. Visit in the late afternoon when the floodlights come on—the way light catches the columns completely transforms the atmosphere.

The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe occupies 19,000 square meters between Brandenburg Gate and Potsdamer Platz, on what was once the death strip of the Wall. New York architect Peter Eisenman placed 2,711 concrete stelae of varying heights on gently undulating ground—as you walk toward the center, the blocks rise above your shoulders and the ground drops away, creating a deliberate sense of oppression. Inaugurated on May 10, 2005, the memorial includes an 800-square-meter underground information center: reading aloud all the victims' names would take 6 years, 7 months, and 27 days.

Head to Friedrichshain to walk along the East Side Gallery, the longest remaining section of the Berlin Wall: 1,316 meters along Mühlenstraße, between Ostbahnhof and the Oberbaumbrücke bridge. Starting in January 1990, 118 artists from 21 countries came to paint the eastern side of the Wall. The most famous murals: the fraternal kiss between Brezhnev and Honecker by Dmitri Vrubel, inscribed with “My God, help me survive this deadly love”; and the blue Trabant breaking through concrete, painted by Birgit Kinder. The entire gallery was restored in 2009 for the 20th anniversary of the Wall's fall.

Karl-Marx-Allee, a 2-kilometer Stalinist boulevard laid out between 1952 and 1960, offers a concrete glimpse into East German monumental urbanism. The buildings lining it—in the so-called “Soviet wedding cake” style—are now protected as historic monuments and represent one of the best-preserved Communist-era architectural ensembles in Europe.

In Berlin, head to Alexanderplatz to explore this large pedestrian square at the foot of the television tower. Find the World Clock and its city names, then take a look at the Fountain of Friendship between Peoples. Around the square, the large buildings and passing trams offer a concrete glimpse of the center of former East Berlin.

At the foot of Berlin's television tower, look up at the sphere above its tall column. From the pedestrian spaces between the tower and Alexanderplatz, walk around the monument to see its silhouette from different angles and photograph its contrast with the buildings around the square.

activities.text: Tiergarten park stretches across 210 hectares in the heart of Berlin—it was the royal hunting ground before being converted into a public park in the 19th century. Rent a bike to cross it from end to end, or push on to the former Tempelhof Airport, now converted into a vast public space where Berliners picnic on the old runways.

On Sundays, Mauerpark in Prenzlauer Berg hosts one of Berlin's largest flea markets, with a giant open-air karaoke session in the afternoon. More compact, the Arkonaplatz market is perfect for hunting down GDR-era objects and vintage furniture.

Final evening in Berlin: climb the Television Tower at Alexanderplatz (368 meters, built in 1969 under the GDR) for a panoramic view of the city at night, then explore the square and its surroundings before heading to the airport the next day.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Around Hanover: Lower Saxony's Most Beautiful Sites
Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea
Northern Germany Road Trip: Lakes, Castles, and the Baltic Coast
Northern Germany Road Trip: Lakes, Castles, and the Baltic Coast

visits.text: More imperial than contemplative, Berlin Cathedral embraces the grandeur envisioned under Wilhelm II. Inaugurated in 1905, it is Germany’s largest Protestant church. Beneath the nave, the Hohenzollern Crypt reopened in March 2026 after about six years of renovation. It contains 91 coffins spanning five centuries, including the Great Elector’s sarcophagus, which weighs 8 to 10 tonnes. Buy your ticket online for around €15; visits pause during services.

activities.text: Climb the roughly 270 steps to the Kuppelumgang, the outdoor gallery around Berlin Cathedral’s dome. From the top, views stretch across the Lustgarten, Museum Island, and the Spree. The climb is included in paid admission; skip it if you are afraid of heights or if winds are strong.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Berliners call the cross of light that sunlight casts on the Fernsehturm’s sphere “the Pope’s revenge”: the tower was erected by an East German state that was removing crosses from churches. Standing 368 m tall, the tower opened on October 3, 1969, and whisks visitors up to around 203 m in about 40 seconds. Standard tickets start at €20. Head up at sunset: the observation deck stays open until 11 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: The Marktplatz in Bernkastel-Kues brings together half-timbered facades best appreciated at a slower pace. The narrow, leaning Spitzhäuschen contrasts with the square’s more imposing houses. Then explore a few nearby lanes. Save the climb to Burg Landshut for a longer visit: it adds an uphill walk and time for a proper visit.

A monument that still cares for local residents: the St. Nikolaus-Hospital, also known as the Cusanusstift, remains a living institution in Bernkastel-Kues. Founded by Nicholas of Cusa, this complex on the opposite bank preserves a Gothic chapel and a library accessible on guided tours. Check access before crossing the bridge and respect the institution’s peaceful atmosphere.

activities.text: You compare Moselle wines at the wine tasting room of the St. Nikolaus-Hospital in Bernkastel-Kues rather than making multiple stops at producers. Set in the complex’s vaulted cellars, it brings together wines from the region. Check the opening hours and tasting options; plan this break after you have finished driving.

days_plan.itin_title: Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier

visits.text: If you attend Sunday Mass at Beuron Archabbey, the monks' Gregorian chant transports you to another century. This Benedictine archabbey, founded in 1077, remains an active center of monastic life. The Beuron Art School, born here in the 19th century, influenced European sacred art with a geometric style inspired by ancient Egypt.
The Danube Valley cliffs around Beuron form a spectacular canyon. The trail following the Danube toward Sigmaringen or Tuttlingen ranks among Baden-Württemberg's finest hiking routes.

activities.text: In Beuron, follow the footpath along the Danube at the foot of the limestone cliffs. From the area around Erzabtei Beuron, observe the wooded cliff faces framing the valley and the views of the archabbey. Return along the same path.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Binz Pier, inaugurated in 1902 and rebuilt in 1994 at 370 m (versus 560 m originally), has a heavy history: a section collapsed in 1912, killing several people, which led to the creation of the DLRG (German lifesaving society). The current pier ends with a pontoon above the waves—in rough seas, you really feel the movement.

The white villas of Binz's Strandpromenade were built between 1880 and 1930 in Bäderarchitektur style: turrets, carved wooden verandas, bay windows. Binz is recognized as the largest coherent ensemble of this style on the island. Binz was officially declared a seaside resort in 1885. The promenade runs along 4 km of fine sand.

The Jagdschloss Granitz is worth the detour from Binz: this mid-19th-century hunting castle sits on a wooded hill 4 km away. Its 38 m central tower offers, in clear weather, a view as far as the neighbouring islands. There is no direct access by car: you get up there on foot from Binz in 1 hour, by the Jagdschlossexpress tourist train from the Seebrücke in Binz, or by the Rasender Roland to the Jagdschloss stop, then on foot.

activities.text: Board the Rasender Roland, the narrow-gauge steam locomotive connecting Binz to Putbus since 1895. The journey crosses forests and marshes, with stops at Sellin and Baabe. The wooden period carriages are original or very close—the steam breath and panting rhythm are part of the voyage.

Islanders call it the Riviera of the East—and the comparison holds better than it seems: blue sea, generous summer sun, white architecture, and waterfront restaurants. Outside July-August, Binz recovers its provincial calm. The best plan remains waking at 7 AM, being on the beach before cruise groups, and swimming in 18-20°C water.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: A monastery where hikers mingle with pilgrims: Kloster Kreuzberg remains an active religious site above Bischofsheim. The Franciscans maintain the pilgrimage church, while the trails and dining options attract other visitors. Start with the church if it is accessible. Respect services and do not assume that brewery tours are offered.

Bischofsheim’s Zentturm provides a vertical landmark in the old town, far from Kreuzberg’s parking lots. The tower, remnants of the town walls, and the Rentamt make for a short town stop before the climb to the monastery. Explore the streets on foot from a suitable parking spot. Check the tower’s opening hours separately if you want to climb it.

activities.text: Climb from Kloster Kreuzberg to the summit crosses along the Stations of the Cross path for views of the Rhön. This short outing complements the church visit, with an ascent that requires more effort than a simple stroll around the courtyard. Wear sturdy shoes and bring a warm layer. If visibility is poor, stay near the monastery.

For a break with a local connection, Klostergaststätte Kreuzberg serves the monastery’s beer among its offerings. Here, tasting the beer accompanies a meal stop; it is not a tour of the brewing facilities. Check opening hours and allow time to get back on the road. The driver should choose a nonalcoholic drink before continuing to Bad Kissingen.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhön and Fulda in 4 days: peaks and spa towns

visits.text: Hohenzollern Castle stands majestically at 855 m on an isolated outlier hill in front of the Swabian Alb. Ancestral seat of the dynasty that gave Prussia its kings and Germany its emperors, the present castle was rebuilt between 1850 and 1867 by Friedrich August Stüler in romantic neo-Gothic style. The Schatzkammer displays Wilhelm II's crown, encrusted with diamonds.

In clear weather, views reach 100 km from the ramparts. The 15th-century Gothic Michaelskapelle is the only surviving medieval element. Around 350,000 visitors annually. Adult admission 26 euros, shuttle from parking lot available.

activities.text: The castle's Biergarten, in the inner garden, serves regional specialties with a view of the Zollerberg.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: The Blautopf (“blue pot”) is Germany's second-largest karst spring, located at the edge of the Swabian Jura 16 km west of Ulm. The funnel-shaped basin reaches 21 meters deep; its intense turquoise-blue color results from light scattering by limestone particles suspended in extremely clear water. During heavy rainfall, the water “boils” as it surges under pressure from the underground karst network of the Blauhöhlen caves, explored for over 18 km by cave divers since 1985—several divers have lost their lives here, leading to a ban on access for non-professionals. Swabian legend tells of a goblin pouring a bucket of ink each morning to maintain the color; another claims a nixie (water spirit) steals the lead ropes that curious visitors attempt to lower to measure the depth—hence the nearby rock nicknamed Klötzle Blei (“little bit of lead”).

The Benedictine monastery of Blaubeuren, founded in 1085 on the heights above the Blautopf, is a monastic complex in Baden-Württemberg. The abbey church houses a Gothic altarpiece from the 15th century and remarkable carved choir stalls.

The Museum of Prehistory in Blaubeuren (Urgeschichtliches Museum) preserves pieces discovered in the surrounding Swabian Jura caves—including replicas of the Venus of Hohle Fels, the female figurine carved from mammoth ivory discovered in 2008 by archaeologist Nicholas Conard in the Hohle Fels cave at Schelklingen (7 km away). Standing 6 cm tall and dating to between 35,000 and 40,000 years ago, it's the oldest known figurative sculpture in the world. The same cave also yielded flutes made from vulture bone and ivory dating to approximately 35,000 years ago—among the oldest known musical instruments.

activities.text: Guided tour of Hohle Fels cave at Schelklingen (7 km from Blaubeuren). The cave is open for guided tours Wednesday through Sunday from May to October. The site sits at an altitude of 616 meters in the Swabian Jura; excavations begun in 1870 have uncovered Upper Paleolithic artifacts in several meters of sediment.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Black Forest & Lakes
Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

activities.text: Perfectly straight paths on one side, Rapunzel letting down her hair on the other: Blühendes Barock embraces both worlds. These 30 hectares of gardens, surrounding the palace on three sides, opened on April 23, 1954, for Ludwigsburg’s 250th anniversary. The Märchengarten brings more than 40 fairy tales to life, and a boat ride along the Märchenbach is included with admission. In the fall, the pumpkin exhibition takes over the paths: August 22 through November 1 in 2026.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Even if you’re not a car enthusiast, the BMW Museum is worth a detour for its building: a silver bowl nicknamed the “salad bowl,” designed by Viennese architect Karl Schwanzer and opened in 1973 at the foot of the four-cylinder-shaped headquarters. Renovated from 2004 to 2008, it displays around 120 exhibits across 5,000 m² and traces the brand’s history from 1916. Admission costs around €10, unlike neighboring BMW Welt.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: You’ll then head to northern Munich for BMW Welt, which opened in October 2007 to designs by the firm Coop Himmelb(l)au and welcomes more than three million visitors a year. Admission is free: you can wander among the models on display beneath the immense roof. The south exit of Olympiazentrum station leads directly to BMW Welt and Olympiapark.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Beneath Deutsches Bergbau-Museum Bochum, the tunnels look like a real mine, yet the museum has never operated one. Its recreated tunnels show the machinery and the miners’ working conditions. Choose this underground route and a few galleries to stay within the allotted time; on weekdays, access to the tunnels requires a guided tour, which you should book according to the available time slots.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

visits.text: The air changes as soon as the Historisches Besucherbergwerk Silberberg takes you beneath the mountain. Near Bodenmais, the tunnels offer another way to read the terrain: here, the rock was also a workplace. Tours are guided, with departure times announced by the operator. The guided tour lasts 45 minutes; bring a warm layer, as the temperature in the tunnels is around 5 °C.

activities.text: You will walk to the Rißlochwasserfälle from the trailhead parking lot, guided by the sound of water. The gorge calls for a slower pace than city walks: roots, stones, and damp conditions require careful footing. Follow the Bo66 trail markers from the start. This is a summer excursion; avoid it in freezing conditions or heavy rain, and return along the marked route.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavarian Forest in 4 Days: From Passau to the Großer Arber

visits.text: Locals still call him the “Lügenbaron” — the lying baron. Hieronymus Carl Friedrich von Münchhausen was born here on 11 May 1720, in what is now Bodenwerder's town hall. The nearby Münchhausen-Museum presents the historical figure and the myth: the real soldier who served the tsarina, then the storyteller whose tales were published without his consent.

The Münchhausen-Museum, housed in the medieval Schulenburg (c. 1300) on the family estate, exhibits first editions of the baron's adventures. The fountain outside the town hall depicts the famous scene of Münchhausen and his half-horse emerging from the swamp — an absurd image that sums up the whole town.

activities.text: On a Sunday from May to October, watch the Münchhausen-Spiel in front of the town hall steps: amateur actors have been performing the baron's adventures here for over twenty years, on the first Sunday of the month. Free performance, local atmosphere guaranteed.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: Stuttgart locals call it the Bohnenviertel, the bean quarter: its residents of modest means grew beans in their gardens and draped the stems like garlands across their facades. Completed around 1415 for tanners and dyers who needed the Nesenbach stream, this district outside the old city walls was defended by its residents in the 1970s. Stop by the Leonhardskirche, enlarged from 1463 to 1466, where the humanist Johannes Reuchlin is buried, then wander among antique dealers, used bookstores, and galleries.

activities.text: If you set aside just one evening for wine, spend it in a Weinstube in the Bohnenviertel. These wood-paneled taverns carry on the tradition of the winegrowers’ taverns of old: vineyards once began just beyond Weberstraße. Order a Viertele, the small local measure, and let your hosts recommend a wine from Württemberg. Tables fill up quickly toward the end of the week: reserve that afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Bonn’s most engaging history lesson is free: you’ll find it at the Haus der Geschichte on the Museumsmeile. Around 4,000 objects tell Germany’s story since 1945, from a section of the Bundestag’s plenary chamber to a homemade escape airplane. Arrive as early as 9 a.m. on weekdays or 10 a.m. on weekends; closed Mondays.

Set aside a good hour for the Beethoven-Haus at 20 Bonngasse: Ludwig van Beethoven was born here in December 1770, and it is his family’s only surviving home. Twelve rooms hold more than a hundred original items, including his last fortepiano, made by Conrad Graf. Closed Tuesdays; expect to pay €15 for admission, a little more during temporary exhibitions.

Completed in 1248, the very year Cologne laid the foundation stone of its cathedral, Bonn Minster rises above the tombs of the martyrs Cassius and Florentius, whose two giant granite heads stand watch outside the apse. Restored from 2017 to 2021, it has regained its Romanesque cloister, open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Saturday.

Bonn’s Altes Rathaus, built in 1737–1738 in the Rococo style, served as a stage for the young Federal Republic. From its gilded staircase, Charles de Gaulle in 1962, John F. Kennedy in 1963, and Mikhail Gorbachev in 1989 greeted the crowds in the Marktplatz. For a photo, step back to the middle of the square.

days_plan.itin_title: Cologne, Bonn, and Aachen in 3 Days: Cathedrals and Treasures

visits.text: If the open-tread stairs make you uneasy, you can also view Bottrop’s Tetraeder from the top of the spoil heap. This steel pyramid stands on Halde Beckstraße, turning mining waste into a lookout point. Climb using the designated paths and skip the platforms if the wind or your fear of heights makes the ascent uncomfortable.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

visits.text: In 1806, Napoleon took the Quadriga atop the Brandenburg Gate to Paris; it did not return to Berlin until 1814. Built between 1788 and 1791 by Carl Gotthard Langhans, the 26 m-high gate features twelve Doric columns and five passageways. The Wall ran along its western side, and the passage through the gate only reopened on December 22, 1989. Walk through toward Pariser Platz, then return after dark: access is free at all hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Two pyramids in the middle of a lake: nobody expects that in the Brandenburg plain. Hermann Fürst von Pückler-Muskau had Branitzer Park laid out between 1846 and 1871 on initially flat, arid terrain. The water pyramid is his tomb, covered in grapevines. The other, on dry land, was intended for his wife Lucie—she was never buried there. Park open year-round, palace April through October.

Inside, Schloss Branitz's Orientzimmer still evoke travel. Pückler, a great traveler, brought back from Egypt and the Near East enough to furnish several rooms in an Orientalist style unique in Brandenburg. The Carl Blechen collection in the restored rooms is, alongside the collection at Berlin's Alte Nationalgalerie, one of the two largest collections of works by this Cottbus-born artist.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Never destroyed, never abandoned: Marksburg is the only hilltop castle on the Middle Rhine to have survived intact. The Deutsche Burgenvereinigung bought it in 1900 for 1,000 gold marks and established its headquarters there. Visits are by guided tour only and last about 50 minutes, taking you from the medieval kitchen to the armory. Park below the castle and allow for 120 steps up to the entrance.

Lovage, butterbur, henbane: Marksburg’s small medieval herb garden smells of dried herbs and old apothecaries. It is tucked away within the walls of the castle, which is perched on a cone of slate above Braubach. Keep your camera ready: from the walls, the view sweeps down over Braubach’s rooftops and the Rhine.

days_plan.itin_title: The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz

visits.text: Touristy, yes, but the Breitachklamm dispels any reservations from the first walkways. The trail runs for about 2.5 km between rock walls roughly 150 m high, and its operators describe it as Central Europe’s deepest rocky gorge. Open to the public since 1905, it welcomes around 300,000 visitors a year: arrive at 9 a.m. and park at Tiefenbach’s P1 parking lot (€5).

activities.text: The Zwingsteg, a footbridge spanning the Breitach high above the river, turns a visit to the Breitachklamm into a loop. From the upper exit, head to Walserschanz, cross the footbridge, then descend via Alpe Dornach and Gsessel to the main entrance: about 5.5 km and 2 hours 30 minutes, including the gorge. In winter, curtains of ice and frozen waterfalls cover the walls; wear shoes with good traction.

days_plan.itin_title: Oberstdorf in 3 Days: Lakes, Gorges, and Kleinwalsertal

visits.text: Bremen's Marktplatz is one of the best-preserved medieval ensembles in northern Germany. The town hall (Rathaus), built in the 15th century in Gothic style then remodeled in Weser Renaissance in the 17th century, and the Roland statue erected in 1404—symbol of municipal freedoms—have been UNESCO-listed since 2004. Bremen had joined the Hanseatic League in 1358; much of its prosperity came from the 17th century onward through coffee and cotton trade.

St. Peter's Cathedral (Dom St. Petri) was founded in 789 by Willehad, the first bishop of Bremen - who died that same year. The present sandstone building was constructed from 1042 onward and remodeled several times. Its two towers with green roofs dominate the Marktplatz.

The Schnoor quarter is the old fishermen's district, whose 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses have remained virtually intact. Its alleyways are so narrow that you can touch both facades by stretching out your arms, and they are home to galleries, artisans, and cafes.

Böttcherstrasse is a 100-meter street rebuilt in the 1920s in the Expressionist style, combining carved red brick with decorative art. It was commissioned by a coffee merchant who had made his fortune from trade with Brazil. At the entrance, a gold relief depicts the Archangel Michael slaying a dragon.

The Kunsthalle Bremen, founded in 1849, is one of Germany's oldest art museums. Its collection covers Flemish and Dutch painting, German Romanticism, French Impressionism—Monet, Pissarro—and modern art. It holds over 200,000 drawings and prints, one of the most important collections of this type in Europe.

activities.text: Stroll along the Schlachte, the riverside promenade along the Weser that runs the entire length of the old town. Terraces and moored boats—very lively on summer evenings.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Around Hanover: Lower Saxony's Most Beautiful Sites
Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea
Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles
Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Five continents in a day: the Klimahaus Bremerhaven follows the 8th meridian East from Niger to Alaska, taking in the Swiss Alps and Samoa along the way. The temperature changes with each room — you go from 35°C desert heat to Antarctica in twenty minutes. A concept unique in the world, open since the late 2000s.

The Deutsches Auswandererhaus (German Emigration Center) hits harder than a conventional museum: located on the quay from which more than seven million Europeans departed between 1830 and 1974, it hands each visitor a “boarding pass” bearing the real biography of an emigrant. Winner of the European Museum of the Year Award in 2007.

activities.text: Stroll the Havenwelten quays and watch container ships pass within arm's reach of the embankment. Bremerhaven is one of Europe's top container ports — the yellow cranes are visible for kilometres. In the evening, a handful of fresh fish restaurants line the basin.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: The vines seem almost vertical, yet the Calmont remains a working landscape. From Bremm and its riverfront surroundings, you can see the rows climbing the hillside and the Moselle curving around its base. Start by taking in the landscape from the village; reaching a viewpoint at the summit requires a climb and extra time.

activities.text: Walk at the foot of the Calmont from Bremm for a nature break during this day of village visits. Routes in the region range from vineyard paths to more demanding trails; the Calmont-Klettersteig includes cables and ladders. Stick to ordinary paths here, turn back according to the time you have available, and bring water.

days_plan.itin_title: Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier

visits.text: Conquer the Brocken, Saxony-Anhalt's highest point and the highest mountain in northern Germany at 1,141 meters elevation. This mythical summit, shrouded in mist and legend, is the gathering place of witches during Walpurgis Night according to Germanic folklore. On clear days, panoramas from the summit extend up to 200 kilometers, embracing the northern plains and neighboring massifs.

Board the Harzer Brockenbahn steam train, one of Germany's last narrow-gauge railways still in regular service. This historic line climbs the slopes of the Brocken through fir forests and highland peat bog landscapes in a nostalgic atmosphere. The 90-minute train journey constitutes an experience as memorable as the destination itself.

Discover Heinrich Heine Rock, named in honor of the famous poet who climbed the Brocken in 1820 and immortalized this experience in his travel narrative. Hiking trails wind through a subarctic landscape unique in central Germany, where stunted vegetation testifies to the extreme climatic conditions. The delicious Brockensplitter chocolates are the gourmet reward for this ascent.

activities.text: Hiking or steam train journey to the Brocken summit

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The Sauerland locals simply call them “die Steine.” Four blocks of volcanic porphyry, 45 to 92 meters high, pierce the forest on the Istenberg's flank at 727 meters elevation. Formed 390 million years ago, designated National Natural Monument in 2017. Peregrine falcons nest in the rock faces. Admission €6.50.

activities.text: Climb up to the Feldstein, the only one accessible to the public. Its summit peaks at 756 meters and offers a circular panorama across the Hochsauerland. The ascent takes 20 minutes from the information center. Closed Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: An archbishop-elector’s residence, then a republic’s ceremonial reception venue: Augustusburg Palace welcomed the federal president’s state guests until 1994. Begun in 1725 for Clemens August and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984, it can be visited on a guided tour, including Balthasar Neumann’s grand staircase. Admission is €15; closed Mondays and from December through February.

activities.text: Crunching gravel, fountains, and ornamental flower beds: Brühl’s Schlosspark, a French formal garden designed by Dominique Girard, takes 30 minutes to explore. Open year-round, it has longer opening hours than the palace. Save this walk for the end, once your guided tour is over.

days_plan.itin_title: Cologne, Bonn, and Aachen in 3 Days: Cathedrals and Treasures

visits.text: Built from 1915 to 1917 with 1.5 million clinker bricks, Burg's Bismarckturm rises 27 meters on the Schlossberg. During World War II, the Wehrmacht used it as a radio center; in 1951, it was renamed “Tower of Youth”; it regained its name on October 3, 1990, during a public celebration. Open from April to November.

You'll cross the Kur- und Sagenpark to reach the other end of Burg. This 60,000-square-meter park depicts Sorbian mythology with themed sculptures—water spirits, forest spirits. More instructive than a simple garden, though the bilingual panels are in German and Lower Sorbian only.

activities.text: Two hours on a punt from Burg is considerably quieter than in Lübbenau. The Spreehafen Burg is one of the Spreewald's oldest harbors; the Kolonistentour goes up to villages founded by Frederick the Great. Budget around €20 per adult.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Burg zu Burghausen stretches 1,051 m along its ridge between the Salzach and Wöhrsee, and Guinness World Records recognizes it as the world’s longest castle. Duke Henry XIII rebuilt it beginning in 1255, and George the Rich expanded it considerably in the late 15th century. Explore the outer courtyards, open at all hours, starting with the sixth and farthest one and working your way toward the Hauptburg.

The Hauptburg is worth the admission price, especially for its upper floors. On the first upper floor, the Staatliches Burgmuseum recreates the apartments of the dukes of Bavaria-Landshut, who kept their gold and silver treasure here; on the next two floors, the Staatsgalerie displays 56 paintings dating from the late Middle Ages to the early 17th century. Tickets are available at the Besucherzentrum in the Dürnitzstock; open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. April through September, and until 4 p.m. in winter.

The daughter of the king of Poland, Hedwig married George the Rich at the famous Landshut Wedding, then lived here with her court from 1475 to 1502. The Stadtmuseum, in the Hauptburg’s Kemenate, devotes its ground floor to this princely life before tracing local history, including the witch hunts. Open from mid-March through fall; a €10 pass covers three castle museums.

A former tax office filled with cameras: the Haus der Fotografie occupies the Rentmeisterstock in the castle’s fifth courtyard. More than 600 cameras from every era trace the history of photography, alongside early photographic processes and old photographs of Burghausen. Founded in 1983, it is open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., from March to early November.

Burghausen’s Stadtplatz, at the foot of the castle, is lined with Inn-Salzach-style screen facades extending to the Taufkirchen-Palais and the Regierungsgebäude, crowned by three Renaissance towers. Nearby, St. Jakob has a 79 m bell tower, and Anton Bruckner played its new organ in 1856. Walk down from the Hauptburg to combine the castle and old town without getting back in the car.

activities.text: Swim at the foot of the ramparts: the Wöhrsee, a former oxbow of the Salzach, has served as a swimming lake for local residents since 1833. In January 2015, its Naturbad even hosted Germany’s first ice swimming championship, followed by the world championship in 2017. Outside the swimming season, walk around the lake; in late November, more than 350 lanterns line its shores.

If the sky is clear, cross the Salzach on the Alte Brücke: on the opposite bank, you are already in Austria. A steep trail climbs to a viewing platform overlooking the old town and the full length of the Burg. The “Über Brücken gehen” loop, 4.3 km and about 1 hour 10 minutes, returns via the Neue Brücke and follows the bronze plaques of the jazz-themed Street of Fame on the Bavarian side.

days_plan.itin_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach

visits.text: Celle's old town (Altstadt) boasts over 500 half-timbered houses designated as historical monuments, the oldest dating back to the 15th century. The town's name derives from the Latin cella—a small monastic chamber—recalling an ancient monastery established on the site. First mentioned in 985 as Kellu, Celle served as the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg from 1378 to 1705. The carved beams above doorways once indicated the occupants' trades.

The Hoppener Haus, built in 1532, stands among Germany's most lavishly decorated half-timbered houses. Its six-level facade is covered with carvings depicting devils, jesters, planetary gods, mythical creatures, and reptiles. Across the street, two lampposts equipped with speakers recount local anecdotes in both standard German and Low Saxon dialect—they activate automatically as you pass.

Celle Castle (Schloss Celle) overlooks the bank of the Aller River from a low hill surrounded by moats and a six-and-a-half-hectare park. Built in the 13th century and serving as the residence of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg for over three centuries, it houses Baroque state apartments adorned with Italian stuccowork and a Renaissance chapel. The Schlosstheater, founded in 1675, is considered Germany's oldest Baroque theater still in operation. Queen Caroline Matilda of Denmark was exiled here from 1772 until her death in 1775.

The Stadtkirche St. Marien ranks among the town's oldest buildings. Its tower offers views across the old town's rooftops and the castle. Access to the tower depends on opening hours posted on the facade.

Celle's synagogue, built in 1740, is the oldest synagogue in northern Germany. This baroque half-timbered building, located at Im Kreise 24, survived Kristallnacht in 1938 because authorities feared fire would spread to neighboring houses. Inside, a collection of objects that belonged to Holocaust survivors.

The French Garden (Französischer Garten) was designed in the 17th century by French landscape architects, though over time it has taken on a more English appearance. Linden tree avenue, flower beds, and a pond—freely accessible.

activities.text: Walk a loop along the Aller and the historic bridges—the best angle to see the castle reflected in the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands
Road Trip Around Hanover: Lower Saxony's Most Beautiful Sites

visits.text: The Biertor, an ocher brick gate with twin towers, is the most striking remnant of Cham's medieval wall. The Marktplatz just behind it features a town hall with a carillon and the Bürgerspital dating from 1300. Cham can be explored on foot in an hour.

The promenade along the Regen, which wraps the old town in a broad loop, explains the nickname “Stadt am Regenbogen.” Century-old trees, wooden footbridges, ducks: a bucolic atmosphere ten minutes from the center.

activities.text: Take the bike path along the Regen toward Chammünster to see the Pfarrkirche Mariä Himmelfahrt, one of the Palatinate's oldest parishes. 6-km round trip, flat, family-friendly.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Touristy to the point of parody, yet steeped in history, Checkpoint Charlie was the only crossing between East and West Berlin open to foreigners, diplomats, and Allied military personnel. In late October 1961, ten Soviet tanks and ten American tanks faced off here about a hundred meters apart. Today’s guardhouse is a replica; the original is preserved at the Allied Museum. Take your photo, then save your time for the neighboring museum.

Packed with exhibits and somewhat disorganized, the Mauermuseum Haus am Checkpoint Charlie is most worthwhile for its escape artifacts. Opened in 1963 beside the border crossing, it displays an armored car, a homemade hot-air balloon, and a miniature submarine powered by a bicycle motor, all designed to reach the West. Open daily from 10 AM to 8 PM; at €18.50 for adult admission, it is best suited to Cold War enthusiasts.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Chemnitz was renamed Karl-Marx-Stadt in 1953 by the GDR and regained its historic name in 1990 after reunification. The Karl Marx Monument, inaugurated in 1971, is a colossal bust weighing 40 tonnes, carved from Siberian granite and placed on a 13-meter pedestal. The locals call it the “Nischel,” a local dialect term for “skull.” In 2025, Chemnitz is European Capital of Culture under the slogan “C the Unseen”—150 projects and 1,000 events distributed throughout the city and 38 surrounding municipalities, in converted former industrial buildings.

The Kaßberg district is one of Germany's largest continuous ensembles of Gründerzeit and Art Nouveau architecture—about a hundred blocks from the late 19th century with their sandstone facades and sculpted ornaments. It had largely escaped the 1945 bombings that devastated the center.

The municipal art collections (Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz) feature works by Karl Schmidt-Rottluff - the Expressionist painter was a native of the city. The museum also includes an important collection of 19th-century paintings and contemporary art.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

activities.text: The 25 m wooden pagoda of the Chinesischer Turm watches over Munich’s second-largest beer garden, with seating for about 7,000. Built in 1789–1790 and destroyed by fire in July 1944, it was rebuilt to match the original in 1952. End the day here with a Maß of beer and a pretzel, preferably before sunset so you can find a table near the tower.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Chorin Abbey gives brick an unexpected lightness: arches and openings still define the spaces of the former Cistercian abbey. The exhibitions explore monastic life and the preservation of the monument, offering more than a simple setting of ruins. Take your time on the architectural tour and check for any concert-related restrictions before your visit.

activities.text: Extend your visit to Chorin Abbey with its digital tour, which helps you understand the sections that have disappeared. The site offers tools for exploring on your phone, including a virtual exploration of the entire complex; the architectural volumes become easier to interpret when you compare them with the remains. Charge your device and check what content is available before starting.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeastern Brandenburg: Abbey, Forest, and Lakes in 3 Days

visits.text: The loveliest prelude to the Christlessee comes in the form of three chapels: the Lorettokapellen, on Oberstdorf’s southern edge. Built one after another starting in the 15th century, they have long drawn pilgrims to the end of a Stations of the Cross route leading from town. Step inside quietly, then continue toward the golf course: the trail to the lake starts there.

It never freezes, yet hardly anyone swims in it: fed by karst springs, the Christlessee stays at 4 to 6 °C year-round. The springs feeding it supply Oberstdorf’s drinking water, and its blue water turns turquoise in places around submerged tree trunks. Walk around the lake on the shoreline trail, then warm up at the nearby café.

activities.text: Set out on foot from the Mühlenbrücke in central Oberstdorf via the Haldenweg and Lorettokapellen: the Christlessee is about 1 hour away along almost flat paths. The trail then continues into the Trettachtal as far as Spielmannsau. For an effortless return, board the Bergsteigerlinie, a shuttle linking the lake to Oberstdorf’s bus station from spring through late fall.

days_plan.itin_title: Oberstdorf in 3 Days: Lakes, Gorges, and Kleinwalsertal

visits.text: An open-air museum in the countryside: the Museumsdorf Cloppenburg assembles some sixty rural buildings from the Middle Ages to the 1980s. Founded in 1934, it's one of Germany's oldest Freilichtmuseen. Count on a good two hours.

The creak of wood beneath the hooves of Heidschnucken, the black-headed sheep grazing between the windmills: the Museumsdorf isn't a frozen museum. Three windmills, a church, a forge and even a rural 1980s disco. Adult admission: around 12 euros.

activities.text: If the Dorfkirmes falls during your visit (July), the museum village comes alive with historic fairground stalls and bread baked over a wood fire. Check the dates on museumsdorf.de.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: The Veste Coburg was Luther's hideout for six months in 1530, while the Diet of Augsburg redefined religious Europe. Luther's apartment is still visitable in the fortress, one of Germany's largest. The Kunstsammlungen preserve works by Cranach, Dürer, and Grünewald - less crowded than in the major museums, so at leisure.

Coburg's Altstadt is more human and more lively than those along the Romantic Road: no souvenir shops at every corner, residents doing their shopping, the Marktplatz with the statue of Prince Albert (born here in 1819). The tourist surplus hasn't settled in yet.

Schloss Ehrenburg, former town palace of the Dukes of Saxe-Coburg, rebuilt after a 17th-century fire, houses what is reputed to be the first flush toilet in German history - installed for Queen Victoria during her 1845 visit. The guided tour lasts one hour.

activities.text: Walk up from the Schlossplatz to the Veste along the Carl-Escher-Weg: about 30 minutes of steep climbing. The effort is rewarded by the view from the ramparts over the town and the hills of Upper Franconia. A bus is available for the way down.

If you are there in July, the Coburg Samba-Festival (second weekend of July) fills the town center with around a hundred samba groups from all over the world. The rest of the year, the Hofgarten behind the palace is a quiet spot for a break.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Arrive in Cochem via the road that follows the Moselle: steep vineyards frame the river's meanders, and the pointed silhouette of Reichsburg appears from afar, perched 100 meters above the village. Stroll along the Moselle quays—promenades lined with terraces, pleasure boats, and slate-roofed half-timbered houses.

The Marktplatz of Cochem and St. Martin's Church, built on the ruins of an 11th-century chapel, form the old town's heart. The square is framed by restored half-timbered houses and a former baroque town hall. From the square, stepped streets climb toward the castle.

Walk up via Schlossstrasse to Reichsburg (20 minutes from Marktplatz), the largest hillside castle on the Moselle. Built around the year 1000, first mentioned in 1051, it was destroyed in 1689 by troops of Louis XIV—then purchased in 1868 by Berlin merchant Louis Ravené, who had it completely rebuilt in the Romantic Gothic Revival style then in vogue. The castle has 50 rooms, 6 of which can be visited on a guided tour: the Gothic-style knights' hall, the Romanesque hall, the Renaissance dining room with its woodwork, and a room housing a 1 km secret passage to the Capuchin monastery in town. In the courtyard, a 50-meter-deep well once supplied water to all inhabitants.

Then take the chairlift (Sesselbahn) up to Pinnerkreuz, a viewpoint at an elevation of 290 meters overlooking the loop of the Moselle. The panorama over terraced vineyards, river meanders, and wooded Eifel hills is the most comprehensive in the entire Cochem region.

Eltz Castle (Burg Eltz) is one of the few castles in Europe never to have been destroyed and to have remained in the same family for 33 generations—the first written record dates to 1157, when Rudolph “of Eltz Castle” was named as a witness in a deed issued by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. The castle rises from the depths of a wooded valley, perched on a 70-meter rocky spur bordered on three sides by the Elzbach River. In 1268, three brothers divided the property under a system of joint inheritance (medieval co-ownership): three family branches lived together in their own quarters around a narrow inner courtyard, hence the mixed styles—Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance—visible in the facades. The guided tour (about 35 minutes) covers the knights' hall, the armory (with the world's oldest cannon arrows), the Rübenach Hall fitted out in 1311—which houses a Virgin and Child by Lucas Cranach the Elder—and the reception hall.

The Schatzkammer (Treasury), accessible with the same ticket, is the only place in the castle where photography is allowed. It houses over 500 pieces accumulated by the family over eight centuries: gold and silverwork, jewelry, weapons, chalices, and armor. It's one of Germany's most important private collections.

activities.text: One-hour panoramic cruise on the Moselle from Cochem marina. The circuit heads upriver toward the wine villages of Beilstein or Ediger-Eller, skirting steep terraced vineyards and medieval castle ruins.

Photo walk on the Moselle bridge in Cochem toward the end of the day: from the bridge, the quays, steeples, and castle silhouette line up in the view—the city's classic composition, particularly flattering in the golden evening light.

From Cochem, allow for a round trip to Moselkern, on the Moselle. Hike from the village to Eltz Castle along a forest trail beside the Elzbach, gradually descending deeper into the wooded valley. The castle suddenly appears around the final bend. This trail is the best way to arrive—and to avoid the lines at the parking lot.

days_plan.itin_title: Germany Road Trip: Castles, Medieval Villages and the Alps
Germany Road Trip: Castles, Medieval Villages and the Alps
Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier

visits.text: Built in 1908 by Bernhard Sehring in just sixteen months, the Staatstheater Cottbus is Lusatia's only Jugendstil theater and Brandenburg's sole state theater. The façade reads like an Art Nouveau manifesto: panther on the roof, nine muses in a frieze. Architectural guided tours take place on Sundays.

Cottbus's Spremberger Turm has dominated the Altmarkt since the thirteenth century—31 meters of medieval red brick at the end of the shopping street. The Altmarkt itself is ringed with Saxon Baroque and Classicist gabled houses: cafés are open from 8 a.m., terraces packed in summer.

activities.text: You'll stroll around the Altmarkt, surrounded by colorful façades, then head up Burgstraße to the Oberkirche St. Nikolai, Lower Lusatia's largest Gothic church. You can walk across Cottbus's center in under an hour; stay around Burgstraße / Mühlenstraße for the concentration of cafés and shops.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Standing in wood on the Elbe embankment since the 18th century, the Kugelbake has guided ships into the river mouth for centuries — it marks the northernmost point of Lower Saxony. The current structure dates from 1945 (the previous one was destroyed during the war), stands nearly 30 metres tall, and has featured on Cuxhaven's coat of arms since 1913.

The Wattenmeer mudflats around Cuxhaven stretch as far as the eye can see at low tide: a flat tidal plain churned by worm burrows, scattered with shells and lit by shifting colours. Listed as a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site, it hosts millions of migratory birds.

activities.text: Set off on a Wattwanderung at falling tide from Duhnen beach — twice a day the sea gives up kilometres of mudflats to be crossed barefoot. Grey shrimps and crabs survive in rock pools. Get back before the tide turns: it comes in fast.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Explore the mysterious Burg Berwartstein, a fascinating castle perched dramatically atop one of the rocky sandstone hills that characterize this border region. Once seized by notorious robber barons during the Middle Ages, this fortress is steeped in amazing myths and legends that the guided tours bring thrillingly to life. The hand-carved, candlelit tunnels beneath the castle create an atmospheric adventure unlike any other.

Discover the castle's remarkable architecture, including a small chapel adorned with medieval paintings that survived centuries of conflict and neglect. The robber baron history adds a thrilling dimension to the visit, with tales of ambushes, ransoms and dramatic escapes echoing through the stone corridors. This hidden gem remains surprisingly untouched by mass tourism, offering an authentic castle experience.

activities.text: Take the guided tour to hear the fascinating legends and explore the candle-lit underground passages

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: The Mathildenhöhe is Germany's most remarkable Art Nouveau site, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2021. On this hill overlooking Darmstadt, Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig founded an artists' colony in 1899, bringing together architects, painters, and sculptors—including Joseph Maria Olbrich and Peter Behrens—under the motto: “Let my Hesse flourish, and art within it.” Four international exhibitions (1901, 1904, 1908, 1914) produced an ensemble of 23 architectural elements: artists' houses, studios, the Swan Pavilion, a water lily pond, and a grove of plane trees. These buildings became a laboratory of emerging modernism, inspired by both the British Arts & Crafts movement and the Vienna Secession.

The Hochzeitsturm (Wedding Tower), standing 48.5 meters tall, is the iconic building of the Mathildenhöhe. Olbrich designed it for the third exhibition in 1908 as a gift from the city to Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig for his remarriage to Princess Eleonore. Locals call it the "Five Finger Tower" because of its five ascending arches. Since 1993, an annex of the registry office has been housed here—weddings celebrated at the top grant access to the panoramic platform.

The Russian Chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene is part of the UNESCO site but predates the artists' colony. It was built between 1897 and 1899 by architect Louis Benois from Saint Petersburg, on the orders of Tsar Nicholas II—who had married Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig's sister Alix of Hesse, later Empress Alexandra, in 1894. Its five golden onion domes stand out against the park's greenery, and the chapel served as a place of worship during visits by the Russian imperial family.

The Hessisches Landesmuseum Darmstadt is one of Germany's most comprehensive encyclopedic museums. It brings together art (including the world's largest collection of works by Joseph Beuys), archaeology, geology, and natural history. One gallery is devoted to fossils from the Messel Pit.

The Messel Pit (Grube Messel), 9 km northeast of Darmstadt, is Germany's first natural site inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1995). This former oil shale quarry preserves the remains of over 40,000 specimens from a 47-million-year-old ecosystem—the Eocene epoch, when the first modern mammals were developing in a tropical forest. Discoveries include primitive horses the size of a dog (Eurohippus messelensis), primates, crocodiles, snakes, and insects with colors still visible. Access to the pit itself is by guided tour only. The finest specimens are displayed at the Senckenberg in Frankfurt and the Landesmuseum in Darmstadt. Anecdote: the pit nearly became a municipal landfill in the 1970s—a strong campaign by citizens and scientists prevented it.

activities.text: Guided tour into the Messel Pit: the descent into the quarry allows you to observe the layers of oil shale from which fossils are still extracted. Replicas showing preparation under real working conditions are on display. The tour lasts approximately two hours.

Explore the scientific quarter of Darmstadt, a city nicknamed “Science City”: the Technical University, GSI (heavy ion research center), ESA/ESOC (European Space Operations Centre), and EUMETSAT are all based here. The facade of the ESOC control center—from which European Space Agency satellites are operated—is visible from the street.

days_plan.itin_title: Hesse, Germany Tour: Cities and Nature Parks

visits.text: Above Daun’s other lakes, Weinfelder Maar calls for a simpler pause. It belongs to the Dauner Maare group and can be reached from the parking areas along the L64. Here, the terrain alone reveals the imprint of volcanic activity, without a museum display. Park in a designated area and observe the lakeshore from the marked trails.

If you are looking for a lake in a deeper basin, stop at Gemündener Maar near Daun. Its wooded shores contrast with the open views at Weinfelder Maar; these neighboring landscapes offer different perspectives. Keep this stop as a brief scenic viewpoint, separate from the walk to the Dronketurm. Check seasonal access if you are considering a water activity afterward.

activities.text: You will climb toward the Dronketurm to compare the lakes rather than walk along all their shores. The viewpoint lets you see Gemündener Maar and Weinfelder Maar in the same landscape. This perspective on the terrain complements the stops by the water. Choose a marked route that suits your pace; skip the climb if conditions become slippery.

The village almost touches the water at Schalkenmehrener Maar, offering a third distinct setting among the lakes near Daun. A walk along the shore places the crater in an inhabited landscape, while swimming and boat rentals depend on the season. For this short itinerary, choose an easy stretch from Schalkenmehren. Treat a possible swim as an alternative to walking, without extending every activity.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: Every Whit Tuesday, a billy goat delivered by the neighboring municipality of Lambrecht is auctioned outside Deidesheim’s Historisches Rathaus as symbolic payment for historic grazing rights. The setting fits the occasion: an exterior staircase from 1724 and the Museum für Weinkultur, established inside in 1986. Continue to St. Ulrich’s Church, built from 1444 to 1473. The museum opens only a few afternoons a week during the season: check before you come.

activities.text: Here you’ll raise a glass in the first place in the Palatinate where estates began producing quality wines in the early 19th century. Reichsrat von Buhl and Bassermann-Jordan, established in 1849 when the Jordan estate was divided, are based in Deidesheim, and many winemakers open their cellars for tastings. Book on weekdays and walk back: the small town is easy to explore without a car.

Saumagen means “sow’s stomach”: hardly diplomatic, yet Helmut Kohl served this Palatinate specialty to Margaret Thatcher, Mikhail Gorbachev, and Boris Yeltsin when he hosted them in Deidesheim between 1989 and 1997. Order it for dinner at a Weinstube in the old town, with a glass of local wine; reserve a table on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen

places.name: Denkmal Fuer Die Ermordeten Juden Europas

visits.text: Head down into the Ort der Information, the information center beneath the eastern corner of the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe: after the abstract stelae, the focus shifts to individual lives. In the Room of Names, the names of Jewish victims are read aloud using data from Yad Vashem. Admission is free, Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with last admission 45 minutes before closing; a free guided tour in English starts at 2 p.m. on the first Sunday of the month.

activities.text: The ground undulates, the concrete blocks grow taller, and the city’s noise fades within a few steps. Designed by Peter Eisenman and inaugurated in May 2005, the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe consists of 2,711 stelae spread across nearly 2 hectares, ranging from 20 cm to 4.7 m in height. Walk through several aisles without looking for a set route: each changes your perspective. This is a place of remembrance; climbing and picnicking are not allowed.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

map_keywords: Denkmal für die ermordeten Juden Europas Berlin

visits.text: Immerse yourself in the Bauhaus universe in Dessau, where this revolutionary art school was founded in 1919 and relocated in 1925. The main building designed by Walter Gropius, with its iconic glass facade, embodies the founding principle of form follows function. Over 300 Bauhaus buildings dot the city, constituting the world's largest architectural ensemble of this movement.

Visit the Bauhaus Museum, which presents an important collection devoted to this major twentieth-century artistic movement. Works by legendary masters Walter Gropius, Marcel Breuer and Wassily Kandinsky are displayed in a contemporary architectural setting. The Masters' Houses, residences of the Bauhaus professors, offer a moving insight into their avant-garde way of life.

Discover the rebuilt city center of Dessau, more than 85% destroyed during World War II. The Residential Palace, Town Hall, and mausoleum testify to the princely history of the town before the Bauhaus era. St. Peter and Paul Church and Georgium Palace, surrounded by its English-style park, complete this diverse architectural heritage.

activities.text: Visit Luisium Park, an 18th-century landscape garden with its small neoclassical palace

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The LWL-Freilichtmuseum in Detmold is Germany's largest open-air museum: 90 hectares, over 120 buildings dismantled at their original locations and rebuilt here, and 500 years of Westphalian architecture, from farming communities to urban workshops. A 1960s filling station turned museum exhibit stands alongside 16th-century farms. Open March to October, Tuesday-Sunday.

Smoke rises from the blacksmith's forge inside a half-timbered building — at the LWL-Freilichtmuseum, smiths, bakers and potters work for real in the historic workshops. Daily demonstrations have no fixed schedule: come in the morning to catch the craftsperson at work. Senner horses, a rare breed, graze within the museum grounds.

The Residenzschloss in Detmold, built in the Weser Renaissance style, is still the residence of the princely zu Lippe family. Its façade and clock tower dominate the Altstadt. The princely apartments can be visited on guided tours by arrangement — the interior is worth the trip.

activities.text: Start early and set aside two to four hours at the LWL-Freilichtmuseum — a full circuit of the site covers 9 kilometres. Horse-drawn carriages run between the entrance and the Paderborner Dorf. Three historic on-site restaurants mean you can have lunch without leaving the museum.
If the Saturday market is open, Detmold hosts a weekly market with regional products from Lippe. Strate's Brauhaus, just a short walk away, has served local beer since 1863 - a good spot for dinner.

days_plan.itin_title: Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken
Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: You’ll spend the afternoon at the Deutsches Museum, founded in 1903 on an island in the Isar, and you’ll need the time. The renovated half, reopened in July 2022, features 19 permanent exhibitions: the first diesel engine, the laboratory table used in nuclear fission experiments, musical instruments, and a large model railroad. The temporary entrance is in the glass pavilion on the Corneliusbrücke side; the museum opens from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with last admission at 4:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Less famous than Rothenburg, and that's its fortune. Dinkelsbühl has preserved its medieval ramparts almost intact with five gates, eleven towers, and a bastide. Focus magazine named it Germany's most beautiful Altstadt - not a scientific ranking, but the evening stroller quickly understands why.

The Münster St. Georg presents a fan vault that astonishes in this late Gothic church from the 15th century. The severe façade doesn't prepare you for the interior ceiling. A curiosity: the bakers' stained-glass window, in the last bay on the right, depicts a pretzel. Free entry.

activities.text: Walk to the Wörnitztor in the morning before the shops open. The ramparts walk in Dinkelsbühl is shorter than Rothenburg's and less crowded; it's a better place to wander without a precise plan. The Weinmarkt in the center is the epicenter of local life.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Dinkelsbühl is often called “Rothenburg's little sister”—but is rightly less well known, and therefore less crowded. The town is surrounded by ramparts dating partly from 1370, with 16 towers and 4 gates still standing, accessible along their entire perimeter. Unlike Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl suffered no damage during World War II—three-quarters of its houses are over 350 years old. Walk along the outer rampart path (2.7 km, about 45 minutes) to see the towers, moats, and gardens bordering the walls.

St. George's Minster (Münster St. Georg) is Dinkelsbühl's central monument. Built between 1448 and 1499 in just 51 years, it's one of the most beautiful Gothic hall churches in southern Germany. The nave and two aisles, covered by net vaulting, are of equal height, creating a sense of unified space that is rare in Gothic architecture. The Romanesque tower predates the nave: it dates from the 12th century.

The Marktplatz and Weinmarkt (wine market), two adjacent squares separated by the Minster, form the historic heart. The Deutsches Haus on Weinmarkt is a patrician half-timbered house in German Renaissance style, with a facade adorned with sculptures, one of the region's finest.

activities.text: Night watchman's round (Nachtwächter): every evening, a guide in medieval costume, lantern in hand, leads visitors through the illuminated old town to recount Dinkelsbühl's history.

days_plan.itin_title: Germany Road Trip: Castles, Medieval Villages and the Alps

visits.text: Pass through the cathedral and its Adamspforte to reach the adjoining Diözesanmuseum. The highlight is the Sternenmantel, Henry II’s star-studded cloak, displayed alongside other medieval imperial garments and pontifical vestments; the cathedral cross exhibited here weighs 600 kg. Admission is €7; the museum is closed on Wednesdays and opens only at noon on Sundays. Allow 45 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: The most intense moment of the trip unfolds in an unsettling setting: the Dokumentationszentrum Reichsparteitagsgelände occupies the north wing of the never-completed Kongresshalle, pierced diagonally by Günther Domenig’s glass-and-steel “stake.” The hall was intended to hold 50,000 party activists; its walls reach only 39 m instead of the planned 68.5 m. The new permanent exhibition, opened in 2026 across 1,600 m², can be explored with a 90-minute French audio guide, included in the €7.50 admission. Opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays and 10 a.m. on weekends.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: If you walk up from the Walhallastraße bus stop, expect 358 steps to reach the Walhalla. Leo von Klenze designed this Parthenon-inspired temple for Ludwig I. Inaugurated on October 18, 1842, above the Danube, it houses approximately 130 busts, including Max Planck since 2022. Open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., April through October.

days_plan.itin_title: Altmühltal and the Danube in 4 Days, from Ingolstadt to Regensburg

visits.text: Deutsches Fußballmuseum deserves its place on this industrial itinerary: it showcases another form of collective culture in Germany. Opposite Dortmund’s central train station, the museum combines objects, images, and interactive exhibits to tell the history of soccer. Focus on the sections that interest you rather than reading everything; check opening hours and buy your ticket before visiting.

activities.text: Finish at PHOENIX See, following the shoreline instead of immediately getting back on the road. In Dortmund-Hörde, the artificial lake transforms the landscape of a former steelmaking district; the paths around the water form a 3.2 km loop. Allow about fifty minutes to walk without a long break, and check municipal notices in case construction affects access.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

visits.text: The Zwinger is Dresden's most iconic monument. Built from 1709 by Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann for Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, it began as an orangery and princely festival arena. Its official inauguration took place in 1719 for the marriage of Augustus's son to Archduchess Maria Josepha of Austria. Six pavilions linked by galleries enclose a vast interior courtyard with fountains and lawns—Augustus the Strong had himself depicted as Hercules above the Wallpavillon. The Kronentor, the gate crowned by a golden crown carried by four eagles, is the complex's most photographed image.

The Old Masters Picture Gallery, housed in the Semper Wing built between 1847 and 1855, contains over 700 paintings from the 15th to 18th centuries. Its greatest treasure is Raphael's Sistine Madonna, painted around 1512 and acquired by Augustus III in 1754 for the colossal sum of 25,000 ducats. Rubens, Vermeer, Rembrandt, Titian, Giorgione, and Botticelli are also represented. The paintings had been evacuated before the 1945 bombings—they were found hidden in underground mines and returned by the USSR in 1955 after being held in Moscow for ten years.

The Zwinger Porcelain Collection houses some 20,000 pieces of Chinese, Japanese, and Meissen porcelain. Augustus the Strong was so obsessed that in 1717 he traded a regiment of 600 Prussian soldiers for 151 Chinese porcelain vases—these pieces are still on display here. The collection also illustrates how the discovery of European porcelain at Meissen in 1708 arose from a royal commission for alchemy: Augustus wanted gold, his chemists invented porcelain.

The Semperoper, standing on Theaterplatz facing the Zwinger, is one of Europe's most renowned opera houses. The first building was designed by Gottfried Semper and inaugurated in 1841, then destroyed by fire in 1869. The second, also designed by Semper but completed by his son Manfred, reopened in 1878—the elder Semper was then banished from Saxony for participating in the 1849 insurrection. Razed by the February 13, 1945 bombings, it was rebuilt to match the original and reopened on February 13, 1985, exactly forty years after its destruction. Richard Strauss premiered several of his operas here, including Der Rosenkavalier in 1911.

The Residenzschloss, palace of the prince-electors and kings of Saxony, is one of Dresden's oldest buildings. Its construction dates to 1220; it was remodeled in Renaissance style between 1548 and 1556, then partially destroyed in 1945 and gradually rebuilt from 1986. It now houses several major museums. The Historic Green Vault (Historisches Grünes Gewölbe) presents 3,000 examples of baroque goldsmithing in their original 18th-century display cases—one of Europe's largest treasure collections. On November 25, 2019, thieves broke a window at 5 a.m. and stole several sets of diamond jewelry from the collection: the case caused a scandal throughout Germany.

The Fürstenzug stretches 102 meters along the outer wall of the Stallhof, the palace stable courtyard. This monumental mural depicts the procession of the 35 rulers of the House of Wettin, from Conrad I in 1127 to King George I in the early 20th century, accompanied by soldiers, artists, and scholars. Originally painted between 1871 and 1876 to celebrate 800 years of the dynasty, it was replaced between 1904 and 1907 by approximately 23,000 Meissen porcelain tiles to withstand the weather—it's the world's largest porcelain artwork. Despite the 1945 bombings, only 200 tiles had to be replaced during restoration.

The Frauenkirche, standing on the Neumarkt, is the symbol of Dresden's resurrection. Built between 1726 and 1743 by municipal architect Georg Bähr, the church has a 96-meter stone dome—the largest north of the Alps—which withstood Prussian cannonballs in 1760 as they bounced off it. The church collapsed, however, on February 15, 1945, two days after the Allied bombings, from the accumulated heat in the sandstone. The ruins remained a memorial for 45 years under the GDR.
