Reconstruction, financed by donations from around the world, lasted from 1994 to 2005: 3,643 original stones blackened by fire were reintegrated into the new edifice, identifiable by their dark color among the light blocks. The golden cross at the top was donated by British donors, including the son of one of the pilots who had bombed the city.

The Neustadt, on the right bank of the Elbe, is Dresden's artistic quarter—it survived the 1945 bombings better than the Altstadt, and its Art Nouveau streets from the early 20th century have kept their character. The Kunsthofpassage, a series of five interconnected courtyards, is the best-known example of this creativity: each courtyard was entrusted to different artists. The most famous is the Court of Elements, whose blue facade is covered with gutters shaped like trumpets and funnels that transform rain into music.

The Brühlsche Terrasse, nicknamed "the balcony of Europe" by Goethe, is a 500-meter elevated promenade along the Elbe above the old ramparts. Developed in the 18th century on medieval fortifications by Count Brühl, it offers the classic view of the Altstadt silhouette with its domes and steeples. It's from this terrace that Romantic painters—notably Canaletto and Caspar David Friedrich—immortalized Dresden's panorama.

The Albertinum houses the Gallery of New Masters, covering painting and sculpture from the 19th century to the present. The collection includes works by Caspar David Friedrich, including Two Men Contemplating the Moon, as well as Impressionist and Expressionist paintings. The building itself, a 19th-century neo-Renaissance arsenal, was flooded during the 2002 Elbe floods—the works had to be urgently carried to upper floors to be saved.

activities.text: Walk or electric scooter ride along the Elbe to admire Dresden's reconstructed skyline
Observation platform at the Frauenkirche for views over the city

Ascent to the Frauenkirche observation gallery for a panoramic view of Dresden's rooftops, the Elbe, and surrounding hills. Access is via an interior staircase to the dome lantern, 67 meters above ground.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea

visits.text: Locals call it “das kleine Meer”: the Dümmer See, Lower Saxony's second-largest lake at 12.5 km², is so shallow that the average depth is 1.2 meters. Common cranes and greylag geese stop here by the thousands in autumn. Bike loop around the lake: 27 km.

activities.text: Rent a bike and circle the lake on the marked cycle path. The east side of the Dümmer offers free-access sandy beaches, ideal for a swimming break. About 90 minutes of leisurely pedaling.

If you come in autumn, bring binoculars: the Dümmer is a wetland of international importance. Observation towers are scattered around the lake. The Naturschutzstation on the west side organizes guided tours.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Greenery is gaining ground at Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord, but the blast furnaces remain in place. This former steelworks now offers walking routes and sports, even within its old industrial facilities. Follow the interpretive trail to understand the facilities rather than simply photograph them; park admission is free, and you should wear shoes suitable for uneven ground.

activities.text: Walk along the quays of Innenhafen Duisburg to see another example of industrial redevelopment. Around the harbor basin, former warehouses stand alongside contemporary buildings; Garten der Erinnerung even preserves fragments of buildings that have disappeared. Stay on the public walkways and keep this loop short before driving to Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

visits.text: Düsseldorf's Altstadt is nicknamed "the longest bar in the world" due to its concentration of pubs and breweries in less than half a square kilometer. Beyond the festive reputation, the quarter preserves notable medieval remnants: St. Lambert's Basilica with its crooked spire (deformed by 14th-century drought according to legend), the 13th-century Schlossturm, the last tower of the princely castle destroyed by fire in 1872 and now a navigation museum, and the Rhine promenade laid out in 1993 when the former main road was buried in a tunnel.

The Königsallee, known as the "Kö," owes its name to an 1848 incident: King Frederick William IV, passing in a carriage on what was then called Kastanienallee, was pelted with horse manure by angry citizens. To smooth over the scandal, the city renamed the avenue "Königsallee" in 1851. Stretching 800 meters and bordered by a 30-meter-wide canal, it's one of Germany's widest avenues and has been a premier shopping street since the late 19th century.

The MedienHafen demonstrates that architectural conversion can be an attraction in itself. This former freight port decommissioned in the 1980s was converted starting in the 1990s with a simple rule: each new building had to dialogue with the harbor's history. Frank Gehry's Neuer Zollhof (1998) is the centerpiece—three buildings with undulating forms and distinct skins (white plaster, brushed steel, brick) that some interpret as a father-mother-child family. The neighboring Rheinturm rises to 240 meters and houses the world's largest decimal clock on its shaft.

activities.text: Stroll along the Rheinuferpromenade, 1.5 km of landscaped quays between Burgplatz and the MedienHafen. The promenade follows the Rhine with views of Oberkassel and its Art Nouveau façades on the opposite bank. In late afternoon, locals gather here for Altbier, the bitter brown beer typical of Düsseldorf.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea

activities.text: More colorful than moving, and all the more valuable for it, the East Side Gallery stretches for 1,316 m along the Spree, painted in spring 1990 by 118 artists from 21 countries. Dmitri Vrubel’s kiss between Brezhnev and Honecker draws every camera; the paintings were redone in 2009. Walk from Ostbahnhof toward the Oberbaumbrücke, staying on the Mühlenstraße sidewalk.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Slate roofs and stone ramparts: Eberbach’s towers add character to a short walk through town. Pulverturm, Haspelturm, Rosenturm, and Blauer Hut mark the old town walls; the last takes its name from its dark roof. Focus on their shapes rather than looking for four interiors to visit. Pick up a route map at the tourist office.

The Museum der Stadt Eberbach provides the context the facades cannot. Its collections trace the history of the town and its residents in the historic center. It is a useful alternative to a long walk if rain sets in. Check opening hours before parking, and choose a few rooms rather than trying to see everything.

activities.text: Follow Eberbach’s Flusspromenade to the flood markers near the ramparts. The route follows the Neckar and reaches the area around Blauer Hut: the inscriptions are a reminder that the river is more than scenery. Keep this walk short if you have already followed the tower route, and keep the shared sections clear for others.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: The calm waters of the Finow Canal contrast with its industrial past. In Eberswalde, this waterway connected the Havel and Oder basins long before the large boat lifts. The banks let you appreciate its scale without traveling the entire canal. Start near the town center to keep this first stop short.

activities.text: Follow the Finow Canal to the Eberswalde Town Lock to watch boats move between water levels. This lock is one of the canal’s historic structures: here, you can understand the mechanism from the bank. Stay on public paths and keep maneuvering areas clear; whether a boat passes through depends on traffic.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeastern Brandenburg: Abbey, Forest, and Lakes in 3 Days

visits.text: The smell of smoke and salt announces Eckernförde well before you reach the harbour: the town has been smoking sprats and eels in wood-fired kilns since the 19th century. The Alte Fischräucherei Eckernförde museum traces this craft. At the harbour, a few artisan smokers still sell directly at the quayside.

St. Nicolaikirche, plain and Gothic, surprises with the quality of its interior woodwork — 17th-century altars and pews inside a building raised in the 13th century. 200 metres from the harbour, usually empty, free entry.

activities.text: Buy smoked sprats directly from fishermen on the quay in the morning — Eckernförder Sprotten, smoked and marinated in vinegar, are the local speciality. On the first Sunday of the month, the fish market sets up along the harbour promenade.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: If you dream of Italy without leaving the Palatinate, Villa Ludwigshöhe will give you that illusion: Ludwig I of Bavaria wanted it built in the region’s mildest climate and had it constructed between 1846 and 1852 to designs by Friedrich von Gärtner. Restored from 2019 to 2025, it features parquet floors made of fine woods and Pompeian-style murals. Open Wednesday through Sunday, €6; French audio guide available for €1.

activities.text: Take the two-seat chairlift from the villa up to Rietburg: an eight-minute ride with an elevation gain of about 220 m brings you to the ruins of a castle built between 1200 and 1204 and destroyed during the Thirty Years’ War. From the top, the view stretches across the vineyards and the Rhine Plain to the Odenwald and, on clear days, the Black Forest; a fallow deer enclosure also awaits you at the summit. A round-trip ride on the Rietburgbahn costs €8.50.

days_plan.itin_title: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen

visits.text: Waldeck Castle is worth the trip for the view, not the furniture. Perched 120 meters above the Edersee, this 12th-century castle served as a prison until 1868. The “Hinter Schloss und Riegel” museum stages torture instruments and cells. The restaurant terrace offers the most complete panorama of the lake and dam.

Like the Möhnetalsperre, the Edersee dam wall was bombed by the RAF in May 1943 (Operation Chastise). The dam was rebuilt in four months. The Sperrmauer Museum at Hemfurth documents the attack. In the evening, a light installation illuminates the stone façade.

activities.text: Take the Waldecker Bergbahn, a 1961 cable car linking the lake shore to the castle in a few minutes. The ride is short and without adrenaline, but the vintage mechanics have a quaint charm. Down below, swimming or kayaking on the Edersee.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: Feel a shiver of vertigo as you peer into the well at Willibaldsburg: it plunges 76.5 meters. The castle of Eichstätt’s prince-bishops houses the Jura-Museum, with an original Archaeopteryx fossil and the only known specimen of the dinosaur Juravenator. Then climb the tower for the view and stroll through the Bastionsgarten, open from mid-April to mid-October; from October through March, the castle’s opening hours are reduced to 10 a.m.–4 p.m.

Behind its Baroque facade, Eichstätt Cathedral conceals a limestone altarpiece approximately 11 meters tall, the Pappenheimer Altar, donated in 1489 by a canon who had returned safely from the Holy Land. Then visit the Mortuarium, a Gothic funerary hall with a twisted column. Admission is free, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., outside service times.

Eichstätt’s most beautiful setting is arguably the Residenzplatz, lined with Rococo facades. At its center, the Mariensäule and its fountain were added between 1776 and 1780 under the direction of Maurizio Pedetti. Take time to walk around the square: fifteen minutes is enough before heading to the Hofgarten.

You’ll finish your visit to Eichstätt at the Hofgarten, the court garden begun in 1735 alongside the Sommerresidenz. In the 19th century, part of the Baroque layout gave way to an English landscape garden; the summer palace now houses the university administration. Save ten minutes to sit on a bench before taking the road through the Altmühltal.

days_plan.itin_title: Altmühltal and the Danube in 4 Days, from Ingolstadt to Regensburg

activities.text: There’s no ocean or beach, yet surfers wait their turn on Prinzregentenstraße: the Eisbachwelle, a standing wave on the Eisbach, forms at the southern edge of the Englischer Garten, near the Haus der Kunst. The city reopened it for surfing on May 8, 2026, for experienced surfers only, with leashes required and no surfing after 10 p.m. Watch from the bridge, stay well away from the banks, and leave your bike farther away: the passage is narrow.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: There is no better place to begin this trip than Wartburg Castle: the first German castle inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, in 1999, it brings together Luther and Saint Elizabeth on a single rocky spur. In the Lutherstube, Martin Luther, hiding under the name Junker Jörg, translated the New Testament in about eleven weeks; the mosaics in the Elisabeth-Kemenate, however, date only to 1902–1906. Arrive at opening time: the Palas can be visited on a guided tour, and the climb from the parking lot is steep.

According to tradition, the young Luther stayed with the Cotta family between 1498 and 1501 in what is now Eisenach’s Lutherhaus, one of Thuringia’s oldest half-timbered houses. The exhibition “Luther und die Bibel” traces his translation across three floors, followed by a room exploring a darker subject: the church-run “Entjudungsinstitut” of 1939–1945, whose members exploited his anti-Jewish statements. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes, and avoid Mondays, when it is closed.

Stop at the Georgenkirche on Eisenach’s Markt: Johann Sebastian Bach was baptized here in 1685, and Luther preached here on May 2, 1521, while fleeing his pursuers. From 1665 to 1797, four members of the Bach family served here in succession as organists. On your way out, look at the gilded Saint George fountain, designed in 1549, then the Baroque facade of the Stadtschloss on the same square.

Bach’s birthplace? There is no proof, yet Eisenach’s Bachhaus became the world’s first Bach museum in 1907. Every hour, short concerts bring the collection’s historical instruments to life, including two organs built around 1650 and around 1750. Save it for late afternoon, since it is open daily until 6 p.m.; a combined Bach–Luther ticket also covers the Lutherhaus.

activities.text: Water trickles beneath the walkways, and moss-covered walls close in: at its narrowest point, the Drachenschlucht leaves a passage just 68 centimeters wide. This gorge, about 3 kilometers long and south of Eisenach, has been protected as a geological natural monument since 1977, along with the neighboring Landgrafenschlucht. Hike up to Hohe Sonne and take the bus back down; strollers and bicycles are prohibited.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature
Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach

visits.text: The Kurfürstliche Burg often flies under the radar, overshadowed by the castles of the Romantic Rhine - wrongly so. Built in the 14th century on the ruins of a fortress destroyed in 1301, it served for 150 years as the residence of the Archbishops of Mainz. The Gutenberg Museum at the top of the tower recalls that the printing press inventor lived here in 1465. Admission: €3.50 adult. Note: the east flank is under renovation in 2026.

If you visit in June, the rose gardens of the Kurfürstliche Burg alone justify the detour. This flowering garden earned Eltville the title of Rosenstadt in 1988. Climb the 123 steps in the Burgturm for views across the Rheingau and Rhine as far as the Rhine plain.

activities.text: Walk down to the Rhine quays along Eltville's car-free promenade. The Rheingau vineyards begin immediately behind the town - the tourist office offers guided walks through the vines with tastings at local wineries. Reservations at +49 6123 9098-0.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Discover Emden, a historic seaport and sailing paradise on the North Sea coast. This maritime city at the mouth of the Ems River has been a center of seafaring for centuries, offering excellent conditions for sailing enthusiasts and water sports. The harbor atmosphere, maritime museums, and Dutch-influenced architecture reflect its rich trading heritage.

activities.text: Set sail from Emden's harbor to explore the stunning East Frisian coastline and nearby islands. The protected waters and steady North Sea breezes create ideal sailing conditions for both beginners and experienced sailors, with opportunities to spot seals and seabirds along the way.

Explore the unique East Frisian culture with its distinctive language, tea traditions, and windmill-dotted landscape. The flat polder lands stretching to the horizon offer superb cycling routes along historic dikes and through charming villages where time seems to stand still.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands

visits.text: Erfurt's St. Mary's Cathedral dominates Domplatz from a raised terrace, flanked by the collegiate Church of St. Severus—together forming one of Central Europe's most impressive religious architectural ensembles. The current cathedral was begun around 1280 with a vast Gothic choir. Its glory is the Gloriosa: cast in 1497, it's the world's largest free-swinging medieval bell. It's rung only on major occasions to protect the structure. The cathedral also houses the “Wolfram,” a 12th-century bronze candelabrum, and Gothic stained glass in the choir.

Fischmarkt is Erfurt's central square, surrounded by Renaissance merchants' houses, some dating from the 16th century. The neo-Gothic town hall, built 1870-1874, overlooks the square with its murals of local legends. Erfurt miraculously survived World War II bombing, explaining the density of its historic fabric - the city is often called «the preserved medieval metropolis».

The Krämerbrücke—“grocers' bridge”—is Central Europe's longest inhabited bridge: 120 meters long, with 32 half-timbered houses built directly on its structure. First mentioned in 1156, its current stone form dates from the 14th century. It recalls Florence's Ponte Vecchio or Venice's Rialto, except that its houses are inhabited and occupied by shops even today.

Erfurt's Old Synagogue, built around 1094, is Central Europe's best-preserved medieval synagogue. Its walls remained intact because after the pogrom of March 21, 1349—when about 900 of the city's Jews were massacred—it was converted into a warehouse and fell into oblivion, which protected it during Kristallnacht. The synagogue, mikveh, and Stone House complex has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023. In the cellar, the Erfurt Treasure—discovered in 1998 in the wall of a neighboring cellar—has been permanently displayed since 2009: 3,141 silver coins, 14 ingots, and more than 700 pieces of 14th-century Gothic goldsmiths' work. The centerpiece is a gold ring adorned with a miniature temple bearing the Hebrew inscription “mazal tov.” The treasure was exhibited at the Musée de Cluny in Paris and the Metropolitan Museum in New York before joining the permanent collection.

activities.text: A visit to Erfurt's medieval Jewish treasure in the Old Synagogue's cellar. Looking through the Gothic goldsmiths' work—gem-studded brooches, gold rings, ceremonial tableware—gives a sense of Erfurt's Jewish community at its height, before its annihilation in 1349.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

places.name: Essen

visits.text: Zollverein’s steel structures spread out like a city within a city. In Essen, this mining complex and its coking plant form a World Heritage Site whose outdoor areas are accessible free of charge. Focus your route on the headframe and the coking plant facilities; pick up a map at the visitor center to avoid unnecessary detours.

Leave time for Villa Hügel: its contrast with Zollverein sheds light on industrial society. This Krupp family residence features reception rooms and a historical exhibition amid park grounds. Check the online calendar, which lists occasional closures of the Main Building; the villa is closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

map_keywords: UNESCO World Heritage Site Zollverein Essen

visits.text: You’ll climb the keep at Burgruine Randeck to see the Altmühltal spread out below you. The ruined castle, probably dating from the 11th century, was partially rebuilt in 1842 at the initiative of Crown Prince Maximilian; its keep, approximately 36 meters tall, now serves as an observation tower. Open from April through October for a small admission fee.

activities.text: The residents of Essing named it Tatzlwurm, after an Alpine monster that is half serpent, half feline, because of its undulating shape. Nearly 190 meters long, this wooden footbridge has spanned the Main–Danube Canal since 1986. Cross it, then return via the old wooden bridge and its Gothic gateway.

days_plan.itin_title: Altmühltal and the Danube in 4 Days, from Ingolstadt to Regensburg

visits.text: Wander through Esslingen's remarkably preserved medieval old town, home to some of Germany's finest half-timbered buildings clustered in atmospheric lanes. The town center features extraordinarily large and beautifully decorated timber-frame houses that survived centuries of war and development pressures. This architectural treasure trove just southeast of Stuttgart rewards visitors who venture beyond the capital.

Admire the historic Altes Rathaus (Old Town Hall) and the twin-spired Stadtkirche that dominate the market square, both masterpieces of medieval civic architecture. The town's wine-growing tradition continues on the steep vineyard slopes that surround the old town, producing excellent local varieties. Canal waterways threading through the center add to Esslingen's picturesque charm.

Visit during Christmas market season to experience one of Germany's most magical medieval markets. The market transforms the old town into a fairy-tale setting with medieval children's rides, torch-lit streets and the unique spectacle of betting on mice running into small numbered wooden houses. Flaming braziers and costumed performers create an authentically medieval atmosphere unlike any other Christmas market.

activities.text: Climb to the castle ruins above town for panoramic views over the half-timbered rooftops and vineyards

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: The carillon at Esslingen’s Altes Rathaus has chimed several times a day since 1926, beneath an astronomical clock that retains its original mechanism. Built around 1420 as a merchants’ hall and tax office, the building gained its Renaissance facade, designed by Heinrich Schickhardt, between 1586 and 1589, while its south side displays exposed timber framing. Steps away, houses 4 through 10 on Hafenmarkt date from 1328 to 1331. Walk around the building: its two facades tell the stories of two eras.

Next, climb to the Burg via the stairs and Burgsteige, among the vineyards. Despite its name, Esslingen’s Burg is not a castle but a section of the medieval fortifications, with the Dicker Turm dating from 1525 and the Hochwacht, an 18th-century watchtower. The Seilergang wall walk overlooks the old town’s rooftops and the Neckar Valley. Allow 45 minutes for the round trip and wear closed-toe shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Mystical or geological, the Externsteine have fascinated people for as long as they have passed this way. These thirteen sandstone pillars rise 40 metres above a pond in the Wiembecke valley, and a Romanesque bas-relief of the Descent from the Cross is carved directly into the rock — first documented in 1129. Installed stairways and a panoramic platform at the summit.

A Romanesque bas-relief of the Descent from the Cross, carved between 1115 and 1130 into the Externsteine sandstone, depicts Christ at life size: it is one of the rare examples of outdoor Romanesque sculpture still in place in Germany. The interpretation of the site — a Germanic place of worship, a Christian pilgrimage site or both — remains a matter of debate among historians.

activities.text: Arrive early in the morning — crowds are significant around midday and in the afternoon at this busy site. The circular one-hour hike around the rocks offers the best viewing angles. Climbing ticket €5 for adults, €2.50 for children aged 6 to 17.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: A 36-second elevator ride takes you to the observation deck at 150 m: inaugurated in February 1956, Stuttgart’s Fernsehturm was the first reinforced-concrete television tower. Fritz Leonhardt had persuaded the broadcaster to replace a simple steel mast with a tower featuring a café and observation decks. On clear days, the view stretches to the Swabian Jura you explored earlier in the day. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with the last ascent half an hour before closing; admission is €12.50. Take U7, U8, or U15 to Ruhbank (Fernsehturm).

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Flensburg has been importing rum from the Danish West Indies since 1755, when the city's merchants supplied Saint Croix, Saint Thomas and Saint John. Of the era's 200 rum houses, two active distilleries remain: Johannsen and Braasch. The Rum Museum inside the Schifffahrtsmuseum traces this colonial trade that most Germans know nothing about.

The Museumshafen with its old sailing vessels is worth visiting even without a festival: the traditional wooden boats moored along the stone quay are accessible on certain days. The former West Indies warehouse stands directly on the basin.

In the inner courtyards of the Norderstrasse, hints of molasses and tobacco seep from the old warehouses. The Kaufmannshöfe — merchants' courtyards — conceal secret gardens behind gates that are often left open. The Marienburg is the best known.

activities.text: Follow the Rum & Zucker Meile from the Nordertor to the harbour: this marked trail links the old warehouses, merchants' courtyards and the two last active distilleries. Tastings are offered at Johannsen Rum — let them know in advance.
The Südermarkt market offers fruit, vegetables, Danish cheeses and smoked fish. Flensburg is officially bilingual in German and Danish — both languages can be heard at the stalls.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Between 1938 and 1945, the SS detained around 100,000 people at Flossenbürg concentration camp and exploited them in the granite quarries. At least 30,000 died there. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was executed here in April 1945. The memorial, one of Europe's most modern memorial sites, is free and open daily.

If you then climb to the Schlossberg, the castle ruin at 732 m offers a striking contrast: a peaceful view over the verdant Upper Palatinate. The ruin is accessible year-round. Seeing the two sites, just a few hundred meters apart, leaves a lasting impression.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: The Römerberg has been Frankfurt's historic heart since the Early Middle Ages. At the center of the square stands the Fountain of Justice (Gerechtigkeitsbrunnen) with its goddess Justitia, and on the west side, the Römer—a town hall with three stepped gables that has served as the seat of city administration since 1405. Inside, the Kaisersaal (Emperors' Hall) preserves portraits of all 52 emperors of the Holy Roman Empire, from Charlemagne to Francis II. This is where coronation banquets were held after the ceremony in the nearby cathedral. From the Golden Bull of 1356 until 1792, the Römer was the site of imperial elections. The hall and inner courtyard are freely accessible.

Continue to the Kaiserdom (St. Bartholomew's Cathedral), whose red Gothic tower rises 95 meters. Consecrated in 1239, it was officially designated the coronation site for Holy Roman Emperors in 1356—ten ceremonies took place here between 1562 and 1792. The current building is a postwar reconstruction, but the cathedral treasury preserves authentic pieces, including a Gothic priestly vestment dated to 1350. Climb the 324 steps of the tower for panoramic views over Frankfurt's rooftops.

Just steps away, the Paulskirche (St. Paul's Church) deserves a stop. In 1848, it served as the seat of Germany's first freely elected National Assembly—the founding event of modern German parliamentarism. It was one of the first buildings reconstructed after the war, a testament to its symbolic importance. The austere interior now hosts exhibitions and official ceremonies.

Cross the Eiserner Steg, an iron footbridge built in 1869 over the Main River, to reach Sachsenhausen on the south bank. From the bridge, the view brings the Römerberg's half-timbered houses, Gothic towers, and the financial district's skyscrapers in the background into alignment, capturing the paradox of Frankfurt—nicknamed “Mainhattan” for this coexistence of medieval and modern. Water levels engraved in the pillars recall the great historic floods.

The Alt-Sachsenhausen quarter preserves its cobbled lanes and half-timbered houses. The city's cider taverns are concentrated here: Apfelwein (or Ebbelwoi in the local dialect) is served from blue stoneware pitchers in diamond-shaped glasses. Wander the alleys around Frankensteiner Platz before heading to the Museumsufer along the waterfront.

The Städel Museum, founded in 1815 by banker Johann Friedrich Städel as Germany's first civic museum foundation, is the crown jewel of the Museumsufer. Its collection spans 700 years of European art: 3,100 paintings, 660 sculptures, and over 100,000 drawings and prints. In 1937, the Nazis confiscated 77 paintings and 700 prints deemed 'degenerate'—the remaining works were evacuated to Bavaria to protect them from bombing. The museum preserves masterpieces by Dürer, Botticelli, Cranach, Rembrandt, Vermeer, Monet, and Picasso. The underground extension inaugurated in 2012, lit by circular skylights at surface level, houses contemporary art.

Head back toward the center to reach the Main Tower, one of the few Frankfurt skyscrapers with a public viewing platform on the 55th floor, at a height of 200 meters. On clear days, views extend to the Taunus to the north and the Odenwald to the south. From here you can best appreciate the “Mainhattan” skyline: 39 glass and steel towers forming continental Europe's densest financial district.

The Palmengarten (botanical garden), open since 1871, is one of Germany's largest, with 13 hectares of greenhouses and themed gardens. The tropical greenhouses house rare species from the Amazon, Africa, and Asia. It's a place to take a breather, popular with families and people out for a walk.

Finish with a stroll along the Museumsufer, the museum boulevard that lines the south bank of the Main for about 2 km. Over thirty museums cluster here—the film museum, architecture museum, Jewish museum, and communications museum. On the last weekend of August each year, the Museumsufer Festival transforms this boulevard into one of Europe's largest outdoor cultural events.

activities.text: Walking tour through the Altstadt: Römerberg → Kaiserdom → Paulskirche → Goethe House (Großer Hirschgraben 23). The writer's birthplace, destroyed during the war, has been reconstructed exactly as it was, with the original furniture and objects. You can see, among other rooms, the study where Goethe wrote The Sorrows of Young Werther at age 23.

One-hour panoramic cruise on the Main departing from the Museumsufer landing stages. The route passes the quay's 39 museums, goes under the Eiserner Steg, and offers a comprehensive view of the city from the river.

Apfelwein tasting in a traditional Sachsenhausen tavern. The local apple cider is served in stoneware pitchers in a glass called Geripptes (ribbed). The tradition of cider taverns in this quarter dates to the 18th century.

visits.text: Fragile in your hand, glass becomes a strong thread through history at Glasmuseum Frauenau. The exhibits trace its artistic and everyday uses from antiquity to contemporary creations. The collections also include works by Daum and Gallé: a detour through Lorraine in the heart of Bavaria. Check which days it is open; the museum is usually closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Continue your visit in Frauenau’s Gläserne Gärten, where glass leaves the display cases behind. The sculptures around the museum extend toward the Moosau workshops and Eisch glassworks. Outdoor light changes how you perceive their forms and colors. Start in the museum area, then continue toward Eisch glassworks if time allows.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavarian Forest in 4 Days: From Passau to the Großer Arber

visits.text: The freestanding octagonal bell tower of the Münster on Fraueninsel, topped with a Baroque onion dome in 1626, is a landmark throughout the Chiemgau. Frauenwörth Benedictine Abbey, founded in the 8th century by Duke Tassilo III, is still home to a community of nuns: pass beneath the Carolingian Torhalle before entering the church, where the chapel of Blessed Irmengard, an abbess who died in 866, draws couples hoping for a child. Be discreet; the convent is still very much in use.

activities.text: Water lapping against the fishermen’s docks accompanies the entire walk: explore Fraueninsel on foot along a waterfront path of approximately 1.4 km. Around 200 residents live on these 15.5 hectares, and six families still earn their living from fishing. Try fish from Lake Chiemsee at an island inn, then stop at the monastery shop for its handmade marzipan: the convent has also been distilling spirits since at least 1470.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: The Fraueninsel is a fishing village set on water, with a Benedictine convent active since the 8th century. You can walk around it in twenty minutes, between vegetable gardens, pottery workshops, and Tassilo's thousand-year-old linden tree. No cars, no noise.
The Abtei Frauenwörth sells its own Klosterlikör and marzipan in a small shop at the entrance. The Carolingian Torhalle, a 9th-century remnant, is the island's oldest building.

activities.text: Settle in at the Klosterwirt for a smoked Renke (whitefish), caught that morning in the Chiemsee. The terrace overlooks the lake and Herreninsel. One of the best combinations of quality and enjoyment on the whole trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: “Teufelstritt,” the devil’s footprint: this is what Munich locals first point out at the Frauenkirche, a footprint in the paving at the entrance. According to legend, the devil thought the church had no windows and stamped his foot while laughing; from this spot, no windows were visible between 1620 and 1858. The two towers, nearly 99 m tall, received their onion domes around 1525. The south tower is open to visitors: after about 90 steps, an elevator takes you up to 80 m, with tickets sold only on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: By around 1225, the Goldene Pforte already adorned the Romanesque basilica that preceded Freiberg Cathedral, and this sculpted portal has been preserved. Inside, the Tulpenkanzel, a tulip-shaped pulpit dating to around 1505, and Gottfried Silbermann’s great organ, completed in 1714 with 2,574 pipes, vie for attention. In the choir, 38 members of the House of Wettin were buried between 1541 and 1696. Choose a guided tour with organ music: Sundays at 11:30 a.m., or Wednesdays at 2 p.m. from May through October.

Even if geology is not your passion, terra mineralia at Schloss Freudenstein is well worth 2 hours of your time. More than 3,500 minerals, gemstones, and meteorites from five continents fill 1,500 m² across three levels, an area equivalent to nearly six tennis courts. They come from the collection of Erika Pohl-Ströher, a member of the family that founded Wella. Save the treasure chamber, beneath a historic vault, for last. The exhibition is closed on Mondays; arrive at least 1 hour before closing.

Next, head to the Obermarkt, Freiberg’s civic heart. The Rathaus, begun in 1410, sounds a Meissen porcelain carillon, while a stone in the pavement marks the spot where Kunz von Kauffungen was executed in 1455. In the center, a statue of the city’s founder towers over a fountain where four lions bearing the arms of Meissen spout water. Return in December if you can: the Christmas market takes over the square then.

If your descent underground has made you want to understand the city, set aside 45 minutes for the Stadt- und Bergbaumuseum at Am Dom 1 on the Untermarkt. The museum is reopening in stages: since March 27, 2026, its second floor has explored mining-inspired art, Freiberg in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the Knappschaft, the miners’ guild. The “Licht im Schacht” exhibition runs there through February 2, 2027. The museum is open Wednesday through Monday, and admission is free for visitors age 16 and under.

activities.text: Ten degrees year-round, with a hard hat firmly on your head: at Silberbergwerk Freiberg, the Reiche Zeche mine cage takes you 150 meters underground. It all began in 1168 with the discovery of silver near Christiansdorf. Led by volunteers, the GrubenTour traces mining activity from the Middle Ages to the present in a mine where students and researchers from the TU Bergakademie, founded in 1765, still work.

days_plan.itin_title: The Ore Mountains in 3 Days: Mines, Toys, and Fichtelberg

visits.text: In 1970, a fall on the Heini-Klopfer-Skiflugschanze became the very image of “the agony of defeat” for an American sports show. This ski flying jump has a 70 m inrun tower, now served by an accessible inclined elevator. Head up to the platform for sweeping views of the Stillachtal, and aim for Thursday at 2 p.m. for the public guided tour.

activities.text: The Freibergsee sits at 930 m, and measurements taken in 1938 even ranked it warmer than every other Bavarian lake. Its 18 hectares offer a designated swimming area, a beach café, and rowboat rentals, just a few minutes from the ski jump. Walk here from the Skiflugschanze: no bus travels up the access road.

days_plan.itin_title: Oberstdorf in 3 Days: Lakes, Gorges, and Kleinwalsertal

visits.text: Three centuries of construction, and a cathedral that leans slightly but remains standing. Freiburg Minster took more than 300 years to complete. What really catches the eye are the gargoyles on the south façade, including one famous for its scatological pose - supposedly the revenge of an unpaid sculptor. The tower is 116 m high and reached by climbing 335 steps. Closed to visitors during Sunday morning services.

Here, the Minster's gargoyles look you straight in the eye - the sandstone originals, rather than the copies displayed outdoors, are installed in the nave of the former Augustinian monastery at a height of almost 12 m. The Augustinermuseum fully reopened in February 2026 after 22 years of renovation work. The medieval sculpture gallery is the highlight. Check admission prices and opening hours at museen.freiburg.de; closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Is the channel that makes you marry someone from Freiburg kitschy? Perhaps – but the legend is told with all the seriousness of a local truth. The Bächle are medieval irrigation channels running through the pedestrian streets. Follow Konviktstraße to see the half-timbered houses, then stop at Hausbrauerei Feierling (Gerberau 46) for a beer brewed on the premises. The terrace overlooks the rooftops. Reservations are not accepted.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: The photo is everywhere on Instagram, but nothing prepares you for the real visual shock. Freudenberg's Alter Flecken lines up over 80 black-and-white half-timbered houses, rebuilt after the 1666 fire following the 1540 plan. Climb to the Kurpark for the full panorama. Designated a monument of international significance by the State.

Locals simply call their quarter the “Flecken.” The 4fachwerk museum on Mittelstraße displays local clockmaking crafts in two restored half-timbered houses. Open Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday 2pm-5pm. Free admission.

activities.text: Walk the Fachwerkweg, a 12-km loop around Freudenberg. The trail passes through the Hohenhain tunnel (former railway), the wooded Gambachtal valley, and offers several viewpoints over the black-and-white ensemble. Allow three hours at a good pace.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: Drive the legendary Black Forest High Road (Schwarzwaldhochstraße) from Baden-Baden to Freudenstadt, one of Germany's most scenic mountain routes. This spectacular drive takes you along the peaks of the Black Forest, with incredible views plunging down into forested valleys at every bend. Numerous viewpoints and trailheads invite you to stop, breathe the pine-scented air and absorb the magnificent panoramas.

Stop at the Mummelsee, a mystical glacial lake surrounded by dark fir forests and shrouded in local legends about water spirits and lake nymphs. Allow for a round trip within a day from Freudenstadt, followed by an uphill walk to the viewing platform on the Hornisgrinde, the highest peak in the northern Black Forest, which rewards visitors with 360-degree views extending to the Vosges mountains in France. Several hiking trails of varying difficulty lead from the road through unspoiled forest landscapes.

Arrive in Freudenstadt, home to Germany's largest market square, a vast open space surrounded by arcaded houses that give the town a distinctly Mediterranean feel. This planned Renaissance town was founded in 1599 and rebuilt after World War II damage with remarkable attention to its historic character. The unique L-shaped Protestant church and covered shopping arcades make it a pleasant base for Black Forest exploration.

activities.text: Stop for short hikes along the route to experience the Black Forest's pristine nature up close

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: Schloss Neuenburg has watched over Freyburg since the 1090s, when Louis the Jumper had it built; it was once five times the size of the Wartburg. Its double chapel dates to around 1180, and the Dicker Wilhelm keep, begun in 1150, has served as a lookout since 1991. Allow 30 minutes to walk from the center; the museum opens at 10 a.m., except on Mondays.

activities.text: A lawsuit lost to a champagne house gave the brand its name: sued in 1894 over its “Monopol” name, Rotkäppchen Sektkellerei, founded in 1856, adopted the name of its red bottle cap, registered in 1895. Its Domkeller, built in 1896, houses Germany’s largest wooden blending cask. Guided tours Wednesday through Sunday: €20 online, €25 at the ticket counter.

“Tuscany of the East”: that is the region’s nickname, and Freyburg’s Herzoglicher Weinberg shows why. Its six-sided Rococo vineyard house, built around 1774, overlooks the terraces; the Schweigenberg has some 90 vineyard cottages from the 18th century. Stroll here on the evening you arrive, then taste a wine from the Winzervereinigung Freyburg, which brings together more than 300 winegrowers.

days_plan.itin_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra

visits.text: An airship four times larger than an Airbus, yet lighter than air: the Zeppelin Museum in Friedrichshafen tells this engineering madness across 4,000 square meters. The Bauhaus building of the former Hafenbahnhof is a perfect setting. More than 1,500 pieces on display.

Step inside the life-size reconstruction of the LZ 129 Hindenburg passenger cabins: 33 meters long, original carpeting, Art Deco dining room. You understand why the wealthy of the 1930s paid a fortune to cross the Atlantic in three days.

You don't expect to find Otto Dix in a dirigible museum, and yet. The Zeppelin Museum's art collection brings together Baumeister, Ackermann, and other artists of the “inner migration,” refugees at Lake Constance during Nazism. An unexpected counterpoint.

activities.text: If your budget allows, you can still fly over the Bodensee in a Zeppelin NT: Deutsche Zeppelin-Reederei offers tours lasting 30 to 120 minutes from Friedrichshafen. It is expensive, but offers an aerial experience above the lake. Booking is required.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: It is hard to believe: Amsterdam has an enclave in Schleswig-Holstein. Friedrichstadt was founded in 1621 by Duke Friedrich III to receive Dutch settlers — Remonstrants fleeing religious persecution. They brought their bricks, their stepped gables and their canals. The town council minutes were written in Dutch until the 18th century.

Founded in 1621 by Duke Friedrich III of Schleswig-Gottorf, the planned town is laid out around the Mittelburggraben — the central canal — on a grid of perpendicular streets. The Gevelsteen, carved and painted stone reliefs above doorways, bear the coats of arms of the original Dutch families and some date back to the town's founding.

activities.text: Board a boat on the Mittelburggraben for a trip along Friedrichstadt's grachten. The gabled red brick houses are reflected in the water. An hour is enough for the main canals.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Light-colored stone, twin towers, and a broad forecourt: Fulda’s Dom St. Salvator immediately conveys the scale of the Baroque quarter. The cathedral houses the tomb of Saint Boniface, which explains its role as a pilgrimage destination as well as its architectural interest. Take time to appreciate the interior space before examining the decorative details. Check visiting hours and give priority to services, especially on Sundays.

A palace in the heart of town, rather than an isolated castle: Stadtschloss Fulda is within walking distance of the cathedral. Its historic rooms and collections of local porcelain tell the story of court life behind the façades of the Baroque quarter. The neighboring garden extends the visit without any additional travel. Check which areas are open to the public and decide which rooms to see before booking a guided tour.

The atmosphere in Fulda’s Altstadt changes as soon as you leave the sweeping vistas of the Baroque quarter. The historic center retains medieval buildings, shopping streets, and squares where you can admire the façades as you walk. This stroll ensures you experience more of Fulda than just two monuments. Follow a short loop between the old town and the palace quarter, leaving your car parked for the entire day.

To build on your cathedral visit without adding an excursion, Fulda’s Dommuseum is a fitting option. Its religious collections and the neighboring Domdechaneigarten complement the cathedral with artifacts and a more intimate setting. Choose this visit if you would rather explore religious heritage in greater depth than take more walks. Check the museum’s and garden’s own opening hours: you cannot infer them from those of the cathedral.

activities.text: Walk through Fulda’s Schlossgarten between the Stadtschloss and the Orangerie to slow down after the indoor visits. Vistas, flower beds, and water features structure this Baroque garden: it is more than a shortcut to the next monument. Save this walk for a break in the weather and choose a bench if you want to rest. Access to the garden does not automatically include the rooms inside the Orangerie.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhön and Fulda in 4 days: peaks and spa towns

visits.text: Who installs a dragon weighing 11 tonnes, 16 m long and 5 m tall in the middle of a Bavarian village? Furth im Wald. The Further Drache “Tradinno” is the world's largest four-legged walking robot (Guinness). It breathes fire and walks toward you. Not a toy: a feat of engineering blending Hollywood and German robotics.

In the Drachenhöhle, the floor trembles and red smoke rises: the museum tells the story of the Drachenstich, Germany's oldest folk play, documented since at least 1590. You also learn how the robot works. Admission + demonstration: €15 for adults, €10 for children.

activities.text: If you're there in August, the Drachenstich festival brings together 350 extras in medieval costume on the Stadtplatz. The dragon moves through the crowd breathing flames. Advance tickets at drachenstich.de.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: The clatter of the wheels in the ravine reaches you before the mill comes into view – you hear it before you see it. The Hexenlochmühle, built as a sawmill in 1825 and owned by the same family since 1839, is the only mill in the Black Forest with two waterwheels. It is still in operation. Local legend says that witches performed their rituals at night in this steep-sided valley. A terrace beside the Heubach. A decent restaurant and a shop selling regional schnapps to take away.

The Deutsches Uhrenmuseum in Furtwangen is closed for renovation. For an activity exploring clockmaking, head to its StattMuseum at Friedrichstraße 3: this temporary venue offers workshops for adults and activities for children. On Thursdays, you can join in without booking; on other days, contact the museum to arrange an appointment. Visit deutsches-uhrenmuseum.de to choose an activity before you set off.

activities.text: Take the damp trail and leave digital navigation behind: the Zweribach waterfall is an option for those seeking two hours of complete solitude. Ferns, mosses, no crowds on weekdays. From Furtwangen, allow for a return trip to reach the start of the hike in the St. Märgen area, followed by a two-hour walk there and back. Bring waterproof footwear: the trail follows a stream, with many slippery stretches after rain.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: Neuschwanstein Castle, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025, is Germany's most visited castle, with more than one million admissions a year. King Ludwig II of Bavaria, crowned in 1864 at the age of 18, commissioned its construction in 1869 on a rocky spur 200 meters high. He had 8 meters of rock blasted away to clear the foundations, and between 1879 and 1880 had some 465 tonnes of Salzburg marble and 400,000 bricks transported to the site. The project used the most modern technology of the era: central heating, running water on every floor, and a steel structure to support the throne room. Ludwig II lived there for only a few months in 1884 before being declared unfit to rule and dying mysteriously in Lake Starnberg on June 13, 1886. The castle was still unfinished—and would never be fully completed.

Walk up to the Marienbrücke, suspended 90 meters above the Pöllat Gorge and its 45-meter waterfall. This bridge, originally built in wood in the 1840s by Ludwig II's father as a birthday gift for Queen Marie, then reconstructed in iron in 1866, offers THE classic photo of Neuschwanstein: the castle stands out in its entirety against a backdrop of forests and Alpine peaks. This silhouette inspired Walt Disney for Sleeping Beauty's castle at the first Disneyland, opened in 1955 in California—it later became the Disney studios logo. The walk up from the Hohenschwangau parking lot takes about 40 minutes.

Hohenschwangau Castle, below Neuschwanstein, was the home where Ludwig II spent his childhood. His father, Maximilian II, had it restored in the neo-Gothic style from 1832 onwards. The rooms, richly decorated with tapestries depicting medieval legends—including that of Lohengrin, the Swan Knight—fired the future king's imagination from an early age. Seeing Wagner's opera Lohengrin in 1861, at the age of 15, was a revelation for Ludwig: the swan would become his emblem, appearing throughout Neuschwanstein. The castle overlooks the Alpsee, whose turquoise waters invite a stroll along the trail that circles the lake.

The Hohes Schloss (High Castle) in Füssen, the summer residence of the prince-bishops of Augsburg from the late 15th century onwards, is one of the largest and best-preserved Gothic castles in Swabia. Its trompe-l'oeil painted façades—false windows, false battlements, and false oriel windows—are unique in Germany and date from the reign of Bishop Friedrich von Zollern (1486–1505). The Rittersaal (Knights' Hall), with its carved coffered ceiling, is worth the climb. The Bavarian State Gallery, housed in the former reception rooms, displays late Gothic paintings and sculptures from the 15th and 16th centuries.

Below the castle, St. Magnus's Benedictine Monastery (Kloster St. Mang), founded in the 8th century and rebuilt in Baroque style between 1697 and 1726, houses one of Europe's finest collections of antique lutes and violins—Füssen is considered one of the cradles of European luthiery. The cultural heritage museum also presents Jakob Hiebeler's “Dance of Death” (1602), Bavaria's oldest mural representation of a danse macabre. The monastery's splendid Baroque halls offer a glimpse of the institution's former wealth.

Wander through Füssen's pedestrianized old town along Reichenstraße, lined with houses with painted façades and following the route of the ancient Via Claudia Augusta, the Roman road that connected Italy to Germania. The luthiers' fountain recalls the town's historic role in the manufacture of stringed instruments. On Schrannenplatz, the site of the former grain hall, historical parades enliven the town in summer. Perched at an altitude of 800 meters at the foot of the Alps, the town has more than 2,000 years of history—its colorful Baroque houses, narrow streets, and mountain views make it a spectacular end point for the Romantic Road.

activities.text: Walk the circuit around the Alpsee, a 5-kilometer trail hugging turquoise waters framed by conifer forests and the rocky faces of the Alps. The panorama of the two royal castles from the south shore is spectacular. The trail is flat and accessible, perfect for unwinding after visiting the castles.

Walk down to Lechfall, the Lech waterfall, 10 minutes from the center of Füssen. The Lech River, which rises in Austria, plunges into a narrow gorge here through a series of natural cascades. The bridge spanning the gorge offers spectacular views of the turquoise water and rocks sculpted by erosion.

Embark on a cruise on the Forggensee, Bavaria's fifth-largest lake by surface area. Boats operate from early June to mid-October and offer panoramas of Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau castles, Füssen's old town perched on its hill, and the surrounding Alpine peaks. Evening cruises at sunset are particularly recommended.

visits.text: If you visit between April 17 and November 8, 2026, finish at the Gärtner- und Häckermuseum, housed in a market gardener’s home dating to 1767 in the heart of the Gärtnerstadt, the gardeners’ district where crops have been grown within the city since the Middle Ages. Behind the house, the Sortengarten preserves around thirty traditional Bamberg crops, including licorice, across 400 m². The museum opens Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; outside the season, stroll along Mittelstraße between the plots, about a ten-minute walk from the train station.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Start with the Partnachklamm, a 700-meter gorge carved by the Partnach River, with walls rising up to 80 meters in places. Designated a natural monument as early as 1912, it's accessible via a path carved into the rock alongside the glacial torrent. In winter, the waterfalls transform into spectacular frozen cascades. Allow 25 minutes on foot from the Olympic stadium.

Then head back up to Partenkirchen's Ludwigstrasse for a stroll through the historic heart. Garmisch and Partenkirchen were two separate municipalities for centuries before being forcibly merged by Hitler in 1935, ahead of the 1936 Winter Olympics. Their character remains distinct: Garmisch is more modern, while Partenkirchen retains its houses with painted trompe-l'oeil facades, a Bavarian decorative style called Lüftlmalerei.

Spend the afternoon on the Zugspitze, Germany's highest point at 2,962 meters, on the Austrian border. In clear weather, the panorama stretches as far as Italy. A 90-year-old cogwheel train connects Garmisch to the glacial plateau at 2,600 meters, from where a 1,000-meter cable car ascends to the summit.

activities.text: Walk around Lake Eibsee, with its turquoise waters surrounded by limestone rocks and pine forests, at the foot of the Zugspitze. The complete loop is about 7 kilometers. In summer, rowboats can be rented on site.
