Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Forests & Medieval Towns
German Alpine Road: Lake Constance to Königssee

visits.text: Walk along Bernauer Straße: the Berlin Wall Memorial follows the former border strip for 1.4 km, with a 70 m section of the original Wall, its patrol road, and a watchtower. The Window of Remembrance brings together portraits of 130 people killed at the Wall, and the Chapel of Reconciliation replaces the church demolished with explosives in 1985 because it stood in the border zone. The outdoor exhibition is free and open daily from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Seen from above, the no man’s land comes into chilling focus. From the five-story observation tower at the Berlin Wall Memorial’s Documentation Center, you look down on the preserved border strip opposite; inside, the exhibition “1961 | 1989. The Berlin Wall” recalls how the border encircled West Berlin for 155 km. Admission is free, Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with the last ascent at 5:45 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Two blocs facing each other, just a few steps apart: Point Alpha brings the Cold War into focus near Geisa. The former American observation post and reconstructed border installations give a tangible sense of Germany’s division. Allow time outdoors as well as indoors. Check ticket details and which areas are accessible before you begin.

If you want to understand how the border affected everyday life, start at Point Alpha’s Haus auf der Grenze. The exhibitions explore Germany’s division and its consequences for residents, looking beyond military equipment. Check the language of the exhibit materials and the opening hours. Then allow some time for the nearby outdoor installations.

activities.text: Follow a short section of Point Alpha’s Weg der Hoffnung to connect the landscape with questions of remembrance. The sculptures stand in the former border zone and evoke resistance to communism. This route complements the exhibitions without requiring a long hike. Wear suitable shoes and keep the walk short to preserve your planned time in Tann.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhön and Fulda in 4 days: peaks and spa towns

visits.text: A well-planned short stop at Nordsternpark is better than an impromptu walk in front of barriers. In Gelsenkirchen, the former mining site is being redeveloped for IGA 2027, with Emscherinsel closed and several paths rerouted. Check the city’s map before coming and limit your visit to areas that are actually open, without planning to cross the island.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

visits.text: More than two years of construction, from October 2022 to March 2025, restored Gendarmenmarkt’s 14,000 m² of cobblestones, now fully wheelchair accessible. Laid out in 1688, the square features Schinkel’s Konzerthaus (1821) between two matching churches, the Französischer Dom and Deutscher Dom, whose domed towers date to 1785. Here, “Dom” refers to the dome, not a cathedral. Return toward the end of the day, when the square empties out.

activities.text: Climb to the Französischer Dom’s panoramic platform, 40 m above Gendarmenmarkt, for a 360° view of the historic center. The tower also houses the Huguenot Museum, recalling the French community that built the church between 1701 and 1705. Tickets cost €8, or €10 with an audio guide; access is by stairs only, Tuesday through Sunday.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: A half-timbered village, certainly. But behind the façades stands a Benedictine abbey founded by the wandering monk Pirmin around 725, which survived the wars along the Rhine, the Reformation, Louis XIV's troops in 1689 and secularisation in 1803. The Baroque church with its 1716 bell tower is still standing. The Marktplatz is worth a stop - 20 minutes is enough, then head for Offenburg, 10 km away.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: Gera is the birthplace of Otto Dix (1891-1969), one of the most important German painters of the 20th century. Born into a working-class family in the village of Untermhaus, he studied decorative arts in Dresden before leaving for war in 1914. His paintings of the Great War—The Trench, the War Cripples—are among the rawest and most disturbing visual testimonies of that conflict. In 1937, the Nazis confiscated 170 of his works as "degenerate art." The Otto Dix House and the Orangery of the Princes of Reuss, dedicated to him, house a selection of paintings and engravings including the famous Der Krieg (The War) series from 1924.

Gera's market square is one of Thuringia's most beautiful, with its Baroque town hall, whose mansard roof and entrance tower were built after the 1686 fire. The neighboring Church of the Savior (Salvatorkirche) is a Thuringian Baroque masterpiece with its frescoed ceiling and ornate galleries.

The Höhler are a network of vaulted cellars dug under the old town in the 17th and 18th centuries to store beer. Since the late 1980s, a section has been open as a museum. In October, the cellars host the Höhler Festival, one of Thuringia's largest folk festivals.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

visits.text: Around 1.3 million objects, with some 25,000 on display: founded in 1852 and built around a former Carthusian monastery, the Germanisches Nationalmuseum is Germany’s largest museum of cultural history. Don’t look for America on Martin Behaim’s Erdapfel, the oldest surviving terrestrial globe, completed in 1492 before Columbus returned. Dürer, Veit Stoß, Rembrandt, and remnants of the original Schöner Brunnen round out the visit. Admission is €10; closed Mondays, with extended hours on Wednesdays until 8:30 p.m. and free admission from 5:30 p.m. (excluding temporary exhibitions).

Dani Karavan’s Straße der Menschenrechte transforms Kartäusergasse, in front of the museum entrance, into a manifesto in white concrete. Each of its 27 pillars bears an article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in German and another language. In the city of the Nazi rallies and the 1945–1946 trial, the symbolism carries considerable weight. Read a few columns as you leave the museum: the street is freely accessible.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Next to the Erlöserkirche, Villa Sarabodis takes you back to a time in Gerolstein long before the church’s mosaics. The Roman remains include traces of underfloor heating: an ancient comfort beneath a newer neighborhood. A combined visit helps explain the relationship between these neighboring sites. From April to October, interior access is available through a guided tour; book with the tourist office.

activities.text: If your legs are up to it, make Munterley the goal of your climb in the Gerolsteiner Dolomiten. These cliffs overlook the town and the Kyll Valley, showing that there is more here than a simple stop for mineral water. The full circuit requires more time than this stop allows. Ask for confirmation of a short access route and save Buchenlochhöhle or Papenkaule for a longer hike.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: To appreciate the Rhön’s open landscapes, Wasserkuppe deserves more than a stop in the parking lot. The plateau is home to an airfield and a gliding museum, with hills surrounding the site. Choose a short walk to accessible viewpoints. Keep a windproof jacket with you and postpone the outing if visibility disappears.

From gliders to model aircraft, the Deutsches Segelflugmuseum mit Modellflug on Wasserkuppe tells a story of technology rooted in this place. The aircraft on display help you understand unpowered flight without having to book a flight experience. Choose this visit instead of a long walk in bad weather. Check the museum’s hours before heading up.

Gersfeld’s Schlosspark offers a more sheltered break after visiting the highlands. The neighboring castles form the park’s backdrop, but these private buildings cannot be toured like a public palace. View the facades from areas where access is permitted. Keep this stop short if you also plan to visit Wasserkuppe and Rotes Moor.

activities.text: Wood beneath your feet, birch trees, and waterlogged ground: Rotes Moor reveals a different side of the Rhön from its peaks. The boardwalk leads to an observation point; the nature reserve offers a short loop of about 3 km. Stay on designated paths and check for restrictions related to restoration work before leaving Gersfeld.

Watch takeoffs at Wasserkuppe airfield from designated public areas. This gliding site lets you observe flight activity without booking an introductory flight, but operations depend on wind and weather. Follow posted instructions and never cross aircraft maneuvering areas. This stop complements the plateau walk.

If you are traveling with children or prefer to stay near Gersfeld, choose Wildpark Gersfeld. This wildlife park in the Ehrengrund area offers an alternative to outings in the highlands, with a walking route around the enclosures. Check opening hours before heading there. On a 3-day trip, replace an outing rather than adding this activity to all the others.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhön and Fulda in 4 days: peaks and spa towns

visits.text: Asleep for more than two thousand years, the Barberini Faun stretches out in a room with barely plastered brick walls: the Glyptothek, on Königsplatz, is Munich’s oldest public museum, built by Leo von Klenze and opened in 1830. The frescoes were lost during the war, and the museum’s 1972 reopening retained these austere walls, which showcase the pediments from the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina. On Sundays, admission drops to €1.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Balthasar Neumann designed this basilica between 1730 and 1739, and the result is a paradox: an austere twin-towered façade for an incandescent Baroque interior. Franconia's main pilgrimage site for the Trinity, it receives about a hundred pilgrimage groups annually according to the parish site. The Friday guided tour at 10:30 a.m. includes an organ concert from May to October.

The Burg Gößweinstein, dating at least to the 11th century according to the first mention in 1076, faces the basilica on the opposite outcrop. Legend says Wagner found inspiration here for the Grail castle in Parsifal - nothing proven, but the silhouette confirms the intuition. Panoramic beer garden open Easter to October.

activities.text: On the Burg terrace, the beer garden overlooks the confluence of the Wiesent, Püttlach, and Ailsbach in the valley. The Balthasar-Neumann-Rundwanderweg (3.6 km from the village) connects the basilica and fortress via a trail that multiplies viewing angles. A car-free detour possible from Gößweinstein.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Görlitz is Germany's best-preserved city—more than 4,000 listed historic buildings in the center, covering five centuries of architecture from late Gothic to Art Nouveau, because the city emerged intact from World War II. Its prosperity in the 15th century rested on cloth manufacturing and trade in woad, a highly prized blue pigment. The Untermarkt, the lower square, is the heart of the old town: its colorful Renaissance and Baroque facades, wrought-iron balconies, and vaulted passages form one of Saxony's most beautiful ensembles. The city serves so often as a film location it's called "Görliwood"—Wes Anderson's The Grand Budapest Hotel, Inglourious Basterds, and The Reader were filmed here.

The Görlitzer Warenhaus, the former Art Nouveau department store from 1913 on Demianiplatz, is the building used as the hotel lobby in The Grand Budapest Hotel. Its large glass-roofed interior courtyard and multi-level shopping galleries are striking—the building was threatened with demolition before the filming saved it.

The Schönhof, dating from 1526, is one of Germany's oldest Renaissance burgher houses still preserved in their original state. It houses the Silesian Museum, which documents the history and art of Silesia, a region shared between Germany, Poland, and the Czech Republic.

The Church of St. Peter and Paul stands directly on the banks of the Neisse, the border with Poland. Its Baroque "sun organ," built in 1703 by Eugenio Casparini, is one of Saxony's most remarkable instruments—its monumental case has remained intact since its creation.

activities.text: Cross the Old Town Bridge (Altstadtbrücke) to Zgorzelec, the Polish side. The pedestrian bridge rebuilt in 2004 bears a European Union plaque at its center. You can stroll for a few minutes on the Zgorzelec side—the two municipal councils have jointly managed many facilities since the symbolic reunification of the two banks.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: New oak posts, but a layout some 7,000 years old: the Sonnenobservatorium Goseck, an enclosure about 70 m in diameter, dates to around 4900 B.C. It opened to the public on December 21, 2005, the winter solstice, and its gates align with sunrise and sunset on that day. Free access year-round.

Goseck Castle deserves as much attention as the circle. Schloss Goseck grew out of a Benedictine monastery founded in 1041; the crypt, choir, and transept survive from the church consecrated in 1053, incorporated into the Renaissance castle of 1609–1635. Its information center opens daily from April through October, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. (€2, €5 including the Schlosskirche).

days_plan.itin_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra

visits.text: A thousand years of ore without interruption: the Rammelsberg is, according to UNESCO, the only deposit in the world exploited continuously for over 1,000 years (until 1988), listed along with the old town in 1992. The guided tour descends into the galleries aboard the old miners' train—allow 2.5 hours, around €18. Book ahead in high season. The Feuergezähe Gewölbe from the 13th century, still visible on site, is presented by UNESCO sources as the oldest vaulted mining chamber in Europe.

At night, Goslar's alleys smell of damp timber and ancient stone—roughly 1,500 half-timbered houses compressed into one square kilometer. The Kaiserpfalz (Imperial Palace), founded by the Ottonians around 1005 and brought to its apex by the Salians in the 11th century, is the largest preserved secular building of that century in Germany. The Marktplatz with its bronze imperial eagle, and the Frankenberg church with its legends of miner ghosts. The old town is compact: everything walkable in two hours.

The Neuwerkkirche, hidden behind the market square, is one of Goslar's most austere Romanesque structures—no guided tour, no ticket. You push the door and enter. A walled garden behind the apse, stone benches, silence. A useful counterpoint after the Rammelsberg. Generally open mornings until noon.

activities.text: Discover the Upper Harz Water Management System, an ingenious network of dams, reservoirs and channels listed by UNESCO, built to power the historic mines. This 800-year-old feat of hydraulic engineering stretches across the Harz mountains, demonstrating how medieval miners harnessed water power with remarkable sophistication.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands
Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken

visits.text: The Georg-August University was founded in 1737 by George II, Elector of Hanover and King of Great Britain, to spread the ideals of the Enlightenment. Napoleon reportedly declared: "Göttingen belongs neither to a state nor to Germany—it is the university of Europe." Since its founding, 47 Nobel Prize laureates have studied or taught here, including Max Born, Werner Heisenberg, and Otto Hahn. One in four residents is a student. The Aula, the main classical-style building on Wilhelmsplatz, is the visible heart of the historic campus.

The Gänseliesel—Lison the goose girl—is the Art Nouveau fountain installed in front of the Altes Rathaus (13th century). Every new doctoral graduate must climb the fountain, offer the statue a bouquet, and plant a kiss on her cheek. The tradition was officially forbidden but always tolerated. On some summer days, the scene repeats almost hourly.
The Old Botanical Garden, created in 1736, houses over 10,000 plant species and 19th-century historic greenhouses—one of Germany's oldest university botanical gardens, still active for research.

The Junkernschänke is a late Gothic 15th-century house with a richly carved facade, one of the most beautiful in the old town. The Stadtwall, a former medieval rampart transformed into a green promenade, circles the historic center.

activities.text: Walk a loop on the Stadtwall, the green ring that follows the route of the old medieval ramparts around Göttingen's center—about 4 km, flat and shaded path.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Around Hanover: Lower Saxony's Most Beautiful Sites

visits.text: The Schnupftabak- und Stadtmuseum in Grafenau holds a surprise: glass is used here to tell the story of snuff. Handmade bottles, antique boxes, and memorabilia from the salt trade connect several local crafts. The collection occupies the town’s former almshouse. Visits are by appointment through the Grafenau tourist office; book before making the detour.

activities.text: Extend your break at KurErlebnispark BÄREAL in Grafenau before continuing to Neuschönau. The park provides a gentle transition between the museum and the national park trails. The brief walk through the center also links the exterior of Spitalkirche with Kirchenwiese. Choose a short stroll and save longer hikes for the following day.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavarian Forest in 4 Days: From Passau to the Großer Arber

visits.text: Friedrich called it 'my beloved ruin'—Eldena Abbey Ruins, founded in 1199 by Cistercians, provided Caspar David Friedrich with his principal motifs for three decades. He was born in Greifswald in 1774, spent his childhood there, and sketched these walls from his adolescent visits. The paintings derived from them are preserved in Berlin and in Greifswald itself at the Pommersches Landesmuseum.

Greifswald's Altstadt stayed standing thanks to a surrender without combat in 1945—the garrison commander chose to surrender rather than let fighting destroy the city. Result: the Gothic brick ensemble is intact. St. Nikolai Cathedral, the Marktplatz, and the university museum (the university dates from 1456) form a compact ensemble visitable in two hours.

activities.text: The Caspar-David-Friedrich-Bildweg follows on foot or by bike from the painter's birthplace in the Altstadt to Eldena Abbey Ruins, passing through the historic port and the fishing village of Wieck with its wooden drawbridge. The route is about 6 km and takes 2 hours on foot. The Caspar-David-Friedrich-Zentrum in the birthplace house opens onto his work and local motifs.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: The Großer Arber offers a vantage point over the ridges, provided the clouds allow a clear view. The gondola makes it easy to reach the heights, followed by a short walk to panoramic viewpoints. The domes of the technical installations are a reminder that the summit is more than a natural landscape. In summer, the gondola usually runs from 9:00 AM to 4:30 PM; allow extra time for the descent and take the wind into account.

activities.text: If you are looking for a less steep walk, the Rundwanderweg around the Großer Arbersee follows the shores below the mountain. Floating mats of vegetation, sometimes called islands, contrast with the wooded mountainside that encloses the landscape. The maintained route offers an easy way to explore, but it remains an outdoor trail subject to the day’s conditions. Stay on the trail and never venture onto the ice in winter.

The lapping of water accompanies your pedal boat on the Großer Arbersee as the shore slowly recedes. Rentals near the Arberseehaus offer another perspective on the mountainside and woods without adding another hike. This outing depends on the season and weather. Confirm that the rental operator is open and check the instructions on site; if the service is closed, simply spend that time along the shore.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavarian Forest in 4 Days: From Passau to the Großer Arber

visits.text: If the sky is clear, climb the observation tower on the Großer Inselsberg: from its 21-meter height, you can see as far as the Wasserkuppe in the Rhön and the Brocken in the Harz. At 916 meters, this summit is the highest point in the western Thuringian Forest. There is an admission fee for the tower; bring a jacket, even in summer.

activities.text: Follow the Rennsteig across the Großer Inselsberg’s summit plateau, which is about 700 meters long: the ridge trail, marked with a white “R,” shares its route here with the E3 European long-distance path. Running some 169 kilometers between Hörschel and Blankenstein, it marked the former border between Saxe-Gotha and the Electorate of Hesse here. For a longer walk, continue to the Kleiner Inselsberg pass and its 1,000-meter summer toboggan run.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach

visits.text: The sandstone warms in the sun among the vines, with Noah depicted as the first winegrower: the Steinernes Bilderbuch in Großjena features twelve scenes carved in 1722. Court jeweler Johann Christian Steinauer dedicated them to Duke Christian of Saxe-Weissenfels to mark his ten years of rule. The Naumburg–Freyburg trail passes close by: come on foot if possible.

Next, head up to the Max-Klinger-Haus, near the Blütengrund where the Unstrut joins the Saale. The painter and sculptor bought this vineyard and its small Baroque house in 1903 and died here on July 4, 1920; his grave lies on a small plateau above the house. Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., from April to early November, €5.50.

days_plan.itin_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra

visits.text: Three concrete cubes connected by terraces overlook the former open-pit mine filling with water before your eyes: Großräschen's IBA-Terrassen are the visitor center for the Lausitzer Seenland, created through the redevelopment of the mining basin. The “IBA meets IBA” exhibition traces 100 years of German building exhibitions. Check whether the renovation closure has been lifted before coming.

activities.text: If you are here on a Thursday, the iba-aktiv-tours guided bus tour leaves at 10 a.m. to show every stage of filling the Seenland's lakes: an active open-pit mine, navigable canals and floating houses. Allow around 3 hours. A public tour is also offered on the first and third Sundays of the month.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: The studio museum of Ernst Barlach, the Expressionist sculptor who lived here, displays his anguished bronze sculptures. The town is quiet, far from the tourist circuit.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Step back in time at the Black Forest Open-Air Museum (Vogtsbauernhof), an extraordinary village of meticulously rescued historic farm buildings spanning 400 years of rural life. Each farmhouse, barn and mill has been carefully dismantled, transported and reconstructed on this picturesque hillside site, complete with authentic furnishings and equipment. This living museum offers an unparalleled window into the traditional way of life in the Black Forest region.

Watch craftspeople demonstrate traditional skills in the working wooden toy workshop, where hand-carved Black Forest toys are made using century-old techniques. If you're lucky, the wood-fired bread ovens will be in operation, filling the air with the irresistible aroma of freshly baked loaves. Farm animals roam the grounds, adding to the authentic atmosphere of a working agricultural community of the past.

Follow the excellent audio guide through the farmhouses to understand how families lived, worked and survived the harsh mountain winters. Interactive exhibits vividly bring agricultural techniques and domestic life to life, engaging visitors of all ages. The traditional Black Forest houses with their distinctive low-pitched roofs represent architectural solutions to the region's heavy snowfall.

activities.text: Purchase authentic Black Forest handicrafts and traditional products directly from the museum workshops

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: Hainich National Park is Germany's largest contiguous deciduous forest with its 13,000 hectares. Established on December 31, 1997, it is Thuringia's only national park. Its uniqueness stems from its military past: vast sectors were restricted zones during the Cold War, leaving them to develop freely for decades. The forest has thus returned to an almost primeval state, with old trees, abundant deadwood, and more than 1,600 identified fungus species. The 1,573-hectare core zone has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011 as part of the “Primeval Beech Forests of Europe.” A 9.5 km World Heritage trail traverses the core zone.

The Baumkronenpfad—canopy walkway—starts at the park center in Thiemsburg. Over 540 meters, the walkway gradually rises to a height of 24 meters, level with the tops of the beech trees, then climbs to an observation platform at 44 meters, with an unobstructed view over the whole Hainich and the Thuringian Basin. Panels at each level explain life in the canopy and the diversity of species.

The national park center features an interactive exhibition on Hainich's limestone geology, forest fauna, and conservation challenges. A reconstructed «root cave» illustrates subterranean life. The center also provides information on the wildcat - an emblematic species visible at the dedicated village of Hütscheroda, a few kilometers away.

activities.text: A hike along the World Heritage trail, a 9.5 km circuit through the primeval beech forest. The path runs alongside areas of deadwood, skirts forest pools, and crosses clearings where the black woodpecker—Europe's largest woodpecker—excavates its nesting cavities in old trunks.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

visits.text: The Wikinger Museum Haithabu, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018 alongside the Danevirke, is one of Germany's most important archaeological museums. Between the 8th and 11th centuries, Haithabu was one of Northern Europe's largest trading ports — around 3,000 people are estimated to have lived here in about 950 AD. The semicircular earthwork that enclosed the town is still visible in the landscape today.

The Danevirke, a 30-km wall that cut across the Jutland peninsula from the Schlei to the North Sea, was built to defend the Viking kingdom against the Franks. It shares its UNESCO listing with Haithabu. A restored section of the earthwork wall can be visited a few kilometres to the north.

activities.text: Walk the boardwalk paths of the Haithabu open-air museum, where seven Viking longhouses have been reconstructed full-size within the ancient rampart. Craftspeople in period costume work here in season. A reconstructed longship is moored at the jetty — boat trips are offered in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Admire Halberstadt Cathedral, a Gothic masterpiece housing one of Europe's most important ecclesiastical treasures. This majestic cathedral, built on the model of French cathedrals, impresses with its harmonious proportions and medieval stained glass windows. St. Martin's Church completes this exceptional religious heritage with its preserved Romanesque architecture.

Explore the Klusfelsen near Halberstadt, impressive sandstone rock formations where medieval troglodyte chapels were carved. These sacred caves, sculpted into the rock by medieval hermits, create a mystical landscape unique in northern Germany. Hiking trails allow you to discover this site between nature and spirituality.

Visit the sandstone caves and Regenstein Castle near Blankenburg, a medieval fortress carved directly into the rock. This rock citadel offers spectacular views of the Harz foothills and bears witness to medieval defensive ingenuity. The cave dwellings of Langenstein, some of which were inhabited until 1916, reveal an unusual way of life maintained for centuries. Regenstein Castle is about half an hour's drive from Halberstadt.

activities.text: Hike to the sandstone caves of Blankenburg and discover the rock-cut Regenstein Castle, about half an hour's drive from Halberstadt

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Discover Halle an der Saale, birthplace of the famous composer George Frideric Handel, whose monument proudly adorns the market square. This cultural center of Saxony-Anhalt is home to Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg, one of Germany's oldest universities, founded in 1502. An academic and artistic atmosphere permeates every street of this multifaceted city.

Contemplate Halle Cathedral and the Market Church of Our Lady with its four emblematic towers dominating the urban skyline. These late Gothic edifices testify to the religious and economic power of the town in the Middle Ages. Giebichenstein Castle, perched on a rocky promontory above the Saale, today houses a prestigious School of Fine Arts.

Marvel at the Nebra Sky Disc at the State Museum of Prehistory, the oldest concrete depiction of the sky ever discovered. This 3,600-year-old bronze disc, adorned with gold representing the sun, moon, and stars, revolutionized our understanding of Bronze Age astronomical knowledge. The Francke Foundations, a Baroque architectural complex dedicated to Pietist education, complete this exceptional heritage.

activities.text: Visit the Halloren Museum and taste the famous chocolate balls, specialty of Germany's oldest chocolate factory still in operation

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The smell of mud and roasted coffee rises from the canals of the Speicherstadt in the early morning. This district of red-brick warehouses was built between 1883 and 1927 on wooden pilings and designated UNESCO in 2015 alongside the Kontorhausviertel. Its 26 hectares and its fleetes (internal canals) make it one of the largest historical warehouse complexes in Northern Europe. Arrive before 9 AM—tour groups start pouring in from 10 AM.

The Speicherstadt vanishes underfoot—and there rises the Elbphilharmonie, perched atop the former Kaispeicher A warehouse from 1963 like a glass iceberg on brick. Inaugurated in 2017 following designs by Herzog & de Meuron, it soars to 110 m. The Grand Hall is considered one of the world's best-designed concert halls acoustically, with its stucco walls cut like lace. The Plaza on the 8th floor is free and open daily.

The Elbphilharmonie still divides Hamburgers—a massive budget overrun, ten years late, and yet no one regrets it anymore. The Reeperbahn a few streets away is the flip side of the city: this is where the Beatles played their first real gigs in 1960-1962 in the clubs on Große Freiheit. At night, the street becomes one of Germany's liveliest—worth seeing even if music isn't your priority.

The Kunsthalle Hamburg, founded in 1869, is one of Northern Germany's largest art museums. Seven centuries of painting coexist here, from Gothic art to contemporary works—with a dense collection of Caspar David Friedrich that echoes Greifswald later on the route. The Neo-Renaissance building adjoins a separate modern gallery. Closed Monday; allow at least 1.5 hours.

HafenCity unfolds along the Elbe on former port lands as Europe's largest intra-city urban renewal project according to developers' data—157 hectares under development until around 2030. On the Elbpromenade side, the Marco-Polo-Terrassen offer a viewpoint over the Elbe free from any construction, rare in a port city.

activities.text: If you climb to the Elbphilharmonie Plaza on a windless day, the panorama over the Elbe, the Speicherstadt, and the harbor cranes captures in a single image what makes Hamburg distinctive. Access is free, but concert tickets sell out months in advance—book now if you want to hear something.

Walk or bike along the Elbe from HafenCity to the Fischmarkt: on Sunday mornings from 5 AM, this century-old fish market spills herring, fruit, and vendors' shouts onto the quay for three hours. It's kitschy and sincere—a way to see Hamburg outside the polished circuits.

An Alster ferry crossing (Alsterdampfer) from Jungfernstieg takes 1 hour and loops the two inner lakes that carve through the city. Seen from the water, Hamburg changes completely: church steeples, ambassadorial villas, and gardens replace the industrial docks. Boats run year-round, more frequently April to October.

Have dinner in the Schanzenviertel, the alternative district north of the Reeperbahn, before heading to the airport. The restaurants on the Schulterblatt are open in the evening, prices are reasonable and the atmosphere less polished than in the HafenCity. Hamburg Airport is about 25 min by S-Bahn from Hauptbahnhof.

Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea
German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: The Fagus-Werk, which requires a round trip by car from Hameln to visit, is a shoe-last factory built from 1911 onward by Walter Gropius - his first independent commission at the age of 27 - in collaboration with Adolf Meyer. Gropius removed the load-bearing corner pillars and placed the structure inside the building, freeing up fully glazed corners - a radical innovation for 1911. The principle of the glass curtain wall, which he would perfect at the Bauhaus in Dessau, is used here. The factory still operates today and continues to produce shoe lasts. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.

Hameln is built along the Weser, with an old town whose half-timbered houses and 16th- and 17th-century sandstone facades illustrate the Weser Renaissance style. In the cobblestones, thousands of small bronze rat-shaped plaques guide visitors to the main sites—a nod to the legend whose earliest written traces date back to a chronicle from 1384.

The Rattenfängerhaus (Pied Piper House), built in 1602, bears on its facade an inscription recalling the event of June 26, 1284: "130 children born in Hamelin were led away by a piper dressed in many colors to Calvary near the Koppen and disappeared there." Some historians see in this legend an allegory of eastward colonization migrations (Ostsiedlung) in the 13th century—the rats, incidentally, only appear in 16th-century versions.

The Hochzeitshaus (Wedding House), built between 1610 and 1617, is the most imposing Renaissance building on the central square. Its mechanical carillon plays the Pied Piper melody three times daily with moving figures—crowds gather to watch.

The Collegiate Church of St. Boniface (Münster St. Bonifatius) is Hameln's oldest religious building, its origins tracing back to a Benedictine monastery founded in 851. The current church preserves Romanesque and Gothic elements.

activities.text: Walk along the Weser from the historic center—the river borders the old town along its entire west side.

Road Trip Around Hanover: Lower Saxony's Most Beautiful Sites
Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken
Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: You’ll find GrimmsMärchenReich in the right wing of Schloss Philippsruhe, a Baroque palace on the banks of the Main. Opened in 2019, this interactive experience takes you through seven fairy-tale worlds and a whispering corridor, and features Jacob Grimm’s frock coat. Visit from 11 a.m., Tuesday through Sunday; the Hanau history museum occupies the rest of the palace.

At midnight, a local legend says, the two brothers swap places on Hanau’s Brüder-Grimm-Nationaldenkmal. Unveiled in 1896 on Neustädter Marktplatz, the monument by Syrius Eberle depicts Wilhelm seated and Jacob standing and rises nearly six and a half meters high. Time your visit to hear the carillon at the Neustädter Rathaus just behind it: 10 a.m., noon, 4 p.m., or 6 p.m.

Reduced to its foundations and two stone gables in March 1945, the Altstädter Rathaus, built in 1538, was faithfully reconstructed in the 1950s. It houses the Deutsches Goldschmiedehaus, whose jewelry and goldsmithing exhibitions change throughout the year, facing the figure of Justice on a fountain dating from 1607–1608. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: A newly built ruin: that is the paradox of Staatspark Wilhelmsbad. As early as 1779, Crown Prince William of Hesse-Kassel had a mock castle ruin built here, its tower concealing a small palace—a precursor to Kassel’s Löwenburg. The park is free to enter; its 1780 carousel runs only a few times a year, so come mainly for a morning stroll.

days_plan.itin_title: Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel

visits.text: Discover Hannover, the vibrant regional capital of Lower Saxony, where modern urban life meets a rich historical heritage. The city boasts magnificent royal gardens, world-class museums and a dynamic cultural scene that hosts the Schützenfest, billed as the world's largest marksmen's festival, as well as the spectacular International Fireworks Competition. From the elegant Herrenhausen Gardens to the lively city centre, Hannover offers endless discoveries.

Explore central Hannover around the New Town Hall, a vast domed building overlooking Maschpark. Step inside to see models illustrating the city's evolution, then follow the park lake and continue to the old town, where the Marktkirche and half-timbered houses line the pedestrian streets. This walk links several major landmarks in the heart of Hannover.

activities.text: Stroll through the magnificent Herrenhausen Gardens, one of Europe's most impressive baroque garden ensembles. The Great Garden features geometric precision with fountains, sculptures, and the famous Grand Fountain reaching 80 meters high, while the surrounding botanical collections offer year-round floral displays.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands

visits.text: Alexander von Humboldt called it one of the seven most beautifully situated towns in the world — and even if the phrase may be apocryphal, it makes sense here. Hann. Münden is a half-timbered town with more than 700 houses, ringed by forests and set where the Werra and Fulda meet and the Weser begins.

On Tanzwerder island, the Werra and Fulda merge into the Weser at the foot of the 1899 Weserstein — the small obelisk bears the famous inscription reproduced in every German geography textbook. The Welfenschloss overlooks the scene from the bank, a Weser Renaissance building that remains intact.

activities.text: Take the river boat towards Kassel if the timetable allows: seasonal services on the Weser connect Hann. Münden to Reinhardshagen and sometimes beyond. Otherwise, cycle along the Weser on the signposted Weser-Radweg to the wooded riverbank at Reinhardshagen — 12 km one way, with no elevation gain.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: Trek the famous Harz Witches' Trail through Germany's northernmost highland region, where stunning panoramic views reward every climb. This legendary trail winds through ancient forests steeped in folklore, offering spectacular vistas across valleys and peaks that have inspired myths for centuries. The Harz mountains combine natural beauty with mystical atmosphere like nowhere else in Germany.

activities.text: Experience the Harz National Park's 3,000 kilometers of trails perfect for mountain biking adventures through pristine wilderness. From gentle forest paths to challenging alpine routes, the varied terrain caters to all skill levels while showcasing the region's diverse landscapes of rocky outcrops, dense woodlands, and crystal-clear mountain streams.

In winter, glide through the white snowy countryside on cross-country skis across the Harz's well-maintained trails. The region transforms into a winter wonderland offering downhill skiing, snowshoeing, and toboggan runs amidst snow-dusted pine forests and frozen waterfalls.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands

visits.text: Locals call it the Kornstadt: Haselünne, the oldest town in Emsland, still counts three Korn distilleries (Berentzen, Heydt, Rosche). In the 19th century, there were 26. The Berentzen Hof offers tours with tasting.
Stop by the Wacholderhain at the town's edge, a nature reserve of junipers across more than 30 hectares. Semi-wild Tarpan horses graze there. Marked trails, free access.

activities.text: The Korndiplom at Rosche is kitsch but well done: you take an exam on historic school benches at the Korn-Academie, then taste the result. Reservation required.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Wood, stone, and an inner courtyard: Burg Guttenberg offers a change from the open ruins along the Neckar. The castle in Neckarmühlbach, in the municipality of Haßmersheim, houses a museum devoted to life in the castle and its history. Combine the visit with the birds of prey program only if the schedule works. Dogs are not allowed in the museum.

activities.text: Birds of prey flying freely above the audience: the Deutsche Greifenwarte at Burg Guttenberg turns the courtyard into an observation area. Eagles, vultures, and eagle owls take part in the demonstrations announced by the center. Check the session times before leaving Bad Wimpfen, as they determine your morning’s schedule. Follow the animal keepers’ instructions and keep your distance.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: From ore to metal, the route through Henrichshütte makes sense of a factory that initially seems impenetrable. In Hattingen, the museum preserves a blast furnace and explains how materials moved through the former steelworks. Focus on this route rather than reading every information panel, and arrive before the last admission, currently at 5 p.m.

activities.text: Dark timber and cobblestone lanes: Altstadt Hattingen offers a change of scenery after Henrichshütte. This preserved old town provides another perspective on the city, far from the museum’s metal structures. Take a short walk through the streets of the historic center before dinner, wearing comfortable shoes for the cobblestone stretches.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

visits.text: If you reach the Hauptmarkt just before noon, look up at the Frauenkirche: as soon as the hour strikes, seven prince-electors circle Charles IV three times. This Männleinlaufen clock, completed in 1509, commemorates the Golden Bull; the church, built from 1352 to 1362, stands on the site of a synagogue destroyed during the pogrom of 1349. On the same square, the Schöner Brunnen rises 19 m, adorned with forty painted figures. From November 27 to December 24, 2026, the Christkindlesmarkt fills the square: arrive as early as 10 a.m.

activities.text: Ask for “Drei im Weggla” at the counter: three Nürnberger Rostbratwürste tucked into a roll with mustard. These grilled, marjoram-seasoned sausages measure just 7 to 9 cm and weigh around twenty grams, and their name is protected throughout the European Union by a geographical indication. Eat them standing at a kiosk near the Hauptmarkt: you still have a busy afternoon ahead.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Annette von Droste-Hülshoff was born in 1797 in this Renaissance moated castle and spent her first thirty years here. The museum inside Burg Hülshoff is closed for renovation, with reopening planned for 2027. Walk through the accessible park: the paths offer views of the moat and the castle façades. The DROSTE 1797 café-restaurant, in the vaulted cellar and on the courtyard terrace, remains open.

The seven-kilometre Lyrikweg links Burg Hülshoff to Haus Rüschhaus near Münster, tracing a path Annette von Droste-Hülshoff walked hundreds of times. Outdoor poetry stations, hedgerow countryside, fields — an open-air museum without barriers. Ideal in the late afternoon.

activities.text: After your visit, stop in at Droste Café 1797 in the castle's vaulted cellar — regional cakes and a view over the moat. Check the Burg website for ongoing restoration works: some areas are closed depending on the restoration phase.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: Germany's only cave navigable by boat: the Wimsener Höhle is explored by rowboat on an underground river that gushes from a limestone cliff. The journey lasts about ten minutes in total silence, broken only by the lapping of water. Open April to October.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Behold Hohenzollern Castle, one of Germany's most spectacular castles and ancestral seat of the Prussian royal family whose members later became German emperors. This fairy-tale fortress, rebuilt in its current neo-Gothic splendor in 1850, crowns a dramatic conical peak rising 855 meters above the Swabian countryside. The castle rivals Bavaria's famous Neuschwanstein in beauty and surpasses it in the authenticity of its royal ties.

Tour the gloriously opulent interiors, where visitors don enormous felt slippers to protect the precious parquet floors while children can dress in royal costumes for an immersive experience. The family still uses the castle for special events, so verify opening times before your visit to avoid disappointment. The treasury displays Prussian crown jewels and personal effects of Frederick the Great.

Hike to the neighboring Zeller Horn viewpoint for the iconic photograph of the castle floating above clouds that has made Hohenzollern Castle famous worldwide. The approach road itself offers increasingly spectacular views as the castle emerges from the forested hilltop. Hot air balloon rides over the castle at sunset provide an unforgettable perspective on this architectural marvel.

activities.text: Visit Hohenzollern Castle during Advent to discover the Königlicher Winterzauber exhibition, with illuminations and Christmas decorations in the castle courtyards and rooms

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: Ruins rather than an intact palace: that is the appeal of Schloss Heidelberg. The castle’s wings and terraces offer views of the old town and the Neckar; explore the complex without expecting a succession of furnished rooms. Save the gardens for more views after the courtyard. When buying your castle ticket, check what it includes, particularly the funicular and guided tours.

The Alte Brücke frames Heidelberg between the water and wooded slopes. This stone bridge connects the old town to the opposite bank of the Neckar; its gateway gives the crossing the feel of a monumental threshold. Walk all the way across: the castle is easier to appreciate from farther away. Come early to photograph the arches without rushing, then return along the riverfront instead of retracing your steps.

A church surrounded by shops: the Heiliggeistkirche retains this informal setting on the Marktplatz. Inside, the spacious nave contrasts with the bustle of commerce in the square. This change of atmosphere is worth a stop even without climbing the tower. Check access conditions on the day of your visit and respect church services; an open door does not mean every area is open to visitors.

Rows of jars, dark wood, and bottles: the Deutsches Apotheken-Museum offers a different perspective on Heidelberg Castle. Its collections tell the history of pharmacy and medicines in the Ottheinrich wing. This is a visit with tangible appeal, worth prioritizing if courtyards and facades leave you wanting more. Include it in your castle visit: museum admission is included in the site ticket; confirm this when purchasing.

activities.text: Walk up to the Philosophenweg to see Heidelberg from the opposite slope across the Neckar. This walk offers the broader perspective missing from the old town’s streets: the castle, bridge, and rooftops appear together. The climb is part of the outing; this is more than a viewpoint where you step out of a car. Wear supportive shoes and shorten the walk if you want to leave time for the museums.

If you prefer level ground, follow Heidelberg’s Neckar riverfront instead of the Philosophenweg. The river offers another view of the facades and hills without adding a climb to your day. This walk is an alternative to the outing on the opposite slope, rather than an additional obligation. Choose a short loop from the Alte Brücke and leave room for cyclists.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest
Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: Founded in 1793 by Duke Frederick Francis I, Heiligendamm is continental Europe's oldest seaside resort. White neoclassical villas line the beach, earning it the nickname Weiße Stadt am Meer. The Grand Hotel (site of the G8 in 2007) can be viewed from outside. 200-meter pier.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Charming in photos, sinister in history: the Henkersteg, a covered footbridge over the Pegnitz, takes its name from the executioner who lived there, employed by the city but kept apart from society. From the 15th to the 19th century, the executioner lived in the neighboring tower; one of them, Franz Schmidt, recorded 361 executions between 1578 and 1617. In 1595, a flood brought down the footbridge, killing eight onlookers. Photograph it from the south bank, with the half-timbered Weinstadel; the Henkerhaus, a museum of judicial history, is open from April through December, Tuesday through Sunday, from noon to 5 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: View from the battlements of Starkenburg: the Rhine plain stretches to the Palatinate, the vines of the Bergstrasse tumble below, Heppenheim looks barely the size of a village. The fortress was built in 1065 to protect the estates of Lorsch Abbey; it's therefore the natural offspring of the previous stop. The observation tower (67 steps) opens in season.

Heppenheim's Altstadt is the Bergstrasse's finest surprise: a Marktplatz with fountain, half-timbered houses, the town hall, and the Stiftskirche St. Peter in a compact, preserved arrangement. On the evening of November 11, 1693, French troops set fire to the town - five buildings survived. What you see today is a meticulous 18th-century reconstruction.

activities.text: Walk up to Starkenburg via the path from the old town (about 30 minutes). The Burgschänke at the top offers Brotzeit and a view: two good reasons to linger. A youth hostel occupies part of the buildings - an original option for an overnight stay.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: The three imperial seaside resorts (Heringsdorf, Ahlbeck, Bansin) have Belle Époque villas lining 12 km of promenade—Europe's longest. Bismarck, Kaiser Wilhelm II, and Fontane took the waters here. Heringsdorf's pier, 508 meters long, is Germany's largest.

activities.text: Walk along the promenade from Heringsdorf to Ahlbeck (4 km) to compare the styles of the three imperial seaside resorts. Each resort has its own personality. Ahlbeck has Germany's oldest pier (1882), the one from the film Pappa ante Portas.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: 53.46 metres of a triumphant Germanic warrior — the Hermannsdenkmal on the Grotenburg is Germany's tallest statue. Ernst von Bandel devoted 40 years of his life to this project, inaugurated the year before his death. Climbing to the panoramic platform costs €5.

From the top, the Teutoburg Forest stretches as far as the eye can see — on a clear day, you can make out the hills of Bielefeld. The monument commemorates Arminius's victory over the Roman legions of Varus in AD 9, in this very forest. The Waldbühne at the foot of the site hosts concerts from June to August.

activities.text: Walk down from the monument to the car park via the Hermannsweg: the dense forest, the reddish sandstone paths and the geology information boards make this twenty-minute descent a real counterpoint to the monument. The nearby Teuto-Kletterpark offers treetop adventure courses for families.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: Ninety-eight meters of mirrors and 33 glass chandeliers: the Hall of Mirrors at Neues Schloss Herrenchiemsee is longer than its model at Versailles. Ludwig II laid the foundation stone on May 21, 1878, but slept here for only a few days in September 1885; when he died, 50 of the 70 rooms remained unfinished. The state rooms can only be seen on a guided tour lasting approximately 40 minutes: book your time slot as soon as you arrive on the island.

More intimate than the gilded salons, the König-Ludwig-II-Museum has occupied the south wing of Herrenchiemsee Palace since 1987. Its twelve rooms trace the king’s life from his christening gown to his death mask, connecting the stops on this journey, from Nymphenburg to Berg and St. Michael. You can explore at your own pace; in winter, the last admission is at 3:45 p.m.

Less gilding, greater consequences: at Herrenchiemsee’s Altes Schloss, a former monastery of Augustinian canons founded shortly before 1130, representatives of eleven West German states and West Berlin drafted, between August 10 and 23, 1948, the text that formed the basis of the Basic Law. The Constitution Museum shares the building with the restored Kaisersaal and a gallery of painters from Lake Chiemsee. Open year-round, with hours of 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from April through October 24.

activities.text: From the Herreninsel landing, you can reach the Neues Schloss on foot in about 20 minutes across the island, or by horse-drawn carriage from April to October. Walkers have an even better option: an 8 km trail circles the entire island, with 4 and 6 km alternatives. Leave plenty of time to catch the next boat, especially in winter, when it runs only once an hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: After you get off the boat, a forest path takes you to Schloss Herrenchiemsee in fifteen minutes (or you can go by carriage, like Ludwig II). The park fountains spout opposite the Great Hall of Mirrors, a copy of the one at Versailles. The king slept there just ten nights before dying in 1886.

Ludwig II bought the island in 1873 and launched construction in 1878 with architect Georg Dollmann. The castle was granted UNESCO status in 2025, along with Neuschwanstein and Linderhof. The ground-floor Ludwig II Museum displays his baptismal gown and death mask.

activities.text: Bavarians call the Chiemsee their "sea." After visiting the castle, walk to the island's southern tip. No tourists, just trees and the lake stretching to the horizon. Allow two hours on the island in total.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Herrstein looks like a movie set: Edgar Reitz filmed “Home from Home: Chronicle of a Vision” here. Granted town status in 1428, it owes its exposed half-timbering to a restoration in the 1970s that removed the plaster and slate cladding. Climb to the Uhrturm, then follow the rampart walk to the tower where Schinderhannes spent a night in 1798.

Step inside Herrstein’s church, the former castle chapel built in a defensive position: a Gothic chancel, a Baroque nave, and a Stumm organ from 1772. The Stumm family, from Rhaunen-Sulzbach, built more than 370 organs over seven generations. On Saturdays at 2:30 p.m., from May through October, a guided tour lasting about 1 hour 30 minutes starts at the Uhrturm.

days_plan.itin_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern

visits.text: No cars on Hiddensee: you get around by bike or on foot. The island stretches 17 km in length and is 250 meters wide at its narrowest, between the Baltic and the Bodden. The Dornbusch lighthouse, in the north, offers a 360° panorama. Gerhart Hauptmann, Nobel laureate, had his summer house here (museum open).

activities.text: Rent a bike at the Vitte landing and circle the island in half a day. The west beaches are deserted; the Dornbusch heathland recalls Scotland. Return by evening ferry.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: St. Michael's Church in Hildesheim was built between 1010 and 1022 by Bishop Bernward. Its symmetrical double-apse plan, characteristic of Ottonian Romanesque art, earned it the nickname "heavenly castle." The painted wooden ceiling of the central nave, created in the 13th century on 1,300 oak planks, depicts the Tree of Jesse and measures 27.6 × 8.7 meters—one of the extremely rare monumental paintings from the Early Middle Ages to have survived, along with those in Zillis, Switzerland, and Dädesjö, Sweden. UNESCO-listed since 1985.

St. Mary's Cathedral (Hildesheimer Dom) dates back to 872. Its present form as a three-aisled basilica was completed in 1061. It houses the Bernward Doors, wrought in bronze in 1015, and the Christ Column of 1020. The thousand-year-old rosebush grows in the cloister: traditionally said to have been planted in the 9th century, it was destroyed during the bombing of 1945 but grew back from its roots. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.

Hildesheim's Marktplatz presents a curiosity: its gabled houses were completely destroyed in 1945 and faithfully reconstructed between 1984 and 1989 from precise architectural records. Renaissance and Baroque facades that appear medieval but are less than forty years old.

The Roemer and Pelizaeus Museum houses one of Germany's most important Egyptian art collections, assembled in the 19th century by merchant Wilhelm Pelizaeus from Cairo. Funerary statues, masks, and papyri spanning over 3,000 years.

activities.text: Urban walk between Michaelisplatz and Domhof—the two UNESCO sites connected on foot in about twenty minutes through medieval alleyways.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands
Road Trip Around Hanover: Lower Saxony's Most Beautiful Sites
Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken

visits.text: Schloss Hirschhorn overlooks a bend in the Neckar, with the old town clustered at the foot of the slope. The castle makes the reasons for choosing this location much clearer than simply driving through. Focus on the accessible areas and the view; not all buildings are open for interior visits. Check the operator’s information before heading uphill.

Small on the map, but rarely level: Hirschhorn’s Altstadt rises in tiers between the Neckar and its castle. The half-timbered houses and narrow streets offer a different experience from the panorama seen from above. Explore the center first to choose your route uphill. Avoid looking for parking in the narrow passageways.

activities.text: Book a guided tour of Hirschhorn’s old town and castle if you want to connect the narrow streets with the castle through explanations. The town offers these guided tours, which provide more insight than a series of photo stops. Confirm the meeting point and language with the tourist office. This option replaces self-guided visits to the same places; it does not add to them.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: Take the U5 line to the Killesberg stop: this former quarry became a horticultural exhibition park in 1939, then the Höhenpark, covering about 50 hectares. Its landmark, the Killesbergturm, is a 40 m cable-supported tower designed by engineer Jörg Schlaich in 2001. Two spiral staircases of 174 steps, one for going up and the other for coming down, lead to the upper platform at 31 m. The tower opens at 7 a.m. and has no elevator: come before the heat sets in.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Corvey — Westphalia's only UNESCO-listed monument to date — was founded in 822 on the orders of Louis the Pious. Its Carolingian westwork has stood intact since the 9th century and earned the UNESCO designation in 2014. In the princely library of some 75,000 volumes, Hoffmann von Fallersleben was working as librarian when he wrote the Deutschland-Lied in 1841.

The Weser shimmers behind Corvey's Carolingian towers — the site is a two-kilometre walk from the centre of Höxter along the river. Along the way, Höxter's Altstadt lines up its Weser Renaissance half-timbered houses between the stones of the old town walls.

activities.text: Walk the two kilometres from the town centre to Corvey along the Weser — this is the Weser-Radweg, a signposted, flat path. The return by bike from Corvey takes ten minutes. On site, the medieval Remtergarten with its medicinal plants is free to enter.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

activities.text: “Stammtisch”: at the Hofbräuhaus, the word refers to more than 125 groups of regulars, and 616 lockers keep their personal beer steins under lock and key. Founded in 1589 by Duke William V, the brewery moved to Platzl in 1607; only the ground-floor Schwemme survived the bombings of 1945. To round off this day of museums, take a seat in this hall with room for a thousand guests, where a band plays daily: reservations are not accepted.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Eight paths converge on the Dianatempel, the central pavilion of the Hofgarten, laid out beginning in 1613 for Duke Maximilian I in the style of Italian Renaissance gardens. Enter from Odeonsplatz through the Hofgartentor, designed by Leo von Klenze in 1816; admission is free. Cross the garden from west to east: its paths lead toward the Haus der Kunst and the southern end of the Englischer Garten.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Here, they say love launched the industry: Karl Magnus Hutschenreuther, son of a porcelain painter, founded the region's first factory in 1814 to stay near Johanna Reuß, the forester's daughter. The Porzellanikon Hohenberg, in his villa, displays 2,000 m² of porcelain history. Closed Mondays.

View Burg Hohenberg from its accessible surroundings: mentioned as early as 1222, it is ringed by round and square towers. Ongoing restoration restricts even exterior visits. Do not enter the construction site or plan to climb the towers until public access has been restored.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Never conquered, but surrendered twice: Hohenneuffen Fortress capitulated in 1519, then again in 1635 after a fifteen-month siege. Perched at around 743 m on the edge of the Swabian Jura, it gained its bastions under Duke Ulrich in the 16th century, served as a state prison, and was then handed over for demolition in 1801. In 1948, a conference of the three German states held here laid the groundwork for the creation of Baden-Württemberg. Admission is free, with a walk of about 20 minutes from the hiking parking lot; on clear days, the view reaches Stuttgart.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Hohenschwangau Castle is Ludwig II of Bavaria's childhood castle. His father, King Maximilian II, had the dilapidated building restored from 1832 in neo-Gothic style, having medieval legend scenes depicted on the walls—including episodes of the swan knight Lohengrin, with whom Ludwig strongly identified. One room still displays the piano on which Richard Wagner played before the young king. It was here, facing the site of two former ruined castles on the opposite hill, that Ludwig II made the decision in 1868 to build Neuschwanstein there.

The Museum der Bayerischen Könige (Museum of Bavarian Kings), on the shore of the Alpsee, traces the Wittelsbach family's history from the Middle Ages to the 20th century. Collections include portraits, jewelry, and personal objects of Bavarian kings.

Walk along the Alpsee, a glacial lake with transparent waters at the foot of both castles. The complete circuit trail is about 3.5 km. In clear weather, the reflections of the Alps and castles in the water are striking.

activities.text: Scout the paths leading to Neuschwanstein and the Marienbrücke bridge in the late afternoon. The ascent from the Ticket Center takes 30 to 40 minutes on foot. Checking the route the day before allows you to set off at opening time without having to find your way.

days_plan.itin_title: Germany Road Trip: Castles, Medieval Villages and the Alps
Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

activities.text: A hike along a section of the Hohenwarte Reservoir trail, a 74.4 km circuit that follows the reservoir through the dense forest of the Thuringian Slate Mountains. In places, the paths overlook the Saale's deeply incised meanders from rocky cliffs, creating a landscape evoking Norwegian fjords—hence the nickname “Thuringian Sea” for this region.

A walk in the Naturpark Thüringer Schiefergebirge/Obere Saale, which covers the Thuringian Slate Mountains and the upper reaches of the Saale. The nature park protects landscapes of heathland, conifer forests, and deep valleys typical of this slate mountain range.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

visits.text: A helmet on your head, sand underfoot, and temperatures of 10–14 °C: bring a sweater to visit Homburg’s Schlossberghöhlen. Excavated to extract quartz-rich sand, they are described as Europe’s largest caves in variegated sandstone. Guided tours last 40 to 50 minutes and cover about 800 m; cash only.

Hohenburg crowns the Schlossberg, just above the caves: the seat of the counts of Homburg in the 12th century, it gave the town its name. Vauban transformed it into a fortress for Louis XIV; his fortifications were dismantled in 1714. Walk up after visiting the caves: you can freely explore the walls, moat, and surviving fortifications.

Head back down to the Marktplatz, the heart of an Altstadt whose layout dates to Vauban’s work. Emperor Louis the Bavarian granted the town its charter in 1330, and St. Michael, a Romanesque Revival church built in red sandstone (1836–1841), stands at the foot of the Schlossberg. The pedestrian streets and fountains date from the renovation launched in 1978: perfect for a coffee break.

The Römermuseum Schwarzenacker deserves much more than a quick detour: the small Roman town destroyed by the Alemanni in 275 comes back to life here. Explore the eye doctor’s house, the house with the five-column cellar, and the reconstructed Temple of Mercury, followed by the Baroque Edelhaus and its garden. Buy a combination ticket for the museum and the caves; both welcome visitors from March through October.

days_plan.itin_title: Saarland in 3 Days: Saarbrücken, the Saarschleife, and Homburg

visits.text: Five main rock pillars rise from the forest floor to 40 meters—nothing but stone and sky. The Externsteine have no archaeological evidence of Saxon worship, but their Romanesque Relief of the Descent from the Cross (circa 1160) is the oldest large medieval rock carving north of the Alps. In the scene: a tilted column that some read as an Irminsul submitting to Christ. Climbing the rocks costs around €4 (April to October). Allow 90 minutes.

activities.text: The Teutoburg Forest unfolds along the Hermannsweg, a 156-kilometer marked trail. From the Externsteine, a 90-minute loop through beech woods shows why Roman legions lost their way here in 9 AD. No technical scrambling, easy terrain. Take the path climbing behind the rock formation and loop back via Bruchsee pond—weekday silence guaranteed.

days_plan.itin_title: Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken

visits.text: Hörnum Odde is Sylt's very end: a sand spit that narrows towards the south and is half-swallowed by winter storms. The island loses several metres of ground here each year on the North Sea side. There is a rare feeling of impermanence — the land is literally slipping away underfoot.

Leuchtturm Hörnum, brought into service in 1907, is the only lighthouse on Sylt accessible on a guided tour — the other four do not open to visitors. Built in cast iron on a 17-metre dune, it rises nearly 50 metres above sea level. Views from the gallery take in Föhr, Amrum and the halligen.

activities.text: Walk to Hörnum Odde point along the marked dune path from the village: 2 km each way, flat terrain, but a headwind can double the effort. Seals often rest on the sandbanks visible from the tip — binoculars are useful.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: The oldest building in town, Hoyerswerda Castle began life in the 13th century as a moated water fortress before being rebuilt as a Renaissance structure in 1592. Today it houses the municipal museum, which traces local history and the Sorbian roots of the region. An anecdote: Napoleon supposedly dined there for a few hours in 1813. A combination ticket covers both castle and neighboring zoo—better value if you do both.

Stroll around Hoyerswerda's Marktplatz, past the Sorbenbrunnen (Sorbian fountain) and the old postal column. The Altes Rathaus, erected in the 15th century, closes off the square with its squat silhouette. A local curiosity: computer inventor Konrad Zuse took his high-school exams in the town's former lyceum. The old town can be covered quickly on foot; the Touristinformation at the Bürgerzentrum provides maps and guided-tour departures.

activities.text: Zoo Hoyerswerda has a history that touches local hearts: residents built it themselves starting in the 1950s, in the former castle park. Across six hectares, it houses roughly 1,100 animals, including brown bears, a Siberian tiger, and zebras. A restaurant and playground occupy the park's center. With children, plan a half-day rather than a rushed hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: A Baroque palace completed in 2020: the Humboldt Forum reconstructed three facades of the former Berlin Palace, demolished by East Germany in 1950, and paired them with a decidedly modern east facade designed by Franco Stella. The Ethnological Museum and the Museum of Asian Art occupy the third and fourth floors. Several areas are free, including the sculpture hall; a day ticket costs €14. Open from 10:30 AM to 6:30 PM, except Tuesdays.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, head up to the Humboldt Forum’s rooftop terrace, 30 m above the ground: roughly 1,800 m² with views of Berlin Cathedral, Alexanderplatz, and Marienkirche. An elevator takes you there from the ground floor. Admission costs €5, and reserving a time slot online avoids the wait.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: The Hundingshütte is a hunting lodge built by Ludwig II in Viking style, inspired by Wagner's The Valkyrie. A structure made of rough timber. A thirty-minute walk from Linderhof, with a gentle uphill slope.

activities.text: Walk back down the forest trail to the Marokkanisches Haus, another exotic pavilion of Ludwig II's in Linderhof park. The contrast between the Viking chalet and the Moorish salon sums up the king's unbridled imagination.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Theodor Storm called his hometown “the grey city by the sea” — and he was right. North Sea skies press down hard on Husum. The Theodor-Storm-Zentrum, installed in the house where the writer lived, displays manuscripts and personal objects belonging to the master of Nordic short fiction. Storm is the author of Der Schimmelreiter — read it before you come.

The Schloss vor Husum is worth visiting less for its interior rooms than for its park: in spring, more than four million violet crocuses carpet the lawn beneath the trees — the spectacle lasts two weeks in March and April. It is the only castle on the North Sea coast in Schleswig-Holstein, built between 1577 and 1582.

At the Binnenhafen, ochre and white façades reflect in the still water of the inner basin — the very image of a Nordic postcard. This is the marina today. The real fishing harbour, with its crab cutters, lies at the Außenhafen, 500 metres further towards the sea.

activities.text: Walk through the Nordfriesland Museum to understand the history of the North Frisians — a seafaring people settled on this coast since the Middle Ages, whose language is still spoken in a handful of villages. Fishing implements, storm charts and traditional costumes sum up a thousand years of coastal life.

If it's March, the Schloss park bursts into crocus bloom for two weeks — this is the time to go. Outside the flowering season, the Herzoginnengarten and Schlosspark take twenty minutes to walk around. The smoked herring brötchen kiosks on the Binnenhafen quay open from 8am.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Even if jewelry is not your passion, the Deutsches Edelsteinmuseum in Idar is worth a visit. Across three floors and 800 m², more than 10,000 pieces span 6,000 years of gem cutting and engraving, from local agates to lapis lazuli and tourmaline. One date to remember: in 1827, emigrants from the region discovered immense agate deposits in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, with shipments reaching Idar and Oberstein as early as 1834. Open daily except from mid-January to mid-February; admission €9.50.

Lying on their stomachs on tilting “Kippstühle,” the gem cutters at the Historische Weiherschleife spent their days bent over the grinding wheel. This mill is the last on the Idarbach still powered by a waterwheel; it operated, with interruptions, until 1945. A gem-cutting demonstration conveys the physical demands of the trade better than any display case. Allow 1 hour, including the gemstone exhibition, plus a pedal boat ride on the Kallwiesweiher pond if the weather permits. Call before visiting (06781 901918), Tiefensteiner Straße 87.

A church in the cliff, with no road leading up to it: Idar-Oberstein’s Felsenkirche, built between 1482 and 1484 in a rocky recess, can only be reached by stairs or a long trail, followed by a tunnel with around 40 steps. Legend has it that a knight had it hollowed out to atone for murdering his brother by throwing him from a castle window. Inside, a Gothic winged altarpiece depicts the Passion. Guided tours only, Tuesday through Sunday at 1:30 p.m. and 3 p.m., from mid-March to mid-November; €5.

The Deutsches Mineralienmuseum occupies a Wilhelmine-era house on Oberstein’s Hauptstraße, at the foot of the Felsenkirche, with 24 rooms across four floors. Its crystal room, described by the city as unique in Germany, is worth the stop on its own. On your way out, look at the B41: since the 1980s, the Nahe has flowed beneath it in a concrete channel nearly 2 kilometers long. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. in season; admission €8.

If your legs are up to it, climb from the Felsenkirche to the two ruins crowning the cliff. Schloss Oberstein, built in 1320, is recorded in 1330 as “the house above the house of the rock,” referring to the older, neighboring Burg Bosselstein. Its rooms, restored since 1981, host receptions, but the view down over Oberstein and the Nahe Valley is the reward for the climb. The trail is steep and includes flights of steps: wear sturdy shoes.

activities.text: Put on a helmet and descend into the Edelsteinminen Steinkaulenberg, described by the city as Europe’s only gemstone mine gallery open to visitors. The 400-meter route follows veins of agate, amethyst, rock crystal, and jasper. Commercial mining ceased in 1875, undercut by larger, cheaper agates from Brazil. After the tour, children can search for stones in the prospecting area for an additional fee.

In Idar-Oberstein, Spießbraten is not described as “grilled”: the word is “braten,” and “schwenken” or “grillen” are considered inappropriate. The Idar version, the most common, marinates overnight in raw onion, salt, and pepper before cooking over a beechwood fire; the Oberstein version is a rolled roast cooked on a spit. The recipe is said to come from the gauchos’ churrasco, brought back along with agates from Argentina and Brazil. Order it for dinner with a beer.

days_plan.itin_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern

visits.text: If Goethe intrigues you more as a government minister than as a poet, start at the GoetheStadtMuseum, in the Amtshaus on Ilmenau’s Markt. Its galleries recount his efforts to revive the town’s copper and silver mines and then its porcelain and technical glass industries; after his first visit in 1776, Goethe returned to Ilmenau 26 times. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday in summer and Wednesday through Sunday from November through April.

The Jagdhaus Gabelbach, a wooden hunting lodge hastily built in the summer of 1783 for Duke Charles Augustus’s hunts, stands a few hundred meters below the summit of the Kickelhahn. Goethe was a frequent guest; today, the museum explores hunting, his scientific research, and the forest through the exhibition “Der Kickelhahn, Goethes Wald im Wandel.” It follows the GoetheStadtMuseum’s opening hours, and a combined ticket covers three of the town’s museums.

activities.text: Climb the Kickelhahn, at 861 meters, from the Herzogröder Wiesen hiking parking lot on the road to Frauenwald: an uphill walk of about 2 kilometers through the forest. Near the summit, the Goethehäuschen, rebuilt in 1874, recalls the cabin where Goethe wrote “Over all the peaks is peace” in pencil on September 6, 1780; returning in 1831, a few months before his death, he wept as he reread these lines. Finish by climbing the 107 steps of the Kickelhahnturm, which is free to enter.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach

visits.text: You don’t have to be a car enthusiast to enjoy the Audi museum mobile at the Audi Forum Ingolstadt.
