Across three levels, more than 100 cars and two-wheelers trace the history of Audi and its predecessor brands since 1899, from Horch cars and DKW motorcycles to a Silver Arrow. One detail is sure to make you smile: eleven cars and five motorcycles circulate continuously on a paternoster lift that runs through all three floors. Arrive at opening time, 9 a.m. on weekdays and 10 a.m. on weekends; adult admission has been €7 since October 2026.

The Kreuztor guards the western entrance to Ingolstadt’s old town, bristling with seven red-brick turrets. This gate dates to 1385 and formed part of the medieval city’s second ring of walls. Start your walking tour here: the Liebfrauenmünster is just a few steps away, and the gate’s interior is only open during exhibitions or cultural events.

Laid in 1425 on the orders of Duke Louis the Bearded, the cornerstone of the Liebfrauenmünster heralded a church to match his ambitions. Its two towers, set at an angle, were never completed. Inside, look for the large altarpiece by Hans Mielich, consecrated in 1572, then consider the roof framework overhead: Bavaria’s tourism office says it is three times as large as that of Notre-Dame in Paris. Allow half an hour, outside service times.

Walk slowly up the central aisle of the Asamkirche Maria de Victoria, keeping your eyes on the pyramid painted on the ceiling: the perspective shifts with every step. Cosmas Damian Asam painted this illusion on a flat ceiling in a room roughly ten meters high for this Rococo church, built from 1732 to 1736. The sacristy houses the gold and silver Lepanto Monstrance, designed in 1708 and decorated with scenes of the battle. On some Sundays at noon, an organ recital brings the nave to life.

If you’ve read Mary Shelley, Ingolstadt’s Alte Anatomie may ring a bell: the novelist sends Victor Frankenstein to study at the city’s university. The Deutsches Medizinhistorisches Museum occupies this Baroque building, where physicians trained from 1735 to 1800, and a room devoted to the character explores the electrical experiments of the period. Finish with the medicinal plant garden, which is free to enter; the museum opens Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with admission at €6.

It’s a war museum, yet the most intriguing object at Ingolstadt’s Neues Schloss is a wheelbarrow. Dating to 1537, it is presented as Europe’s oldest and stands in the siege room alongside a model of the fortress around 1570. The Bayerisches Armeemuseum occupies this 15th-century Gothic castle, where its exhibition “Forms of War 1600–1815” unfolds. Save it for the end of the day: it stays open until 5:30 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday.

days_plan.itin_title: Altmühltal and the Danube in 4 Days, from Ingolstadt to Regensburg

visits.text: Twenty-seven euros to see flowers is steep. But Mainau Island delivers what it promises: 45 hectares of gardens, a tropical Schmetterlingshaus (Germany's second-largest butterfly house), a Bernadotte baroque palace, and lake views at every turn. Children free up to age 12.

Take the boat from Konstanz to arrive by lake: the approach is more beautiful than the road bridge. The 18th-century Deutschordensschloss stands at the center, private residence of Count Björn Bernadotte. The Palmenhaus shelters more than 20 palm species.

activities.text: In May, a million tulips cover Mainau's slopes. In summer, roses take over in the Italienischer Rosengarten. In autumn, 12,000 dahlias bloom. The Schlosscafé, between the palm trees and the exhibition, is a good place for a break.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: Rothenburg is more famous, but Iphofen has kept its Stadtmauer intact without becoming a theme park. The medieval ramparts with their three gates and towers still encircle the town; you can follow them entirely along the Herrengraben. The Rödelseer Tor, built between 1455 and 1466, is the oldest of the three and serves as the town's official symbol.

The Knauf Museum at the edge of the Marktplatz presents reliefs from the great cultures of Antiquity through modern times - five millennia, four continents, in a contemporary building constructed with stones from the Schwanberg castle destroyed in 1525. The Knauf company, based here since 1936, finances the museum.

activities.text: The vines of the Julius-Echter-Berg bake in the sun above Iphofen - the walk from town takes about twenty minutes to reach the terroir f viewpoint with its interpretation panels. More than twenty winemakers work in the town; some offer Weinproben directly in their cellars without reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Five oaks aged 600 to 1,000 years stand in Ivenack Park, Germany's first National Natural Monument. Their trunks exceed 14 meters in circumference. A treetop walkway lets you approach them at canopy height. Fallow deer roam freely in the enclosure.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Perched atop Tempelberg hill, Jagdschloss Granitz overlooks Rügen's beech forests. Its central tower houses a freestanding spiral cast-iron staircase of 154 steps. The view from the top sweeps the island's east coast. Access on foot, by carriage, or via the Rasender Roland.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Schiller's Garden House in Jena is the modest dwelling the poet occupied from 1797, when he was teaching at the university. It's in this pastoral setting that he began his creative collaboration with Goethe - who had brought him to Jena - and started «Wallenstein». The original building is preserved with some period furniture.

The Zeiss-Planetarium, inaugurated on July 18, 1926, is the oldest continuously operating projection planetarium in the world. It was designed by Carl Zeiss engineer Walther Bauersfeld, who simultaneously developed the thin-shell concrete dome—an architectural invention that revolutionized construction in the 20th century. The dome measures 25 meters in diameter. Current projections use a Zeiss Velvet full-dome laser system. The original idea dates back to 1913, when the founder of the Deutsches Museum approached Zeiss for a “Himmelsschau”—a representation of the sky.

The JenTower is a 160-meter cylindrical tower built during the GDR era to serve as a Zeiss research center—hence its local nickname “Keksrolle” (roll of cookies). At 128 meters high, the panoramic platform offers views over the deeply incised Saale Valley and the surrounding limestone hills.

The Kunstsammlung Jena (Jena Art Collection) brings together more than 5,000 works ranging from the Middle Ages to the present, with a particular focus on German Expressionism. The museum is housed in several buildings in the historic city center.

activities.text: A hike along a section of the SaaleHorizontale, a 91 km trail that follows the limestone ridges overlooking the Saale River around Jena. The cliffs rising sheer above the river offer views down into the valley and over the city. Several possible starting points from the city center.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

visits.text: If there is one building in Berlin that speaks through its architecture, it is Daniel Libeskind’s Jewish Museum, opened in 2001: a zigzag intersected by voids around 20 m high. The Holocaust Tower, a 24 m concrete silo, is lit only by a slit, while the Garden of Exile features 49 pillars topped with Russian olive trees. The permanent exhibition is free; reserve a time slot online and arrive before 5 p.m., the last admission time. The museum is closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: “Der hohle Zahn,” the hollow tooth: this is Berliners’ nickname for the ruined tower of the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church, left standing at 71 m after the bombing of November 22, 1943. At its foot, Egon Eiermann’s church (1959–1963), which they compare to a tube of lipstick and a powder compact, is bathed in blue light from 21,292 stained-glass windows by Gabriel Loire, inspired by Chartres. Sit for a few minutes in the octagonal nave; open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: The best place to start exploring Nuremberg is at the top, at the Kaiserburg. Louis IV of Bavaria stayed here 74 times, and the Golden Bull of 1356 required every new ruler to hold his first assembly, the Hoftag, in Nuremberg. The €10 combination ticket gives you access to the Palas and its two-level chapel, the museum, the Tiefer Brunnen—a well more than 50 m deep cut into the rock and presented during a guided demonstration—and then the Sinwellturm, where peregrine falcons nest. Arrive at opening time (9 a.m. from April through September, 10 a.m. afterward): tickets are sold only on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: In AD 9, three Roman legions were annihilated here by a Germanic coalition led by Arminius. The site was only identified in 1987, when a British officer and amateur archaeologist found Roman coins in a field. The museum exhibits the famous iron Reitermaske and eight Roman gold coins.

From the top of the 40-meter tower, your gaze sweeps the Kalkrieser Berg and the Großes Moor. Below, the Germanic rampart has been reconstructed on the probable route. The 20-hectare park features themed pavilions and a treetop adventure course.

activities.text: Grab the audio guide and walk through the archaeological park following the battle route. The reconstructions of the Germanic palisade and the swamp give a concrete idea of the trap set for the legions. Admission: €9.50 adult.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Kandinsky and Gabriele Münter spent the summer of 1903 in this village at the confluence of the Naab and Vils. Since then, Kallmünz has never lost its painters. The colorful houses of the Vilsgasse, the old millstone, the gardens suspended in the rock: everything here is, in the literal sense, picturesque.

The Haus ohne Dach, carved into the limestone cliff above the Vilsgasse, was inhabited until 1937. You can still make out a corridor, two storage niches and a chamber for smoking food. Open once a year, on Tag des offenen Denkmals.

activities.text: Walk down to the confluence of the Naab and Vils for the finest view of the castle ruin. The ruin itself, reached by a steep staircase, dates to the 13th century and offers a view covering the entire Naab valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Climb Bad Tölz's Kalvarienberg for the panorama over the Isar valley and the Karwendel range. At the top, the Heilig-Kreuz-Kirche houses a Heilige Stiege, a copy of Rome's Scala Santa. Gentle ascent, fifteen minutes.

activities.text: From the Kalvarienberg summit, the baroque Way of the Cross leads back down past the Leonhardikapelle. The panorama stretches from Bad Tölz's rooftops to the Karwendel massif. Descent in ten minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Kamenz's red Rathaus stands out with its Venetian palazzo airs: built around 1847–1848 in an Italian neo-Renaissance style, it marks the old town. Kamenz is the birthplace of Enlightenment writer Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, born here in 1729. Worth knowing: the Lessing Museum is closed for renovations until spring 2027, so you follow his traces around town, not in the museum. Park near the center—everything is walkable afterward.

Completed around 1510, the Klosterkirche St. Annen blends church and sacred-art museum on the northern edge of Kamenz's old town. It preserves a rare ensemble of carved late-Gothic altarpieces, among the religious treasures of Lusatia. The painting 'Law and Grace,' painted in 1542 by a pupil of Cranach, numbers among the notable pieces. Check opening hours—they're more restricted outside peak season.

Climb the 117 steps of the Roter Turm, a remnant of Kamenz's old fortifications, a former guardpost turned prison. From its 32-meter height, the view sweeps across the old town's rooftops. The key is picked up at Kamenz-Information, so stop by before the ascent. The opening slot is limited—midday is usually your best bet.

activities.text: If blooms attract you, climb the Hutberg, the hill on Kamenz's outskirts, planted with rhododendrons and azaleas that burst into color in spring. The landscaped park rises gently to the Hutbergbühne, an amphitheater-style open-air stage. At the summit, a small viewing platform overlooks the town. Spring for flowers, summer for a concert: choose according to the program.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: Kampen carries the steepest price tag on Sylt — €8 breakfasts, luxury boutiques, villas tucked behind hedgerows. But the beach and the cliff are free. The Rotes Kliff owes its name to the iron-rich clay that turns blood-red in the late afternoon light — 30 metres of cliff face stretching 4 km between Kampen and Wenningstedt.

The Rotes Kliff runs 4 km along Sylt's west coast between Kampen and Wenningstedt: the 30-metre cliff crumbles steadily into the sea — keep 5 metres back from the edge. A wooden boardwalk has run along the top since 1979, designated a nature reserve. Kampen Lighthouse dates from 1855 and stands 40 metres tall.

activities.text: Climb the Uwe-Düne via 110 wooden steps from Kampen: at 52.5 metres, it is Sylt's highest natural point. The wooden platform gives a 360° view over the island, from List in the north to Hörnum in the south. Free and accessible at any time.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Three towers on a Nordic promontory—it's too many, and yet each deserves a stop. The Schinkelturm (1827, the oldest) was designed following plans by the Prussian Architecture Commission and remains the second-oldest lighthouse on the German Baltic coast. The Great Lighthouse (1902, 35 m) is active. The Peilturm (1927) served as a radio beacon for the Sassnitz-Trelleborg ferry line.

The Schinkelturm, built in 1827 in square red brick, is the oldest lighthouse still standing on the German Baltic coast after Travemünde lighthouse. At its feet: the Burgwall of Jaromarsburg, a Slavic rampart from the 6th to 12th centuries protecting the temple of the god Svantovit. In 1168, Danish King Valdemar I conquered and razed it. Only the circular embankment remains.

activities.text: Leave the car at Putgarten (paid parking) and walk the 1.3 km to the cape's tip—no traffic, sea wind, views over the 45-m cliff. In good weather, the Danish coast of Møn is visible on the horizon, about 30 km away. The village of Vitt, 200 m below the cape, is an untouched fishing hamlet with an octagonal 19th-century chapel.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Three bell towers, three naves, three altars, three round towers: everything comes in threes in the Dreifaltigkeitskirche Kappl. Georg Dientzenhofer built it between 1685 and 1689 on a cloverleaf plan. From the Glasberg at 599 m, the view takes in the Egerland all the way to Czechia. Free admission, open 8 a.m.–6 p.m. April to October.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe is Europe's largest terraced park (240 hectares) and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2013. Art historian Georg Dehio described it as “perhaps the most magnificent combination of architecture and landscape that the Baroque ever dared to attempt.” Construction of the park began in 1689 at the initiative of Landgrave Carl of Hesse-Kassel and continued for 150 years. Reservoirs and a hydropneumatic system feed a 350-meter Baroque cascade, a grotto with sound effects, rapids, and the Grand Fountain—a 50-meter-high geyser, the tallest in the world when it was created in 1767. The water features run every Wednesday, Sunday, and public holiday from May 1 to October 3.

The Hercules monument dominates the Bergpark from an elevation of 596 meters. The hammered copper statue, standing 8.30 meters tall, reproduces the 3rd-century Farnese Hercules. It's visible from across the city and serves as Kassel's symbol. Below the statue, a pyramidal octagon houses the head of the cascade. The entire ensemble—statue, octagon, and grotto—measures 71 meters in total height.

Kassel's documenta is the world's most important contemporary art exhibition. Held since 1955 every five years for 100 days, it takes place across multiple city venues—including the Fridericianum (1779, continental Europe's first public museum), the Documenta-Halle, and urban spaces. Permanent works from past exhibitions are visible throughout the city year-round.

The Grimmwelt, opened in 2015, is the world's largest exhibition space devoted to the Brothers Grimm's work. Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm worked in Kassel in the early 19th century, where they began collecting folk tales from the region. The annotated copies of Children's and Household Tales are inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register. The museum also presents their role as linguists and their contribution to the German dictionary.

activities.text: Walk through the iconic documenta sites in the city: the Fridericianum on Friedrichsplatz, the Documenta-Halle, and the in-situ works scattered throughout Kassel's public spaces. Even outside exhibition periods, permanent installations are visible.

An evening of illuminated water features at Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe: on selected dates listed in the program, the cascades and the Grand Fountain are lit up at nightfall. In 2026, these evenings take place on June 5 and 6 and September 11 and 12; the BergparkLeuchten festival does not take place that year.

days_plan.itin_title: Hesse, Germany Tour: Cities and Nature Parks
From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip
Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days
Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel

visits.text: The pastel façades along Kaufbeuren's Kaiser-Max-Straße survived the war without a scratch. The town, founded as a Frankish royal court around 740, kept its medieval lanes intact. You can walk the center in an hour.

Built in 1420, the Fünfknopfturm is the town's former watchtower. Its five cupolas give it a toy-like air. 92 steps with no elevator, but the panoramic rooftop view rewards the effort. Open weekends in summer.

The Crescentiakloster isn't on the usual tourist circuit, and that's just as well. This 13th-century Franciscan convent still operates. You can visit the Gedenkstätte dedicated to Crescentia Höss, beatified in 2001.

activities.text: If you pass through in July, the Tänzelfest transforms Kaufbeuren for twelve days. It's Bavaria's oldest historical children's festival: parades in medieval costume, torchlit camps. Book accommodation well in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Beneath the Befreiungshalle’s 45-meter dome, 34 white marble figures of Victory hold hands as if in a circle dance. Ludwig I had this monument built on the Michelsberg to commemorate the wars against Napoleon; it was inaugurated on October 18, 1863. The €13 combination ticket purchased at Prunn is valid here and at the Walhalla.

Unassuming when viewed from the river, the church of Kloster Weltenburg becomes theatrical the moment you step inside. At the Asam brothers’ high altar, Saint George on horseback, illuminated by a high window in the apse, emerges against the light with his flaming lance raised against the dragon. Also look for the bust of Cosmas Damian Asam, dated 1721, at the edge of the dome.

You’ll return from Weltenburg in time to visit the Archäologisches Museum, housed in the Herzogskasten, a ducal granary from the late 15th century. The exhibits trace 200,000 years of history, from the Neanderthals of the Altmühltal to the Celtic oppidum of Alkimoennis, with 13 meters of its original rampart occupying the courtyard. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., from Easter through the fall school break.

activities.text: A boat is still the most beautiful way to arrive at Kloster Weltenburg. From Kelheim, it travels upstream in about fifty minutes through the Donaudurchbruch, a gorge approximately 5.5 km long lined with cliffs up to 80 meters high; the downstream trip takes half as long. Watch for the rock nicknamed “Napoleon’s suitcase.” Service generally runs from mid-March to early November.

Sources mention monks brewing beer at Weltenburg as early as 1050; today, the Klosterbrauerei describes itself as the world’s oldest monastic brewery. Its Barock Dunkel, a dark beer, won the World Beer Cup in 2004, 2008, and 2012. Try it on-site before boarding the boat, and leave the afternoon driving to a sober driver.

days_plan.itin_title: Altmühltal and the Danube in 4 Days, from Ingolstadt to Regensburg

visits.text: Kempten calls itself Germany's oldest city, and the proof lies beneath your feet. The Greek geographer Strabo mentioned Kambodounon over two thousand years ago. Today it's a small metropolis of 70,000 inhabitants, lively and unpretentious.
Descend into the underground Erasmuskapelle, a vaulted space rediscovered beneath the market square. The atmosphere is striking: medieval walls and modern theatrical lighting. Open Tuesday to Sunday.

The gilded stucco of the Fürstäbtliche Residenz hits you the moment you step into the Thronsaal. Bavaria's first baroque residence, built in the mid-17th century. The state rooms rank among the state's finest rococo interiors.

Beneath your feet, the Cambodunum archaeological park reconstructs a Roman quarter with baths, forum, and temples. Open March through November, Tuesday to Sunday 10 a.m.–5 p.m. Allow an hour for the visit.

activities.text: If you are traveling with children, explore the Cambodunum archaeological park in Kempten. The baths and temples offer a chance to discover Roman life on site. Interactive stations and the park's app complement the visit.

The people of Kempten call the Rathausplatz their living room. In the morning, cafés roll out their tables and the vibe turns Italian. Grab a Milchkaffee facing St. Mang church and its 66-meter bell tower.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Kiel was 80% destroyed in 1944, but its waterfront was rebuilt with care around the Kieler Förde — the 17-km fjord that opens onto the Baltic. The Kiellinie, a 4-km promenade along the fjord's west bank, is the meeting point of joggers, cyclists and families. In June, Kieler Woche turns it into one of the world's largest sailing regattas.

The Kiellinie runs 4 km along the Förde from the city centre to the botanical garden: Scandinavian ferries, cargo ships and racing yachts pass within metres. At the far end, the Düsternbrooker Gehölz is a waterside woodland park.

activities.text: Take the Schlepp- und Fährgesellschaft's F2 line from Reventlou across the Kieler Förde to Dietrichsdorf or Wellingdorf. From the boat, watch the sailing boats and harbour facilities on both shores. Check the company's departure schedule before heading to the landing stage; a fare is charged for the crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Walk upstream along the opposite bank on the Am Leinritt path: according to the tourist office, this is where Klein Venedig looks its best. The former fishermen’s quarter in the Inselstadt lines the Regnitz with half-timbered houses that seem to lean against one another, complete with small gardens and moored boats. During Sandkerwa, Bamberg’s major annual festival, the facades are decorated and illuminated. The path has no steps and is wheelchair accessible; sightseeing boats pass right alongside the houses.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Hard to resist life-size dinosaurs: Saurierpark Kleinwelka, Germany's largest dinosaur park, lines up more than 200 sculptures across sixteen hectares. It all started in sculptor Franz Gruß's private garden, where he shaped his first concrete dinos as early as 1978. Entry now passes through the “Mitoseum,” opened in 2017. Open mainly April through November; buy tickets online to skip the queue.

activities.text: Lose yourself for real in the Irrgarten Kleinwelka, the maze attached to the dinosaur park. Hedges, dead ends, and false trails test young and old alike, especially at visit's end when legs tire. Count on half an hour to an hour depending on your sense of direction. Separate ticket from the Saurierpark—check if a combination deal exists on the day of your visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: Film buffs recognize these corridors instantly: during winter 1985-1986, Jean-Jacques Annaud shot the interiors of The Name of the Rose here with Sean Connery. Founded in 1136 by twelve Cistercian monks, Eberbach Abbey ranks among Germany's best-preserved abbeys. The basilica, the 13th-century lay brothers' hall, and the wine cellars each deserve an hour of exploration. Open daily 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Eberbach Abbey's basilica reveals an austere façade that contrasts with late Cistercian exuberance. Romanesque nave, Gothic choir - two centuries of construction legible in a single crossing. Its acoustics make it one of the Rheingau Music Festival's venues each summer: check the program.

activities.text: Finish with a tasting at the Cabinet-Keller or WineBar1136 in the monastery cellars. The Hessische Staatsweingüter GmbH still works the vineyard surrounding the abbey, including the Steinberg, an exclusive property since 1239. A bottle of the house Riesling feinherb costs under €10.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Thirty-two marbled columns, a balustrade that ripples like a wave, and a ceiling painted by Franz Georg Hermann: the Bibliothekssaal at Wiblingen Abbey is a visual shock. This 23-meter-long rococo hall, built between 1740 and 1750, rises through two stories. The inscription above the door promises “all the treasures of wisdom and science.”

The Benedictine abbey, founded in 1093, was secularized in 1806. Its books were scattered between Munich and Stuttgart. Only about sixty original volumes remain in the hall today. The small adjoining museum recounts this turbulent history. Around 90,000 visitors annually.

activities.text: Pair your visit with the adjacent Klosterkirche: its ceiling frescoes, painted in late baroque style, rank among Württemberg's most colorful. The complex forms part of the Upper Swabian Baroque Route.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Count Bothmer lived at 10 Downing Street before it became the Prime Minister's residence. A Hanoverian diplomat, he helped George I ascend the throne. His Schloss Bothmer at Klütz (1726-1732) is northern Germany's only English country house. Thirteen brick buildings, 12 hectares of parkland. Around €8.

activities.text: Walk along the Festonallee, an avenue of linden trees pruned into garlands, a landscape axis unique in the north. Open-air concerts in the park in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: The Energiefabrik Knappenrode occupies a former lignite briquette factory, state-of-the-art for its era. The last crew left in 1993; today, this site of the Saxon Museum of Industry tells the rise, fall, and future of the Lusatian coal basin. The red-brick halls provide the backdrop for the visit. Closed Mondays: schedule your stop another day.

activities.text: Serious industrial museum on one side, playground on the other: at the Energiefabrik Knappenrode, the youngest race off into the slide-tunnel and labyrinth while adults marvel at the giant excavators. The enormous bucket-wheel machines convey the scale of work done to extract lignite. Factor in time for a coffee at the bistro in between. Workshops and temporary exhibitions rotate—glance at the schedule.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: The Deutsches Eck juts out like a ship’s bow where the Moselle meets the Rhine. William I sits astride his horse here: a 14-meter equestrian statue atop a monument more than 37 meters tall, inaugurated in 1897. The original was dismantled after World War II; the current replica was placed on the pedestal in 1993. Climb the monument at sunset, when both rivers catch the light.

In 842, the Basilika St. Kastor hosted a decisive meeting between the sons of Louis the Pious; the following year, the Treaty of Verdun divided the Frankish Empire. Consecrated in 836, the oldest church in Koblenz now has a Romanesque appearance dating from the mid-12th century. It stands close to the lower gondola lift station; in winter, it is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

You come up for the view and stay for the ramparts: Festung Ehrenbreitstein deserves at least two hours. Perched 118 meters above the Rhine, this Prussian fortress took its present form between 1817 and 1828; the Koblenz tourist office describes it as Europe’s largest historic fortress after Gibraltar. The Landesmuseum occupies four buildings, and the Rhein-Mosel-Blick viewing platform overlooks the confluence. From March 29 to November 1, 2026, it is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Onion-domed bell towers rise above the rooftops: the Liebfrauenkirche marks the heart of Koblenz’s old town. Nearby, the Vier Türme display their ornate corner oriel windows, while the Romanesque Florinskirche watches over the Florinsmarkt. Take the Kunstgässchen, the alley linking the church to Münzplatz, one of the city’s oldest squares.

An apparently well-behaved little bronze figure, the Schängel on the Schängelbrunnen spits a jet of water well beyond the basin every few minutes. Created by Carl Burger and inaugurated in 1941 in Koblenz’s city hall square, the fountain takes its name from a local nickname derived from the French “Jean,” which originated under French rule in the 19th century. Keep your distance when taking photos.

activities.text: Cross the Rhine by gondola lift: Koblenz’s Seilbahn travels 890 meters and climbs 112 meters to the fortress. Opened in 2010 for the 2011 Bundesgartenschau, it can carry 7,600 passengers per hour in each direction in its 18 cabins. As you ascend, look for the Deutsches Eck below, at the tip of the confluence.

If the evening is mild, follow Koblenz’s Rhine promenade upstream from the Deutsches Eck to the Kurfürstliches Schloss. The former residence of the prince-electors of Trier stretches its classical facade toward the river, surrounded by extensive gardens. Sit on a riverside bench: the fortress you visited that afternoon stands silhouetted across the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier
The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz

visits.text: Climb the Herzogstand, a hikers' paradise rising to 1,731 meters between two strikingly beautiful lakes. This iconic peak offers one of Bavaria's most beautiful panoramas, taking in the Kochelsee with its steely reflections and the turquoise waters of the Walchensee in a single view. A cable car makes access easier, but reaching the summit requires walking from the upper station.

Discover the Walchensee, one of Germany's deepest and purest Alpine lakes. Its intensely blue waters, often compared to tropical lagoons, contrast magnificently with the surrounding snow-capped peaks. This naturally dammed lake served as the setting for numerous films and remains a well-kept secret among Bavarians.

Contemplate the Kochelsee, a more peaceful and accessible lake bordered by green meadows and traditional villages. It was here that painter Franz Marc, a major figure of German Expressionism, found inspiration for his famous works. The Franz Marc Museum in the nearby village pays tribute to this master of color.

activities.text: Panoramic ridge hike on the Herzogstand

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: St. Bartholomä stands on a peninsula formed by sediment deposited by the Eisbach, beneath the Watzmann’s east face. Rebuilt in 1697–1698 on the site of a chapel consecrated in 1134, the church has three red domes crowning its trefoil-shaped choir, with a layout reminiscent of Salzburg Cathedral. Admission is free; on the Saturday after August 24, pilgrims arrive on foot from Maria Alm via the Steinernes Meer.

activities.text: There is no engine noise: since 1909, electric boats have crossed Königssee between cliffs that plunge almost vertically into a lake nearly 190 m deep. Halfway to St. Bartholomä, the boatman plays a few notes facing the Echowand, and the cliff echoes the melody once, rarely twice. Buy a ticket to Salet, allowing about 1 hour 45 minutes for the round-trip boat ride, and board before 10:30 a.m. on fair-weather days.

Get off at Salet, the last stop on Königssee, and walk 15 minutes to Obersee. The trail then follows its shore, with a railing along the rock face, to Fischunkelalm; beyond it, Röthbachfall drops about 470 m, making it Germany’s highest waterfall. Allow for a 5.5 km round trip, wear shoes with good traction, and keep an eye on the last boat’s departure time.

The best shot of Königssee is taken at Malerwinkel, reached on foot, rather than from a boat deck. This viewpoint takes in the entire lake, with St. Bartholomä on its peninsula and the 2,653 m Schönfeldspitze in the background. The Malerwinkl-Rundweg loop covers 5 km, takes about 1 hour 30 minutes, and includes 160 m of ascent: save it for late in the day, after your boat ride.

days_plan.itin_title: Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits

visits.text: Walk across the Hohenzollernbrücke toward the end of the day, with the cathedral behind you and the Rhine beneath your feet. More than 1,200 trains cross it each day, and hundreds of thousands of love locks have been attached to it since 2008. Its 409 meters take about ten minutes to cross, including photo stops.

The KölnTriangle offers something the cathedral tower cannot: a view of the cathedral itself. An elevator takes you to the 28th floor, then a few steps lead to the viewing platform, more than 100 meters up, with the cathedral at eye level beyond the Hohenzollernbrücke. Admission is €5, open until 8 p.m.; closed during thunderstorms.

A shower of colored squares falls across the south transept of Cologne Cathedral: Gerhard Richter’s stained-glass window, installed in 2007, combines 11,500 pieces of glass randomly arranged by computer. The cathedral around it took more than six centuries to complete, from 1248 to 1880, including its 157-meter spires. Leave time for the Shrine of the Three Kings, made between 1190 and 1225 by Nicholas of Verdun. Since July 1, 2026, admission has cost €12: book your time slot online, between 10 a.m. and 5:30 p.m. on weekdays.

The Domschatzkammer occupies medieval vaulted cellars beneath the cathedral’s sacristy, housing reliquaries, liturgical vessels, and textiles from the 4th to the 20th century. Displays include the archbishops’ insignia, Frankish tombs from the early Middle Ages, and the Heiltumskammer, which holds the cathedral’s most precious relics. Get the combined ticket with the tower for €12 instead of €8 each, online or at the Kurienhaus ticket counter, Roncalliplatz 2.

For anyone who loves 20th-century art, the Museum Ludwig, next to the cathedral, makes a stop in Cologne worthwhile all on its own. Founded in 1976 with a donation from Peter and Irene Ludwig, it brings together around 900 works by Picasso, one of Europe’s largest collections, Pop Art by Warhol and Lichtenstein, and the most comprehensive collection of Russian avant-garde art outside Russia. Closed Mondays; on the first Thursday of the month, it stays open until 10 p.m., and a free guided tour starts on Tuesdays at 2 p.m.

Head below Groß St. Martin before looking up at its crossing tower: the excavation area reveals the foundations of Roman warehouses on which the church was built, on the site of a former island in the Rhine. The current Romanesque basilica dates from 1150 to 1250; it was devastated by bombing in 1942 and 1945, and its interior was not restored until 1985. Admission is free, but the church is closed on Mondays and remains a place of prayer: avoid service times.

Gothic in its facade, Roman underground: Cologne’s Rathaus, Germany’s oldest city hall with some 900 years of documented history, stands on the site of the ancient praetorium. Its tower dates from 1407–1414, its Renaissance loggia from 1569–1573. Afterward, walk through the nearby Alter Markt and listen: the tower’s carillon plays four times a day.

Follow the Rhine south to the Rheinauhafen peninsula: the Schokoladenmuseum, opened there in 1993 by chocolatier Hans Imhoff, welcomes around 700,000 visitors a year, more than any other museum in the city. A tropical greenhouse measuring 10 meters on each side and planted with cacao trees, a glass-walled factory, and a chocolate fountain around 3 meters tall: touristy, but well done. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; book online to go straight into the exhibition.

activities.text: “Köbes”: in the Brauhäuser of Cologne’s Old Town, this is the server who replaces your 0.2-liter Stange of Kölsch without waiting to be asked. This beer, protected in the European Union since 1997, must be brewed less than 50 km from the city. To stop the rounds, place your coaster on your empty glass.

If your calves are up to it, climb the 533 steps of Cologne Cathedral’s south tower: a spiral staircase takes you up to 75 meters, followed by a metal staircase to the platform at around 100 meters. Along the way, you pass through the chamber where eight of the cathedral’s twelve bells hang. Allow 30 to 45 minutes; there is no elevator or bag storage, and only small backpacks are allowed.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea
Cologne, Bonn, and Aachen in 3 Days: Cathedrals and Treasures
Cologne, Bonn, and Aachen in 3 Days: Cathedrals and Treasures

visits.text: Pure white against deep blue: the Königsstuhl is Rügen's tallest and best-known chalk cliff, at 118 m above the Baltic. The chalk dates from about 70 million years ago. The Skywalk, a suspended walkway above the void, opened in 2023 and offers a direct view of the wall face. Jasmund National Park (3,000 ha) is Germany's smallest national park.

The Königsstuhl cliff plunges 118 m into the Baltic and erosion makes it one of the coast's most unstable formations. Entire sections regularly fall into the sea—a natural process since the last glaciation. The Stubnitz beech forests bordering the cliffs have been designated UNESCO World Natural Heritage since 2011.

activities.text: Descend to the pebble beach from Sassnitz (8 km from the National Park Center) via the coastal trail—allow 2 hours round-trip. From below, the view of the chalk cliffs is more impressive than from the summit. Early morning, the site is calm and the raking light brings out the chalk's whiteness.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen

visits.text: Königstein Fortress occupies 9.5 hectares on a sandstone plateau rising 240 meters above the Elbe—it's one of Europe's largest mountain fortresses. Never taken by storm, it was nicknamed the “Bastille of Saxony”: a state prison from 1591 to 1922, it notably housed Johann Friedrich Böttger, inventor of European porcelain, who was imprisoned there to try to recreate his secret formula. During World War II, it served as a prisoner-of-war camp for Allied officers—General Henri Giraud escaped on April 17, 1942, by descending a rope made of knotted sheets, an action that sent Hitler into a fury. The well dug between 1563 and 1569 to supply the garrison is 152.5 meters deep—the deepest in Saxony.

activities.text: Walk around the fortress ramparts (1.7 km) with panoramic views of the Elbe valley, Saxon Switzerland National Park, and Bohemia. A panoramic elevator provides access to the plateau from below.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Saxon Switzerland in 3 Days: Bastei and Sandstone Peaks

places.name: Konigswartha

visits.text: At the heart of Germany's largest pond network, the Haus der Tausend Teiche serves as gateway to the Upper Lusatian Heath and Pond Landscape UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. The multimedia exhibition recounts carp farming, practiced here since the 13th century, and the wildlife of the reed beds. A large aquarium closes the visit. The center is located in Wartha; closed Mondays, open mainly during the day.

activities.text: Ride a bike along the Seeadlerweg, the 'white-tailed eagle path,' which winds between the ponds from the reserve's center at Wartha. The dikes offer observation points over waterbirds; in the quiet, you may encounter herons and raptors. In August, the heath turns purple—it's the most beautiful time. Bring binoculars and mosquito protection near the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

map_keywords: House of a Thousand Ponds Wartha

visits.text: Explore Konstanz on the shores of the Bodensee (Lake Constance), Germany's largest lake straddling the border with Switzerland and Austria. The lovely lakeside promenade is lined with restaurants and cafes offering views across the shimmering waters toward the Swiss Alps. The famous rotating Imperia statue at the harbor entrance completes one revolution every three minutes, a modern monument with medieval satirical roots.

Visit the fascinating open-air lake-dwelling museum in Unteruhldingen, a UNESCO World Heritage site that reconstructs Stone Age and Bronze Age settlements built on wooden stilts above the water. Allow for a round trip from Konstanz, taking the ferry to Meersburg and then continuing to Unteruhldingen. These remarkable reconstructions offer a glimpse of human life on Lake Constance more than 4,000 years ago. Archaeological finds from the lake bed vividly bring these ancient communities to life through engaging exhibitions.

Cross to Mainau Island, the famous “island of flowers” where subtropical botanical gardens, a Baroque palace and a butterfly house create a Mediterranean paradise in the heart of Europe. The gardens burst with color throughout the year, from spring tulips to summer roses and autumn dahlias. To visit Meersburg Castle, take the ferry from Konstanz to Meersburg on the opposite shore of the lake. Germany's oldest inhabited castle rises spectacularly above the lake, with some sections still occupied by the family that owns it.

activities.text: Take a boat cruise across the Bodensee to appreciate the stunning Alpine panorama from the water

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest
Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: A basalt arc so slender it seems unreal: the Rakotzbrücke, known as the 'Devil's Bridge,' reflects in Lake Rakotz to form a perfect circle. Built between the 1860s and 1880s in basalt stone, it cannot be crossed—you admire it from the shore. The reflection depends on wind and light, so aim for a calm morning. On fine days, you won't be alone in front of this backdrop.

activities.text: Reducing Kromlau to its Instagram shot would be a shame: the Rhododendron Park surrounding the bridge deserves a proper stroll. Across roughly 200 hectares, you'll encounter curious stone structures, like the 'Basaltkirche' jutting out of the water and the 'Heaven and Hell' grotto. The rhododendron bloom runs from May to July—that's the prime time. Outside peak season, check the opening hours for the village cafés; many close.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: Stop in Wismar along the way, approximately 41 kilometers from Kühlungsborn, a 40-minute drive—the Hanseatic old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002. The Marktplatz, one of the largest in northern Germany, is surrounded by red-brick Gothic façades. The town belonged to Sweden from 1648 to 1803, giving it a blend of German and Scandinavian architecture that is rare in the region.

Kühlungsborn was founded in the late 19th century when three independent coastal villages merged in 1938. The promenade follows the sea for several kilometers, lined with seaside villas whose wooden façades are typical of the Bäderarchitektur style. Head down to the beach through one of the access points between the streets—the fine sand stretches as far as the eye can see.
The pier at Kühlungsborn East measures 240 meters and extends into the Baltic Sea—it's the best spot to watch ferries offshore and observe sunsets over the water.

activities.text: Rent a bike and head into the Kühlung Forest, 133 hectares of beech and pine that extend directly behind the resort. You'll find Bronze Age burial mounds, enormous glacial erratics deposited by ice sheets, and paths that emerge onto coastal panoramas. The Strandkorb—the woven wicker beach chair typical of Baltic beaches—awaits you on the sand for your afternoon break.

Bastorf Lighthouse stands on Cape Bukspitze, a few kilometers west of Kühlungsborn. At 20.8 meters tall, it's one of Germany's smallest lighthouses but one of the best positioned—it towers on a cliff at a remarkable height above the sea.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: Lakes, Castles, and the Baltic Coast

activities.text: Head east along Kurfürstendamm, from Adenauerplatz to Breitscheidplatz: this 3.5 km boulevard was West Berlin’s premier shopping showcase during the economic miracle. Beginning in 1875, Bismarck had it developed into a 53 m-wide avenue along an old road leading to the Grunewald hunting lodge. Save some energy for KaDeWe, which opened in 1907, and its sixth-floor gourmet food department.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: At the Benediktinerabtei Maria Laach, take time to slow down rather than simply ticking off its facades. The Romanesque church serves an active monastic community beside a lake formed by volcanic activity. The contrast between architecture and landscape makes the visit rewarding. Check the service schedule before setting off: reflection may take precedence over photography and tourist access.

activities.text: You can extend your visit to Maria Laach at the Klostergärtnerei instead of getting straight back behind the wheel. The abbey runs several businesses, including a garden center and a shop selling products. This detour reveals a working monastery beyond its church. Check the shops’ opening hours separately, and keep purchases light before your walk along the shores of Laacher See.

If the sky clears, prioritize the shores of Laacher See over the shops. This lake fills a volcanic depression surrounded by woods and reed beds; Maria Laach owns the land. Choose an out-and-back walk that fits your schedule instead of a long loop. Stay on permitted paths and bring a waterproof jacket.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: The Lech cascades down five stone steps over a drop of 7.7 meters at the Lechfall, a ten-minute walk from the old town. It's no accident: Füssen locals built these tiers in 1787 to harness water power. In spring, snowmelt makes the spectacle impressive.

activities.text: From the Maxsteg or the 2014 panoramic platform, watch the Lech's power as it rushes into the gorge. Best moment: early morning, when light hits the turquoise water. Free access.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: The worm-eaten planks creak, the reed roofs smell of damp hay: the Freilandmuseum Lehde recreates four nineteenth-century farms from different parts of the Spreewald. One of Brandenburg's oldest open-air museums. A family bedroom where seven people slept in a single alcove bed—the panels present this as a fact hard to imagine today. Open April through October, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.

activities.text: You'll reach the Freilandmuseum in Lehde on foot from the parking area in Lübbenau-Ortsteil Lehde. On the way, count the stepped wooden bridges characteristic of the Spreewald.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Less well known than Lehde, Leipe is the real island village. Perched on an 800-by-400-meter sandbank surrounded by the Spree and the Leiper Graben, it's home to a handful of residents and wasn't connected to the road network until 1969. Before that, the doctor, the mail carrier, children going to school—everything was done by boat. The Heimatstube displays Sorbian costumes and utensils from another era.

activities.text: If you have a canoe or kayak, the channels are calmest around Leipe. Several Lübbenau rental operators offer return shuttles; count on about 3 hours of paddling one way from the Großer Hafen for a peaceful arrival in the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: The Thomaskirche is Leipzig's musical heart. Johann Sebastian Bach was cantor here from 1723 until his death in 1750—he composed the St. Matthew Passion, the Christmas Oratorio, and more than 150 cantatas here. His tomb stands before the altar. The Thomanerchor, founded in 1212, is one of the world's oldest choral ensembles and still performs motets every Friday and Saturday. Martin Luther himself preached from this pulpit.

The Gewandhaus Orchestra, founded in 1743 by Leipzig's merchant bourgeoisie—a clean break from the tradition of princely or ecclesiastical orchestras—is one of the world's oldest symphony ensembles. Felix Mendelssohn was its director and it was under his direction that Bach's St. Matthew Passion was rediscovered in 1829, after a century of oblivion. Richard Wagner is a native of Leipzig, Robert Schumann lived and composed here. More than 500 composers have reportedly resided in the city.

The Nikolaikirche, a Gothic church remodeled in the 16th century with a green and white palm-themed neoclassical interior, is the church of the Peaceful Revolution of 1989. It was here that the Monday demonstrations (Montagsdemonstrationen) began, with prayers for peace organized every week since 1982. On October 9, 1989, 70,000 people marched through Leipzig's streets—it was the turning point that precipitated the fall of the Berlin Wall.

The Völkerschlachtdenkmal, inaugurated in 1913 for the centenary of the Battle of the Nations, is Germany's largest monument: 91 meters high, an interior staircase of 500 steps, colossal sandstone statues of warriors in the Wilhelmine monumental tradition. The October 1813 battle, which pitted Napoleon against the allied Prussian, Austrian, Russian, and Swedish forces, left 90,000 dead in four days at Leipzig's gates—one of the Napoleonic era's deadliest.

The Spinnerei, in the Plagwitz district in the west of the city, is a former cotton mill built in 1884 that employed up to 3,500 workers. Since the 1990s, its 10 hectares of industrial buildings have been converted into artist studios, galleries, cafes, and cultural spaces—more than 100 artists work there. The “Neue Leipziger Schule,” a figurative painting movement influential in global contemporary art in the 2000s, was born here.

The Mädlerpassage, one of the historic covered passageways in central Leipzig, houses Auerbachs Keller in its cellars—a tavern whose origins date back to 1525. Goethe frequented it during his Leipzig student years and made it the setting for a scene in Faust: Mephistopheles makes wine gush from a wooden table. Two groups of statues at the entrance depict the scene.

activities.text: BMW factory tour
Concert or motet at the Thomaskirche. Friday evening and Saturday afternoon motets with the Thomanerchor are free and open to all—it's one of Germany's most authentic musical experiences.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

visits.text: View the Burgruine Leuchtenberg from outside, perched on a granite cone at 585 m. Mentioned as early as 1124, it belonged to the landgraves whose title was eventually borne by an emperor of Brazil and a king of Sweden. The interior and outer courtyard are currently closed to the public: do not plan to visit the chapel or the knights' hall.

activities.text: From the Marktplatz in Leuchtenberg, look at the fortress silhouette dominated by its square keep. The castle's current closure prevents access to the courtyard and the view from the keep. The Burgfestspiele are usually held in summer: check their program before planning to attend a performance in the courtyard.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Dubbed the “Märchenschloss Württembergs,” Lichtenstein Castle perches at 817 m above the village of Honau. Count Wilhelm von Württemberg commissioned it after reading Wilhelm Hauff's novel in 1826. The neo-Gothic castle, completed in 1842, remains the private property of the ducal family of Urach.

The 30-minute guided tour winds through period-furnished salons and concludes on a balcony with vertiginous views over the Echaz valley. The 2009 film Dornröschen was shot here. Closed January–February.

activities.text: Combine your visit with the nearby Nebelhöhle: 141 steps lead down into this stalactite cave in the Swabian Alb. Open from April to October. The Maultaschenwirt at the cave entrance serves homemade Maultaschen.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: At 80 meters up, the wind cuts through the structure and the rivets rumble: Lichterfeld's Abraumförderbrücke F60 is as much a physical experience as a historical one. At 502 meters long and weighing 11,000 tonnes, the F60 operated for only 13 months in 1991–1992 before being shut down for economic reasons. Nicknamed “der liegende Eiffelturm der Lausitz”. Ninety-minute guided tours starting at 11:30 a.m.

activities.text: The Bergheider See adjoins the F60: a body of water formed by flooding the same open-pit mine, with a fine sandy beach accessible on foot from the parking lot. Twenty minutes' walk under the structure to finish the itinerary with your feet in the water.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

activities.text: If your legs are still up to it after the fortress, climb Lilienstein from its trailhead parking lot. Two routes reach the plateau: the southern slope has the steepest stairs, while the northern route offers a gentler climb. Choose the northern route for the out-and-back hike and keep well away from the edges.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxon Switzerland in 3 Days: Bastei and Sandstone Peaks

places.name: Limburg An Der Lahn

visits.text: Seven towers, a red-and-white façade, a limestone outcrop above the Lahn: Limburg Cathedral (1235) strikes first by its silhouette. The interior mixes massive Rhenish Romanesque with early luminous Gothic. No other church in Germany has seven towers.

Limburg locals claim that Römer 2-4-6 is Germany's oldest freestanding half-timbered building, dated 1289. True or not, the Fischmarkt lane around it concentrates 13th-century façades in a tiny space. The contrast with the cathedral looming overhead is striking.

Cross the old stone Lahnbrücke (replaced in 1315, rebuilt since). On the other side, the view of the cathedral rising above the slate rooftops is the city's postcard shot. The Farbmühle, an old dye mill at the foot of the rock, makes a good photo landmark.

activities.text: If you stay for dinner, restaurants on Salzgasse and Fischmarkt serve Hessian cuisine in half-timbered settings. The cathedral is illuminated after sunset. Limburg is well served by train (ICE at Limburg-Süd), convenient if you're returning the car here.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

map_keywords: Limburg an der Lahn Old Town

visits.text: Begin the route on Lindau Island on Lake Constance (Bodensee). The old town occupies a 70-hectare island that's been linked to the mainland by a railway bridge since 1853. Two iconic guardians stand at the harbor entrance: the Mangturm, a former 13th-century lighthouse 37 meters tall that guided boats on the lake from 1230, and the new white lighthouse built between 1853 and 1856—Bavaria's only lighthouse. The 6-meter sandstone statue of the Bavarian lion, the work of sculptor Johann von Halbig unveiled in 1856, completes the scene.

Stroll down Maximilianstrasse, the old town's main artery, lined with burgher houses in varied architectural styles—Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque—forming a surprisingly harmonious row. Along the way, stop at Reichsplatz to see the 15th-century Altes Rathaus with its fresco-painted facade. Lindau was a free imperial city from 1275 to 1805 and hosted several Diets of the Holy Roman Empire at this town hall.

Continue east along the Deutsche Alpenstraße—Germany's oldest tourist route, inaugurated in 1933, which links Lindau to Berchtesgaden over 450 km along the Alps. The first major stop is Bad Hindelang and its Oberjochpass: 106 bends over 5 km to climb 300 meters, including 9 hairpins winding spectacularly above the village. Built in 1895, the Jochstraße was already a feat of road engineering—in 1662, 15,850 barrels of salt passed through here each year on the backs of 300 horses. Allow for a round trip within the day from Lindau to Bad Hindelang and the Oberjochpass.

Halfway up the Oberjochpass, stop at the Kanzel, a viewpoint offering a panoramic view of the Ostrach valley, Bad Hindelang and Bad Oberdorf below, with the Nagelfluhkette and the 2,224-meter Nebelhorn in the background. It is one of the best viewpoints accessible by car in the Bavarian Alps. Allow for a round trip within the day from Lindau to reach this viewpoint.

activities.text: Take a ferry from Lindau harbor along the shores of the Bodensee toward Bregenz (Austria) or Friedrichshafen. From the water, the silhouette of the island's old town, with its two lighthouses and colorful facades, comes fully into view—it is from out on the lake that Lindau truly reveals itself.

A self-guided walk at the Aussichtspunkt Kanzel on the Oberjochpass, with a short path from the parking lot leading to the viewpoint in 2 minutes. In fine weather, the panorama extends to the Austrian ranges. Allow for a round trip within the day from Lindau for this walk.

German Alpine Road: Lake Constance to Königssee
