Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: Schloss Linderhof is the only castle Ludwig II saw completed. Small in size, extravagant in décor: the bedroom drowns in gold, and the Venus Grotto recreates a Tannhäuser scene with an artificial lake and colored lighting. Online booking recommended.

activities.text: Linderhof's Italian-style park unfolds its terraces, fountains, and Moorish pavilion in a valley of the Ammergauer Alpen. The grand fountain spouts every hour in summer. Allow an hour to stroll.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: At the Ellenbogen — Sylt's “forearm”, the island's northern tip — the wind cuts in from both sides at once: North Sea to the west, Wadden Sea to the east, Denmark visible 12 km away. It is private land that the owner opens for an €8 car toll; walkers and cyclists pass freely on the dune paths.

The Lister Hafen, in the north of the island, sends ferries to Rømø (Denmark). Fishing boats sell Sylt oysters directly on the quay — Sylt is one of the few places in Germany where oyster farming still survives.

activities.text: Take a ferry to Rømø from List — 45 minutes to the Danish island. Rømø has the widest beaches in Scandinavia at low tide: up to 2 km of dry sand. The wind drives the land yachts.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: “Ley” for rock, “loren” for listening: the Loreley is said to be the rock that listens to the echo of the rapids. On the plateau, the Kultur- und Landschaftspark Loreley, which is free to enter, links six viewpoints; a passage through a cleft leads to the Felsenspitze, around 125 meters above the Rhine. Come early in the morning to have the tip almost to yourself.

A touch theatrical, but effective: the Mythoshalle, which opened in 2025 on the Loreley plateau, stages a recreated rock with light, sound, and mist. The sorceress first appeared in 1800 in a ballad by Clemens Brentano set in Bacharach, before Heine’s 1824 poem, set to music by Silcher in 1838, established her here. In November and December, opening hours are 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz

visits.text: Lorsch Abbey was founded in 764 during the reign of Pepin the Short, Charlemagne's father. It became one of the most important cultural centers of the early Middle Ages, housing one of Europe's largest libraries and a renowned scriptorium. Upon the death of Louis II the German in 876, the abbey became the necropolis of the Carolingian kings of East Francia. Of this once immense complex, only the Königshalle (Torhalle) remains standing: a monumental 17-meter portico built around the mid-9th century with a polychrome facade alternating light and dark bands over arcades inspired by antiquity. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991, it's one of the rare Carolingian buildings to have retained its original appearance. Its exact function remains debated—library, reception hall, or ceremonial gateway? The Lorsch Pharmacopoeia, written around 800 in the abbey, has been inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register since 2013 as the first herbal medicine treatise.

activities.text: Walk through the Lorsch Abbey site: the footprints of buildings that no longer stand (basilica, cloister, monastic buildings) were marked out in the lawns during the 2017 renovation by Topotek1. The medicinal herb garden behind the tithe barn is planted with species mentioned in the Lorsch Pharmacopoeia.

days_plan.itin_title: Hesse, Germany Tour: Cities and Nature Parks
From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Touristy, yes, but Lübben's Schlossinsel delivers on its promise. This six-hectare island in the town center brings together the castle museum (including the hall of coats of arms), a water activity course, and the SpreeLagune footbridge that stretches 107 meters above the water. Avoid the Christmas market weekend: the lines spill onto the bridges.

The scent of old timber still lingers in the Paul-Gerhardt-Kirche, a late-Gothic church with a nave and two aisles named for the local Lutheran poet. The bell tower's platform is 22 meters up—Vera Städter, the only female tower keeper in Brandenburg and Berlin since 2011, guides visitors up 115 steps through history three times a week. Schedule details at luebben.de.

activities.text: You'll find a punt boatman first thing in the morning at the Schlossinsel's small harbor. The Spree boats carry about twenty people and leave on demand. Budget 90 minutes for a basic loop; the boatman stands to propel the boat with a pole called a Rudel.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Kitsch on the outside, but Lübbenau's Spreewald-Museum in the Torbogenhaus on Topfmarkt is worth the hour it takes to visit. The museum recreates a regional town circa 1900 with a grocery selling colonial goods, a furrier's workshop, and steam locomotive 99 57 03 from the Spreewaldbahn. Founded in 1899 by Paul Fahlisch, who launched tourism in the Spreewald.

Lübbenau locals simply call it “der Große Hafen” and gather there every morning as they would at a café. Lübbenau's Großer Spreewaldhafen is where Theodor Fontane boarded more than 150 years ago for his excursions in the Hochwald. Today the Gurkenmeile has a row of pickle producers along the waterfront.

activities.text: If you have a choice, take the Wotschofska-Tour: a 5-hour 30-minute round trip along channels without motor traffic to the forest inn on the island of alders. Departure at 10:30 a.m., €28 per adult. The 2-hour version at €17 works if the afternoon is packed.

You'll taste the pickles on the Gurkenmeile: more than ten local producers offer different recipes with garlic, herbs or mustard. A fresh, crunchy pickle is quite different from what you find in a jar.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Built between 1464 and 1478 under the direction of Hinrich Helmstede, the Holstentor leans slightly on its marshy foundation—and it's precisely this flaw that makes it human. Its two round red-brick towers appear on the German two-euro coin. It's one of only two of Lübeck's four medieval gates still standing. The interior museum traces Hanseatic commercial power: allow one hour, arrive early.

Lübeck's seven spires hover permanently over the city, but it's the Marienkirche that induces vertigo. Its two towers reach 125 m—it was for a long time the city's tallest structure. Its melted bells, which fell during the 1942 bombing, remain in place on the floor as testimony. A lesser-known detail: Dietrich Buxtehude served as organist here from 1668 to 1707, and the young Bach traveled from Arnstadt to hear him play.

The people of Lübeck saved their Altstadt from a wave of demolitions in the 1970s through a citizens' campaign—the city was listed by UNESCO in 1987. The ensemble covers 81 hectares of medieval streets, gabled houses and the six Salzspeicher (salt warehouses, built between 1579 and 1745) facing the Holstentor. The marzipan made here since the 15th century is sold by the piece in the Niederegger shops.

The European Hansemuseum, opened in 2015 in the former convent buildings of the Burgkloster, traces a thousand years of Hanseatic trade across three floors and 5,000 m². It's the largest museum dedicated to the Hansa in Europe. The scenography avoids archive mode—reconstructions of merchant offices in Bruges, Novgorod, and Bergen give flesh to what this network was.

activities.text: Stroll along the Fischergrube, the old seafarers' street running down to the Trave. A stone's throw from the top of the street, the Jakobikirche, the seafarers' church, keeps in one of its chapels a lifeboat from the sailing ship Pamir, lost at sea in 1957. Opposite, the Schiffergesellschaft, the sea captains' guild house built in 1535, is now a restaurant whose great hall is hung with model ships.

The scent of marzipan invades Breite Straße from morning on. The Niederegger confectionery, installed opposite the Rathaus since 1806, sells its almond paste in two hundred forms—in slices, figurines, cakes. The upstairs café offers a view of the pedestrian street without having to order anything expensive.

Crossing the Trave by rowboat from the Holstenbrücke quay takes 20 min and provides a view of the Salzspeicher and Holstentor from the river—an angle street photographers don't capture. Boatmen also offer longer circuits to the outer harbor. Season April-October, departures as demand arises.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen

visits.text: Dubbed “Versailles of the North,” Ludwigslust Palace surprises with its resemblance to a French palace set on the Mecklenburg plains. A ducal residence from 1765 to 1837, it conceals a Goldener Saal whose papier-mâché decorations imitate stucco. The 127 ha English-style park is free to enter, with free parking.

activities.text: Walk up Schlossstrasse from the palace: this straight baroque avenue, lined with courtiers' houses, reveals a town designed entirely as the palace's setting. Stop for a craft beer at the Orangerie.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Built in 1271 on a sandbar in the meanders of the Stever river, Burg Vischering is one of the oldest and best-preserved castles in the Münsterland. A 16th-century fire led to a Renaissance rebuild that has remained intact ever since. The museum offers a combined Vorburg + Hauptburg ticket for €7.50.

Defensive and austere — and yet the park between Lüdinghausen's two castles, open since 2018, reveals a bucolic path with eight-hundred-year-old trees, a stork's nest on the north side and tiny bridges over the Stever. Burg Vischering and Burg Lüdinghausen are ten minutes apart on foot.

activities.text: Follow the moat toward Burg Lüdinghausen along the Kapitelweg, lined with busts of clergymen - an atmosphere blending the grotesque with serenity. Allow ten minutes on foot. Burg Lüdinghausen hosts cultural events.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: You expect a hedge maze and find a colossal granite boulder field. The Felsenlabyrinth Luisenburg, designated a national natural monument in January 2026, has boulders several meters across, between which you weave along walkways and metal stairs. Goethe visited in 1820 and was astounded. Admission: €4.50 for adults, €9 for a family ticket.

activities.text: Allow a good two hours for the marked circuit (blue arrows up, red arrows down). Wear proper hiking shoes, even in summer: the granite turns slippery the moment it rains. At the summit, the Bundesstein offers a view worth the effort.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Lüneburg grew rich on salt for a thousand years, then nearly sank into the ground: the city is built on a pillar of salt that is slowly dissolving beneath its foundations. The result is Gothic façades tilted like exhausted dominoes — and the charm comes precisely from that instability. The salt works closed in 1980, but the houses are still standing.

Built from 1405, Lüneburg's Altes Rathaus is an accumulation of styles spanning six centuries — Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque — stacked together without contradiction. The councillors' chamber with its 16th-century glazed tiles is accessible on a guided tour. Check with the tourist office for opening times.

Head down to the Stintmarkt, the old harbour on the Ilmenau, where the medieval wooden crane from the 14th century still stands on the quay. It was used to load barges with salt bound for Lübeck. Today the terraces have taken over from the cargo — views across half-timbered warehouses included.

activities.text: The Deutsches Salzmuseum is worth two unhurried hours: housed in the former salt works that closed in 1980, it traces the salt industry from antiquity to the 19th century. Giant extraction vats, horse-powered wheels, the long rivalry with Lübeck — all meticulously reconstructed.

The weathered brickwork and tilting houses of the old town are best seen in the evening: the gabled façades of Am Sande and Grapengießerstraße are lit up and the day-trippers are gone. End with a glass of Lüneburger Pils at one of the Kneipen on the Stintmarkt.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands
Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Immerse yourself in the history of the Protestant Reformation at Lutherstadt Wittenberg, cradle of a movement that transformed Europe. It was here, on October 31, 1517, that Martin Luther allegedly nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, triggering a spiritual and intellectual revolution. This monumental portal, now in bronze, attracts visitors from around the world who come to pay tribute at this symbolic site.

Visit St. Mary's Church where Martin Luther preached regularly, a Gothic edifice at the heart of the old town listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Castle Church houses the tombs of Luther and his collaborator Philipp Melanchthon. The market square, dominated by the Luther monument and Renaissance facades, forms one of the finest urban ensembles in central Germany.

Explore the many historic buildings in the old town that bear witness to this pivotal period in European history. The Lutherhaus is closed for renovation until 2027; instead, discover the temporary exhibition devoted to Martin Luther in the neighboring Augusteum. Cross the Elbe bridge to reach the floodplain meadows, where preserved nature offers a peaceful contrast to this intense cultural heritage.

activities.text: Walk through the Elbe meadows to enjoy the preserved natural surroundings

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The Lychen Timber Rafting Museum gives concrete meaning to the lakes visitors come to admire. Timber was once floated out of the region toward major cities; tools, clothing, and models reveal the work behind this vacation landscape. Pay particular attention to the miniature model tracing the trees’ journey to the waterways. The museum is normally open on Tuesdays from 12 p.m. to 4 p.m.; call before visiting.

activities.text: The reflections on Großer Lychensee invite you to finish without another list of monuments. This lake belongs to Lychen’s network of seven lakes, within Uckermärkische Seen Nature Park; here, water connects both the landscapes and the history of timber rafting. Choose a short walk from a public access point, keep private shorelines off your route, and plan your return trip before lingering.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeastern Brandenburg: Abbey, Forest, and Lakes in 3 Days

visits.text: Discover the Green Citadel, an architectural masterpiece designed by Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser. This unique building with its organic shapes, vibrant colors, and green roofs represents a revolutionary vision of urban architecture. Its colorful columns and irregular windows create a fascinating visual experience that defies traditional architectural conventions.

Admire the majestic Magdeburg Cathedral, the first Gothic edifice erected on German soil. This imposing cathedral, whose construction began in 1209, houses the tomb of Emperor Otto I the Great. Its soaring vaults and medieval sculptures bear witness to eight centuries of spiritual and artistic history at the heart of Germany.

Explore the Elbauenpark and its Millennium Tower, an interactive attraction tracing 6,000 years of scientific and technological history. This 60-meter tower offers hands-on experiences across five levels to understand humanity's great discoveries. The park also houses the famous Sandman figure, an iconic character from East German television.

activities.text: Stroll through the Old Market and discover Otto von Guericke's Magdeburg hemispheres
Visit the Johanniskirche, a Gothic church rebuilt after World War II

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Imposing outside, almost intimate inside: St. Martin’s Cathedral in Mainz strikes both notes. Archbishop Willigis began construction around 975; the building burned on the very day of its consecration in 1009, and Archbishop Bardo consecrated it again in 1036. Look for the two facing choirs and the funerary monuments of more than forty archbishops. Admission is free from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and from 1 p.m. on Sunday.

Mainz’s most precious treasure can now be seen in a natural history museum. While its new building is under construction, the Gutenberg-Museum reopened in November 2024 in the left wing of the Naturhistorisches Museum under the name Gutenberg-Museum MOVED. In a walk-in vault, two copies of the 42-line Bible face each other. Time your visit for one of the hourly printing demonstrations; admission is 10 euros, with extended hours on Thursday until 8 p.m.

Head to St. Stephen’s Church in Mainz and let your eyes adjust to the blue. Marc Chagall began designing its nine stained-glass windows in 1978, at age 91: six in the east choir and three in the transept. Continue into the cloister dating from 1499, with its net vaults and pendant bosses. From March to October, the church is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and from noon on Sunday; in winter, it closes at 4:30 p.m.

The Kirschgarten fits into a small cobblestone square, yet packs in so much: half-timbered houses from the 15th to the 18th century, sandstone, and a fountain of the Virgin Mary in the center. Built around 1500, the Haus zum Aschaffenberg is the oldest known half-timbered house in Mainz. Continue along Augustinerstraße, a main street in the southern old town, and step into the Augustinerkirche, spared by the wars, to admire its stucco work and 18th-century organ.

activities.text: The smell of fresh bread, the voices of produce growers, crates stacked at the foot of the towers: Mainz’s Wochenmarkt fills the squares around the cathedral on Tuesday, Friday, and Saturday from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Come at 9 a.m. to browse without having to elbow your way through.

Weather permitting, spend the end of the afternoon on Mainz’s Rhine promenade near Fischtorplatz. With lawns, wide paths, and river views, it is also one of the locations for Saturday’s Marktfrühstück. Walk from the cathedral to the riverbank in just a few minutes, then follow the water downstream.

“Weck, Worscht und Woi”: this is how Mainz locals sum up their national dish—a bread roll, a sausage, and wine. Mainz has been part of the Great Wine Capitals network since 2008, and wine here is often ordered as a “Schoppe,” mixed with sparkling water. Settle into a Weinstube in the old town in the evening to sample wines from Rheinhessen.

days_plan.itin_title: The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz

visits.text: Malchow is an “island town” set between two lakes, linked by a swing bridge (Drehbrücke) that opens every hour to let boats pass.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: These two neighboring castles did not form a single complex: the Manderscheider Burgen face each other above the Lieser. Oberburg and Niederburg define the valley’s skyline, with the river running between their sites. Start with the viewpoints to understand why their proximity is misleading. Check access to Niederburg and avoid turning each ruin into a lengthy separate visit.

The Maarmuseum Manderscheid deserves a place on your itinerary if the lakes have left you with more questions than answers. An easy-to-understand model explains the structure of a maar, and the displays connect volcanic activity with the landscapes of the Eifel. It is a useful stop in bad weather. Check opening hours before you come and focus on the geological exhibits rather than rushing through without reading.

activities.text: You can follow a short section of the Manderscheider Burgenstieg to see how the ruins sit within their valley. The trail combines wooded terrain with views of the Manderscheider Burgen; it complements visits inside the sites without repeating them. Ask the tourist office for a suitable route. Keep to a short loop and wear shoes with good traction, as the day continues toward Gerolstein and then Vogelsang.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: A single ground-floor room: that was all the Schiller family rented when Friedrich was born here on November 10, 1759. Schillers Geburtshaus, a craftsman’s house rebuilt after the fire of 1693, became a museum in 1859, making it one of the oldest literary memorial sites in the German-speaking world. Inside, you can see a christening cap and a period child’s outfit. Open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. April through October, and from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. in winter.

Next, climb to the Schillerhöhe, developed as a place for celebrations in the 1830s, to visit two neighboring museums. The Schiller-Nationalmuseum, opened in 1903, has presented the “Schiller!” exhibition since 2025, with some 400 items exploring the political poet. Next door, David Chipperfield’s Literaturmuseum der Moderne displays more than 180 manuscripts and objects from the 20th century. Between visits, stroll through the half-timbered old town, rebuilt after the fire set by Mélac’s troops in 1693. Both museums are closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Few churches can claim such an early start: begun in 1235, Marburg’s Elisabethkirche is considered Germany’s oldest purely Gothic church. Its two towers, about 80 meters tall, watch over the reliquary of Saint Elizabeth, made of oak clad in gilded silver and completed in 1249, and Hindenburg’s tomb, installed here in 1946. During the ongoing restoration, the rear choirs remain outside the visitor route; the nave and reliquary can be visited from 10 a.m.

Copper wings flap above the square: every hour, the rooster on the clock of Marburg’s Rathaus comes to life as the neighboring trumpeter sounds. The town hall, built from 1512 to 1527, occupies the south side of the Marktplatz, opposite Saint George’s Fountain. Stand near the fountain a few minutes before the hour for a good view of the gable dating from 1581.

“I believe there are more steps in the street than in the houses,” wrote Jacob Grimm, and the climb to the Landgrafenschloss proves him right. At the top, the 482 m² Fürstensaal ranks among Central Europe’s largest secular Gothic halls, the chapel dates from 1288, and the castle was where Luther and Zwingli debated in 1529. Open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. except Mondays; bus 10 saves you the climb.

Marburg’s Alte Universität is a reminder that, since 1527, the city has been home to the first Protestant university to endure, founded at the initiative of Landgrave Philip. Its current wings date from 1873 to 1891 and stand beside the Universitätskirche, a former Dominican church begun in 1291. The Brothers Grimm studied here under the jurist Savigny from 1802 to 1806; look on the church for the light installation Sterntaler, station 5 on the Grimm-Dich-Pfad.

You will end the day at the Kunstmuseum Marburg, Biegenstraße 11, a museum opened in 1927 and renovated in 2018. Paintings by artists from the Willingshausen colony in the Schwalm region and works by Otto Ubbelohde, a celebrated illustrator of the Grimms’ fairy tales, share space with Kirchner and the postwar avant-garde. Open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Tuesdays; a combination ticket includes the Landgrafenschloss.

activities.text: There are no large signs for the Grimm-Dich-Pfad: its fairy tales hide on Marburg’s walls. Its 15 stations lead from the fish in The Fisherman and His Wife, at the Old Botanical Garden, to Snow White’s mirror against the castle wall and Cinderella’s red slipper in the vineyard below. Pick up the brochure at the tourist office, Wettergasse 6, and wear good shoes for the stairs.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip
Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel

visits.text: Few mining town squares look as geometric as Marienberg’s Marktplatz: a square covering about one hectare, part of the grid plan drawn up by Ulrich Rülein von Calw for the town’s founding in 1521. Nearby, St. Marien lost its interior in the fire of 1610. Finish at the Roter Turm and Zschopauer Tor, remnants of the town walls.

The Museum sächsisch-böhmisches Erzgebirge occupies the Bergmagazin, a granary built for the mining community between 1806 and 1809 and converted into a museum in 2006. Three stories intersect here: the mining town, Germans and Czechs living as neighbors, and the building’s own history. Exhibits are in German and Czech; open Tuesday through Sunday until 4 p.m., so arrive before 3 p.m.

If you visit on a weekend, aim for 1 p.m. or 2:30 p.m. at the Rudolphschacht horse whim in Lauta: horses turn the mechanism that hauled ore from 1838 to 1877. Restored in 2006, the site also offers access to the shaft down to a depth of 20 m. On weekdays, guided tours run at 1 p.m. and 2:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: The Ore Mountains in 3 Days: Mines, Toys, and Fichtelberg

visits.text: It was called “Marienglas,” or Mary’s glass: this transparent gypsum was used in place of glass over pictures of the Virgin Mary. In the Marienglashöhle, between Friedrichroda and Bad Tabarz, the crystal cave discovered in 1784 holds crystals up to 90 centimeters long, preserved since their extraction was banned in 1848. The guided tour lasts about 45 minutes and involves around a hundred steps: bring a fleece, as temperatures stay at 8 to 10 °C even in the height of summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach

visits.text: If you reach Marienplatz shortly before noon, find a spot facing the Neues Rathaus: the Glockenspiel and its 43 bells reenact a wedding tournament from 1568, followed by the coopers’ dance, at 11 a.m. and noon, plus 5 p.m. from March through October. This neo-Gothic backdrop was only completed in 1905, after nearly forty years of construction. Afterward, two elevators take you to the top of the 85 m tower, with 20-minute time slots starting at €7.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

activities.text: The Markthalle came within one vote of disappearing: that was the margin by which the city council decided to preserve it in the early 1970s. Completed in 1914 to designs by Martin Elsaesser, it conceals 33 stalls behind its Jugendstil facade, beneath a glass roof supported by concrete beams without a single pillar. Put together a quick lunch here, then head upstairs for home goods and gifts. Open weekdays from 7:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. and Saturdays from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Two churches face each other across Ludwigsburg’s Marktplatz: the Protestant Stadtkirche to the west and the Catholic Dreieinigkeitskirche to the east, on opposite sides of a square measuring about 110 m by 80 m, designed in the 18th century by Donato Giuseppe Frisoni. At its center, the fountain bears a statue of Duke Eberhard Ludwig, the city’s founder, who was nevertheless reluctant to fund a church. Come on Tuesday, Thursday, or Saturday morning for the market, starting at 7 a.m.

activities.text: End the day beneath the arcades of the Marktplatz, where restaurants and shops occupy the ground floors. This square also hosts Ludwigsburg’s Barock-Weihnachtsmarkt during Advent and its Venezianische Messe. Settle into an outdoor seat facing one of the two churches: the Baroque setting is all you need for an aperitif, and the palace is just a few minutes away on foot.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: It is hard to find a more complete example: UNESCO, which listed Kloster Maulbronn in 1993, considers it the best-preserved medieval monastery north of the Alps. The Cistercians settled here in 1147. Step through the Paradies, a porch dating from the 1210s–1220s where Romanesque arches meet the emerging Gothic style, then head to the cloister and the Brunnenkapelle, whose three-tiered fountain retains its original lower basin. Choose the €13 ticket with an audio guide, available in French.

Doctor Faust is said to have stayed around 1516 in the Faustturm, at the southeastern corner of Maulbronn’s enclosure, summoned by the abbot to make gold. Another legend credits the monks with inventing Maultaschen, those Swabian ravioli, though no documents support the claim. On firmer ground: the Protestant seminary that opened in 1556 educated Johannes Kepler, Friedrich Hölderlin, and Hermann Hesse. From March through October, it is open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.; in winter, it is closed on Mondays, with last admission at 3:45 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: A fortress can also tell the story of everyday life: the Genovevaburg houses the Eifelmuseum above Mayen’s market square. The visit connects the castle with life in the region, taking you beyond its walls. First, step back in the square to get a sense of its setting. If time is limited, choose the galleries that interest you instead of attempting a comprehensive visit.

The lighting narrows your field of vision at the Deutsches Schieferbergwerk beneath the Genovevaburg. This underground museum showcases slate mining, revealing a second visit hidden beneath the castle, this one focused on the miners. Do not treat the descent as a quick stroll through the courtyard. Check museum access and opening hours, then leave time to get back on the road toward Nürburg.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: The first stones of Burg Meersburg reportedly date back to the 7th century, under Merovingian King Dagobert I. It's Germany's oldest still-inhabited castle: not a ruin, not a frozen museum, a living fortress. More than 30 rooms to explore, from dungeon to knights' hall.

Poet Annette von Droste-Hülshoff died here on May 24, 1848. Her apartments and death chamber are part of the circuit. Guides offer special Droste tours by reservation, with access to normally closed rooms.

Walk up to the Neues Schloss for the view from the Baroque terrace: the lake, the vineyards and the Alps in the background. The palace was built in the 18th century for the prince-bishops of Konstanz.

activities.text: The terraced vineyards descend to the lake between the two castles. The Winzerverein Meersburg produces dry whites typical of the Bodensee. Buy directly from the cellar, modest prices for the quality.
If you're visiting on a Thursday evening, the Burg hosts a tasting of four Winzerverein wines within its medieval walls. Lake view included. Book at burg-meersburg.de.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: The Albrechtsburg dominates Meissen from a rocky promontory above the Elbe. This late Gothic castle, begun in 1471 by architect Arnold of Westphalia, is considered one of Germany's first residential palaces—designed as a princely residence rather than a fortress. In 1710, Augustus the Strong installed Europe's very first porcelain manufactory here, under the direction of alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger, who had promised to make gold and discovered porcelain instead. The manufacturing secret was so well guarded that workers were not allowed to leave the castle. Production remained here until 1863, when it was transferred to new buildings below. The interior walls are covered with 19th-century frescoes illustrating Saxony's history.

The Cathedral of Saints John and Donatus, adjoining the Albrechtsburg on the same promontory, was built from 1250 on the ruins of a 10th-century Romanesque church. Construction continued until the end of the 15th century. It houses 14th-century Gothic sculptures depicting Emperor Otto I and his wife Adelaide of Burgundy, as well as paintings by Lucas Cranach the Elder.

The Meissen Porcelain Manufactory, in its current buildings at the foot of the hill, houses the most comprehensive museum on the history of European porcelain. The demonstration workshops allow you to watch the different stages of production—modeling, wheel throwing, glazing, hand painting—carried out according to methods unchanged since the 18th century. The trademark of two crossed blue swords, created in 1722, is one of the oldest trademarks still in use in the world.

activities.text: Porcelain painting workshop at the Meissen Manufactory. The workshops offer introductory sessions where visitors paint a design on a piece of porcelain themselves, supervised by an artist from the manufactory.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

visits.text: Two rulers died here: Henry I in 936, then Otto the Great in 973. At Kloster Memleben, Otto II and Theophanu founded an abbey no later than 979 whose church measured about 82 m in length; ruins and a Romanesque crypt, the only intact chamber, survive. Open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. during the season, March 14 to November 8 in 2026.

The silence of the ruins extends into the medieval garden at Memleben Monastery, which is open to visitors along with the exhibitions. The site also appeals to wine lovers: the wines of Memleben Abbey, mentioned in 998, are the first documented wines of Saale-Unstrut. Stop by the monastery shop before heading up toward Wangen and the Arche.

days_plan.itin_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra

visits.text: The scent of fresh bread drifts across Memmingen's Marktplatz, lined with patrician houses with ornate gables. A former Free Imperial City that gained its status in 1268, the town built its fortune on salt and spice trading. The market runs Tuesday and Saturday mornings—perfect for sampling Allgäu cheese.

Seven gates, twenty-six towers: Memmingen's Stadtmauer is the town's largest complex of fortifications. The 13th-century ramparts still stand at their original height in the Ulmer Vorstadt district. Walk along the Stadtbach at dusk, when the lights reflect in the water.

Small but mighty, the Stadtpfarrkirche St. Martin rises above the rooftops with its refined Gothic proportions. It was completed in 1499. The choir stalls are worth a look. Free entry, closed during services.

Take the lane along the Stadtbach toward the weavers' quarter. The Frauenkirche, one of Swabia's oldest churches, hides a surprising medieval fresco: a unicorn hunt. It's easy to miss—ask the tourist office for a map.

activities.text: If it's Tuesday or Saturday, the Wochenmarkt on Memmingen's Marktplatz lines up stalls of cheese, honey, and local schnapps. The market is compact—you can circle it in thirty minutes. Try the Allgäuer Bergkäse, the local mountain cheese.
Head to the tanners' quarter along the Memminger Ach. The old half-timbered houses are reflected in the stream. This is the town's most photogenic corner, especially in the late afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: A heavy silence falls as soon as you enter Courtroom 600: at the Memorium Nürnberger Prozesse, the International Military Tribunal tried 21 Nazi leaders from November 20, 1945, to October 1, 1946, over 218 hearings, and handed down twelve death sentences. The courtroom remained in judicial use until 2020; the “Zeitreise Saal 600” installation now recreates the trial there. Admission is €7.50, with a free multimedia guide in French; closed to visitors on Tuesdays. Take subway line U1 to Bärenschanze.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Built between 1824 and 1828, Meppen's Koppelschleuse is a double-chamber work of engineering, designed to overcome more than four meters of elevation between the Ems-Hase Canal and the river. It can be visited in its original state, open-air. Free access.

The Renaissance gables of the old Rathaus, built in 1408 from glacial erratics, deserve a look. The baroque red-and-yellow Gymnasialkirche, a stone's throw away, contrasts with the northern Protestant sobriety.

activities.text: Climb up to the Höltingmühle on the island between the Dortmund-Ems Canal and the Hase. The windmill is photogenic, and the Mühle café serves good homemade cakes.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Here, time unfolds from top to bottom: a visit to the Mercedes-Benz Museum starts on the ninth floor in 1886, then spirals down toward the present. Opened in 2006, UNStudio’s building arranges seven “Legend” rooms and five “Collection” rooms along a double helix, letting you switch between them as you please: more than 160 vehicles across 16,500 m². Admission is €16, with an €8 evening ticket from 4:30 p.m., but ticket counters close at 5 p.m. Take S-Bahn S1 to NeckarPark; the museum is closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Schloss Mespelbrunn owes its survival to discretion: hidden in a side valley of the Spessart, it was never stormed. Every war spared it. The Renaissance moated castle - begun in 1427, completed in its current form in 1569 - remains inhabited by descendants of the original family. The guided tour lasts about 40 minutes, admission €5.50.

In good weather, the castle's reflection in the pond is the true postcard of the Spessart. In 1958, the film Das Wirtshaus im Spessart starring Liselotte Pulver was shot here - you can still ask the Schlosshof café owner which scene was filmed in which room.

activities.text: Explore the Spessart trails from the castle parking lot. The Gruftkapelle of the Counts of Ingelheim (1875) stands a few hundred meters uphill toward the Echterspfahl. The forest is dense and silent - the Spessart is one of Germany's most extensive forest massifs.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Two kilometers as the crow flies, nearly ten along the river: from the Cloef viewpoint, the Saarschleife reveals the full detour the Saar River takes between Besseringen and Mettlach. The overlook stands about 180 m above the water. Head up when you arrive from Saarlouis, then return the following morning for the Baumwipfelpfad, which starts right beside the Cloef-Atrium.

The most intriguing detail at Villeroy & Boch The Experience involves the Titanic: its ceramic bathroom fixtures rank among the company’s landmark projects. More than 2,000 m² of exhibition space fill the Baroque abbey built between 1727 and 1780, which Jean François Boch purchased in 1809. Open Monday through Saturday, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.; booking tickets online is recommended.

If you visit just one medieval monument in Saarland, choose Mettlach’s Alter Turm, built around 990–994 as a funerary chapel for Saint Lutwinus. This Ottonian octagon, inspired by Aachen Cathedral, is the oldest medieval building still standing in the state. Admire it from the Abteipark, an English landscape garden with more than 30 tree species.

activities.text: Follow the gentle incline of the Baumwipfelpfad Saarschleife, which opened above the Cloef in 2016. The 1,250 m trail runs up to 23 m above the ground among beech, oak, and Douglas fir trees, then spirals up a 42 m tower. Arrive when it opens at 9:30 a.m. so you can drive to Homburg in the late morning.

days_plan.itin_title: Saarland in 3 Days: Saarbrücken, the Saarschleife, and Homburg

visits.text: Michelstadt’s Historisches Rathaus warrants a stop even without a guided tour: the half-timbered building anchors almost the entire square. The town dates its construction to 1484, long before photo tourism. View the arcades from several angles. Arrive before the crowds and do not mistake the chance to admire the facade for guaranteed access to the rooms inside.

The Kellereihof and Diebsturm reveal a less cheerful side of Michelstadt than its main square. The old courtyard, defensive walls, and tower recall the center’s defensive role, while the nearby Stadtkirche rounds out the route. Combine these monuments into a single walk. Ask for the town map and check opening hours for each interior separately.

A small synagogue with a history that reaches far beyond Michelstadt: the Dr. I. E. Lichtigfeld-Museum presents the life of Jewish communities in the Odenwald. It occupies the synagogue built in 1791, which is also used for worship. Find out about visiting arrangements before coming, and respect the customs of the site when access is available.

Built for Einhard, a close associate of Charlemagne, the Einhardsbasilika in Michelstadt-Steinbach takes you to a different era as well as a different neighborhood. Its austere forms contrast with the half-timbered buildings in the center and make its Carolingian architecture easy to appreciate. Plan a separate trip from the old town. Check the operator’s opening hours; do not assume the church is always open.

Schloss Fürstenau is worth the detour mainly as part of a walk that includes the neighboring Einhardsbasilika in Michelstadt-Steinbach. The estate comprises several buildings and retains elements of an earlier moated castle. Choose areas that are actually accessible rather than assuming an interior tour is available. Check entry conditions on site and respect private areas.

If you prefer collections to facades, choose the Gräfliche Sammlungen at Schloss Erbach, near Michelstadt. Antiquities and collectibles reflect the interests of Count Franz I. Visits are guided; the Rittersaal is currently closed for investigations into the building’s structure. Book a time slot and check which rooms are included.

The Deutsches Elfenbeinmuseum at Schloss Erbach showcases a craft whose story is absent from Michelstadt’s streets. The carved works document the history of this local specialty in a wing of the castle. Prioritize this museum over other interiors if the subject interests you. Check opening hours and distinguish its ticket from the one for the count’s collections.

activities.text: Book a guided old town walk in Michelstadt to connect the Rathaus, Kellerei, Diebsturm, and synagogue through their history. The town offers this guided walk, which keeps the center from becoming merely a list of photographed facades. Ask about the language and starting point when booking. This route replaces self-guided stops in the center and does not automatically include Steinbach or Erbach.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: Miltenberg’s Schnatterloch brings together a Renaissance fountain and half-timbered facades in a compact space. The square serves as a starting point for exploring the old town, squeezed between the Main and the hills. It is a good stop before choosing a museum. Walk here from parking outside the historic center to preserve the walking experience.

A fortress with more than suits of armor: the Museum Burg Miltenberg juxtaposes icons and contemporary art inside the Mildenburg. This contrast adds another dimension to the castle above the rooftops. The climb and the collection require more time than a photo of the square. Check the museum’s seasonal opening schedule before heading uphill.

Housed in several old houses on the Schnatterloch, the Museum Stadt Miltenberg tells the town’s story through its objects and residents. It complements the square rather than the castle’s art museum: the two visits appeal to different interests. Choose whichever draws you in. Check opening hours, especially during the Mildenburg’s winter closure.

activities.text: Follow the banks of the Main in Miltenberg for a broader view of the old town. The hills of the Spessart and Odenwald frame this stretch of the river, which feels very different from the narrow lanes around the Schnatterloch. Take a short walk before continuing toward Wertheim. Keep this break simple if you have chosen a museum.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: The small Schloss Mirow, on its island in the lake, is the birthplace of Sophie Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, future Queen of England (wife of George III). The exhibition traces her journey. The palace park overlooks the lake—absolute calm.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Arche Nebra, a 60 m building resembling a solar boat, tells the story of the Sky Disc: approximately 32 cm across and weighing 2 kg, it was unearthed by looters in 1999 and seized in 2002 during a sting operation at a hotel in Basel. Its 42-seat planetarium screens two 25-minute shows per hour. Admission is €8.50; the original is on display in Halle.

activities.text: If you’re traveling with children, set aside half an hour for Outer Space, Arche Nebra’s UFO, which opened on July 9, 2025. You can explore both its interior and its roof, with a command center, interactive stations, and a panoramic rooftop walkway. Admission is free, as is access to the outdoor area at Mittelberg.

You’ll finish at Mittelberg, about 3 km from Arche Nebra, where the disc lay for some 3,600 years. At the foot of the 30 m tower, which tilts at 10°, the Himmelsauge, a 3 m polished steel disc, marks the discovery site; on clear days, the view extends to the Kyffhäuser. Access is free, but there are no restrooms, so plan accordingly.

days_plan.itin_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra

visits.text: Six hundred and fifty meters long, 40 meters high, built entirely of rough stone blocks: the Möhnetalsperre is Westphalia's heaviest listed monument. Inaugurated in 1913, it was then Europe's largest reservoir. On the night of May 16, 1943, a British bouncing bomb blasted a 77-meter breach. The floodwaters claimed over 1,600 lives downstream.

activities.text: Book a guided tour inside the dam through the Ruhrverband (€2.50 per person, 1h30 duration). You'll see a replica of the 1943 bomb. Outside tours, the promenade along the dam crest is free and offers a plunging view over the Ausgleichsweiher.

When the dam overflows, water cascades down 105 arches. The spectacle is rare but impressive. Otherwise, the boat cruise on the Möhnesee (April to October, departing from the Staumauer) lasts about an hour and shows the lake's arms.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: Three hundred sixty meters of Douglas fir planks, nearly 100 meters above the ground: the Hängeseilbrücke Geierlay, inaugurated on October 3, 2015, and modeled on Nepalese footbridges, connects Mörsdorf to Sosberg. It was Germany’s longest until 2017. Allow for a 1.8 km walk from the Besucherzentrum, and leave your stroller in the car: strollers are prohibited.

activities.text: Walk the longer Geierlayschleife loop, about 5.5 km: after crossing the Geierlay, the trail joins the Saar-Hunsrück-Steig and passes beneath the footbridge before climbing back toward Mörsdorf. From below, you can appreciate its full scale. Short on time? The shorter 3.6 km loop cuts through the meadows.

days_plan.itin_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern

visits.text: Next, head up toward the Monopteros along the Schwabinger Bach, where the Japanisches Teehaus, built for the 1972 Olympics, regularly hosts tea ceremonies. Leo von Klenze’s small round temple, about 16 m tall and completed in 1836, crowns its hill and offers a sweeping view of the city. The path up has a grade of more than 6% and is not wheelchair accessible.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Monschau, nicknamed the “Pearl of the Eifel,” is nestled at 517 meters altitude in the steep valley of the Rur. First mentioned in 1198, the town today preserves more than 330 listed buildings, including an ensemble of 17th- and 18th-century half-timbered houses stretching along both riverbanks. Its 13th-century medieval castle, built by the Counts of Limburg, overlooks the valley from a rocky spur. During the Battle of the Bulge in December 1944, Monschau marked the northernmost point of the German offensive front and was one of the few towns spared from destruction.

The Rotes Haus, the Red House, is an 18th-century patrician residence that tells the story of Monschau's golden age of cloth industry. In the 17th and 18th centuries, the town was one of Europe's great centers for fine cloth production—its woolen cloth was renowned throughout Europe. The house, converted into a museum, presents remarkably preserved period interiors with their Baroque and Rococo furnishings.

activities.text: Hike in the Rur valley around Monschau: several marked trails follow the river, cross meadows, and climb toward the forested hills of the Eifel. The Eifelsteig trail passes through Monschau and offers loops suitable for all levels. In spring, the valleys are covered with millions of wild daffodils, a spectacular natural phenomenon of the region.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea

visits.text: Moritzburg Castle rises in the middle of a vast artificial pond, its silhouette with four round towers topped by copper roofs reflecting in the water—the image is striking, especially in misty weather. The first hunting lodge was built here between 1542 and 1546 by Duke Moritz of Saxony, whose name the castle bears. Augustus the Strong had it completely rebuilt in Baroque style from 1703, with the help of Pöppelmann, architect of the Zwinger. The interiors of its more than 200 rooms are lined with painted leather depicting hunting scenes—unique 18th-century pieces—and house the world's largest collection of deer trophies. Napoleon stayed here in 1806, on the occasion of the coronation of his ally the King of Saxony. In winter, the castle hosts the Three Nuts for Cinderella exhibition, named after the 1973 Czechoslovak fairy-tale film that was shot here and remains a cult classic throughout Central Europe.

The Fasanenschlösschen, the little pheasant palace, is located 2.5 km from the main castle at the end of a long vista laid out through the forest. This bright pink rococo pavilion, built between 1769 and 1782, was used as a secondary residence during hunting parties. Its miniature harbor with a jetty and Saxony's only lighthouse—a pink lighthouse, too—served as the setting for reenacted naval battles that the princes organized on the ponds.

activities.text: Walk around the pond to see the castle from all angles. The promenade around the lake is about 3 km and takes 45 minutes. The most impressive view of the castle is from the opposite shore.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

visits.text: One hundred and seven meters above the Wupper, the Müngstener Brücke is Germany's highest steel railway bridge. Completed in 1897, it measures 465 meters long. Every ten minutes, an S-Bahn rumbles overhead. The Brückensteig offers a guided climb onto the lower parabolic arch for the more daring.

activities.text: Head down to Brückenpark Müngsten for a riverside picnic. Minigolf, lawns, beer garden. A floating ferry (Schwebefähre) crosses the river without an engine, pulled by cable. Free, operates weekends April to October.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: In 1648, inside the Friedenssaal of the historic Rathaus, delegates from across Europe brought thirty years of war to a close — it isn't a large room, and that's precisely what surprises you. The 37 portraits of sovereigns and envoys, purchased by the council as early as 1649, still gaze down from oak-panelled walls dating to 1577. Entry €3; closed Monday mornings.

The scent of hot pretzels drifts up from the market at Domplatz, just behind the Prinzipalmarkt. This arcaded street — nicknamed the Gute Stube by Münster residents — runs 300 metres between the Rathaus to the south and the Lambertikirche to the north. The gabled houses, destroyed in 1945, were rebuilt in Baumberge sandstone between 1947 and 1958. Stroll here early in the morning, before deliveries.

Three iron cages hang from the tower of the Lambertikirche — in these late-Gothic cages, the bodies of executed Anabaptist leaders were displayed in 1536. The church itself is free to enter, and the organ is worth a stop. The contrast between the beauty of the place and the history of the cages is quite striking.

activities.text: Pick up a bike at the central station: Münster is one of Germany's best-equipped cities for cycling. A tour of the Schlossgarten, Schlaun's princely palace and the botanical garden takes under two hours on two wheels. Avoid riding the wrong way along cycle lanes — local cyclists won't give way.

If you're passing through on a Wednesday or Saturday morning, the Domplatz market is a good place to go: fruit, Westphalian cheeses and cured meats in front of the cathedral. Arrive before 10am for the best picks. The stalls pack up around 1pm.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles
Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: The Belchen remains little-known outside Germany despite steady visitor numbers—and that's its greatest asset. From the Ballon d'Alsace, 73 km to the west, the sun rises precisely over this summit at the equinoxes: according to Basel cantonal archaeologist Rolf d'Aujourd'hui, this system of five peaks named Belchen formed a druidic calendar roughly 2,300 years old. The name likely comes from Belenus, the Celtic sun god. At 1,414 m, the Belchenhaus serves hot soups on a south-facing terrace. Arrive early if you want the Vosges-Jura-Alps panorama to yourself.

The 'devil's stone' stands near Saint-Ulrich monastery: it is a carved sandstone basin, rather than an isolated rock in the woods. According to legend, Satan brought the stone to claim the saint's soul, but the saint outwitted him. Look at the figures carved around the basin. From Münstertal, allow for a return trip for this visit, separate from the excursion to the Belchen.

activities.text: Allow four and a half hours if you set out on foot from Neuenweg – 12 km with 700 m of elevation gain. Otherwise, the cable car from Multen gets you there in 8 minutes. Bicycles are recommended if your knees are troublesome, particularly with the option of walking back down. Bring water: the Belchenhaus does not always open early. In September, the pastures are still open and the cows are gone.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: Mühldorf’s Stadtplatz stretches nearly 500 m from Münchner Tor to Altöttinger Tor. Its Inn-Salzach-style facades rise above the roofs to conceal them, a fire protection measure adopted after major fires. An enclave of Salzburg until 1802, the city retains the air of a small capital. Walk the length of the square, from one gate to the other.

Tree trunks cut straight across mark the mass grave deep in the forest at KZ-Gedenkort Mühldorfer Hart. Beginning in the summer of 1944, thousands of deportees, including many Hungarian Jews, built a bunker here for the aircraft industry in a Dachau subcamp. Open to the public since 2018, the Waldlager and the grave can be explored along paths lined with information panels.

days_plan.itin_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach

visits.text: Neuschwanstein sits on a rocky spur at an elevation of 970 meters, overlooking the valley from 200 meters above. Ludwig II had it built from 1869 as a “temple worthy of the divine friend”—meaning Richard Wagner, whose operas inspired all the interior frescoes: Tannhäuser in the singers' hall, Lohengrin in the bedrooms, Parsifal in the throne room. The castle was never completed. Ludwig II spent only 172 nights of his life there. In June 1886, doctors appointed by the government had him declared insane and committed him to care; three days later, he was found dead in Lake Starnberg. The unfinished rooms were opened to visitors just seven weeks after his death—to repay his debts. Today, 1.4 million people visit the castle annually. Be sure to book in advance.

The Marienbrücke bridge stands 92 meters above the bottom of the Pöllat Gorge and spans a 45-meter waterfall. Originally built in wood and then rebuilt in iron in 1866, it bears the name of Marie of Prussia, Ludwig II's mother. The world's best-known view of the castle is from this bridge. In high season, lines form here—go early in the morning.

Arrive in Munich mid-afternoon. First discovery walk: Isartor → Viktualienmarkt → Marienplatz. The Viktualienmarkt is Munich's permanent open-air market, founded in 1807, selling Bavarian specialties, charcuterie, cheese, and beer at the central Biergarten. Marienplatz has been the city's heart since 1158: the Marian column (Mariensäule), erected in 1638 to celebrate the end of Swedish occupation, stands at the square's center.

The Munich Residence (Residenz) is Germany's largest urban palace—130 rooms, 10 interior courtyards, 40,000 m² of floor area. Seat of the Wittelsbach dynasty from 1508 to 1918, it offers a comprehensive overview of architecture and decorative arts from the 16th to the 19th century. Its jewel is the Antiquarium, a Renaissance hall 69 meters long built between 1568 and 1571 by Duke Albert V to house his collection of ancient sculptures—it's the largest secular Renaissance hall north of the Alps. The barrel vault is pierced by 17 pairs of windows and covered with 102 frescoes in lunettes depicting Bavarian towns.

The Schatzkammer (Treasury), accessible with the same ticket, houses over 1,200 precious objects from Bavarian ruling dynasties: crowns, scepters, reliquaries, jewels, and gold and silver tableware—spanning two millennia of history. The Cuvilliés Theater, designed between 1751 and 1755 by architect François de Cuvilliés, is one of Europe's finest rococo theaters. Mozart's opera Idomeneo premiered here in 1781.

Marienplatz and the Neues Rathaus: the Glockenspiel sets its 32 life-size figures in motion at 11 a.m. and noon, and also at 5 p.m. from March to October. The two scenes depicted—the tournament at William V's wedding in 1568 and the coopers' dance (Schäfflertanz) commemorating the end of a plague epidemic—have been performed since 1908.

The Frauenkirche (Cathedral of Our Lady), with its two 99-meter onion-domed towers, is Munich's symbol. Its Gothic construction dates from 1468 to 1488. Inside, look for the mysterious “devil's footprint” (Teufelstritt) in the entrance floor—a footprint left, according to legend, by Satan himself, who came to inspect the building.

The Englischer Garten (English Garden), created in 1789, is one of the world's largest urban parks—larger than New York's Central Park with its 370 hectares. In the southern section, the Eisbachwelle is a permanent artificial wave where surfers practice in the heart of the city, an emblematic Munich image.

activities.text: Walk up from the Ticket Center to the castle (30–40 minutes) for the morning opening slot, before tour buses arrive. Visitor numbers exceed 6,000 people per day in summer—the earliest slots are significantly less crowded.

Walking tour through the Innenstadt: Odeonsplatz → Feldherrnhalle → Theatinerkirche (yellow baroque facade, built from 1663 as a votive offering for the birth of an heir) → Hofgarten → return toward Marienplatz.

visits.text: It was here, in Murnau's Münter-Haus, that Kandinsky and Gabriele Münter lived between 1909 and 1914 and invented abstract art. The small house with blue shutters, nicknamed the “Russenhaus,” has remained in its original state: painted furniture, reverse glass paintings on the walls. Closed Mondays.

Climb to the Schloßmuseum Murnau, whose Blaue Reiter collections have gained international stature since the 2023 KK-Stiftung donation. Kandinsky, Münter, Marc, Jawlensky: the originals are here, in the village that inspired them.

From the shore of the Staffelsee, the light changes hour by hour. Franz Marc called this region the "Blaues Land," the Blue Land. You understand why at day's end, when the mountains turn gray and the lake deep green.

activities.text: If weather permits, rent a pedal boat on the Staffelsee. The lake is calm, shallow, and reed-lined. An hour is enough to cross and return.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: The Murnauer Moos is Central Europe's largest undrained peat bog. A boardwalk trail crosses this landscape of mosses, dwarf birches, and reeds. Binoculars are useful: curlews, snipes, and harriers nest here.

activities.text: Allow an hour for the boardwalk loop through the Murnauer Moos. The trail is walkable even after rain. Free access, no ticket booth.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: The Zwingerweg runs along Nabburg's intact wall with its towers, gates and viewpoints over the Naab valley. Below, storks nest on the steeples. The complete circuit takes 30 minutes and is worth it for the atmosphere alone.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: The Königsstuhl, a 118-meter chalk cliff, is Rügen's symbol. The Nationalparkzentrum presents the ecosystem of ancient beech forests (UNESCO world heritage). The Königsweg, a suspended walkway, replaces the old cliff-edge access. Plan on the shuttle from Sassnitz or Hagen—cars prohibited.

activities.text: Hike the Hochuferweg, a ridge trail along the chalk cliffs between Sassnitz and Königsstuhl. The path winds through beech forest, with openings onto the Baltic. About 6 km, two hours.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Kellerwald-Edersee National Park, created in 2004, covers 5,724 hectares in northern Hesse—the state's only national park. Since 2011, part of its beech forests has been included in the UNESCO site “Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe.” These beech forests are among the best-preserved in Central Europe: some trees exceed 200 years of age and 30 meters in height. The forest is left to develop naturally without human intervention, creating “tomorrow's wilderness.” Wildcats (which reappeared in 2007 after 60 years of absence), black storks, and 15 species of bats can be encountered there.

The park center in Vöhl-Herzhausen offers exhibitions on beech forest ecology and the Eder Dam, which closes off the park's eastern boundary. The dam, 400 meters long, was built in 1914 and holds back the Edersee—Germany's second-largest reservoir at 27 km long. During World War II, it was targeted in May 1943 by Operation Chastise, one of the first uses of the "bouncing bomb" by the RAF. The breach caused catastrophic flooding downstream.

The Edersee's shores offer 50 km of waterfront to explore. The turquoise waters of the lake—fed by Kellerwald streams—are among the clearest in inland Germany. In some summers, low water levels allow the remains of the village of Asel, submerged when the reservoir was filled in 1914, to reappear along the former shoreline.

activities.text: Hike through the UNESCO-listed beech forests on the Urwaldsteig Edersee, a 68 km trail that loops around the lake in 4 to 5 stages. The sections on the northern side, in the heart of the national park, are the wildest. The trail is perfectly marked with "U-E" in white on a blue background.
Boat trip or water activities on the Edersee: sailing, windsurfing, kayaking, and swimming at equipped beaches. Sightseeing boats tour the lake from the Waldeck pier.

days_plan.itin_title: Hesse, Germany Tour: Cities and Nature Parks

visits.text: Nothing quite prepares you for Uta’s gaze. In the west choir of Naumburg Cathedral, twelve life-size donor statues surround visitors: eight men and four women carved in the mid-13th century by the workshop of the Naumburg Master. Uta is paired with Margrave Ekkehard II. The Cranach-Triegel altarpiece, criticized for obscuring these two statues, has been on a two-year loan to Rome since fall 2025. Admission is €9.50, including an audio guide; on Sundays, worship services occupy the morning, and visits resume at noon.

A 45 kg missal and a 14th-century Pietà: the Domschatzgewölbe displays the treasury of the cathedral, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018, across 285 m². In the Elisabethkapelle, three stained-glass windows by Neo Rauch, installed in 2007, contrast with the medieval stonework. Finish in the Domgarten, nearly a hectare of regional plants that served as models for some 200 foliage carvings in the west choir: compare a living leaf with its stone copy.

Naumburg’s Markt centers on a Renaissance town hall built between 1517 and 1528. On the square, the Hohe Lilie, whose street-facing tower dates to around 1250, houses the Stadtmuseum: visitors can trace 750 years of occupation, from a private well to traces of the fire of 1517. Admission is €5.50, free for visitors under 18, Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; the ticket also includes same-day admission to the exhibitions at the Galerie im Schlösschen.

The rumble of bass notes makes the nave of Stadtkirche St. Wenzel vibrate as the Hildebrandt organ comes to life. Built between 1743 and 1746, the instrument was inspected on September 27, 1746, by Johann Sebastian Bach and Gottfried Silbermann; it has three manuals and more than fifty stops. From May through October, a 30-minute concert takes place at noon on Wednesdays, Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays (€6.50): take your seat a few minutes early.

You’ll climb 202 steps to reach the Wenzelsturm platform, 53 m above Naumburg’s rooftops. Until 1892, a tower watchman lived here at a height of 45 m, keeping watch for enemies and fires; the bell tower houses Saxony-Anhalt’s only fully preserved medieval peal of three bells, the largest weighing 2,309 kg. You can climb the tower from April 1 through October 31, Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., for €3.

The philosopher of “God is dead” grew up a few streets from a cathedral, at the Nietzsche-Haus at Weingarten 18. His mother, Franziska, rented an upstairs apartment there in 1858, bought the house in 1878, and lived there until her death in 1897. The museum, which opened in 1994 and has been supported by a neighboring documentation center since 2010, traces the philosopher’s life and work. Come in the afternoon: on weekdays, the house opens at 2 p.m., except on Mondays.

If you pass through just one gate, make it the Marientor, the only one of Naumburg’s seven gates still standing. Its tower dates to the second half of the 14th century, and its barbican, added around 1456, formed a courtyard designed to trap attackers. From April through October, Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., admission costs €1, paid in coins at the ticket machine; in summer, the courtyard hosts theater performances and concerts.

activities.text: Hop aboard the Naumburger Straßenbahn, in service since 1892: line 4 connects the Hauptbahnhof with the Salztor every 30 minutes using streetcars built in Gotha. It is Germany’s smallest streetcar network with daily service. Expect to pay a little over €2 per ride, or board with the Deutschlandticket, which is accepted on board: a convenient way to reach the station after your visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra

visits.text: The bracing air at 2,200 m hits you as soon as you step out of the cabin. At the Nebelhorn summit, at 2,224 m, the operator advertises views of more than 400 peaks; in 1930, its first mountain lift was considered the world’s longest open to passengers. Take one of the first cabins in the morning, before clouds gather along the ridge, and bring a fleece even in July.

activities.text: If heights draw you in without leaving you frozen, the Nordwandsteig awaits around the Nebelhorn summit station. Opened in 2016, this approximately 600 m trail follows a ledge along the north face and is accessible to people with limited mobility. Keep a warm layer handy: on the north side, the air stays cool even in midsummer.

Ride down one section to Höfatsblick station, then follow trail no. 4 toward the Zeigersattel pass at 1,900 m. From the pass, you look down onto Seealpsee, described as the deepest mountain lake in the Allgäu Alps at 42 m. Marmots and chamois frequent the slopes. To reach the water, allow about four hours round-trip from the station, including the steep climb back up.

days_plan.itin_title: Oberstdorf in 3 Days: Lakes, Gorges, and Kleinwalsertal

visits.text: Four castles for a small town: Neckarsteinach immediately sets the tone for the Neckar. Vorderburg, Mittelburg, Hinterburg, and Schadeck occupy the nearby heights; their silhouettes stand out from the riverbanks. Do not assume that every building is open for interior visits. For a brief stop, focus on the views and check access information before heading uphill.

Neckarsteinach’s Hinterburg is worth leaving the riverfront for: its ruins make the valley’s terrain much easier to understand. The walls frame the Neckar rather than a collection of furnished rooms. Choose this climb if you only want to visit one castle here. Check the trail’s condition and allow extra time for the descent.

activities.text: Follow Neckarsteinach’s Uferpromenade to take in views of the castles without moving your car. The town describes it as a promenade free of car traffic; it offers a less demanding break than the ridge trails. Turn back when your schedule requires, without trying to cover the entire riverbank before continuing to Hirschhorn.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: A castle associated with Götz von Berlichingen: Burg Hornberg puts a face to Neckarzimmern’s history. The ruins occupy a spur above the Neckar, surrounded by vineyards. The visit is as much about understanding the landscape as exploring the walls. Check access hours and wear shoes suitable for stairs.

activities.text: If you enjoy wine, book a Burg Hornberg tasting in Neckarzimmern. The estate offers guided tastings and vineyard walks, a way to see the vines from a different perspective than the ramparts. Choose an option that fits with the next leg of your trip. Designate a driver who will not take part in the tasting, and confirm your reservation before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: Neubrandenburg possesses northern Germany's best-preserved medieval brick wall. Four Gothic gates (Stargarder, Treptower, Friedländer, Neues Tor) frame 25 Wiekhäuser—small half-timbered houses embedded in the wall. Now workshops, cafés, and galleries.

The Konzertkirche St. Marien presents a stark contrast: a Brick Gothic exterior and an interior transformed into a modern concert hall (glass, concrete, wood). The acoustics are as impressive as the sight.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: After the cathedral’s restraint, the Neue Residenz embraces Baroque extravagance, and is all the better for it. Its wings, built from 1697 to 1703 to designs by Leonhard Dientzenhofer for Prince-Bishop Lothar Franz von Schönborn, conceal the Kaisersaal, where Melchior Steidl painted sixteen emperors larger than life-size from 1707 to 1709. Guided tours of the prince-bishop’s apartment run every half hour in German; the other rooms can be explored independently. Admission is €7 and free for visitors under 18.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Old brickwork, faded frescoes, and contemporary spaces play off one another at the Neues Museum, which reopened in October 2009 after its reconstruction by David Chipperfield. The bust of Nefertiti, sculpted around 1345 BC and unearthed at Amarna in 1912, takes pride of place here; its left eye was never given an iris. Before leaving the floor devoted to prehistory, see the Berlin Gold Hat, whose decoration can be read as a calendar. Reserve a time slot online and arrive right at 10 AM; the museum is closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Stop in Oranienburg, 35 kilometers north of Berlin, to visit the Sachsenhausen memorial; allow for a return trip from Neuruppin. Built in 1936 by prisoners from other camps, it was designed as the SS “model camp”: its triangular layout allowed a handful of guards to watch the whole site from a single central tower. Between 1936 and 1945, more than 200,000 people were imprisoned here and around 84,000 died. This is where Himmler established his headquarters and where the first methods of mass extermination, including gas vans, were tested. After 1945, the Soviets reused the site until 1950 to imprison their own political opponents.

Neuruppin, nicknamed Fontanestadt, is the birthplace of two of Prussia's greatest cultural figures: architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel, born March 13, 1781, and writer Theodor Fontane, born December 30, 1819. Fontane's father's pharmacy still stands on the central square. A devastating fire razed nearly the entire town in 1787—Schinkel was six years old, and his father, a superintendent, died of exhaustion shortly after. The town was rebuilt between 1788 and 1796 in a rigorous neoclassical style that makes it one of the best-preserved classicist ensembles in northern Germany. Fontane himself thought the town resembled a suit too large for the wearer.

Walk to the Klosterkirche Sankt Trinitatis by the lakeside—it was the first Dominican monastery east of the Elbe, founded in 1246. Its two tall neo-Gothic towers, built between 1904 and 1907 from plans inspired by Schinkel, are visible from the entire lakeside promenade. Just behind it, the old high school where both Schinkel and Fontane were students bears the inscription on its pediment: CIVIBUS AEVI FUTURI—“To the citizens of the future.”

The Tempelgarten was laid out for Crown Prince Frederick during his stay in Neuruppin between 1732 and 1736. Here, Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff—who would later build Sanssouci in Potsdam—created his very first work: a round temple completed in 1735.

activities.text: Stroll along the Ruppiner See, Brandenburg's longest lake at 14 kilometers. Excursion boats sail in summer under the name Kronprinz Friedrich, and the view from the water of the Klosterkirche's twin towers is well worth the trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: Lakes, Castles, and the Baltic Coast

visits.text: The ossuary in Perschen, a Romanesque rotunda from 1150, preserves original unrestored frescoes whose color intensity astonishes art historians. It adjoins the church of St. Peter und Paul and the Edelmannshof, a 17th-century farm. Free admission.

activities.text: Continue to the Freilandmuseum Oberpfalz: 30 hectares of reconstructed historic farms with heritage-breed animals. Five themed villages to explore on foot. Allow at least 2 hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: To understand the forest before exploring it, Hans-Eisenmann-Haus is worth taking the time to visit. This center at Nationalparkzentrum Lusen, near Neuschönau, explains the national park’s habitats and how the park is changing. It helps you see dead trees as more than an abandoned landscape: they also contribute to forest regeneration. Stop here before heading onto the trails, then ask about the day’s conditions and any access restrictions.

The Pflanzen- und Gesteins-Freigelände encourages you to slow down and notice what you often walk past on a hike. Around Hans-Eisenmann-Haus, native plants and blocks of gneiss or granite make the forest easier to understand. Some stones have a polished corner, making it easier to compare the materials. Save this outdoor visit for a break in the weather, look for differences in texture, and stay on the designated paths.

activities.text: Gain a higher perspective on the Baumwipfelpfad Bayerischer Wald without climbing a tree. The walkway leads to a 44-meter tower and changes the scale of the landscape: treetops become the foreground, with hills in the background. Admission is charged, unlike the national park’s neighboring outdoor areas. Check the operator’s hours and the weather before going up; dense fog makes the panoramic view less rewarding.

If the lynx stay hidden at Tier-Freigelände, your walk is still worthwhile: their enclosures also give the animals places to retreat. The site presents regional wildlife, including wolves, bears, and birds, in a forest setting. The full circuit covers 7 kilometers and takes three to four hours; marked shortcuts allow a shorter loop. Follow them without rushing from one enclosure to the next.

Climb Lusen via Sommerweg and Himmelsleiter, whose steps make the final ascent noticeably steeper. At the summit, a mass of granite boulders replaces the forest floor: the change in scenery is more striking than the elevation. The Luchs loop from Lusenparkplatz returns via Winterweg; the listed route is approximately five kilometers long. Check the Igelbus service for access to the trailhead, wear sturdy shoes, and postpone the climb if the rocks are slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavarian Forest in 4 Days: From Passau to the Großer Arber

places.name: Neustadt An Der Weinstrasse

visits.text: Neustadt’s Stiftskirche conceals a wall right down the middle: since 1708, a partition has separated the Catholic choir from the Protestant nave, one of the few such partitions still standing in Germany. Begun in 1356, the church borders the medieval Marktplatz, and its Kaiserglocke is reputed to be the world’s largest cast-steel bell. The Protestant section opens mainly for services, so take a walk around the square too.

In the Palatinate, you may be offered a hunting license for the Elwetritsche, an imaginary bird said to hide in the vineyards. Neustadt, its unofficial capital, dedicated Gernot Rumpf’s Elwetritschebrunnen to it in 1978 on Marstallplatz: 21 bronze creatures, including a bird with a fox’s head representing the mayor. Allow 15 minutes and look for the little mouse, the sculptor’s signature, near the lantern.

In our view, no castle on the Weinstraße carries as much historical weight as Hambacher Schloss: on May 27, 1832, 20,000 to 30,000 people climbed up here to demand unity, freedom, and popular sovereignty, many beneath black, red, and gold flags. The “Deutschlands Wiedergeburt” flag carried that day is displayed in the museum and may not be photographed. Open daily, €6.50; allow 90 minutes for the exhibition, then visit the terrace overlooking the Rhine Plain.

days_plan.itin_title: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen

map_keywords: Collegiate Church Neustadt an der Weinstraße

visits.text: Neustrelitz lost its palace (destroyed in 1945) but kept its baroque star-shaped layout. Eight streets radiate from the central square. The Schlosspark, with its orangery and neoclassical temple, remains the lake district's finest park. Logical final stop before Berlin.
