days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: A 36-meter difference in elevation, and the entire boat takes the elevator at the Niederfinow Boat Lift. Opened in 1934, the original structure carries vessels in a water-filled caisson instead of through a series of locks. Choose your tour route according to how comfortable you are with stairs, and check which access routes are open before heading up.

The same principle, a different silhouette: the Niederfinow North Boat Lift completely changes how you see the site. Opened in 2022, the new lift stands beside the one from 1934; having them side by side makes comparison immediate. View both structures from permitted areas and check which ticket grants access to the route you want to take.

activities.text: A technical explanation is worth more here than another photo of the Niederfinow Boat Lift. Guided tours offered at the site show how the caisson, counterweights, and boat traffic work together; watching the movement alone does not tell the whole story. Check tour times before setting out and choose a short option that fits your onward journey to Chorin.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeastern Brandenburg: Abbey, Forest, and Lakes in 3 Days

visits.text: Dating back to around 1200, the Nikolaiviertel was destroyed during World War II, then rebuilt for Berlin’s 750th anniversary in 1987: reconstructed houses stand alongside prefabricated apartment buildings. At its center, the Nikolaikirche, begun around 1230 and rebuilt from 1980 to 1987, houses a museum devoted to its history. Stroll through the lanes and along the Spree in the late afternoon before dinner at one of the neighborhood’s traditional restaurants.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Stone giants deposited on the heath: the Lausitzer Findlingspark Nochten lines up more than 6,000 erratic boulders, torn from Scandinavia by glaciers and then unearthed here during coal mining. Opened in 2003 on a former opencast mine, it covers about twenty hectares divided into seven themed gardens. Allow one to two hours. Avoid windy and cold days—the site is wide open.

activities.text: Climb up to the Feldzeichen, the high point of the Findlingspark, for an unobstructed view over Lusatia. Below, children rush toward 'Die Wüste,' an adventure area with boulders to climb, a labyrinth, and water features. The paths are stabilized gravel, so strollers and wheelchairs can get almost everywhere. The bistro at the visitor center covers lunch.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: The Nördlingers call it the Daniel: the 90-meter-high bell tower of St.-Georgskirche, whose watchman still calls out every night between 10 p.m. and midnight - "So, G'sell so!" - a tradition uninterrupted since the Middle Ages. Climbing the 350 steps to see the town inscribed in its meteorite crater is the best way to grasp the site's cosmic origin.

Nördlingen's Stadtmauer makes a 2.7-km circuit: it's entirely walkable and intact, with five gates and eleven towers. One of the rare complete medieval enclosures in Germany still entirely closed and walkable. Nördlingen sits at the center of the Ries, a crater about 14.5 million years old with a diameter near 25 km.

activities.text: Climb onto the ramparts before 9 a.m. and walk the complete circuit. The five Stadttore carry collectible stamps - the Entdeckerpass distributed at the tourist office turns the walk into a game for the whole family. Entry to the towers is free and open.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: You smile at the nickname “the Westphalian Versailles” — and then you arrive in front of Schloss Nordkirchen and understand. This Baroque castle surrounded by water, designed by Pictorius and completed by Schlaun, is the largest moated castle in Westphalia. Since 1959 it has housed a finance school of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Guided tours run on Sundays and public holidays.

Twenty-three avenues radiate from Schloss Nordkirchen through a French-style Baroque park. The reconstructed Venusinsel, the sculptures punctuating the parterres, the right-angled canals: an almost dizzying geometry. The park is free to enter.

activities.text: Rent a bike: Nordkirchen has marked cycle routes through the hedgerow countryside of Münsterland. A circuit of the entire estate takes about an hour. Avoid weekends with open-air concerts, when visitor numbers rise.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: For a breather in Nürburg, Burg Nürburg offers a counterpoint to the nearby racetrack. The village brings together the castle and the Nürburgring, two reasons to stop with very different atmospheres. Approach the ruins for a fresh perspective on this landscape associated with motorsports. Check opening hours before climbing up; on this short stop, choose either the castle or the guided racetrack tour.

activities.text: You can replace the climb to Burg Nürburg with the Nürburgring Backstage Tour. The guided tour takes you behind the scenes at the racetrack and lasts about 1 hour 30 minutes, according to the official description. It is a better option than an impromptu stop with no view of the track. Book a departure time that fits the rest of your route; the ring°werk museum is currently closed for construction work.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

visits.text: Immerse yourself in the history of Nuremberg (Nürnberg), Bavaria's second-largest city and an imperial city of crucial importance in the Middle Ages. This powerful city where the Diets of the Holy Roman Empire were held and where the imperial crown jewels were kept retains an authentic medieval atmosphere behind its imposing walls. Its Christmas market, the Christkindlesmarkt, is Germany's most famous.

Visit the Kaiserburg, the imperial fortress dominating the city from its rocky promontory. This complex castle, enlarged over the centuries, was the residence of all the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire. The view from its ramparts encompasses the red roofs of the old town, the church towers and the meanders of the Pegnitz River.

Discover the old town rebuilt after the destruction of 1945, where half-timbered houses stand alongside the Gothic churches of St. Sebaldus and St. Lawrence. The Nuremberg Trials courthouse, Albrecht Dürer's house and the Documentation Center on Nazism bear witness to both the dark and bright chapters in the history of this city of art and culture.

activities.text: Visit the Germanic National Museum, the largest museum of German art and culture
Stroll through the medieval lanes of the artisans' quarter

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps

visits.text: Visit Linderhof Palace, the most intimate of Ludwig II's palaces and the only one he saw completed in his lifetime. This rococo gem nestled in an Alpine valley enchants with its hilly park dotted with gushing fountains, sculpted groves and exotic pavilions. The Venus Grotto, artificially lit, recreates a scene from the opera Tannhäuser with a navigable underground lake.

Discover Ettal Abbey, a masterpiece of Bavarian Baroque founded in 1330 by Emperor Louis IV. Its monumental dome, one of Germany's largest, houses celestial frescoes of breathtaking magnificence. The Benedictine monks still perpetuate the tradition of monastic brewing and liqueur distillation to this day.

Wander through the lanes of Oberammergau, a village world-famous for its facades painted with biblical frescoes and fairy-tale scenes. This tradition of Lüftlmalerei, trompe-l'oeil painting on plaster, transforms every house into a work of art. The village has also hosted the famous Passion Play every ten years since 1634.

activities.text: Discover the local craft of woodcarving

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: The Oberbaumbrücke spans the Spree on two levels: the roadway below and the subway above, beneath pointed brick Gothic arches. Completed in 1896 by Otto Stahn, the bridge became a pedestrian crossing reserved for West Berlin residents in December 1963. Walk across toward Kreuzberg, then board the U1 at Schlesisches Tor.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: The Obere Pfarre, the Church of Our Lady in the upper town, is Bamberg’s only purely Gothic church, according to the tourist office. The foundations of its choir date to 1375, the nave followed some fifty years later, and flying buttresses support the lofty choir. Stop at the bridal portal with its Gothic statues, then look inside for Tintoretto’s Assumption, a particularly valuable work. In December 2026, the “Poetischer Krippenweg” is performed here on the 12th, 19th, and 23rd at 3:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: The sheer scale of Gasometer Oberhausen draws your eyes toward the ceiling. This former gas holder hosts major temporary exhibitions; the industrial structure is as much a part of the visit as the artworks. Book your ticket and bring an extra layer: the building is unheated in winter.

days_plan.itin_title: Industrial Ruhr in 3 Days, from Duisburg to Dortmund

places.name: Oberhof

visits.text: An alpine garden in Thuringia may seem an odd idea, yet this is the stop on the trip that feels most like another world. On the Pfanntalskopf, at 868 meters, Oberhof’s Rennsteiggarten brings together nearly 4,000 species from the mountains of Europe, Asia, the Americas, and New Zealand, including gentians and edelweiss, across 7 hectares of a former quarry. Snow covers the site for about 150 days a year; the garden closes in winter and announces its reopening in May 2027.

activities.text: The LOTTO Thüringen ARENA am Rennsteig hosts biathletes near the Grenzadler, about 2.5 kilometers west of Oberhof. During the 2023 World Championships, 152,000 spectators attended over nine days; nearby, a two-meter boundary marker topped with a Prussian eagle recalls the former border between Prussia and the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. Park in the large Grenzadler parking lot and walk along the Rennsteig for a while.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach

map_keywords: LOTTO Thüringen ARENA am Rennsteig Oberhof

visits.text: Hitler began vacationing on the Obersalzberg in 1923; after 1933, this mountainside became the second center of Nazi power after Berlin. Dokumentation Obersalzberg traces this history first through the “Idyll und Verbrechen” exhibition, which opened in 2023 and features around 350 objects and documents, then through a network of period bunkers. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours and wear sturdy shoes: the tunnel floors are uneven in places.

activities.text: Next, take the Roßfeld-Panoramastraße from Klaushöhe on the Obersalzberg: billed as Germany’s highest scenic toll road, it reaches nearly 1,600 m. Along the ridge, it runs through Austrian territory for about 1.5 km, while the Salzach Valley and Salzburg unfold a thousand meters below. Set aside €9.50 for the toll and descend on the northern side toward Oberau.

days_plan.itin_title: Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits

visits.text: In May 1865, the fire that devastated Oberstdorf left only the tower and exterior walls of St. Johannes Baptist standing. Rebuilt in the Gothic Revival style and reconsecrated in 1872, the church nevertheless retains a Madonna carved in Ulm around 1430, the “Schöne Oberstdorferin.” Continue to the cemetery’s Seelenkapelle, which escaped the fire and served as a temporary church, avoiding Mass times.

More engaging than many resort museums, Oberstdorf’s Heimatmuseum occupies a mountain farmhouse whose core dates to the 17th century. Inside, you’ll find skis from the 1890s and a 3-meter mountaineering boot billed as the world’s largest. Visit Tuesday through Saturday, between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m.; a guided tour starts every Tuesday at 4 p.m.

Head up to the Orlen Arena at the foot of the Schattenberg: this is where Oberstdorf kicks off the Four Hills Tournament every winter. An inclined elevator climbs to the base of the inrun tower, then a panoramic elevator takes you to the observation platform above a stadium with a capacity of 27,000. The site opens daily at 10 a.m.; guided tours for groups of eight or more can be booked by phone.

days_plan.itin_title: Oberstdorf in 3 Days: Lakes, Gorges, and Kleinwalsertal

visits.text: Crisp air and sweeping views toward Bohemia: at the 1,215 m summit of Fichtelberg, you stand at Saxony’s highest point, facing Klínovec in the Czech Republic. The weather station has recorded conditions here since 1916. Climb the Fichtelberghaus’s 31 m tower on a clear day; spotting the Brocken, 220 km away, is still rare.

Oberwiesenthal deserves more than a passing visit from skiers: at over 900 m, it is Germany’s highest town. On the square, the Postmeilensäule of 1730 indicated distances to travelers; the Martin-Luther-Kirche, rebuilt from 1863 to 1866, houses a nativity scene carved in 1896. It is displayed only from Advent through the end of February.

You can watch for the Fichtelbergbahn’s arrival at Bahnhof Oberwiesenthal, Saxony’s highest train station, at nearly 894 m. This 750 mm gauge railway has operated since 1897, with steam trains running daily on a fixed schedule. The full round-trip journey to Cranzahl takes about 2 hours 30 minutes.

activities.text: The Fichtelberg-Schwebebahn, in service since December 1924, is Germany’s oldest cable car. Its cabins climb 303 m from Oberwiesenthal in about 3 minutes 30 seconds. Buy a one-way ticket, €12 per adult in 2026, if you plan to walk back down.

Walk down from Fichtelberg via the Kammweg and Sachsenbaude, then through the Zechengrund along the Pöhlbach. This route follows the second half of the 10.9 km loop described by Bergwelten, starting at Oberwiesenthal station. Cross the B95 carefully at Neues Haus; the Zechengrund requires sure footing.

days_plan.itin_title: The Ore Mountains in 3 Days: Mines, Toys, and Fichtelberg

visits.text: The 191-meter antenna is visible from kilometers away: the Ochsenkopf, at 1,024 m, is the second-highest summit of the Fichtelgebirge. The Asenturm at the top houses the region's highest restaurant. On clear days, views stretch all the way to Bayreuth. Arrive before 10 a.m. to beat the weekend family crowds.

Carved into the granite summit, an ox's muzzle gives the mountain its name. The Ochsenkopf-Wahrzeichen, a sculpture hewn from the rock, goes unnoticed if you're not looking for it. Spot it on the southern side, left of the tower.

activities.text: Take the cable car from Bischofsgrün to ascend 250 m without effort. In summer, the Ochsenkopf Coaster—a kilometer-long toboggan ride on rails—races downhill at 40 km/h. Family thrills guaranteed, with individual braking.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Offenburg conducted two waves of witch trials: the first between 1586 and 1608, and the second between 1627 and 1631. According to the city council minutes, a total of 89 people were executed - women and men from all walks of life, including members of councillors' families. The first sentences of the second wave were handed down as early as 1 December 1627, when three women were burned alive. The Ritterhaus (the municipal museum at Ritterstraße 10) has a well-documented section on these trials. The displays are mainly in German.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: You don't expect such a castle right in the center of Oldenburg. The Schloss, residence of counts then grand dukes since the 12th century, houses the Landesmuseum für Kunst und Kulturgeschichte. The state rooms and chapel are worth the admission.

The rhododendrons of the Schlossgarten fill the air with fragrance from May onward. This 16-hectare English park, laid out by Duke Peter Friedrich Ludwig, preserves specimens planted in 1828 among the oldest in Germany. Open daily from 8 AM.
The Lappan, a 15th-century bell tower isolated from its church, stands as the city's symbol. Three minutes' walk from the Schloss, it marks the entrance to the pedestrian shopping zone.

activities.text: Make a detour to the Schlossgarten's Tropenhaus to see tropical plants in the middle of Lower Saxony. Free, open in the afternoon. In the evening, bats take over the park.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

activities.text: If the sky is clear in the late afternoon, climb Olympiaberg, the freely accessible hill in Olympiapark. From the top, the view takes in Frei Otto and Günter Behnisch’s tensile roofs, designed for the 1972 Games, the Olympic lake, and the city’s rooftops. The park covers 85 hectares: head back down along the lakeshore to reach the Olympiazentrum U-Bahn station.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Experience Osnabrück, the historic university city where the Peace of Westphalia was signed in 1648, ending the Thirty Years' War. This cultural hub seamlessly blends medieval heritage with youthful energy, featuring impressive Gothic architecture, the magnificent Town Hall, and a vibrant pedestrian zone. The city's 1,200-year history unfolds through its stunning churches and well-preserved old town.

activities.text: Explore the surrounding Osnabrücker Land, ideal for mountain hiking with routes ranging from short day walks to multi-day treks. The rolling hills and ancient forests offer scenic trails through the Teutoburg Forest and peaceful countryside dotted with traditional farms and historic villages.

Cycle through the Osnabrück region on well-marked paths suited to road cycling and leisure rides. Flat sections offer gentle riding through meadows and along rivers, while the surrounding hills provide challenging climbs rewarded with expansive panoramic views.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands

visits.text: Osnabrück and Münster vie for the title of “City of Peace.” It was here, in the Friedenssaal of the Rathaus, that the Treaty of Westphalia was signed in 1648. The 42 portraits of sovereigns and ambassadors still hang on the walls. The 1512 building has carried the European Heritage Label since 2015.

The broken angles of Daniel Libeskind's Felix-Nussbaum-Haus (1998) unsettle you before you even enter. The museum preserves more than 200 works by the painter born in Osnabrück in 1904, murdered at Auschwitz in 1944. Architecture and content speak to each other.

Push open the door of the Remarque-Friedenszentrum to discover the life of Erich Maria Remarque, author of All Quiet on the Western Front, born here in 1898. The permanent exhibition is compact but well done. Free admission.
The Dom Sankt Peter blends Romanesque and Gothic over a length of 109 meters. The cloister and the treasury are open to visitors. The square of the Dom hosts a market on Saturdays.

activities.text: If you're there on a Saturday, the Wochenmarkt on Domplatz is one of the region's best: smoked sausages, rye bread, cheeses from the Osnabrücker Land. Cheerful atmosphere, well-stocked stalls.
Head down into the Altstadt to try a Grünkohl (slow-cooked kale) in season. The pedestrian quarter around the Heger Tor is full of small restaurants.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles
Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: Explore the German Wadden Sea National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site ranked alongside the Grand Canyon and Great Barrier Reef as a natural wonder of global significance. This unique tidal ecosystem stretches along Lower Saxony's North Sea coast, hosting millions of migratory birds and remarkable marine life. The dramatic interplay of ebb and flow creates ever-changing landscapes of mudflats, sandbanks, and salt marshes.

Discover the seven East Frisian Islands, one of Germany's finest coastal treasures, offering unspoilt beaches and distinctive island atmospheres. These islands feature sandy shores, imposing dunes and endless skies where the rhythm of life follows the tides. Each island has its own character, from lively seaside resorts to tranquil nature reserves.

activities.text: Embark on a guided mudflat walking tour across the exposed seabed during low tide, an experience unique to the Wadden Sea. Wade through this lunar-like landscape teeming with shellfish, crabs, and marine worms while expert guides reveal the secrets of this extraordinary ecosystem. The sensation of walking on the ocean floor as seabirds wheel overhead is truly unforgettable.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands

visits.text: From outside, Ottobeuren's Basilika looks like any large country church. Open the door: the interior explodes with stucco, frescoes, and gilding. Built between 1737 and 1766, it's nicknamed the Swabian Escorial. Self-guided visits, organ concerts in summer.

In the Kaisersaal, sixteen Habsburg emperors in marble stare down at you from their pedestals. The monastery's reception hall gives a sense of the abbey's power and wealth in the baroque era. Accessible by guided tour only.

Founded in 764, Ottobeuren's Benedictine abbey has continued uninterrupted through the centuries. The Klostermuseum traces this history in the monastery's former rooms. There's also a monastery shop where the monks sell jams and liqueurs.

activities.text: Attend an organ concert in the Ottobeuren Basilika during summer. The acoustics are remarkable, and concerts are often free or by donation. Check the monastery website for the schedule.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: Cruise ships built 30 km from the sea, in a covered hangar perched on a river: Meyer Werft in Papenburg defies logic. The visitor center exhibits full-size cabins and a six-meter-diameter propeller. 90-minute guided tour, reservation required.

Stroll along the Hauptkanal, the most unusual pedestrian promenade in the north. Replicas of historic sailing ships are moored right in the shopping district. No parking meters anywhere in town, free parking everywhere.

activities.text: If you're lucky, an Überführung of a cruise ship on the Ems happens during your stay: a 300-meter giant glides a few meters from the banks, escorted by tugboats. Dates depend on weather and tides, announced at the last minute.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Humboldt called it the “most beautiful basalt cone in Europe.” The Hoher Parkstein, a volcanic plug 24 million years old, raises its hexagonal columns 38 m above the village. Designated a natural monument since 1937, it's one of Germany's 77 notable geotopes.

Climb the Kreuzweg, a steep five-minute ascent, and at the top you'll find the Bergkirche St. Marien (1852) and a 360-degree panorama of the Upper Palatinate. On clear days, Czechia is visible on the horizon.

activities.text: At the Vulkanerlebnis, the floor rumbles and red smoke rises from it: the museum simulates a volcanic eruption every hour. Fun and well done, especially with children. Admission: €3.50 for adults.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: The white stucco decoration of Dom St. Stephan catches the light all the way up into the vaults. In Passau, the blue-green domes already hint at the richness of the interior, while the organ adds another dimension to the space. View the ceilings from the nave instead of rushing toward the choir. Check visiting hours and respect worship services.

Veste Oberhaus offers the best vantage point over Passau: the city reveals its layout at a glance. From above, the waterways frame the old town and explain its location on a peninsula. Focus on the terraces and courtyards; the fortress museum deserves a separate visit. Wear shoes suitable for the climb.

Three rivers meet without immediately blending into one: Dreiflüsseeck lets you compare the Danube, Inn, and Ilz. Their colors can differ, but the effect depends on the flow and the light. This point is a natural endpoint for a walk through the old town. Keep your distance from the riverbanks and stay away if a flood-related closure is posted.

activities.text: Follow the waterfront in Passau’s old town, moving from tightly packed facades to views of the Inn. Residenzplatz, Altes Rathaus, Schaiblingsturm, and the grounds around Kloster Niedernburg mark out a varied urban loop. The round Schaiblingsturm tower is an easy landmark along the riverbank. Leave your car in the parking lot and view the buildings from the outside on this walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
Bavarian Forest in 4 Days: From Passau to the Großer Arber

visits.text: In 1943, the first V2 rocket was launched from Peenemünde. The Historisch-Technisches Museum traces the history of this research site, the ambiguous birthplace of space exploration. The former Soviet submarine U-461, moored in the harbor, can also be visited. Allow at least two hours.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Pillnitz Castle is actually an ensemble of three palaces set in a 28-hectare park on the banks of the Elbe, 15 km southeast of Dresden. Augustus the Strong had received it from a disgraced former mistress—the Countess of Cosel—and decided to make it a pleasure palace “in the Indian style,” meaning exotic. Between 1720 and 1724, architect Pöppelmann built the Wasserpalais and Bergpalais, two symmetrical buildings with characteristic pagoda roofs, framing a Baroque courtyard. A wide staircase descends from the Wasserpalais to the Elbe, where royal gondolas docked directly. In 1791, it was here that the Emperor of Austria and the King of Prussia signed the Declaration of Pillnitz, threatening military intervention in France if the French royal family were mistreated—which precipitated the declaration of war.

The New Palace, built between 1819 and 1826 after the fire of 1818 destroyed the Renaissance wing, closes off the eastern side of the courtyard. Its Classical dome is the only one of its kind in Dresden. The park also contains a Chinese pavilion from 1804 and a Neoclassical English pavilion from 1780. The garden's camellia, imported from Japan around 1780 and planted in 1800, stands 8.9 meters tall and produces up to 35,000 carmine-red flowers between February and April.

activities.text: Stroll in Pillnitz Park between the three palaces, French gardens, English garden, and greenhouses. You can also walk along the Elbe on the landscaped banks below the Wasserpalais.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

visits.text: Pirna is the gateway to Saxon Switzerland—and a medieval town worth a stop in itself. Its lanes around the Marktplatz have remained almost intact since the 16th century, with Renaissance facades with Gothic porticoes and houses with Baroque elements in adjacent streets (Schmiedergasse, Schössergasse). The painter Bernardo Bellotto, known as Canaletto, worked there in the 1750s and left several paintings of the town that show how little it has changed—some are visible at the Residenzschloss in Dresden.

The Marienkirche, whose steeples dominate the Marktplatz, is a Gothic church built from the 14th to 16th centuries. Its interior, modified in the Baroque era, retains Gothic ribbed vaults and a Renaissance altarpiece.

Sonnenstein Castle dominates the town from a rocky spur. Built from the 13th century for the Margraves of Meissen, it became a psychiatric hospital in 1811—the first establishment of this type in Saxony. Between 1940 and 1941, as part of the Nazi euthanasia program Aktion T4, more than 13,700 people with mental and physical disabilities were gassed in its cellars. A memorial on the site documents these crimes and honors the victims. The castle now houses the district administrative headquarters.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
Saxon Switzerland in 3 Days: Bastei and Sandstone Peaks

visits.text: Plau am See received its town charter in the 13th century and retains a compact historic center with medieval lanes and half-timbered houses around the river port. The town hall, designed in Dutch Renaissance style, is one of the most striking buildings on the central square.

Climb up to the ruins of Plau Castle, which still dominate the center from their promontory. Two steps away, the Gothic church of Sankt Marien deserves a stop for its distinctive bell tower and austere interiors typical of northern Germany.

The Hubbrücke is the town's liveliest spot: this historic lift bridge spans the Elde River right in the center and regularly raises to let pleasure boats pass. Settle into a terrace table by the quay to watch the maneuver—it's Plau am See's essential ritual.

activities.text: The Plauer See, Mecklenburg's third-largest lake at 38 square kilometers, is surrounded by reeds where cranes and ospreys nest. The bike path around it extends for 55 kilometers—a 10-kilometer section toward Bad Stuer passes the lift bridge and follows wild shorelines.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: Lakes, Castles, and the Baltic Coast

visits.text: More compact than the Mercedes-Benz Museum, the Porsche Museum packs a bigger punch: around 80 cars across 5,600 m², in a structure that seems to float on three supports, designed by Delugan Meissl and opened in 2009. Look for the 1948 356 “Nr. 1” Roadster, weighing 585 kg with a top speed of 135 km/h, then the 917 that won Le Mans in 1970. Arrive before 10 a.m.: the Early Bird ticket costs €12 instead of €15. Free multimedia guide; take S-Bahn S6 to Neuwirtshaus (Porscheplatz). Closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Climb the vineyard terraces to Sanssouci Palace, the summer palace Frederick the Great had built from 1745 to 1747 to live “without a care.” Its ten main rooms retain their 18th-century decor, on the scale of a private retreat rather than a royal court. The €14 ticket requires a timed entry: book online, download the free SANSSOUCI app, and bring your own headphones, as none are provided. Closed on Mondays.

The Sanssouci Picture Gallery, built starting in 1755 to house Frederick II’s paintings, is described as Germany’s oldest surviving gallery building. Caravaggio’s The Incredulity of Saint Thomas, painted around 1601, hangs alongside seven works by Rubens. It is open only from May through October: individual admission costs €8, or is included in the €22 sanssouci+ ticket, valid for one day at Potsdam’s palaces.

A summer residence on paper, a display of power in reality: the New Palace, built from 1763 to 1769 following the Seven Years’ War, has more than 200 rooms and over 400 sandstone statues. Among its highlights are the Grotto Hall, encrusted with shells, quartz, and semiprecious stones, and the two-story Marble Hall. Choose the €14 Grand Tour ticket; the palace is closed on Tuesdays, and also on Mondays from January through March.

End the day in the Holländisches Viertel: 134 red brick houses built in the 1730s to attract Dutch craftspeople to Potsdam. The Soldier King, Frederick William I, commissioned them from Jan Bouman, and his son Frederick the Great completed the neighborhood after 1740. Walk there along Brandenburger Straße, the pedestrian street that starts at Potsdam’s Brandenburg Gate: the city has its own, with two facades in different styles.

The Museum Barberini makes Potsdam a destination for Impressionism: 34 paintings by Claude Monet are on permanent display among more than 100 works collected by Hasso Plattner. The museum opened in 2017 on the Alter Markt, in a palace reconstructed on the model of Rome’s Palazzo Barberini, and refreshes its displays with three exhibitions a year. Avoid Tuesdays; admission is €16 on weekdays, €18 on weekends, and €10 from 5:30 p.m.

On February 10, 1962, U-2 pilot Gary Powers was exchanged here for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel: the Glienicker Brücke, which connects Potsdam to Berlin-Wannsee across the Havel, witnessed two more exchanges of agents in 1985 and 1986. Steven Spielberg drew on this history for his 2015 film Bridge of Spies. Walk across this bridge, built in 1907 and reopened to pedestrians on the evening of November 10, 1989.

activities.text: It was not until 1991 that Frederick the Great was laid to rest where he had wished: in the crypt on the highest terrace of Sanssouci Palace, buried at night without pomp, as stipulated in his will. Then descend the terraces, planted with grapevines beginning in 1744, to take in the park’s parterre. Admission to Sanssouci Park is free, daily from 8 a.m. until dusk.

The gold of the Chinese House’s columns and statues emerges between the trees as you round a bend on a path in Sanssouci Park. The park covers nearly 300 hectares, crossed by an east–west axis more than 2 km long; Johann Gottfried Büring’s pavilion, built from 1755 to 1764 on a trefoil plan, can be admired along the way. The interior is open only from May through October (€5), but you can admire the exterior year-round.

Climb the 223 steps of Schinkel’s Nikolaikirche to the gallery encircling its dome, 42 m above the ground: the Alter Markt unfolds at your feet, with its 16 m obelisk, the Altes Rathaus topped by a gilded Atlas, and the Landtag, whose facade replicates that of the former palace. The climb costs €5; hours vary depending on services and concerts.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci
Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Nine degrees all at once, in the middle of summer, when you enter the Teufelshöhle in Pottenstein: the 1,900-meter-long cave - of which 800 meters are accessible to the public - maintains this temperature year-round. The guided tour lasts 45 minutes and passes through the "Barbarossadom," a grand chamber measuring 45 × 18 × 15 meters according to site data, and past a complete cave bear skeleton. Open all year, including winter.

The Burg Pottenstein dominates the village from a limestone outcrop. The thousand-year-old enclosure today houses a restaurant and a small exhibition; the official site indicates seasonal opening. The view across the dolomitic valleys of Franconian Switzerland deserves the ascent.

activities.text: After the cave, take the trail toward Schöngrundsee along the Weihersbachtal stream. The Teufelshöhle café, open April to October, offers a terrace facing the cliff - the route's most spectacular coffee break. Franconian Switzerland counts more than 1,000 caves in total.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: The Darßer Ort lighthouse, at the peninsula's tip, is reached on foot or by bike through the Darß primeval forest. The Natureum, museum of the Boddenlandschaft national park, sits right beside it. The Darß's west beach is one of the Baltic's wildest.

activities.text: Look for the Darßer Haustüren, painted and carved house doors, a local tradition recognized as intangible cultural heritage. Each door tells the owner's story. Prerow's Darß Museum documents them.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Board a boat from Prien-Stock harbor to reach Herreninsel Island on Chiemsee, Bavaria's largest lake. The crossing takes about 20 minutes. In 1873, Ludwig II purchased the entire island for 350,000 florins from an industrialist who planned to clear its entire forest. Construction of the palace began in 1878 under the direction of Georg von Dollmann.

Tour Herrenchiemsee Palace, Ludwig II's final and most lavish construction project—and the one where he spent the least time: just 16 days. The king spent more money on this single construction than on Neuschwanstein and Linderhof combined. At his death in 1886, 50 rooms remained unfinished. The Great Hall of Mirrors, inspired by the one at Versailles, measures 98 meters—25 meters longer than its French model. To illuminate it, 70 servants had to light 33 candelabras and 52 chandeliers.

After the palace, take the boat to Fraueninsel (Women's Island), where the Frauenwörth Benedictine convent has existed for 1,200 years—one of Germany's oldest monastic communities still in operation. Walk around the small island (one hour on foot) among fishermen's houses and monastery gardens. The nuns produce a renowned local spirit.

activities.text: At the end of the day, back in Prien, stroll along the shores of Chiemsee on the Priener Uferweg. Enjoy the sunset over the lake with the Alps in the background.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
German Alpine Road: Lake Constance to Königssee
Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip
Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Prora deserves a separate stop beyond the visit from Binz. The Dokumentationszentrum traces the history of the KdF complex, intended to accommodate 20,000 vacationers simultaneously. The contrast between the ideology and the fine-sand beach just behind it is striking.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Putbus is Rügen's only neoclassical town, created in the early 19th century by Prince Malte zu Putbus. Its Circus, a circular square lined with white houses, evokes Bath more than the Baltic. The Rasender Roland, a steam train traveling at 30 km/h, departs from here for Binz and Sellin.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Quedlinburg has approximately 2,000 half-timbered houses spanning six centuries of construction—from the 14th to the 19th century. UNESCO-listed in 1994, the town owes this distinction to its imperial origins: first mentioned in 922 in a charter by Henry I the Fowler, it became the favorite residence of the first Kings of Germany. Between 922 and 1207, German rulers stayed here 69 times.

The Collegiate Church of St. Servatius dominates the town from the Schlossberg. Built from 1070 to 1129 on 9th-century foundations, it is classified by UNESCO as a masterpiece of Romanesque art. In its crypt lie Henry I and his wife Matilda—Germany's first rulers. Under the Third Reich, Heinrich Himmler transformed the crypt into a neo-pagan sanctuary dedicated to Henry I, whom he considered “the most German of German leaders.”

The Lyonel Feininger Gallery presents works by the German-American master who joined the Bauhaus in 1919 and taught there until the Nazis forced it to close. He had a personal connection with Quedlinburg and deposited a series of works there that make up this permanent collection.

The Marktplatz is framed by the town hall mentioned as early as 1310 and its Roland statue, a medieval symbol of municipal freedoms. The inner courtyards hidden behind the facades are worth exploring.

activities.text: Climb to the Schlossberg for views over Quedlinburg's rooftops and the Harz plain, then descend through cobbled alleyways. About 15 minutes from the market square.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Around Hanover: Lower Saxony's Most Beautiful Sites
Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns
Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken

visits.text: The exterior looks like a genuine ninth-century Slavic fortress—because it is an exact reconstruction. Slawenburg Raddusch was excavated from 1984 to 1990 before being rebuilt from 1999 to 2003. The circular rampart measured 57 meters in diameter, 10 meters wide and 9 meters high. The museum has been closed since February 2026: interior visits are not possible.

activities.text: From Naturhafen Raddusch, follow the Libellenpfad along the embankment, parallel to the canal used by the punts. The trail's installations introduce dragonflies and offer a view of their world through models. Return to the harbor to watch the punts set off along the Spreewald's channels.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: The Karl May Museum occupies two buildings: Villa Shatterhand, where the writer lived from 1895 until his death in 1912, and Villa Bärenfett, a Wild West-style log cabin built next door. Karl May—who had never set foot in America when he wrote his novels about Winnetou—owned a collection here of over 800 Native American ethnographic objects from the 18th and 19th centuries. His study, library, and Oriental drawing room are preserved exactly as they were in Villa Shatterhand. May is the most-read German novelist of all time, with 200 million copies sold worldwide.

The vineyards of Radebeul cover the slopes above the town, facing due south on terraces supported by stone walls. This 507-hectare region is one of Germany's northernmost—vines have been cultivated here since at least the 12th century. The dominant grape varieties are Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, and Pinot Blanc. Wackerbarth Palace, a state-owned wine estate founded in 1728, is the best-known in the valley.

activities.text: Hiking in the Radebeul vineyards with views over the Elbe valley. Marked trails cross the vineyard terraces to the Bismarckturm at the hilltop. Allow about 2 hours for a complete circuit with views of Dresden in the distance.

Saxon wine tasting at a Radebeul winery. Local winemakers offer guided tastings in the cellar or on the terrace with views over the vines—Riesling, Pinot Blanc, and Goldriesling are the region's flagship wines.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland

visits.text: Look up inside St. Georg Church in Raitenhaslach: across three bays, Johannes Zick painted the life of St. Bernard in 1743 for the monastery’s 600th anniversary. Established here in 1146 as the first Cistercian monastery in Old Bavaria, it served as the burial place of the dukes of Burghausen in the 15th century. The reception rooms in the Prälatenstock can be visited by reservation.

Burghausen calls it “the pearl of the Salzach Valley”: on its plateau, the Wallfahrtskirche Marienberg raises its twin towers about 3 km from the center. Franz Alois Mayr rebuilt it from 1760 to 1764; Johann Martin Heigl, a pupil of Johann Baptist Zimmermann, painted its ceilings devoted to the Virgin Mary. Stop on your way to Burghausen; 30 minutes is enough.

days_plan.itin_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach

visits.text: The murmur of the Ramsauer Ache accompanies the view that made Ramsau famous: the Pfarrkirche St. Sebastian, framed from the Malerwinkel with the Ertlsteg in the foreground and the Reiter Alm in the background. Construction of the church began in 1512 under Prince-Provost Gregor Rainer. Its pews still bear the nameplates of village families, whose seats were assigned starting in 1615. The church is always open: step inside after taking your photo.

Keep four euros handy for the Wimbachklamm, reached from the Wimbachbrücke parking lot: buy your ticket from the machine at the gorge entrance. For about 200 m, wooden walkways and bridges follow the rock walls as water gushes from the rock and tumbles down in cascades. The gorge is open from late April to early November; on hot days, it is the coolest stop of the day.

activities.text: About 3,500 years ago, part of the Hochkalter collapsed: some 15 million m³ of rock blocked the valley and created the Hintersee. The Zauberwald grew among this jumble of boulders; explore it along the Naturlehrpfad (3.3 km, 1 hour 15 minutes), then follow the lakeshore. In the early 19th century, Carl Rottmann and other painters set up their easels here; park at the Zauberwald parking lot in Seeklause.

days_plan.itin_title: Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits

visits.text: The Basteibrücke spans the ravines from rock to rock. This stone bridge dates to 1851; from the surrounding area, the Elbe looks almost motionless below the cliffs. Take your time at the Bastei viewpoints, but keep the bridge clear: photo stops quickly slow foot traffic.

activities.text: You’ll climb from Rathen toward the Bastei before descending the Schwedenlöcher stairs. The detour published by the tourist information office goes through Rathewalde: 8.72 km and 3 hours 30 minutes of walking. Follow this alternative, as the lower Amselgrund remains closed after the storm; it bypasses the classic loop via the Amselsee.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxon Switzerland in 3 Days: Bastei and Sandstone Peaks

visits.text: Ravensburg has preserved its medieval profile intact: towers, gates, and ramparts frame an old trading town that has prospered since the 14th century. The Mehlsack, a 51-meter white tower, dominates the skyline. Climb it for views of Lake Constance and the Alps.
The Veitsburg, a former Guelph fortress above the town, offers 360° panoramas and a Biergarten popular with locals. The Museum Ravensburger, devoted to the board game publisher, appeals to families.

The Museum Humpis-Quartier occupies a complex of 15th-century patrician houses in the center. It traces Ravensburg's history as a member of the Great Ravensburg Trading Society, a commercial network that rivaled the Hanseatic League.

activities.text: Stroll down Marktstraße under the arcades and sample a Seele, an elongated bread roll typical of Swabia, crisp and sprinkled with salt and cumin. They're found almost exclusively in Upper Swabia.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: White beneath the walls: the Burgruine Weißenstein stands on a quartz outcrop near Regen. Its geological foundation matters as much as the castle in understanding this landform, known as the Pfahl. From the ruins, views stretch across the forest and the area around the town. From mid-May to mid-September, the ruins open daily from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM, then only on weekends until mid-November; they close in rainy weather.

The Gläserner Wald grows without leaves at the foot of the Burgruine Weißenstein. Its glass trees bring regional craftsmanship into the landscape, with colors that change with the light. After Frauenau and Zwiesel, this installation provides a fitting conclusion to the route’s glassmaking theme. Visit while it is still daylight and view the sculptures from a distance without touching them.

The name Museum im Fressenden Haus sparks curiosity even before you visit: why a house that is “devouring”? This former granary associated with the castle also preserves the memory of the writer Siegfried von Vegesack. The building adds a human story to the nearby ruins and glass trees. Check its hours separately from the castle’s; one being open does not guarantee that the other is.

activities.text: You will finish with a short walk through Weißenstein, the part of Regen that brings together the castle, museum, and sculptures. The quartz of the Pfahl provides a visible link between the buildings and the terrain, while the glass trees echo the trip’s craft theme. The three sites are within a few minutes’ walk of one another; park just once.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavarian Forest in 4 Days: From Passau to the Großer Arber

visits.text: The Steinerne Brücke has spanned the Danube for approximately 336 meters since 1146, following eleven years of construction. For nearly 800 years, until 1935, it was Regensburg’s only safe crossing over the river, and the tourist office describes it as Germany’s oldest surviving stone bridge. Cross it when you arrive in the late afternoon: the old town, which it connects to Stadtamhof, has been UNESCO-listed since 2006. From April through October, the Besucherzentrum in the Salzstadel sells tickets for the bridge tower.

In the nave of Dom St. Peter, light streams through an almost complete collection of medieval stained-glass windows, some dating to the 1220s–1230s. Begun in 1275, the Gothic cathedral took approximately six centuries to build: its 105-meter spires were only completed between 1859 and 1869. Arrive early the following morning—the building opens at 6:30 a.m.—and listen carefully: the Regensburger Domspatzen are the cathedral choir.

Under Marcus Aurelius in the 2nd century, Roman soldiers entered their camp through the Porta Praetoria, whose gateway still stands just steps from the cathedral. This surviving structure is a reminder that Regensburg’s historic fabric spans nearly two thousand years. Stop by right after the cathedral; beneath the neighboring church, document Niedermünster displays remains dating from the year 179, accessible only on a guided tour.

If you fit just one guided tour into your day, choose Regensburg’s Altes Rathaus. From 1663 to 1806, it housed the Perpetual Diet of the Holy Roman Empire; the Imperial Hall and conference rooms remain largely in their original condition, while the Fragstatt, a medieval torture chamber, occupies the basement. The tour, called document Reichstag, is available only with a guide: sign up at the tourist office on the ground floor of the Rathaus and allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

The Goldener Turm on Wahlenstraße has stood nine stories and 50 meters tall since the second half of the 13th century. More than 60 patrician towers once rose above this trading city, and several still survive in the old town. Walk up Wahlenstraße and then Bachgasse, looking up as you go: this 15-minute stroll fits easily between two guided tours.

Once a Benedictine abbey, Schloss Thurn und Taxis is now a palace still inhabited by the princely family, who have lived at St. Emmeram since 1812. The Thurn und Taxis family arrived in Regensburg in 1748 to represent the emperor at the Imperial Diet and received these buildings as compensation for their postal rights in Bavaria. According to the tourist office, the palace has more than 500 rooms. Visits are by guided tour only: from late March to mid-November, tour times run from 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; book online.

You’ll end the day at the Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte on Donaumarkt, beside the river. Its permanent exhibition tells the story of how Bavaria became a free state, covering the period from 1800 to the present through about 1,000 objects spanning nine generations. The panoramic show in the lobby is free. Adult admission is €7, with free admission for visitors under 18; the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: Regensburg’s simplest meal is also its most enjoyable: charcoal-grilled sausages and sauerkraut at the Historische Wurstkuchl. Located at the foot of the Steinerne Brücke for more than 500 years, it bills itself as the world’s oldest sausage kitchen; the sauerkraut comes from its own cellar, and the mustard follows Elsa Schricker’s recipe. Look for the flood marks on the facade, then sit down early: the kitchen closes at 7 p.m.

You’ll cross the Steinerne Brücke to reach Stadtamhof on the opposite bank as evening colors settle over the old town. Covering 0.66 km², this district is the smallest of Regensburg’s 18 districts. It only became part of the city in 1924 and is included in the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Walk through it to the Rococo St. Mang Church, then return to the banks of the Danube to look at the cathedral spires above the rooftops.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
Altmühltal and the Danube in 4 Days, from Ingolstadt to Regensburg

visits.text: Founded in 724 by itinerant bishop Pirmin, Reichenau Abbey was one of Carolingian and Ottonian Europe's major cultural centers. UNESCO since 2000, Lake Constance's largest island keeps its three Romanesque churches, its vegetable fields, and its calm.

Benedictine monks returned to the island in 2001, two and a half centuries after the last ones left. The abbey also serves as town hall. The Minster's Schatzkammer houses reliquaries and illuminated manuscripts of considerable value.
Visit Sankt Georg church for its 10th-century murals: the most complete Ottonian cycle preserved north of the Alps. The colors have survived a thousand years. Free entry.

activities.text: Small but erudite, the reconstructed Kräutergarten behind the cloister follows the prescriptions of Walahfrid Strabo, 9th-century abbot and author of the botanical treatise Hortulus. Medicinal herbs, aromatic plants, flowers. Guided tours in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: The best introduction to Berlin starts on the roof of the Reichstag. Norman Foster’s glass dome, completed in 1999, crowns the federal parliament building, and its 230 m ramp offers panoramic views of the government district, accompanied by an audio guide lasting about twenty minutes. Admission is free with online registration confirmed at least two hours in advance: bring an original ID document, as copies are not accepted. During some weeks, only the rooftop terrace remains accessible; check the calendar at bundestag.de.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: The Residenz grew over more than six centuries, and your legs will remember it. The highlight is the Antiquarium, a Renaissance hall nearly 66 m long, completed in 1571: it is the palace’s oldest space and one of the largest halls of its style north of the Alps. Next come reception rooms from every era of Wittelsbach rule. Get the combined ticket with the Schatzkammer for €15, and allow nearly two hours for the museum alone.

Next, head to the Residenz’s Schatzkammer: more than 1,200 pieces of jewelry and precious objects, spanning late antiquity to neoclassicism, made of rock crystal, gold, enamel, and ivory, including the crown of the kings of Bavaria. It all began with Duke Albert V’s decision in 1565 to prohibit the dispersal of the family treasury. Arrive at least an hour before closing: last entry is at 5 p.m. in summer and 4 p.m. in winter.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Four hundred fifty-two rooms across eighteen buildings: even the guided tour gives up on showing all of Residenzschloss Ludwigsburg. Begun in 1704 as a hunting lodge for Duke Eberhard Ludwig and made a residence in 1718, it blends Baroque, Rococo, and Neoclassical styles. Look out for the Schlosstheater and its almost complete original stage machinery. The interiors can only be seen on a guided tour, costing €10, with several departures daily, some in English.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Schloss Rheinsberg was Frederick the Great's residence in his youth, before his accession to the throne in 1740. The palace on the Grienericksee inspired Tucholsky (Rheinsberg: Ein Bilderbuch für Verliebte, 1912). Rococo rooms, palace theater, English-style park.

activities.text: Circle the Grienericksee by canoe or on foot (5 km loop). The palace is reflected in the water in the morning, with ideal light for photos. Canoe rental at the harbor.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: In 1575, the manuscript of the Nibelungenlied found at Prunn was sent to the ducal library in Munich; it has since been known as the Prunner Codex. Burg Prunn, perched on an almost vertical cliff above the Altmühl, can only be visited on a guided tour in German lasting approximately 45 minutes. From April through October, tours depart hourly, with the last at 5 p.m.

activities.text: If you’re passing through Riedenburg between mid-March and mid-October, set your watch by the Falkenhof Schloss Rosenburg: flight demonstrations take place at 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. Eagles, falcons, vultures, and owls soar above the courtyard of the castle, which has housed a falconry center since 1978. Expect to pay €12 per adult, with no shows on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Altmühltal and the Danube in 4 Days, from Ingolstadt to Regensburg

visits.text: The Bavarian Forest National Park (Bayerischer Wald) is Germany's oldest national park, created in 1970. It covers 24,000 hectares along the Czech border, continuous with Šumava National Park on the Bohemian side—together they form the largest protected forest area in Central Europe.

Start at the Tierfreigelände in Neuschönau, a 250-hectare natural enclosure where 45 animal species live in conditions close to their wild habitat: wolves, brown bears, lynx, European bison, otters, beavers, deer and large raptors. A 7-kilometer trail winds through the site—allow 3 to 4 hours. Bring binoculars, as some animals keep their distance. Entry is free.

Then head to Rachelsee, a mountain lake at an altitude of 1,071 meters, surrounded by century-old beeches and spruces. Local legend says its name derives from the devil's grandmother and tells of an evil woman who was the last to travel across its waters, her coffin accompanied by a flock of black ravens. The trail from Spiegelau is well marked.

Stop at the Hans-Eisenmann-Haus visitor center in Neuschönau, which presents the park's history and wildlife. It's also the starting point for the Baumwipfelpfad, a 1,300-meter aerial walkway that winds through the forest canopy.

activities.text: Hike the marked trails of the park from Riedlhütte or Neuschönau. Over 500 kilometers of paths crisscross the park, some passing through “primeval forest” zones where no human intervention has been permitted for decades. The areas around Lusen and Großer Rachel are the wildest.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Forests & Medieval Towns

visits.text: The fragrance reaches you before the view: some 4,500 rosebushes bloom each summer in the Neue Residenz’s Rosengarten, designed by Balthasar Neumann and framed by linden trees. Statues by Ferdinand Tietz, carved in 1760–1761, punctuate the paths, and the terrace looks out toward the Michaelsberg and the old town’s rooftops. Open from 9 a.m. to 6:45 p.m. from April through September, and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. the rest of the year; the pavilion houses a café.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: The Lokschuppen alone makes Rosenheim worth a stop. The former locomotive depot of the first train station, which opened in 1858, has hosted exhibitions since 1988 that have drawn up to 280,000 visitors. Through August 1, 2027, RÖMER brings together 1,228 objects from around thirty lenders. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; arrive when it opens.

Max-Josefs-Platz is lined with Inn-Salzach-style facades rebuilt after the great fire of 1641; the square became pedestrian-only in 1984. At one end, the Mittertor is the only one of the market town’s five gates still standing; its core makes it Rosenheim’s oldest building. Allow 30 minutes on foot, continuing as far as the onion-domed bell tower of St. Nikolaus.

To understand the sources of Rosenheim’s prosperity, head upstairs to the Städtisches Museum, housed in the Mittertor. Its 23 rooms display around 4,000 objects covering everything from river shipping on the Inn to trade, and from tiled stoves to popular piety. It opens Tuesday through Sunday from noon to 5 p.m., so save it for early afternoon.

Take the “Himmelsleiter,” the staircase nicknamed the ladder to heaven, to reach the Holztechnisches Museum, which opened in 1990 in the Ellmaierhaus on Max-Josefs-Platz. Across more than 400 m², original objects, models, and tools trace woodworking from the craftsperson to the engineer. Half an hour is enough; the museum opens Tuesday through Sunday starting at noon.

days_plan.itin_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach

visits.text: Kröpeliner Straße, Rostock's wide thoroughfare converted into a pedestrian zone in 1968—one of East Germany's first—is well-restored and honest, without the commercial staging of other Hanseatic cities. It stretches from Neuer Markt to Kröpeliner Tor for about 600 m, alternating brick Gothic, Renaissance, and some GDR-era concrete buildings. The Universitätsplatz midway is the historic heart.

The Kröpeliner Tor tower rises 54 m above the end of the pedestrian zone, built around 1270 as part of the city fortifications. Of the twenty-two gates Rostock once possessed, four have survived. A small local history museum lodges in the tower. The view from the rampart walk justifies the stairs.

The Marienkirche houses a medieval astronomical clock still in operation. This clock dates from the 14th century and displays the liturgical calendar, moon phases, and solar time with a precision its builders took a century to perfect. Each day at noon, the upper dial's figurines parade. The church itself dates from the 13th century and its 117-m spire is visible from Warnemünde on clear days.

activities.text: A 15-min S-Bahn ride separates Rostock from Warnemünde, the historic seaside district at the Warnow estuary. The white sand beach, aligned Strandkörbe, and old red-brick lighthouse form the most repeated image of the Mecklenburg coast. Less touristy than Binz, the waterfront remains local and calm outside August.

If you are there in August (usually the second weekend), the Hanse Sail brings together on the Warnow each year one to two hundred traditional sailing ships and museum vessels. It is one of the great maritime gatherings of northern Germany, open to the public and free from the quays. Trips out to sea are also on offer.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: Lakes, Castles, and the Baltic Coast
German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: The Brunnenhalle in Bad Münster am Stein’s Kurmittelhaus, built in 1911, displays in glass cylinders the three springs collectively known as the Rheingrafenquelle. A small exhibition tells the story of salt and of brine and radon baths. A graduation tower still operates in the Kurpark: pause at its base before heading to the ferry.

More than its walls, largely rebuilt in the 19th century, it is Ebernburg’s history that leaves an impression. Franz von Sickingen offered Luther asylum here in 1521; Luther declined, but Bucer and Oecolampadius came, and Ulrich von Hutten nicknamed it the “inn of justice.” A small exhibition traces the history of the castle, which is open year-round.

activities.text: A sheer 200-meter wall of red rhyolite: admire the Rotenfels from the banks of the Nahe in Bad Münster am Stein. To protect peregrine falcons, climbing is normally prohibited east of the Bastei from January 1 to June 30, and west of it year-round. Parts of the rock formation and the hiking trails are currently closed following a fire: do not plan on walking along the ridge.

If the ferryman is at his post, board the Nahefähre in the Huttental: pulled by hand along a cable, it is the only ferry of its kind in Rhineland-Palatinate. On the opposite bank, a trail followed by steps cut into the rock leads to the ruins of Rheingrafenstein, perched on a 135-meter spur. Expect to pay €1.50 for the crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern

places.name: Rothenburg Ob Der Tauber

visits.text: Rothenburg ob der Tauber is one of Europe's best-preserved medieval towns. Perched on a plateau above the Tauber, it has remained virtually unchanged since the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which ruined the town but paradoxically preserved it: too poor to modernize, it retained its medieval appearance intact. Its 13th- and 14th-century ramparts still stand for 4 kilometers, punctuated by 42 towers and gates. The wall walk (Turmweg) is free to access and offers a walk of about an hour and a half at a height of 6 meters, with views looking down over the red-tiled roofs and the valley. After the bombing of March 31, 1945, destroyed more than a third of the old town, international aid enabled it to be faithfully rebuilt—the donors' names are engraved on the stones of the restored ramparts.

The Plönlein—from the Latin planum, “little square”—is Rothenburg's most photographed corner and one of Germany's most reproduced images. At the intersection of two sloping streets, a slightly crooked yellow and red half-timbered house stands between the Siebers Tower (1385) on the left and the Kobolzeller Gate on the right, which leads down toward the Tauber valley. This setting inspired the village in Disney's animated film Pinocchio. Come early in the morning to avoid crowds and enjoy the low-angle light. From there, climb the Röder Tower or the Renaissance town hall's belfry for a 360° panorama of the town.

St. James's Church (St. Jakobskirche), built between 1311 and 1484, rises above the Marktplatz with its Gothic silhouette. It houses the Holy Blood Altarpiece, a masterpiece by the sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider.

The Burggarten, at the western tip of town, occupies the site of the Hohenstaufen castle built in 1142, from which King Conrad III ruled the Holy Roman Empire. Of the double fortress, only St. Blaise's Chapel remains, now converted into a memorial. This terraced garden offers Rothenburg's finest panorama: unobstructed views of the Tauber valley, vineyards, town rooftops, and the double row of ramparts.

The Medieval Crime Museum (Kriminalmuseum), housed in the former commandery of the Order of St. John, displays over a thousand years of the history of law and justice across four floors. Public humiliation masks, dunking cages, “shrew's fiddles” for punishing talkative women: these instruments reveal the brutal realities of medieval law enforcement. In complete contrast, the German Christmas Museum (Deutsches Weihnachtsmuseum) celebrates German holiday traditions year-round through thousands of decorations, nutcrackers, and historic Advent calendars—Rothenburg hosts one of Germany's oldest Christmas markets.

The Imperial City Museum (Reichsstadtmuseum), housed in the former Dominican convent founded in 1258, preserves an intact medieval monastic kitchen, Rothenburg's Stations of the Cross (1494)—a cycle of twelve panels painted by Martinus Schwarz—and Mayor Nusch's drinking cup, the famous 3.25-liter cup adorned with the emperor surrounded by the seven prince-electors (1616), which illustrates the Meistertrunk legend.

Fifty kilometers south of Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl is the forgotten “little sister” of the Romantic Road—and that's precisely its charm. This former Free Imperial City, fortified by Emperor Henry V, has kept its ramparts intact thanks to an edict by King Ludwig I of Bavaria and was spared from bombings in both world wars. The walls feature about twenty towers, the oldest dating from 1370. The Wörnitztor, the town's oldest gate, opens onto streets lined with patrician houses with colorful gables, the Wine Market square (Weinmarkt), and St. George's Church, one of the finest Gothic hall churches in southern Germany, built between 1448 and 1499, with its net vaulting and St. Aurelian's reliquary.

activities.text: Join the Night Watchman's tour (Nachtwächter), which leaves from the Marktplatz. Dressed in medieval costume, with a lantern in his hand and a halberd on his shoulder, the watchman guides visitors through the dark lanes of the old town, recounting Rothenburg's legends, scandals, and anecdotes - a tradition dating back to the Middle Ages, when watchmen patrolled to prevent fires and disturbances.

Try a Schneeball (snowball), Rothenburg's specialty: puff pastry rolled into a ball, fried, and dusted with powdered sugar or coated in chocolate. This Franconian pastry comes in dozens of variations at bakeries along Schmiedgasse and Herrngasse.

map_keywords: St. Jakobskirche Rothenburg ob der Tauber

visits.text: A bright octagon beneath a painted dome: at the Klosterkirche St. Marinus und Anianus in Rott am Inn, start by looking up. Johann Michael Fischer rebuilt the church from 1759 to 1763, Matthäus Günther painted the frescoes, and Ignaz Günther designed the altars. Bring binoculars to view the statues of Emperor Henry II and Cunigunde.

A striking contrast in the shadow of the Rococo: Franz Josef Strauß, Bavaria’s minister-president, who died in 1988, rests in the cemetery of Rott’s former monastery. His wife Marianne, who came from a local brewing family, is buried with him. The grave lies along Franz-Josef-Strauß-Weg; 10 minutes is enough.

days_plan.itin_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach

visits.text: Kitsch, certainly, but the Drosselgasse commands its own atmosphere: 144 meters of pedestrian street lined with Weinstuben, live music, outdoor tables. Touristy to the point of caricature in season - and yet it's exactly what you come for. Arrive at opening around 10:30 a.m. to catch it still empty.

The Niederwald Monument stands 38.18 meters high and weighs 75 tonnes according to official site measurements. Erected between 1871 and 1883 to commemorate German unification, it overlooks the Rhine from the Niederwald forest. The cable car (Seilbahn) climbs from town in a few minutes - the view over the valley is well worth the ticket.

activities.text: Take the cable car up to the monument, then walk back down along the Niederwald trails towards Assmannshausen: about 3 km of woodland with panoramic views over the Rhine.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Twelve and a half meters tall, the Germania figure of the Niederwalddenkmal holds the imperial crown above the Rhine. Inaugurated on September 28, 1883, the monument sculpted by Johannes Schilling stands 38 meters tall and faces Bingen on the opposite bank. Walk around the base, then find a bench in the shade of the Niederwald’s trees.

Crowded, noisy, yet endearing: Rüdesheim’s Drosselgasse does nothing by halves. This cobblestone lane, 144 meters long and 2 meters wide, welcomes around three million visitors a year amid wine taverns and live music. Stop by before noon, while there’s still room to breathe, and greet people with a “Gude,” just like the regulars.

Wind in your face, water lapping against the hull: on the roughly six-minute ferry crossing from Rüdesheim to Bingen, turn to look downstream. The Mäuseturm rises from its little island; the archbishops of Mainz built it between 1298 and 1371, and legend has it that Archbishop Hatto was devoured there by mice. Stay at the front of the ferry for the photo.

activities.text: Leave your car at the bottom and ride Rüdesheim’s Seilbahn up to the Niederwald: rows of vines glide beneath the gondolas all the way to the area around the monument. Rebuilt in 2005, it operates daily in 2026 from March 21 to November 1, starting at 9:30 a.m. Take one of the first rides up to find the terrace almost empty.

days_plan.itin_title: The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz

places.name: Ruhestein

visits.text: The name may sound dull, but the content is impressive. The Black Forest National Park visitor centre at Ruhestein explores the ecology of the primary forest that has been reclaiming its territory since the park was created in 2014. It is a restrained exhibition about the fabric of the forest and the species that are returning. Stop for 30 minutes before heading down to the Mummelsee, 8 km farther on.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

map_keywords: Ruhestein National Park Center Black Forest

visits.text: Saalfeld's Feengrotten—“fairy grottoes”—are the galleries of a former alum mine worked from 1530. After closing in 1850, the mine was rediscovered in 1910, and the third chamber—the “Fairy Realm”—was discovered in 1913. The grottoes opened to the public on May 31, 1914. In 1993, the Guinness Book of World Records designated them “the most colorful grottoes in the world”: the mineral formations—stalactites, stalagmites, concretions—display hues ranging from blue to red, including yellow, due to the oxidation of iron phosphate (diadochite), a rare mineral. Since 1914, more than 20 million visitors have traversed the three chambers connected by galleries.

Since 1937, a gallery of Saalfeld's grottoes has housed Germany's first “Emanatorium”—a gallery used for treatment by inhaling underground air. The gallery's microclimate (constant temperature, mineral-rich air) was used to treat respiratory conditions. This therapeutic gallery is Germany's oldest.

The Grottoneum, an interactive museum adjacent to the grottoes, presents the site's geological and mining history along with exhibitions on the region's minerals and crystals. Children's activities are offered.

activities.text: Forest adventure trail near Saalfeld's Feengrotten, with family-friendly routes through the woods above the grottoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

visits.text: Baroque wings, glass and steel at the center: the Saarbrücker Schloss embraces its dual character. Friedrich Joachim Stengel built it between 1738 and 1748; after structural stability problems, Gottfried Böhm renovated the interior and designed the modern central section, inaugurated in 1989. Admission is free, and a free guided tour starts at 3 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday: keep it in mind if you arrive on the weekend.

Fourteen meters beneath Schlossplatz, the castle fortifications have been accessible through the Historisches Museum Saar since 2007. You walk past the remains of the medieval castle, Renaissance casemates, and an 18th-century dungeon before reaching the galleries devoted to Saarland from 1870 to the end of the 20th century, including the Nazi period. Get the combined ticket for the Schlossplatz museums for €8; on Thursdays, admission is free after 5 p.m.

Nothing on Schlossplatz shines quite as brightly as the treasure of the Celtic princess of Reinheim, displayed at the Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte. Dating to around 370 BCE, it brings together gold jewelry, amber, and bronze; the museum also displays gladiator murals from a Roman villa in Mechern. Allow 40 minutes, and aim for Thursday after 3 p.m. if you can: admission is free then.

Step inside the Schlosskirche on Schlossplatz: its museum of sacred art is free. A chapel stood here as early as 1261; the current church dates to the late 15th century, and Stengel topped it with a Baroque onion dome in 1743. Inside, look for the tombs of the counts and princes of Saarbrücken, dating from 1700 to 1768, then head up toward Ludwigsplatz, a few minutes away on foot.

Rows of palace facades and statues perched on the balustrade: Ludwigsplatz provides the setting for the Ludwigskirche, Stengel’s masterpiece. Consecrated in 1775 and reduced to its outer walls by the bombing of October 1944, the church was rebuilt in stages; only 13 of the balustrade’s 28 figures survive. The interior is open free of charge Friday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; on Sundays, the 11 a.m. service takes priority.

In 1938, about 61 facades around St. Johanner Markt were remodeled in two months to create a uniform Baroque backdrop for Hitler’s visit. Reach the square via the Alte Brücke, built from 1546 to 1548 on the orders of Charles V and reserved for pedestrians since 1964. Look for the Baroque fountain dating to 1759–1760, then slip into Fröschengasse: bars, bistros, and restaurants line the street, so save them for dinner.

If you enjoyed the Protestant Baroque of the Ludwigskirche, the Basilika St. Johann reveals Stengel’s Catholic side. He built it from 1754 to 1758, the tower followed in 1763, and restoration work from 1972 to 1975 returned it to its original Baroque appearance. Then continue to the Gothic Revival Rathaus St. Johann, whose tower rises to 54 m: its carillon rings daily at 3:15 p.m.

A little blue horse alone makes the Saarlandmuseum’s Moderne Galerie worth a visit. Franz Marc painted Blaues Pferdchen in 1912 for Walterchen, the son of his friend August Macke, and the dedication is still visible in the upper-right corner of the canvas. Nearby are works by Liebermann, Corinth, Kirchner, and Pechstein; in the sculpture garden, Maillol’s armless Venus. Open Tuesday through Sunday, until 8 p.m. on Wednesdays; free for visitors under 18.

activities.text: Finish the afternoon on the Staden, the leafy promenade that follows the Saar through the city. Lawns, playgrounds, and beer gardens line the route beside the meadows, and the pace finally changes after three museums and two Baroque churches. Set aside just under 1 hour to enjoy the promenade, sitting or strolling, then head back to St. Johanner Markt for dinner.

days_plan.itin_title: Saarland in 3 Days: Saarbrücken, the Saarschleife, and Homburg

visits.text: Saarlouis is nicknamed “the royal hexagon”: at its center, the Großer Markt, a parade ground designed by Vauban, forms a square measuring about 135 m on each side. The Kommandantur, built in 1680–1683 and reconstructed to match the original in the 1970s, housed the governor. Park around the square, which offers more than 300 parking spaces.

A Gothic Revival bell tower in front, exposed concrete behind: St. Ludwig is a puzzling sight even from the Großer Markt. In 1970, Gottfried Böhm, who also redesigned Saarbrücken Castle, replaced the nave with a Brutalist structure whose folded ceiling evokes a tent. The porch facing the square is always open: a few minutes are enough to appreciate the effect.

Sit down for a meal in the Kasematten on either side of the Deutsches Tor: the Prussians built these casemates between 1824 and 1829 to shelter soldiers and horses during bombardments. Those along the east side of Deutsche Straße now house numerous restaurants. Have lunch there, then look up at the gilded Prussian crown adorning the gate.

The Vauban-Insel, a former ravelin in the fortifications, holds monuments to Marshal Ney and the soldier Lacroix. Ney, “the bravest of the brave,” was born in Saarlouis on January 10, 1769, the son of a cooper; his birthplace stands on Bierstraße, in the heart of the Altstadt. Finish by exploring these narrow lanes before driving to Mettlach.

days_plan.itin_title: Saarland in 3 Days: Saarbrücken, the Saarschleife, and Homburg

visits.text: Built in 1334 under the name Zapfenburg to protect pilgrims on the road to Gottsbüren, the Sababurg was later transformed into a hunting lodge by Landgrave William I from 1490 onward. Between 1571 and 1591, a thorn hedge three metres high and five kilometres long encircled it — the very image said to have inspired the Brothers Grimm for Sleeping Beauty. The state of Hesse has been restoring the castle since 2018.

Sababurg and its garden cannot be visited in 2026: the entire castle complex is closed for renovation. Do not plan a walk among the roses or a fairy-tale performance in the courtyard on Friday, Saturday or Sunday. The neighbouring Tierpark Sababurg remains accessible: its enclosures let you observe wood bison, lynx and wild horses in the Reinhardswald.

activities.text: Tierpark Sababurg, open since 1571 — one of Europe's oldest animal parks — is home to wood bison, lynx and wild horses in the Reinhardswald. Allow two hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days
