visits.text: Salem Abbey, a former Cistercian monastery founded in 1134, is one of southern Germany's largest monastic complexes. After the 1803 secularization, the Margraves of Baden made it their residence. Salem boarding school, one of Europe's most prestigious, occupies part of the buildings.

The rococo stuccowork by Johann Georg Dirr in the palace salons displays exceptional finesse. The Feuerwehrmuseum, installed in the former stables, traces firefighting history with a collection of vintage vehicles. Combined ticket available.

activities.text: Salem's park and gardens are freely accessible. A craft market is regularly held in the courtyard. Salem lies midway between Ravensburg and Lake Constance.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Savor Salzwedel, the town of Baumkuchen, where this traditional spit cake has been made according to ancestral recipes for centuries. This sweet specialty with its multiple golden layers, slowly cooked on a rotating cylinder, has become the culinary emblem of the Altmark. The old Hanseatic town with its half-timbered houses and Gothic brick churches provides a charming setting for this gourmet discovery.

Cruise across Lake Arendsee aboard the Queen Arendsee paddle steamer, which glides peacefully over the waters of this 5 km² natural lake. This nostalgic cruise recalls the atmosphere of old steamships while offering delightful views of the wooded shores. The lake, the largest in the Altmark, is a popular destination for relaxation and water activities. It is about half an hour's drive from Salzwedel.

Discover the singular story of Gustav Nagel, a legendary itinerant preacher and natural healer of the early twentieth century. This eccentric figure lived in a hut he had built near Lake Arendsee and walked barefoot through the region to spread his messages of peace and communion with nature. His legacy reflects the spiritual appeal that this peaceful region already exerted. The site is about half an hour's drive from Salzwedel.

activities.text: Tasting of the famous Salzwedel Baumkuchen in a traditional pastry shop

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Cold stone, dark corridors, wind on the ramparts: exploring Burg Rheinfels engages all the senses. Founded in 1245 by Count Dieter V of Katzenelnbogen, it is the largest castle ruin on the Middle Rhine; it withstood a French army of 28,000 men before being destroyed by revolutionary troops in the late 18th century. The mine tunnels can only be visited with a guide. During the season, it is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with last admission at 5 p.m.

Before dinner, make a detour to the Stiftskirche in Sankt Goar, a two-minute walk from the train station. Until the Reformation, pilgrims came here to venerate the tomb of St. Goar, and late Gothic wall paintings are still visible. Then head down to the riverbank: the Loreley rock rises directly opposite.

days_plan.itin_title: The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz

visits.text: Jasmund National Park, established on September 12, 1990—one of the last acts of the East German government before reunification—is Germany's smallest national park at 3,003 hectares. It occupies the Jasmund peninsula in northeastern Rügen and is home to Germany's highest chalk cliffs: the Königsstuhl rises 118 meters above the Baltic. The chalk that forms these cliffs was deposited about 70 million years ago. Every storm carries off entire sections of cliff into the sea, exposing fossils of sea urchins and sponges. Painter Caspar David Friedrich immortalized these cliffs in 1818 in his painting Chalk Cliffs on Rügen, which made them a symbol of German Romanticism.

The Hochuferweg, a trail that follows the cliff between Sassnitz and Lohme for several kilometers, is one of the most spectacular on the Baltic coast. It passes through the Stubnitz beech forest—493 hectares of old-growth beech woods listed as a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site—and offers overhanging views of the sea. At the Königsstuhl, since 2023, an elliptical 185-meter walkway floats above the cliff from a cable-stayed mast, offering a vertiginous perspective on the chalk white and Baltic blue.

activities.text: Hike from Sassnitz to the Königsstuhl along the coastal Hochuferweg through the beech forest and past viewpoints on the cliffs. The trail alternates between stretches deep in the forest and openings overlooking the sea. The park is also accessible by bus from Sassnitz to the Königsstuhl visitor center.

The harbor of Sassnitz, former ferry port to Sweden and Poland, now hosts fishing and pleasure boats. Walk along the quays in late afternoon to watch fishermen return and the fish halls. Several terraces serve freshly smoked herring, a local specialty.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea

visits.text: Schierke is the last village before the summit—a handful of inns, a church, fir trees. Ideal for observing the atmosphere on Walpurgis Night eve (April 30th) before the Brocken ascent the next morning. Outside of April 30th, it's simply quiet and well positioned.

activities.text: Goethe climbed it on 10 December 1777 through snow and fog - today you can reach the Brocken (1,141 m) from Schierke via the Eckerlochstieg in 3 hours, or take the Brockenbahn steam train from Wernigerode (return fare about €49). At the summit: the Brocken spectre optical phenomenon (your shadow projected with a halo onto the mist), a museum about alpine flora and the history of the East/West German border - the Brocken was a closed Soviet military zone until 3 December 1989. Check the weather on brocken.de before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken

visits.text: The view draws you in, but the subject is disturbing: Vogelsang IP occupies a former training school for officials of the Nazi regime. The exhibition “Bestimmung: Herrenmensch” examines the ideology and history of this complex overlooking the valley. The landscape should not overshadow the buildings’ purpose. Start with the historical information and choose a guided tour if you want to better understand their layout.

For a different perspective after exploring Vogelsang’s history, the Wildnis(t)räume exhibition offers another way to understand the area. The Nationalpark-Zentrum Eifel uses interactive exhibits to explain nature and the relationships between habitats. The visit also appeals to travelers who are less drawn to traditional museums. Check the exhibition’s ticketing arrangements and opening hours before combining the two visits.

activities.text: You can finish your visit to Vogelsang IP with a walk through the permitted outdoor areas facing the Urftstausee. The buildings occupy terraced terrain above the landscape of Eifel National Park: their placement is easier to understand outdoors than from a map. Follow the visitor center’s directions and stay in the open areas, without adding a long hike to this stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Volcanic Eifel and the Ahr: Lakes and Castles in 4 Days

activities.text: In the Franconian dialect, “Schlenkern” describes walking with a swinging motion of the arms: it became the nickname of Andreas Graser, the owner in 1875, and later the name of the Schlenkerla tavern. Its history dates back to 1405, the brewery to 1678, and the establishment passed from the Graser family to the Trum family. Order the Rauchbier, a smoked beer that divides opinion around the table from the first sip, in the Dominikanerklause, beneath a painted Gothic vault restored by the Germanisches Nationalmuseum in the 1920s. Open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 11:30 p.m.; food is served from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Founded in 1985 on an 1818 farm that's been a listed historic monument since 1960, the Bauernmuseum Schlepzig is the only museum in the Unterspreewald. Across 5,000 square meters you'll find farming tools from the German Empire through the GDR, a reconstructed living room, and the clay oven where cake is still baked during demonstrations. Open April through October, Tuesday to Sunday from 10 a.m.

activities.text: Take the towpath along the Spree to reach the heart of Schlepzig village, one of the few settlements in the Unterspreewald to have preserved its traditional network of farms intact. Twenty minutes is enough for a complete loop through the lanes.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: The Nydam Boat, a 4th-century rowing vessel excavated in 1863, is displayed in the Nydamhalle at Schloss Gottorf: 23 metres long, 28 oars, built from clinker-laid oak with no keel. It was probably a Germanic war vessel. No other archaeological find of this size and age is as well preserved anywhere in Northern Europe.

Dom St. Petri dominates the Schleswig skyline from every angle — its 112-metre spire towers over the Schlei fjord. Inside stands the Brüggemann Altarpiece, a masterwork of early 16th-century wood carving composed of 392 individual figures.
Schloss Gottorf looks like a pleasure palace, but it is actually a converted medieval fortress — the dukes of Schleswig-Gottorf ruled here from the 12th to the 18th century.

activities.text: Walk through Gottorf's reconstructed Barockgarten, a terraced garden descending towards the Schlei: the clipped hedges, flower beds and view over the water recreate a 17th-century original.

The shores of the Schlei smell of seaweed and wood tar from old boats — a brackish-water scent characteristic of Baltic fjords. The promenade follows the waterfront from the old town harbour to the cathedral: twenty minutes on foot, with views of sailing boats.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: For Prussian splendor, Charlottenburg Palace rivals anything in Potsdam. Built around 1700 for Sophie Charlotte, wife of Frederick I, the Old Palace houses a Porcelain Cabinet with thousands of pieces; in the New Wing, the Golden Gallery and White Hall rank among Europe’s finest Rococo creations, according to the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation. The charlottenburg+ ticket (€19) covers both wings; closed Mondays.

activities.text: Weather permitting, continue into the gardens of Charlottenburg Palace, laid out beginning in 1697 in the Baroque style by Siméon Godeau and bordered by the Spree. At the end of the paths, Queen Louise’s mausoleum, built in 1810–1812 in a Neoclassical style, houses her tomb. Allow 30 minutes for a stroll, longer if you continue to the riverbank.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Around the bend of the forest path, Schloss Neuschwanstein's white towers surge above the fir trees. Ludwig II launched construction in 1869 on the site of two medieval ruins. The castle mixes Romanesque Revival and Gothic Revival, inspired by Wartburg and Pierrefonds. He lived there just 172 days.

The Singers' Hall, on Schloss Neuschwanstein's fourth floor, reproduces Wartburg's. Ludwig II designed it as a "worthy temple" to Richard Wagner. The castle was never finished, and this interrupted construction is part of its legend.

activities.text: Book your tickets online the day before at hohenschwangau.de. Morning slots sell out first—aim for 9 a.m. The walk up from the Ticket Center takes 30 to 40 minutes. Large backpacks are forbidden inside.

days_plan.itin_title: Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: One room alone would justify the trip: the three-story Steinerner Saal at Nymphenburg Palace has retained its Rococo stucco and ceiling painted by Johann Baptist Zimmermann since 1758. Farther on, Ludwig I’s Schönheitengalerie displays portraits of beauties painted by Joseph Stieler, including Lola Montez, while a bedroom hung with green silk recalls that Ludwig II was born here on August 25, 1845. Arrive at opening time: 9 a.m. in summer and 10 a.m. in winter.

Finish your tour of the interiors at the Marstallmuseum in the palace’s south wing: more than forty carriages and sleighs, including carriages used by Ludwig II, as gilded as you might imagine. Upstairs, the displays feature Nymphenburg porcelain from the 18th through the 20th centuries. Buy the combined ticket for the palace, Marstallmuseum, and pavilions from the outset; it costs less than separate admissions.

activities.text: Weather permitting, set aside 45 minutes for Nymphenburg Park: 229 hectares of landscaped grounds, a canal about 3 km long between two paths, and scattered pavilions, including the Rococo Amalienburg. Entry to the park is free from 6 a.m., and from April through the end of October, gondolas glide along the canal in fair weather.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: Nothing beats Schlossplatz for taking in Stuttgart at a glance. In the center, the Jubiläumssäule, about 30 m tall, commemorates the jubilee of William I’s reign in 1841; a statue of Concordia crowns it because the king refused to have his own statue placed there. Opposite, the Neues Schloss, built from 1746 to 1807 and rebuilt after the 1944 bombings, now houses government ministries. Come early, when you still have the fountains and Baroque flower beds to yourself.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Schloss Wilhelmsburg was inaugurated in 1590, while the construction begun by Landgrave William IV of Hesse was still underway. In the chapel, Daniel Meyer’s organ, with its 252 wooden pipes, was played at the consecration; it ranks among the oldest instruments of its kind still playable in Central Europe. The castle also displays a replica of the Iwein cycle, Germany’s oldest secular murals. From November through March, the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Closely packed half-timbered buildings, cobblestones, and two mismatched towers: Schmalkalden’s Altmarkt reveals itself at a glance. The Rathaus dates from 1419, and the town hosted seven of the Schmalkaldic League’s 26 assemblies; in the nearby Stadtkirche St. Georg, a watchman’s dwelling perched about 50 meters up remained occupied until 1935. Walk around the church to compare its two towers, then wander the streets: nearly 90% of the late medieval half-timbered houses have survived.

In February 1537, Martin Luther stayed at Schmalkalden’s Lutherhaus, a house built in 1530, during the assembly of the Schmalkaldic League. He preached at the Stadtkirche, but a bout of kidney stones then prevented him from attending the meeting. Look for the facade as you explore the lanes, then extend your walk to the Siechenteich ponds and the Stadtpark, which provided the setting for the Thuringian Horticultural Show in 2015.

activities.text: Take a sweet break at Viba Nougat-Welt in Schmalkalden: through the factory windows, you can watch nougat being made step by step. The company has produced nougat and marzipan since the 1920s, was known throughout East Germany, and opened this visitor attraction in 2012. The exhibition floor is free to visit and open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.; hands-on workshops require a ticket.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach

visits.text: Closed to the public during the Cold War (a military zone until 1996), the Schneeberg is Franconia's highest summit at 1,052 m. The Bundeswehr's former telecommunications relay station still crowns the top. No refreshment stand up there: bring your own picnic.

activities.text: Climb up to the Backöfele, the wooden observation tower offering a complete panorama over the horseshoe of twelve Fichtelgebirge peaks. According to local legend, bread was baked here in wartime. Allow 1.5 hours from the Bischofsgrün parking lot.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

places.name: Schoenau Am Koenigssee

activities.text: The Jenner is well worth a morning: from its summit, Königssee stretches out some 1,200 m below, opposite the Watzmann. The glass-sided ten-person gondolas, in service since June 2019, reach the station at 1,800 m in about 20 minutes. From there, a trail equipped with safety features leads to the summit cross at 1,874 m in 20 minutes. Aim for the first ride up at 9 a.m., as the summit gets very busy.

Next, follow the 360° Panoramaweg, a 400 m loop around the upper station and Jenneralm. Just 15 minutes on this easy, marked trail, dotted with photo spots, brings changing views from the Watzmann to the Steinernes Meer. Before heading down, stop at the national park information point, with step-free access just outside the gondola exit.

days_plan.itin_title: Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits

map_keywords: Jennerbahn valley station Schönau am Königssee

visits.text: Board one of the Königssee's electric boats at Schönau to explore this lake, protected since 1978 within Berchtesgaden National Park. The lake, 8 km long and 190 meters deep, is enclosed by vertical limestone walls. Halfway along, the skipper plays a trumpet toward the rock face to demonstrate the exceptional echo.

Disembark at St. Bartholomä, a peninsula accessible only by boat. The baroque pilgrimage church, built from 1134 onward and remodeled in the early 18th century, is recognizable from afar by its red onion domes. The church and former royal hunting lodge, silhouetted against the east face of the Watzmann (1,800 meters of vertical rock face), form one of Germany's most famous photographic subjects.

Continue by boat to Salet to walk to the Obersee—a flat 15-minute walk from the dock. This smaller lake, with no boats whatsoever, has absolutely clear water and perfect reflections of the surrounding rock walls. Since commercial fishing ended in 1978, the lake has returned to its wild state.

Then board the Jennerbahn to reach the Jenner summit at 1,800 meters. The view takes in the entire Königssee, the east face of the Watzmann, and the Berchtesgaden Alps on the Austrian side. Salzburg is 30 km away—this area is the natural endpoint of the circuit for those returning their car in Austria.

activities.text: Hike the Malerwinkel-Rundweg, a scenic forest trail above the Königssee offering the classic view of the lake from above. In 2015, this spot was ranked Germany's 12th tourist attraction. Allow 1 to 2 hours depending on your pace.

days_plan.itin_title: German Alpine Road: Lake Constance to Königssee

visits.text: Explore Schönebeck, the salt town, whose millennial history is intimately linked to the extraction of white gold. The Salt Museum (Salzlandmuseum) takes you on a fascinating journey through the centuries to understand the economic and social importance of this precious resource. The picturesque old town with its colorful half-timbered houses invites leisurely strolls through streets steeped in history.

Relax in the spa district of Bad Salzelmen, where the majestic Gradierwerk (graduation tower) diffuses therapeutic salt spray into the air. This monumental wooden structure, where salt water trickles over blackthorn bundles, creates a unique iodine-rich microclimate. The salt bath offers an authentic wellness experience inherited from German spa traditions.

Admire Europe's longest inhabited half-timbered house on the Elbe, a spectacular testimony to traditional German architecture. La Fleur de Sel, a contemporary art installation on the river, dialogues with this historical heritage. St. Johannis Church completes this architectural panorama with its tower dominating the town.

activities.text: Visit the Pömmelte sanctuary, a cultic site over 4,000 years old with its reconstructed circular ditch

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Schotten is the gateway to the Naturpark Vulkanregion Vogelsberg, Germany's oldest nature park. The Vogelsberg is Europe's largest contiguous volcanic massif: it formed approximately 20 million years ago during a period of intense Tertiary volcanic activity. Basaltic lavas created a topography of rounded domes, peat bogs, and springs. The Vulkaneum in Schotten, a museum and interpretation center renovated in 2018, presents the geology and ecology of the massif with interactive stations.

The Vogelsberg landscapes are characterized by their mixed beech and spruce forests, flowering meadows, and dry-stone walls. The central plateau—the Oberwald—is covered with forests threaded with springs and small streams. The slopes are dotted with basaltic formations with distinctive silhouettes. The region forms a groundwater recharge zone for much of Hesse.

The Hoherodskopf (764 m) is the most iconic accessible summit in the Vogelsberg alongside the Taufstein (773 m). The nature park's information center is located here, with a permanent exhibition on volcanic geology and the massif's biodiversity. In winter, cross-country ski trails are groomed on the plateau. In summer, a 7 km trail loops around the summit, passing the peat bog, streams, and several viewpoints.

activities.text: Hike a section of the Vulkanring Vogelsberg, a circular long-distance trail that crosses the massif along its most remarkable geological formations: basalt flows, volcanic columns, and "Bilstein" cliffs. Nature guides offer guided excursions from Hoherodskopf.
Cycling or e-biking in the Vogelsberg on the marked trail network. Elevation changes remain moderate on the plateau. Bicycles can be rented in several park villages.

days_plan.itin_title: Hesse, Germany Tour: Cities and Nature Parks

visits.text: Discover Schwäbisch Hall, a beautiful and charming town that was once a major center of salt production, the precious “white gold” that created its wealth. Winding streets lined with magnificent half-timbered buildings lead through the old town center to a gorgeous central market square dominated by the imposing St. Michael's Church. The covered wooden bridge spanning the Kocher River creates one of Germany's most photographed scenes.

Visit the local museum to learn about the fascinating history of salt making that gave the town its name and fortune. Salt has been extracted here since Celtic times, and the industry shaped every aspect of local life, architecture and culture. The Hällisch-Fränkisches Museum brings this heritage to life through engaging exhibits about the salt workers and merchants who built the town.

Explore the Großcomburg monastery complex perched on a hill just above the town, where 16th-century defensive walls still stand to protect the Romanesque chapel and cloister within. The monastery's peaceful courtyards and historic architecture offer a contemplative contrast to the bustling town below. Check the town's festival calendar, as Schwäbisch Hall hosts excellent cultural events throughout the year.

activities.text: Relax in the riverside park along the Kocher and admire views of the picturesque covered bridge

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: Locals call it the “Buttermilchturm”: according to tradition, the besieged inhabitants of Treysa coated the Totenkirche’s tower with buttermilk to suggest their supplies were still intact. Parish accounts do record milk purchases, for a white casein paint. A ruin since around 1835, the church can be viewed from the lanes, between stretches of town wall and the Hexenturm; it also hosts cultural events.

Next, in Ziegenhain, you will follow the earthen ramparts of the Wasserfestung, built from 1537 to 1546 for Landgrave Philip the Magnanimous: its 65-meter glacis could be flooded by the Schwalm. The castle, incorporated into a prison, can be viewed from outside. The red cap of the traditional Schwalm costume is said to have inspired Little Red Riding Hood; the Museum der Schwalm displays it in the afternoons during the season.

days_plan.itin_title: Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel

visits.text: Above ground, the town has lost most of its charm: a bombing in April 1945 destroyed 70% of the buildings. But underground, Schwandorf hides Bavaria's largest labyrinth of rock cellars. More than 130 rooms carved from sandstone follow one another over nearly a kilometer.

Book the guided tour of the Felsenkeller-Labyrinth to understand how these cellars were used to brew bottom-fermented beer starting in the late 15th century. During World War II, thousands of civilians took refuge here.

activities.text: The temperature drops to 8 °C when you enter the galleries. Bring a jacket even in midsummer. The tour lasts around 45 minutes; reserve through the tourist office (09431-45-550). Please note: spaces are limited.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: 'Come to Schwarzkollm, to the Black Mill': that's the summons that opens the Sorbian legend of Krabat, the boy who became apprentice to a sorcerer miller. The Krabat-Mühle recreates this 'Black Mill' as a four-sided Lusatian farmstead—six buildings on a large site. You discover Sorbian traditions and the story behind the tale, via guided tour or audio guide. Ideal for families; check the dates for 'Krabat-Saga' performances.

activities.text: Bake your own bread in the Krabat-Mühle's historic wood-fired oven: 'family baking days' must be reserved in advance. Around it, a discovery trail dotted with panels tells the Krabat saga to children. The site comes alive mainly around its events, so everything depends on the day's calendar. Outside special activities, the visit stays short—an hour suffices.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: Monumental though it is, cars no longer pass through it: the Deutsches Weintor, a gateway clad in pink sandstone and built in 1936 to promote Palatinate wines, admits only pedestrians and cyclists. On the side facing Wissembourg, the imperial eagle once held a swastika, which was removed in 1945. Beneath the arch, graffiti from March 1945 salutes Mineral Wells, Texas. A staircase on the east side leads to the gallery.

activities.text: If you take just one walk through the vineyards, choose the Erster Deutscher Weinlehrpfad, opened in 1969 and starting at the Alte Kelter near the Weintor. Its 26 stations, from the statue of Saint Urban to the carved grape thief, lead up the Sonnenberg to a hut with views stretching across the Rhine Plain to the Black Forest. The trail continues into France without border checks if you feel like going farther.

Finish the Wine Route with a glass in hand: book a tasting with a winemaker in Schweigen-Rechtenbach, some of whom also tend vineyards on the French side, or sit down for a meal at the Weintor restaurant, run by the Deutsches Weintor cooperative. Staying overnight in the village means you won’t have to drive after the tasting.

days_plan.itin_title: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen

visits.text: Schwerin Castle floats on its lake—and we're hardly exaggerating; it sits on an island connected to the mainland by a narrow bridge. The current castle was rebuilt in neo-Gothic historicist style between 1847 and 1857 by Friedrich Franz II. It houses today both a museum and the Landtag (regional parliament), making it one of the few historic residences still in political use in Germany.

In Schwerin Cathedral (Dom zu Schwerin), silence is absorbed by the Gothic brick walls. The main construction dates from the 14th century, but older parts date from the 13th. The nave contrasts with the lightness of its columns—a classic of Mecklenburg Backsteingotik. The tower is accessible and provides views over the lake and rooftops.

Schwerinians call it the 'Neuschwanstein of the north'—this isn't flattering hyperbole but sincere architectural comparison, both castles being contemporaneous and sharing the aesthetic of 19th-century romantic historicism. The Schlossgarten designed by Peter Joseph Lenné in the 1840s surrounds the castle with French-style gardens and an orangery.

activities.text: Rent an electric boat on Schwerin Lake: the lake surrounds the castle on three sides and offers a perspective that tourists who stay on the lawns never see. The south shore is uncrowded on weekdays. Rental at the marina 10 min walk from the castle.

Cross the Alter Garten, the large square facing the castle, framed by the Mecklenburgisches Staatstheater and the Staatliches Museum Schwerin. Reopened in late October 2025 after four years of renovation work, the museum houses a Flemish and Dutch collection assembled by the dukes in the 17th century. From its grand staircase, the view takes in the square, the bridge and the castle.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: Lakes, Castles, and the Baltic Coast
German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Lose yourself in the magnificent gardens of Schloss Schwetzingen, a splendid summer palace with hectares of meticulously landscaped grounds that rank among Germany's finest baroque gardens. The salmon-pink palace provides an elegant backdrop to formal parterres, romantic temples and winding woodland paths designed to delight at every turn. This princely retreat was created for the Electors Palatine as an escape from court life in Heidelberg.

Discover the garden's extraordinary follies, including a mosque, Roman temple and bath house that reflect 18th-century fascination with exotic cultures. The circular parterre and grand water features demonstrate the height of baroque garden design and horticultural artistry. If visiting in May, the town's famous white asparagus festival celebrates this prized local delicacy with culinary events throughout the region.

activities.text: Enjoy lunch at one of the charming restaurants along the road leading to the palace gardens

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: Locals call it “der rostige Nagel”, the rusty nail—and it truly is. Sedlitz's Landmarke Lausitzer Seenland is a 30-meter Corten steel tower built in 2008 at the mouth of the Sorno canal into the Sedlitzer See. The rust color is intentional: it recalls the machinery of the former open-pit mine. From the platform you can make out the Sedlitzer See and three other lakes (Geierswalder, Partwitzer, and Großräschener). Free access, year-round.

activities.text: Just north of the tower, the Schwimmender Steg reaches out over the Sedlitzer See: a floating walkway a few dozen meters long to see the lake at water level, without the 162 steps. Short but effective before heading out.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Black water, 18 metres deep, nobody knows the colour of the lake bed. The Mummelsee is a glacial lake at an elevation of 1,029 m, with a circumference of 800 m. Eduard Mörike set his 1829 ballad “Die Geister am Mummelsee” here, with a procession of ghosts descending towards the lake. Grimmelshausen had already sent Simplicissimus to the centre of the earth here. Walking around the lake takes 20 minutes. Do not throw stones: legend says it causes a storm.

At 1,163 m, the Hornisgrinde is the highest point in the northern Black Forest. It is a 3 km walk from the Mummelsee, with 135 m of elevation gain, taking 45 minutes. At the summit are the Bismarck Tower and views across the Rhine plain as far as Strasbourg on a clear day. The complete Mummelsee-Hornisgrinde loop is 6 km and takes about 2 hours. In October, fog rises from the valley and envelops the Mummelsee on the way back.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: Seiffen is the iconic village of the Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge), nestled at an altitude of 700 meters on the Czech border. When the region's mines were exhausted in the 18th century, inhabitants turned to woodworking. In the 19th century, the village established itself as the world center for miniature toys and Christmas decorations. There are more than a hundred craftspeople and around forty shops. The wood-turning technique called “Reifendrehen”—a log slice is turned then cut like a pie to obtain dozens of identical animal silhouettes—is unique to Seiffen and inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

The Seiffen Toy Museum traces the village's history and its craftsmanship since the 18th century. Christmas pyramids—those wooden candle carousels that rotate by thermal convection—are displayed in historical versions. Nutcrackers shaped like Saxon soldiers, whose first version was created in the region to ridicule authority figures, are the other local specialty. The tradition of the miner's angel and the Schwibbogen, the illuminated wooden arch placed in windows, is also explained here: these objects recall the candles that miners placed at the mine entrance on Christmas Eve.

activities.text: Hiking in the Ore Mountains from the village. Marked trails cross conifer forests and ridges with views over the Czech border. In winter, the cross-country ski trail network is one of Germany's densest.

Travel on a historic steam train on the Fichtelbergbahn, the narrow-gauge railway that has linked Cranzahl to Oberwiesenthal since 1897. First drive to Cranzahl, approximately 54 km from Seiffen, a 55-minute drive, then take the train. The historic steam locomotives pass through the villages and forests of the Ore Mountains.

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
The Ore Mountains in 3 Days: Mines, Toys, and Fichtelberg

visits.text: Leuchtenburg overlooks the Saale Valley from an altitude of 395 meters and is nicknamed “the Queen of the Saale Valley.” Its first documented mention dates to 1221, when it was a military base of the Lords of Lobdeburg. It changed hands frequently and became the administrative center of the Wettin villages in 1396. In 1553, an 80-meter-deep well was dug into the rock—Thuringia's second-deepest at the time. After its administration closed in 1705, it served in turn as a prison, a poorhouse, and an asylum. Between 1920 and 1997, Thuringia's first youth hostel operated there. The castle was purchased at auction in 2007 by the Leuchtenburg Foundation and restored, and a new permanent exhibition opened in 2014.

Porzellanwelten Leuchtenburg traces 800 years of Thuringian porcelain history in the castle's halls. The exhibition explores the art, technology, and culture of this craft, for which the town of Kahla, at the foot of the castle, is a historic center. Modern installations deliberately contrast with the medieval walls.

The Mythos Burg exhibition presents the castle's medieval history and legends linked to Leuchtenburg. The keep, accessible by a steep staircase, offers a 360-degree panorama over the Harz, the Thuringian Forest, and the deeply incised Saale Valley.

activities.text: Panoramic view from Leuchtenburg's keep: on clear days, the vista extends to the Harz in the north and the Thuringian Forest in the south. The ascent is via a path or stairs from parking areas below.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

visits.text: From the outside, the former Rosenthal factory looks like a medieval fortress with its massive chimneys. Inside, the Porzellanikon devotes several thousand square meters to the production of “white gold.” You'll find pieces from the Rosenthal collection, bought by the Oberfrankenstiftung in 2009. Selb remains the heart of Germany's porcelain industry.

Walk through the Porzellanikon's six halls to understand each step: kaolin grinding, molding, firing, glazing, decoration. The "Keramik Technique" space shows surprising applications: medical prosthetics, electrical insulators, aerospace components. Closed Mondays.

activities.text: The smell of damp kaolin still drifts through the Porzellanikon workshops where you can paint your own plate. Porcelain decoration courses offered regularly, including for children. Check the calendar at porzellanikon.org.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Sellin Pier measures 394 m and is Rügen island's longest pier. Its first version, inaugurated in 1906, measured 508 m before being reduced by storms and ice—the last destruction dates from winter 1941/42. The current pier, rebuilt in 1998 following models from 1906 and 1927, descends from the top of the cliff to the sea in a spectacular staircase, with a diving gondola at the end.

Destroyed multiple times by ice and storms, then rebuilt in 1998 exactly identical to the 1927 model: this is the Seebrücke's story, but also a metaphor for Sellin itself. The villas of Wilhelmstraße, in carved white wood and open terraces, passed through the GDR era in a state of disrepair then were restored after 1990 one by one. The result is strangely intact.

activities.text: Walk down Wilhelmstraße lined with Bäderarchitektur villas from the Rasender Roland station to the sea in 10 min on foot. The street is steeply sloped—which is why the pier also descends via a monumental staircase to beach level. Below, the restaurants over the water serve fresh fish and pretzels at sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: A Renaissance fortress serving as a mining museum: few places combine that. The Schloss und Festung Senftenberg dates from the sixteenth century and now houses the Museum des Landkreises Oberspreewald-Lausitz. The showpiece is in the cellars: a full-scale reconstructed mine gallery shows coal extraction as it was practiced last century. Closed Mondays.

The Senftenberger See deserves a stop: a former open-pit mine converted into a lake in the late 1960s, it now offers 18 kilometers of shoreline with fine sandy beaches and a town harbor with an 80-meter pier over the water. In summer, sailboats and paddleboarders share the water with rental electric boats.

activities.text: You'll board a boat at the Stadthafen to reach the neighboring Geierswalder See via the Koschener canal. Electric boat rental operators are on-site; count on 2–3 hours for a leisurely cruise and €15–25 depending on boat size.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Lusatia: Spreewald and Mining Lakes in 6 Days

visits.text: Rubens was probably born here in 1577, under inglorious circumstances: his father was under house arrest for adultery. The Oberes Schloss, perched on the Siegberg at 307 meters, houses the Siegerlandmuseum with nine original canvases by the Flemish master. The basement conceals a reconstructed 14-meter-deep mine shaft.

From the castle park, spring tulips frame a panorama over the city. The Nikolaikirche below wears a gilded “Krönchen” atop its spire, the city's emblem. Siegen claims 86% green space across its municipal area.

activities.text: If you enjoy contemporary art, the Museum für Gegenwartskunst occupies the old postal building, a 10-minute walk from the castle. Rotating collections, modest admission. Otherwise, a café at Marktplatz suffices to observe the easygoing rhythm of this university town.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: Seen from the bridge over the Danube, the massive bulk of Sigmaringen Castle seems to weigh down the limestone rock. Residence of the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen family since 1535, it's Germany's second-largest urban castle. The Waffenhalle displays some 3,000 pieces, one of Europe's largest private arms collections. An audio guide is available in several languages.

In 1944–1945, the castle briefly served as seat of the Vichy government in exile. Louis-Ferdinand Céline described the atmosphere in 'Castle to Castle.' The Marstallmuseum, in the stables, presents 17 princely carriages and sleighs.
Walk along the Danube downstream from the castle. Naturpark Obere Donau is one of Germany's most beautiful nature parks.

activities.text: In the evening, the Biergarten terrace facing the illuminated castle is one of the town's finest spots. The castle still belongs to the Hohenzollern family, who live in part of it.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Simmern’s Neues Schloss, built from 1708 to 1713 on the site of the ducal castle destroyed in 1689, houses the Hunsrück-Museum. Its exhibits trace the town’s history, from the dukes of Palatinate-Simmern to the outlaw Schinderhannes. Visit Wednesday through Sunday: the museum is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays, and on weekends it opens only from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m.

Dim light, carved stone, and silence: inside the Stephanskirche, built from 1486 to 1510, St. Anne’s Chapel holds a row of tombs of the dukes of Simmern, with epitaphs by Johann von Trarbach. Beneath the bell tower, a crypt holds the coffins of the last ducal couple, who died in 1674 and 1688. If the door is closed, ask at the castle’s Tourist-Information.

Reputed to be escape-proof, the Schinderhannesturm nevertheless let two prisoners slip away: “Schwarzer Peter” in November 1798, then Schinderhannes himself on the night of August 19–20, 1799. His hat, his pistol, and a replica of the blade that beheaded him in Mainz in 1803 are on display, with free admission. The full tower can only be visited with a guide.

Less conspicuous than the Stephanskirche, the Baroque Sankt Josef church (1749–1752) rewards a look upward: its ceiling frescoes, painted from 1752 to 1756 by Francesco Bernardini, court painter in Mannheim, depict the Adoration of the Christ Child. The organ, delivered by the Stumm family in 1753, complements the one in the Stephanskirche, which dates to 1776.

If you have an hour left, drive 9 km to Ravengiersburg: the Romanesque facade of the “Hunsrückdom,” flanked by two towers about 40 meters tall, dominates the village. The monastery was founded in 1074 for twelve canons. Beneath the dwarf gallery between the towers, look for Christ enthroned within a mandorla, carved in the late 12th or early 13th century.

days_plan.itin_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern

visits.text: Seen from the air, Schloss Clemenswerth resembles a star set in the forest. Eight pavilions arranged in an octagon around the central pavilion: it's the last preserved Parforce-Sternanlage in Europe. Designed by Johann Conrad Schlaun, built between 1737 and 1747 for Prince-Bishop Clemens August.

The silence of the Klostergarten, broken only by birdsong, contrasts with the baroque pomp of the Festsaal. The painted chapels and the hunting pavilion with its trophies are worth the visit. Count on 75 minutes with the guided tour.

activities.text: Eight pavilions in a star around a central castle, eight avenues of lime trees, a pond with five islands: stroll through the park to grasp the Baroque geometry at eye level.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Take the cable car (Seilbahn) up to Schloss Burg rather than climbing on foot. This 12th-century fortress, the largest restored burg in North Rhine-Westphalia, towers 110 meters above the Wupper. The Bergisches Museum traces the lives of the Counts of Berg. Admission €10, closed Mondays.

In the lanes of Gräfrath's old town, the scent of bakeries mingles with slate-grey walls. This historic Solingen quarter clusters half-timbered houses and cobbled courtyards around the Klosterkirche. Less touristy than Freudenberg, more authentic too. Park at Gräfrather Marktplatz.

activities.text: The Klingenpfad is an extensive waymarked loop around Solingen, not a short trail directly linking Gräfrath to Schloss Burg. From Gräfrath, its first major stage follows the Wupper, passes through Müngsten and continues towards Burg. Plan on a full-day hike rather than a short walk.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: Experience the breathtaking Lüneburg Heath, one of Germany's most enchanting natural landscapes. This vast expanse of purple heather moorland, dotted with ancient juniper bushes and grazing Heidschnucken sheep, creates a magical atmosphere especially during the August-September flowering season. The heath's peaceful beauty has inspired poets and painters for centuries.

Get your adrenaline pumping at Heide Park Soltau and on its wooden roller coaster. This leading theme park combines breathtaking rides with themed landscapes, live shows and family attractions spread across beautifully landscaped grounds. Thrill-seekers and families alike will find endless excitement at this German amusement park.

activities.text: Marvel at exotic species from around the world at Walsrode Bird Park, about 29 km from Soltau, a 25-minute drive, one of the world's largest bird parks. More than 4,000 birds from 650 species inhabit this spectacular 24-hectare garden, which features astonishing aviaries, tropical greenhouses and interactive feeding experiences. From tiny hummingbirds to majestic eagles, the diversity of birdlife creates a colourful paradise.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands

visits.text: The winemakers simply call it the Weininsel - the wine island. Sommerach and Nordheim occupy a meander of the Altmain across about 750 hectares of vineyards. The Pfarrkirche St. Eucherius, whose late Gothic silhouette has dominated the village since the 16th century, is one of the rare sanctuaries in Europe dedicated to this saint.

Sommerach's Pfarrkirche, whose steep tower structures the village skyline, took its current form in 1560, with the choir enlarged in 1756-1757. The Kirchplatz surrounding it is the village's natural center - benches, fountain, views across the vineyards.

activities.text: Step through the door of the InfoVinothek on the Kirchplatz for a guided tasting of the Weininsel's wines. The Winzerkeller Sommerach, founded in 1901, is Franconia's oldest wine cooperative. On Friday evenings in season, the terrace atmosphere often surpasses that of big-city bars.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: The Bärenhöhle at Sonnenbühl takes its name from the cave bear skeletons discovered inside. Limestone formations sculpt spectacular shapes in this Swabian Alb cave. Guided tour about 30 minutes.
The Swabian Alb plateau around Sonnenbühl offers easy hikes with panoramas over valleys below. The UNESCO-recognized Swabian Alb Biosphere Reserve begins here.

activities.text: Walk the 'Hochgehträumt' trail linking Lichtenstein Castle to the Nebelhöhle over 10.9 km, with viewpoints overlooking the Albtrauf escarpment. Easy difficulty, moderate elevation gain.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Lichtenstein Castle stands on a rocky spur at 817 meters altitude, above the Echaz valley in the Swabian Jura. In 1826, writer Wilhelm Hauff published a historical novel featuring the medieval castle of Lichtenstein as its setting. The novel was a resounding success, and Count Wilhelm von Urach, cousin of the King of Württemberg, was so enthused he purchased the site and had the current neo-Gothic castle built between 1840 and 1842—a few years before Ludwig II of Bavaria did the same at Neuschwanstein. The interior houses a collection of medieval weapons and wall frescoes. From the ramparts, the view over the valley and Swabian Jura plateaus is remarkable.

Hohenzollern Castle is perched at an elevation of 855 meters atop Mount Zoller, an isolated erosional remnant above the Swabian plain. It's the ancestral seat of the Hohenzollern family, from which Prussia's kings and Germany's emperors descended. The first fortress was erected in the 11th century, destroyed in 1423 after a ten-month siege, and rebuilt from 1454 to 1461. The current castle, the third version, was commissioned in 1846 by King Frederick William IV of Prussia and built by architect Friedrich August Stüler in a neo-Gothic style. Among the collection's pieces: the Prussian royal crown, a letter from President George Washington thanking Baron von Steuben for his role in the American War of Independence, and personal effects of Frederick the Great. On clear days, views from the ramparts extend to the Black Forest.

activities.text: From Sonnenbühl, allow for a round trip to the Hohenzollern Castle parking lot. Twilight views from the viewpoints below the parking lot. The fortress silhouetted at sunset against the Swabian hills is one of Baden-Württemberg's most photographed panoramas.

days_plan.itin_title: Germany Road Trip: Castles, Medieval Villages and the Alps

visits.text: Speyer’s Kaiserdom makes an imposing impression with its 134 m length: it is the largest Romanesque church still standing, commissioned by Conrad II, consecrated in 1061, and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1981. Eight emperors and kings lie in the crypt dating from 1041 and the adjacent burial vault. In front of the entrance, each new bishop would fill the Domnapf, a large stone basin, with wine for the townspeople. There is an admission charge for the crypt; the Kaisersaal and tower can be visited from April through October.

The air grows cooler with every step at the Judenhof: a long staircase passes through a Romanesque portal and descends to the pool of the mikveh, built around 1120 and described as Europe’s oldest surviving monumental ritual bath. Above ground, the walls of the 1104 synagogue and the 13th-century Frauenschul remain. The €5 ticket includes the SchPIRA Museum, which opened in 2010; from April through October, admission is daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Walk up Maximilianstraße, a former triumphal route about 700 m long, to the Altpörtel, a 55 m city gate first mentioned in 1176. Its gallery, some 30 m above ground, is reached by 154 steps and overlooks the entire old town. Visits run in time slots, with fifteen people at a time: from April through October, aim for Wednesday or Friday afternoon, or Saturday morning.

In 1529, at the Diet of Speyer, Lutheran princes issued a solemn protest in defense of their faith. The Gedächtniskirche der Protestation, built from 1893 to 1904, commemorates the event with a 100 m tower, the tallest in the Palatinate. In the ground-floor hall, a bronze Luther tramples the papal bull excommunicating him. Allow 20 minutes; open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

At the Technik Museum Speyer, you can climb onto the left wing of a Lufthansa Boeing 747, some 20 m above the ground. Farther along, the Buran OK-GLI, a Soviet prototype with four jet engines, made 25 test flights before traveling up the Rhine on a pontoon in 2008. Add the U9 submarine and the 5,000 m² space exhibition, covering nearly three-quarters of a soccer field. Open daily from 9 a.m., admission €25: save it for the following morning.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest
Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen

visits.text: Walk up to the choir of the Lorenzkirche and look up: Veit Stoß’s Englischer Gruß, a wooden Annunciation measuring 3.72 m by 3.20 m, encircled by 55 gilded roses and carved in 1517–1518, floats above you. The work fell in 1817 and was almost completely shattered before being restored. Nearby, Adam Kraft’s Sakramentshaus, a sandstone tabernacle nearly 20 m tall, carved from 1493 to 1496, soars toward the vault; Kraft included a depiction of himself in it. Allow 35 minutes, and bring binoculars if you have them.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: The Augustinian abbey of St Märgen, founded in 1118, houses a museum of folk traditions featuring wood carvings and Fasnet masks from the local Alemannic carnival. This carnival is the closest thing in the Black Forest to an openly pre-Christian procession, with animal-headed masks and demon costumes. The Baroque church is worth a quick look. The grounds are free to visit; admission is charged for the museum.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: Fourteen years of work and some €43 million: St. Michael’s Church, closed in 2012 after a piece of plaster fell from the vault, reopened on April 25, 2026. Founded in 1015, the Benedictine abbey crowns the Michaelsberg; behind Leonhard Dientzenhofer’s Baroque facade, look up at the Himmelsgarten, a ceiling where restorers have identified 585 plants, then seek out the tomb of Saint Otto. Admission is free, Friday through Sunday and on public holidays, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. only.

activities.text: Then head down through the Michaelsberg’s terraced gardens, Baroque grounds of the former monastery planted with old fruit varieties. A vineyard was replanted here for the 2012 Bavarian horticultural show, a nod to a city that grew wine grapes until the 18th century. From the rows of vines, the view stretches toward the cathedral; the garden café invites you to take a break.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: The thread running through this trip begins with a tomb, and that feels entirely fitting. In the Wittelsbach crypt of St. Michael, a church completed in 1597, Ludwig II rests among some thirty members of his family. Above, the barrel vault spans more than 20 m without a single pillar, a span exceeded at the time only by St. Peter’s in Rome. Budget €3 for the crypt, which is closed on Sundays.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: The hush of stone, then the gleam of bronze: inside the Sebalduskirche, Nuremberg’s oldest parish church, the Sebaldusgrab stands over the grave of the city’s patron saint. Peter Vischer the Elder and his sons cast this tomb, shaped like a small building, between 1508 and 1519. Damaged by bombing from 1940 to 1945, the church was reconsecrated in 1957, but many of its furnishings survived after being moved to safety in time. Allow 20 minutes; avoid service times.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Controversial when it opened in 1984, admired today: James Stirling’s Neue Staatsgalerie ranks among Germany’s great postmodern buildings, with Henry Moore’s “Liegende” in front of the entrance. Founded in 1843 by King William I, the museum displays around 800 works, from Rembrandt’s “Paul in Prison” to Picassos, along with Monet, Cézanne, and Oskar Schlemmer, whose archives it holds. Admission to the collection is free on Wednesdays; the museum stays open until 8 p.m. on Thursdays and is closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Experience Stade, a jewel among Germany's Hanseatic cities boasting remarkable maritime charm on the banks of the Schwinge River. This 1,000-year-old trading port features a beautifully preserved old town with half-timbered houses, historic merchant buildings, and the iconic wooden harbor crane. The atmospheric harbor quarter and winding lanes transport visitors back to the glory days of Hanseatic trade.

activities.text: Cycle along the North Sea Cycle Path that winds along the embankments between grazing sheep and the vast coastal landscape. This scenic route offers peaceful riding through traditional fishing villages, past historic lighthouses, and along dikes with panoramic views of the North Sea and Elbe estuary.

Explore Stade's maritime heritage at the harbor where traditional sailing vessels still moor alongside the historic quays. The town's museum in the Swedish Storage House tells the story of centuries of trade, fishing, and seafaring that shaped this Hanseatic gem.

days_plan.itin_title: Lower Saxony, Germany: Harz Mountains, Heathland and North Sea Islands

visits.text: Pure white, with the hush of a cathedral: the “heart” of the Stadtbibliothek is a void several stories high, lit through the roof, with galleries of books stacked around it. Korean architect Eun Young Yi completed this roughly 40 m cube in 2011 on the site of the former freight station, and it was named “Library of the Year” in 2013. In summer, head up to the rooftop terrace for one of the city’s best panoramic views. Since February 2026, the library has closed at 7 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: In 1539, an alchemist was found in pieces in his room after an explosion. Room 5 of the Gasthaus zum Löwen still exists – the inn is mentioned as early as 1407. The fresco on the façade shows Mephistopheles snapping Faust's neck. Also admire the cracks in the medieval centre, the result of a failed geothermal drilling project in 2007: locals say the devil came back to claim his due.

The climb smells of resin and ripe Gutedel grapes - the Schlossberg vineyards cling to the hillside all the way up to the ruins. It is a twenty-minute walk from the market square to the remains of the castle of the Lords of Staufen, whose line died out in 1602. On a clear day, the view stretches as far as the Vosges. Do not expect a reconstruction: there are only dry stones, turtledoves and a panorama to keep to yourself.

activities.text: If the dates coincide, the Mephisto Tour is the highlight of the trip: a theatrical tour through the lanes of Staufen, performed by local actors. Check prices and dates directly at stadtgeschichten-staufen.de before you leave - tours do not run all the time. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes. October, with low fog hanging over the rooftops, is the perfect time for it.

days_plan.itin_title: The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: You’ll reach the Amtshaus, a half-timbered house built in 1562 at the far end of its courtyard, where the Grimm family lived from 1791 to 1796: this is the Brüder Grimm-Haus. Downstairs, the brothers’ lives and paintings by their younger brother Ludwig Emil; upstairs, ten fairy-tale rooms to see, touch, and listen to. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., it can be visited before the castle.

A five-sided dry moat, high retaining walls, and a keep around forty meters tall: Schloss Steinau retains the look of a fortress beneath its Renaissance reconstruction, carried out from 1528 to 1555 for the Counts of Hanau. Since 2015, a major exhibition here has traced the lives and work of the Brothers Grimm. You can visit the tower without a guide, while guided tours of the rooms are offered on weekends; the castle is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: A small town with a harmonious feel: in Steinau an der Straße, the Rathaus of 1561 and the Amtshaus of 1562 complement each other at the foot of the castle. The town’s name recalls the Via Regia, the trade route between Frankfurt and Leipzig. Save this walking tour for late afternoon, when the museums close at 5 p.m., then get back on the road to Alsfeld.

days_plan.itin_title: Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel

visits.text: Steinhausen claims the title of “world's most beautiful village church.” The Wallfahrtskirche, built between 1728 and 1733 by Dominikus Zimmermann (the same architect as Bavaria's Wieskirche), packs an unusually dense decorative scheme into an oval space. Johann Baptist Zimmermann's frescoes cover the entire ceiling.

The village itself comprises just a handful of houses around the church. The impact comes entirely from the contrast between the modest setting and the exuberant interior. Free admission, donation box available.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Discover Stendal, proud Roland town of the Altmark, whose monumental statue in the market square symbolizes medieval civic liberties. This Hanseatic city prosperous in the Middle Ages preserves a remarkably homogeneous Gothic brick architectural heritage. Narrow alleyways lead to picturesque squares and hidden treasures revealing the historical importance of this former merchant town.

Marvel at St. Mary's Church which majestically towers above the town. This Gothic brick hall church impresses with its soaring architecture and refined artistic details. St. Jacobi Church, another Gothic jewel, completes this exceptional religious heritage with its star vaults and medieval stained glass windows.

Pass through the monumental Uenglingen and Tangermünde gates, impressive witnesses to the town's former fortifications. These Gothic brick gates, among the finest in northern Germany, tell of Stendal's strategic importance in medieval history. The Powder Tower and Renaissance Town Hall complete this remarkable architectural panorama.

activities.text: Visit the Altmark Museum tracing the history of this historic region

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Lopsided but endearing, the Stiftskirche has two mismatched towers: the Reformation halted work on the western tower’s spire, leaving it with a flat roof at around 61 m. Against the choir wall, eleven armored counts of Württemberg, commissioned from sculptor Sem Schlör in 1574, stand like an ancestral gallery. The interior, remodeled after the 1944 bombings, reopened in 2003. On your way out, cross Schillerplatz, where the poet’s bronze statue watches over the market on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday mornings.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: Explore Stolberg, a picturesque town in the southern Harz whose medieval center is miraculously preserved. Historic half-timbered houses lining the steep alleyways create a setting from another time at the foot of the castle overlooking the valley. Stolberg Castle, residence of the eponymous counts, and St. Martin's Church constitute the emblematic symbols of this romantic town.

Discover the birthplace of Thomas Müntzer, radical theologian and leader of the Peasants' War born here in 1489. A statue commemorates this controversial figure who defied the established order in the name of social justice. His revolutionary legacy makes Stolberg an important memorial site for the history of social movements in Europe.

Climb the 200 steps of Joseph's Cross, the world's largest iron double cross erected on the Großer Auerberg. This impressive 38-meter-high metal structure, built in 1896, offers a magnificent view of the Harz massif from its observation platform. The 360-degree panorama rewards the climbing effort with a grandiose natural spectacle.

activities.text: Climb to Joseph's Cross for the panorama over the southern Harz

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: The old town of Stralsund has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002, jointly with Wismar. It has preserved its medieval urban plan intact, with narrow streets, six large Gothic brick churches, and merchants' houses on parcels typical of the Hanseatic era. Stralsund was one of the most powerful cities of the Hanseatic League in the 14th and 15th centuries, before becoming a Swedish administrative center in the 17th and 18th centuries—Swedish occupation lasted until 1815 and left traces in the architecture and coat of arms.

The Alter Markt, the old market square, is dominated by the Gothic Rathaus, whose origins date back to around 1250. Built in four wings forming a 30-by-60-meter rectangle, it's one of the most remarkable Gothic secular buildings in northern Germany. Its northern façade, adorned with the coats of arms of Hanseatic cities—Stralsund, Hamburg, Lübeck, Rostock, Greifswald—recalls the commercial power of the Hanse. Just beside it, St. Nicholas Church, consecrated in 1276, is the city's oldest church: its baroque lantern spire, added in 1667 after a fire, and its medieval astronomical clock make it an essential stop.

The Ozeaneum, opened in 2008 in Stralsund's harbor, is Germany's largest maritime museum. Its giant aquariums recreate the ecosystems of the North Sea and the Baltic—the largest tank holds millions of liters of seawater. Outside in the harbor, the Gorch Fock I, a training ship launched in 1933, is now a museum vessel moored at the quay.

activities.text: Evening walk in Stralsund harbor: the quays overlook the Strelasund, an arm of the Baltic that separates the city from the island of Rügen. The view across the water with the Gothic spires in the background is characteristic of Pomerania's maritime atmosphere. In summer, short cruises to Rügen or Hiddensee depart from the harbor.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Germany Road Trip: From Dresden to the Baltic Sea
German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen
The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: The entire town sits on a limestone spur so steep the houses look ready to slide. Sulzbach-Rosenberg mixes half-timbering, a Gothic town hall and a castle complex whose foundations go back to the 8th century. It's the heart of the Bayerische Eisenstraße, the old iron road.
Schloss Sulzbach towers over the rock and offers a panorama of the Upper Palatinate Jura countryside. Exterior visits are free.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Wander through Tangermünde, considered one of the most beautiful small towns in Germany. This picturesque town at the confluence of the Elbe and Tanger rivers captivates with its cobblestone streets lined with historic half-timbered houses and impressive red brick buildings. The preserved medieval atmosphere instantly transports you several centuries back in time.

Contemplate the imposing medieval Tangermünde Castle, former imperial residence of Charles IV in the 14th century. This fortress overlooking the Elbe offers spectacular views of the town and river banks. The massive ramparts and watchtowers testify to the strategic importance of this town in the history of the Holy Roman Empire.

Admire the Gothic brick Town Hall, an architectural gem of northern Germany with its characteristic stepped gables. St. Stephen's Church, an impressive 14th-century brick building, dominates the town's skyline with its slender bell tower. The Owl Tower (Eulenturm) is among the remarkably preserved remains of the medieval fortifications.

activities.text: Walk along the medieval ramparts with panoramic views over the Elbe
Discover the statue of Grete Minde, a legendary figure of the town

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: With its two round towers, the Tanner Stadttor provides an unmistakable gateway to Tann. This Renaissance gate connects today’s streets with the former town walls without requiring a lengthy visit to the center. Look at the exterior first. If you want to enter the exhibition, check its opening hours before continuing to the castle.

One castle, but three colors: Schloss Tann brings together the complexes known as Rotes, Blaues, and Gelbes Schloss. Their proximity makes for a different kind of stroll than a visit to a palace with a uniform appearance. Take time to admire the façades from areas where access is permitted. Do not assume the apartments are open, and respect the private areas.

Taxidermied animals and recreated landscapes: Naturmuseum Tann offers an introduction to the Rhön before you head into its highlands. Its dioramas depict the habitats and wildlife of the biosphere reserve. It is an alternative to walking if the weather worsens. Check opening hours and choose this visit instead of a second museum in Tann.

activities.text: If you prefer spoken explanations to information panels, book a guided walking tour in Tann. The tourist office offers guided town tours that help connect the gate, castle, and historic streets. Confirm the language and meeting details before your visit. This option replaces the self-guided walk already described; it is not an addition to this stop’s short itinerary.

days_plan.itin_title: Rhön and Fulda in 4 days: peaks and spa towns

visits.text: Westphalians call it “the balcony of Münsterland”: perched on the Teutoburger Wald, Tecklenburg offers a clear panorama over the plain. The medieval town is compact, all cobbled lanes, 16th-18th century half-timbered houses and stiegen (staircases) carved into the rock.

Tucked into the ruins of Burg Tecklenburg, founded in the 12th century, is a Freilichtbühne: more than 2,300 seats for musicals performed in summer. The acoustics of the old ivy-covered walls are remarkable.

The uneven cobblestones and half-timbered facades of the Altstadt lead to the Puppenmuseum and the Wasserschloss Haus Marck, a moated manor hidden in the woods below. This is where the first negotiations of the Peace of Westphalia took place in 1643.

activities.text: Book a seat for a musical at the Freilichtbühne if you're there in summer (June-September). Performances are in the evening, 1,800 seats are covered. Tickets at freilichtspiele-tecklenburg.de.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles
Westphalia and the Weser Valley — Münster to Kassel in 9 Days

visits.text: The former Kloster Tegernsee now houses a high school, a restaurant, and the Wittelsbachs' ducal brewery. The mix is improbable but works. The Bräustüberl serves beer brewed on-site, within the walls of an abbey founded in the 8th century.

The Pfarrkirche St. Quirinus is worth a stop: a baroque interior, and the Wittelsbach crypt where Sissi's mother, Duchess Ludovika, rests. The crypt is closed to visitors, but mentioned on a sign at the entrance.

The lake shimmers blue-green beneath the Wallberg mountains. Six kilometers long, a kilometer and a half wide, and water that is once again among Europe's cleanest thanks to the efforts of the lakeside municipalities.

activities.text: Circle the Tegernsee by boat: shuttles link Tegernsee, Rottach-Egern, Bad Wiessee, and Gmund. An hour's cruise, cappuccino on deck, views of the peaks. Departures every hour in season.

Founded in the 8th century, the Benedictine monastery was secularized in 1803 then converted into a royal residence. The Wittelsbachs' brewery still operates in the north wing. Order a Tegernseer Spezial and a Brezn at the Bräustüberl—it's a local ritual.

days_plan.itin_title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
Allgäu and Wieskirche: a 9-day baroque road trip

visits.text: A complete town wall surrounds a lively town: the Templin Town Wall still encircles the historic center. Its stone perimeter stretches for 1,735 meters and retains three major gates, enough to trace the former entrances without searching for scattered remnants. Start by locating a gate, then alternate between the inside and outside of the wall instead of repeating the same views.

activities.text: Follow the Templin Town Wall on foot to compare the gates and the small structures along it. The route forms a loop around the old town, so no long connecting walk is needed to return to your starting point. Keep a map of the center handy and plan a break before continuing toward Lychen.

days_plan.itin_title: Northeastern Brandenburg: Abbey, Forest, and Lakes in 3 Days

visits.text: The smell of hops floats over Tettnang in summer. The small town is one of Europe's great hop terroirs: Tettnanger Hopfen goes into the composition of beers worldwide. The Hopfenmuseum explains everything, from cultivation to harvest.

Less known than the lake castles, the Neues Schloss of Tettnang is visited in peace. Baroque residence of the Counts of Montfort, 18th century, state rooms with stucco and frescoes. Open April to October.

activities.text: Visit the Hopfenmuseum to understand why this small town feeds breweries around the planet. Models, tools, tasting possible. In September, the Hopfenernte (harvest) transforms the surrounding fields into a green, fragrant spectacle.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: Ascend to the Hexentanzplatz, the legendary witches' dance floor, accessible by a panoramic cable car soaring over the Bode Valley. This rocky plateau at 454 meters elevation is the scene of numerous legends surrounding the Harz witches who allegedly gather here every Walpurgis Night. The plunging view over the wild Bode Gorge and surrounding forests creates a panorama of striking beauty.

Climb the Roßtrappe, a 400-meter granite rock offering a fantastic view of the Harz Mountains. According to legend, the horseshoe-shaped imprint visible in the rock comes from Princess Brunhilde's horse, which leapt across the gorge to escape the knight Bodo. The latter, having fallen into the abyss, allegedly gave his name to the Bode River that winds 200 meters below.

Hike on the Harzer Hexenstieg, the famous hiking trail following the Bode River through a spectacular gorge. The Devil's Bridge spans the tumultuous waters in an enchanted forest setting worthy of the Brothers Grimm fairy tales. St. Peter's Church and Goethe's Rock, which the writer visited during his travels in the Harz, complete this immersion in a German romantic landscape.

activities.text: Hike along the Bode on the Hexenstieg trail through the wild gorge

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns
Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken

visits.text: Egg-yolk yellow outside and white stucco inside, the Theatinerkirche St. Kajetan brightens Odeonsplatz. Elector Ferdinand Maria and Henriette Adelaide of Savoy had it built starting in 1663 to give thanks to heaven for the birth of their heir, Max Emanuel; Agostino Barelli drew inspiration from Sant’Andrea della Valle in Rome, and the dome rises to about 70 m. Admission to the church is free; the princes’ crypt opens only at set times.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: The Topography of Terror occupies a restrained building on a large open site near Potsdamer Platz. From 1933 to 1945, this was home to the Gestapo and its prison, the SS leadership, and the Reich Security Main Office. The documentation center, opened in 2010, traces their crimes, while an outdoor trail with 15 stations follows a surviving stretch of the Wall about 200 m long. Admission is free, daily from 10 AM to 8 PM; allow more than 1 hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: In the morning, junipers rise from the mist in dark clumps across this bowl-shaped hollow — a scene that draws nature photographers from across Germany. Totengrund owes its brooding name to old local legends whose meaning no one quite agrees on. What is certain: the hollow, likely formed at the end of the last ice age, looks unlike anything else in the region.

This 30-hectare hollow was bought in 1906 by Pastor Wilhelm Bode using donor funds — a founding gesture that gave rise to Germany's first major nature reserve, established in 1921. A memorial stone to investor Andreas Thomsen marks the viewpoint at the rim of the hollow.

activities.text: Walk the loop around Totengrund on the marked paths that trace the rim of the hollow — descending into the bowl itself is prohibited to protect the vegetation. The full circuit takes about 45 minutes. Keep an eye out for snipe and northern lapwings in the wetland areas.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: A bridge gate designed by an Art Nouveau architect: the Brückentor introduces a different side of the Moselle in Traben-Trarbach. Bruno Möhring designed the bridge and its gate in the late 19th century, followed by other buildings for wine merchants. Cross on foot and look at the facades on both banks without adding a driving detour.

activities.text: Beneath the streets, the cool air immediately changes the atmosphere: the Traben-Trarbacher Unterwelt opens up the wine merchants’ former cellars. A guided tour connects several historic cellars and tells the story of the wine trade; it lasts about an hour and a half. Book a departure that fits your schedule and bring an extra layer: allow 90 minutes and save this visit for a less busy day.

days_plan.itin_title: Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier

visits.text: The Tränenpalast owes its name, “Palace of Tears,” to the farewells between visitors from the West and loved ones who remained in the East. From 1962 to 1989, this hall at Friedrichstraße station was used exclusively for departures to West Berlin; the permanent exhibition “Site of German Division” tells the story of the country’s division. Admission is free, Tuesday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., and weekends from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci

visits.text: Not touristy in the facade-seaside sense, but authentically Baltic: Travemünde still lives with its ferries to Helsinki and Stockholm, its fishermen, and its 19th-century resort villas. The waterfront combines an active port, a pedestrian promenade, and the museum sailing ship Passat (1911) moored at the quay, accessible for visits.

The Leuchtturm Travemünde, brought into service in 1827 and decommissioned in 1972 when a hotel blocked its light, is now a maritime museum 31 m high. Its 142 steps lead to a viewing gallery looking straight down on the Baltic and the ferries manoeuvring in the channel.

activities.text: Rent a Strandkorb—the woven wicker beach chair, symbol of the Baltic—and watch the ferries on the Helsinki-Travemünde line pass a few hundred meters from shore. These orange-hulled Finnlines vessels are impossible to miss. The white sand beach is pleasant even off-season; parking near Strandbahnhof remains affordable.

days_plan.itin_title: German Baltic Coast in 12 days: Hanseatic Towns and Rügen

visits.text: Morning stop in Unteruhldingen on the way to Triberg for the Pfahlbaumuseum (pile-dwelling museum), founded in 1922. Allow for a road journey from Triberg for this visit. Twenty-three Neolithic and Bronze Age dwellings (from 4000 to 850 BC) have been reconstructed on stilts above Lake Constance, based on underwater excavations. The site is part of the 111 prehistoric pile-dwelling sites around the Alps, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2011. Walkways cross the village on the lake; the reconstructed houses contain scenes of daily life with mannequins, tools and domestic animals from the period.

The Triberg Waterfalls are Germany's highest waterfalls outside the Alpine zone, with a total height of 163 meters across seven distinct tiers. The Gutach River cascades over granite rocks amid a conifer forest. Three marked trails allow the ascent (between 45 minutes and 1.5 hours). The site is illuminated every evening until 10pm.

The Schwarzwaldmuseum in Triberg, built in 1873, presents traditional Black Forest life across 1,600 m²: cuckoo clock manufacturing, regional costumes (including the Bollenhut with red pompoms for married women or black ones for unmarried women), mining life, and one of Europe's largest collections of barrel organs. Triberg has established itself as the historic capital of Black Forest clockmaking since the 18th century—the first mechanical cuckoo clocks were manufactured here.
