activities.text: Hike on one of the marked trails around the Triberg Waterfalls. The cascade path (Kaskadenweg, ~45 min) follows the successive tiers from bottom to top. Squirrels and uncommon forest bird species are frequently observed along the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Forests & Medieval Towns
Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Black Forest & Lakes
The Occult Black Forest - 7 Days in the Footsteps of Faust

visits.text: The dark stone sets the tone before you even pass through the Porta Nigra: Trier brings the journey to a close on a different historical scale. This Roman gate is part of the World Heritage site inscribed in 1986; its upper levels also show traces of its conversion into a church during the Middle Ages. Climb up to look out over the city through its openings. Scaffolding has been announced, but the monument remains open; check the last admission time.

The atmosphere grows quieter beneath the vaults of Trierer Dom, a few streets from the Porta Nigra. St. Peter’s Cathedral combines elements from several periods and preserves Roman structures; right next door, the Liebfrauenkirche introduces Gothic architecture. Visit the two as a single complex rather than making two separate trips. Check service times: these remain active churches, and sightseeing visits must fit around them.

An imperial hall turned church: the Konstantinbasilika shows how much a building’s function can change. This vast brick structure, also known as the Aula Palatina, is part of Trier’s UNESCO World Heritage site and recalls the power of the Roman court. The sheer scale of its interior makes the visit worthwhile without a lengthy explanation beforehand. Check opening hours before you come; if a service or event prevents access, view the exterior and continue to the baths.

If you enjoy understanding what lies behind a monument, Trier’s Kaiserthermen offer more than the outline of ruins. The imperial bath complex preserves remains of the Roman project and is part of the World Heritage site; its underground passageways make the site’s layout easier to understand. Plan a full visit rather than simply taking a photograph from the street. Wear sturdy shoes and check seasonal hours: last admission is before closing time.

The detour to the Römerbrücke is worthwhile above all for one simple experience: crossing the Moselle on a structure that retains Roman elements. Trier’s bridge is part of the World Heritage site, alongside the baths and the Porta Nigra. Look at its piers from the riverfront before heading back to the center. Stay in the pedestrian areas and save this crossing for the end of the day if your indoor visits have run behind schedule.

activities.text: Walk between the Porta Nigra, the Hauptmarkt, and the cathedral area to rediscover the city between its monuments. Trier’s pedestrian zone lets you move from major Roman remains to the facades and squares of the city center. Take a break along the way rather than adding another museum. A guided tour offered by the tourist office can replace this self-guided loop; choose an option that fits with the visits you have already made.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Forests & Medieval Towns
Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier

visits.text: Fall in love with Tübingen, a charming university town that many consider Germany's most beautiful city. The picturesque old town features a magnificent castle, cobblestone streets lined with half-timbered houses and a picturesque waterfront along the Neckar River. The century-old university gives the town a youthful, intellectual energy that fills the winding lanes and historic squares.

Climb to Hohentübingen Castle, perched on a ridge overlooking the town, where university students attend classes in buildings that have educated scholars for over 500 years. The castle courtyard offers panoramic views over the red-tiled roofs and church towers of the old town below. The surrounding vineyards produce local wines that feature on menus throughout the town.

Experience a traditional Stocherkahn boat ride, Tübingen's version of Venetian gondolas, where flat-bottomed punts glide along the Neckar past willow-draped banks. The annual Stocherkahnrennen boat race is a beloved local tradition featuring costumed students and much hilarity. The Holzmarkt square and surrounding streets come alive on summer evenings with locals enjoying the outdoor café culture.

activities.text: Explore the old town's atmospheric squares and imagine yourself on a Harry Potter film set

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest

visits.text: Tüchersfeld resembles an urban planning error: half-timbered houses wedged between dolomite needles that tower twenty meters above them. The limestone towers are former coral reefs from the age of dinosaurs. The village is an ortsteil of Pottenstein and remains inhabited, which heightens the strangeness - not an open-air museum, a real life among the stones.

The Fränkische-Schweiz-Museum in the former Judenhof - a complex of half-timbered buildings financed in 1750 by Jews from Bamberg - presents across 43 rooms the archaeology, geology, and traditions of Franconian Switzerland. The interior setting is as remarkable as the content.

activities.text: Climb to the Fahnensteig in 10 minutes from the village parking: the viewpoint offers a vertical plunge onto Tüchersfeld and its rock needles. The trail continues to the Kühloch (a natural cave) and the Zeckenstein - count one hour round-trip for the whole route.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Überlingen closes the journey on the shores of Lake Constance. The medieval old town slopes gently toward the lake. The Münster St. Nikolaus houses a limewood altarpiece carved by Jörg Zürn in 1613, considered one of Germany's finest late Gothic altarpieces.
Überlingen's Stadtgärten, terraced gardens facing the lake, hosted the 2021 Landesgartenschau. The cactus collections and the rampart garden are worth a stroll. Modest admission fee.
The Städtisches Museum, housed in the 1462 Reichlin-von-Meldegg-Haus, presents a Renaissance ballroom with painted ceiling and regional art collections. The building itself is a monument.

activities.text: Finish with a swim in Lake Constance from the Therme Überlingen or the public beaches below the promenade. The view of the Swiss Alps from the lake provides the perfect endpoint for the road trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days
Lake Constance Loop: 6 Days Around the Bodensee

visits.text: Birnau Basilica overlooks Lake Constance from a hillside planted with vines. Completed in 1750, it brings together the best of Swabian rococo: Joseph Anton Feuchtmayer's stuccowork and Gottfried Bernhard Göz's frescoes. The Honigschlecker, a putto licking honey, is the most photographed figure on the entire Baroque Route.
From Birnau's forecourt, the view looks down over Lake Constance and takes in the Swiss Alps. The vineyard terraces around the church produce wine sold at the monastery shop. Free admission.

activities.text: The Pfahlbauten at Uhldingen, a reconstructed lake-dwelling village with UNESCO status, is a few minutes' drive away. The Bronze Age stilt houses offer family-friendly visits.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Kochberg Castle is a moated castle (Wasserschloss) built around 1600 in Renaissance style, surrounded by a moat. It's known worldwide for its connection to Goethe and Charlotte von Stein. The von Stein family acquired the estate in 1733. Goethe was a regular guest of Charlotte von Stein from 1775 to 1788—it was at Kochberg that he met Friedrich Schiller for the first time on September 7, 1788, before inviting him to Jena. He wrote the dates of his visits in ink on the castle's secretary desk, where they are still visible today. More than 1,700 letters from Goethe to Charlotte von Stein testify to this thirteen-year relationship. The museum reconstructs the period's apartments with original furniture, portraits, and handwritten documents.

The six-hectare landscape park was transformed by Carl von Stein (Charlotte's son) between 1800 and 1840, from a Baroque garden into a Romantic English park. Under imposing old trees, winding paths lead to a canvas hut, a ruined tower, a grotto with a burial site, a swimming lake, and the flower garden with its floral staircase.

The Liebhabertheater is a 75-seat private theater built around 1800 by Carl von Stein, modeled on Weimar's court theater. It's a jewel unlike any other in the world: the classical columned portico, the auditorium with its hand-marbled wallpaper and floral friezes, the stage, and the orchestra pit are fully restored. It belongs to the “European Route of Historic Theatres” and hosts operas, chamber concerts, and theatrical performances every weekend from May to October.

activities.text: Performance at Kochberg's Liebhabertheater: Baroque opera or chamber concert in this 75-seat theater, in the authentic atmosphere of the 18th century. Productions are conceived specifically for this space and employ historically informed performance practices.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

visits.text: 768 steps spiral up to the top of Ulm Minster's bell tower, Germany's tallest at 161.53 m. The viewing platform at 143 m offers views stretching to the Alps on clear days. Founded as a citizens' church in 1377 and converted to Protestant worship in 1530, it survived the 1944 bombings. Free admission to the church; a fee applies to the tower climb.

The Fischerviertel, the old fishermen's and tanners' quarter, snakes along the Blau just before it flows into the Danube. Leaning half-timbered houses, cobbled lanes, and the Schiefes Haus, one of the world's most tilted houses. A five-minute walk from the Minster.

Ulm's Stadtbibliothek, a glass pyramid designed by Gottfried Böhm, deliberately contrasts with the Gothic Minster it adjoins. Bold contemporary architecture in a city rebuilt after the war. Free admission.

activities.text: Sample Maultaschen at a city-center Gaststätte: these hefty Swabian dumplings filled with meat and spinach are served in broth or pan-fried. Legend has it monks invented them to hide meat during Lent.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

activities.text: Cut flowers, cheeses, draft beer: let your nose lead the way through the Viktualienmarkt. King Max I Joseph moved part of the market here in 1807, and more than a hundred vendors now have stalls around the maypole and fountains honoring Munich comedians such as Karl Valentin. At the beer garden, the city’s six major breweries take turns supplying the beer; bring your own food if you like, but drinks must be purchased on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II

visits.text: The terrace of the Vogelsburg: at your feet, the Main, 527 kilometers long, forms its famous Schleife. This viewpoint belongs to a former monastery turned restaurant dating from the 10th century, tucked among the vines a few hundred meters above the river. The panorama takes in the vineyards of Escherndorf and Nordheim and, on the horizon, the Steigerwald.

Volkach's Altstadt concentrates the Echterhof, the old Zehnthof, and the Schelfenhaus around a Marktplatz with fountain and 16th-century Rathaus. The Wallfahrtskirche Maria im Weingarten possesses an altarpiece by Tilman Riemenschneider - if time is limited, this detail alone justifies entry.

activities.text: Tasting Silvaner facing the Mainschleife on the Vogelsburg terrace is one of Franconia's rituals. The restaurant charges reasonable prices for such a view. Otherwise, head down to Astheim and rent a canoe at the river station - paddling up the loop is the best way to understand why the river stopped there.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Rheingau to Bayreuth - 12 Days in Germany

visits.text: Rust, girders, and steel stairways as far as the eye can see: exploring the Völklinger Hütte feels like walking through an industrial city frozen in 1986, when pig iron production stopped. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994, it offers a climb to the panoramic platform atop the blast furnaces. Wear sturdy shoes: more than 5,000 m of walkways await.

The Gebläsehalle at the Völklinger Hütte houses the giant blowers that supplied compressed air to the hot-blast stoves and blast furnaces. Built between 1905 and 1914 according to UNESCO, these machines now provide a backdrop for major exhibitions. Check the program before visiting: the site hosts up to three exhibitions a year.

If you’re traveling with children, set aside 45 minutes for Ferrodrom, the Völklinger Hütte’s science center. More than 100 interactive stations explain iron, steel, and the four elements, from fire to air. Visit after the blast furnaces: hands-on activities help restore attention when the machines start to look alike.

activities.text: A coking plant turned wild garden: Paradies at the Völklinger Hütte has an almost ironic name. Plants and animals have reclaimed these former industrial grounds, between Mosko’s street-art leopard and Ottmar Hörl’s 10 m King Kong. Save it for last: after the industrial halls, this green retreat gives your eyes a rest.

days_plan.itin_title: Saarland in 3 Days: Saarbrücken, the Saarschleife, and Homburg

visits.text: Waren is the gateway to Müritz National Park. The Müritzeum, an interactive museum on lakes and forests, has a freshwater aquarium spanning two levels, where a school of whitefish swims in circles. Immersive effect guaranteed. Lake Müritz itself (117 km²) is Germany's second-largest.

activities.text: In autumn, head to Rederangsee at dusk: up to 10,000 common cranes gather before migration. Guided observation by national park rangers. In summer, canoe trips on the canals between lakes.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Over in Warnemünde, the beach is empty before 9 a.m. Fishermen's houses converted into fish restaurants line the Alter Strom. Buy smoked fish straight from the boat for a few euros.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltic and Castles: Mecklenburg in 13 Days

visits.text: Walk across the Innbrücke for the classic view of Wasserburg, with its pastel facades clustered above the Inn. The former wooden bridge was swept away by ice almost every year, for the last time in 1929. At the far end, the Brucktor preserves murals from 1568 on its river-facing side: two armored guards still watch over the entrance to town.

Marienplatz brings two eras face to face: the Gothic town hall, built from 1457 to 1459, whose small hall retains its 1564 decoration, and the Rococo facade of the Kernhaus, the work of Johann Baptist Zimmermann between 1738 and 1740. During the season, a guided tour of the town hall’s rooms takes place on weekdays at 1 p.m.

The lion and tower on Wasserburg’s coat of arms come from the Frauenkirche: its 65 m bell tower served as a watchtower. The city’s oldest church, documented as early as 1324, preserves a Gothic Madonna from around 1420 beneath its Baroque decoration. Fifteen minutes is enough to see the Madonna and the nave.

St. Jakob’s finest feature is its pulpit, carved in 1638 by Martin and Michael Zürn. This 17th-century masterpiece stands out in a Gothic hall church built from 1410 to 1478 by Hans von Burghausen, Hans Stethaimer, and Stephan Krumenauer. On your way out, walk around the choir to find the “tree of life” on its exterior wall.

Four floors, 52 themes, around 8,000 objects: Museum Wasserburg occupies a Gothic patrician house typical of the Inn-Salzach region on Herrengasse. River shipping, the salt trade, and thirteen craft workshops tell the story of the city that served as Munich’s port until the railroad arrived. Open Tuesday through Sunday from 1 p.m.; adult admission is €2.50.

activities.text: Climb for about 20 minutes along Kellerbergweg to Schöne Aussicht, south of the bridge: from up here, Wasserburg reveals its setting in a bend of the Inn that almost completely surrounds it. The Innleiten, slopes on the opposite bank, rise as high as 70 m. Save this climb for clear skies, since the view depends on them.

A flood levee turned open-air gallery: along the bend of the Inn, more than 30 sculptures, some very large, line a stretch of about 1.5 km. The AK 68 artists’ association, founded in 1968, began commissioning them in 1988. Look for Leonard Schlögel’s limestone head, “Isis.”

days_plan.itin_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach

places.name: Weiden In Der Oberpfalz

visits.text: Weiden isn't the most picturesque town in the Palatinate, but its pedestrian center around the Oberer Markt has character. Good base for restocking, finding a decent restaurant and fueling up before the rural stages that follow.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

map_keywords: Weiden in der Oberpfalz old town

visits.text: Weilburg Palace occupies half the old town, set on a rocky spur above the Lahn. The baroque residence of the Nassau-Weilburg dynasty preserves its terraced gardens with orangery, among Hesse's finest. The Renaissance Hochschloss (1530-1572) is one of the state's best preserved.

Inaugurated in 1847, Weilburg's ship tunnel is Germany's oldest and longest still-navigable tunnel: 195 meters beneath the Mühlberg. Duke Adolph of Nassau had it bored to bypass the Lahnschleife rapids. Ten years later, the railway made it obsolete.

activities.text: Rent a canoe to pass through the ship tunnel by river. The Lahn flows gently through the vaulted tunnel, lit by a few bulbs. The experience lasts five minutes but leaves a lasting impression. Rental available at Weilburger Bootsanleger, at the tunnel's north entrance.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

places.name: Weimar

visits.text: Tiefurt Palace is a small summer residence on the banks of the Ilm east of Weimar. Originally a modest manor from the mid-16th century enlarged in 1765, it became Duchess Anna Amalia's favorite retreat from 1781 until her death in 1807. Despite its seven rooms per floor, it hosted literary and musical soirées bringing together Goethe, Wieland, and Corona Schröter, making Tiefurt a pastoral «Museion». The music room and the duchess's apartments are restored to their late 18th-century state with original furniture. Tiefurt is part of the UNESCO site «Classical Weimar».

The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar on April 12, 1919, by architect Walter Gropius, who merged the city's Academy of Fine Arts and School of Applied Arts. His manifesto proclaimed that “the aim of all visual art is building.” Among the recruited masters: Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, László Moholy-Nagy, and Oskar Schlemmer. The school left Weimar in 1925 under pressure from a conservative regional government and moved to Dessau, before being closed by the Nazis in 1933. The Bauhaus Museum Weimar, opened in 2019 for the centenary, holds the world's oldest Bauhaus collection—started by Gropius himself—with 13,000 objects spread across three floors. The Bauhaus sites in Weimar have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 1996.

Goethe's House at Frauenplan is the residence the poet occupied for 50 years, from 1782 to his death in 1832. It is preserved as he left it: his study with the mineral collection carefully arranged on shelves, his 5,000 volumes, the bed in which he died. It's the world's most important museum dedicated to Goethe. The house is part of the UNESCO site «Classical Weimar» inscribed in 1998.

Schiller's House is the dwelling the poet occupied during his last three years of life, from 1802 to his death in 1805. It's here that «The Bride of Messina» and «William Tell» were written. The study is preserved with the inclined desk at which Schiller worked standing, his cane, the manuscripts. The modest rooms contrast with the grandeur of the works born there.

The Duchess Anna Amalia Library is housed in the Renaissance “Green Palace” (1562–1565), converted into a library in 1761. Goethe was its director from 1797 to 1832 and doubled the holdings to reach 80,000 volumes. The three-story oval Rococo hall, built of wood, is one of Germany's most photographed interiors. On September 2, 2004, a fire destroyed 50,000 volumes and damaged 118,000—a national tragedy. After restoration, the library reopened in 2007. It preserves the world's largest collection of Goethe's Faust.

The House of the Weimar Republic (Haus der Weimarer Republik), opened in 2019, traces the history of Germany's first democracy. In 1919, the National Constituent Assembly met in Weimar's German National Theater—Berlin was deemed too dangerous amid revolution—and adopted the Constitution of August 11, 1919, instituting universal suffrage and social rights that were pioneering for the time. The permanent exhibition illuminates the birth, crises, and fall of this Republic.

activities.text: Stroll through Tiefurt's English landscape park along the Ilm River. Open meadows, century-old trees, and small monuments punctuate the main avenue: an artificial grotto, a temple of the muses, a Japanese-style wooden bridge. The park was designed in the spirit of 18th-century «natural» English gardens.

Bauhaus walking tour through Weimar's streets to discover buildings linked to the school: the Haus am Horn (1923), a Bauhaus housing prototype built for an exhibition, and Henry van de Velde's buildings where the school had its first workshops. Specialist guides offer guided tours.

days_plan.itin_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature
Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature

map_keywords: Goethe Gartenhaus Park an der Ilm Weimar

visits.text: With 6,666 pipes, the Gabler organ in Weingarten Basilica ranks among Germany's largest baroque instruments. Built in 1750, it resonates through a 102-meter-long nave locals call the “Schwäbischer Petersdom.” The ceiling frescoes are by Cosmas Damian Asam.

Every year on the Friday after Ascension, Weingarten's Blutritt gathers horsemen from across Swabia for an equestrian procession honoring a relic of Christ's Blood. It's Europe's largest mounted procession.

activities.text: Weingarten is 3 km from Ravensburg. The two towns complement each other well in a single day. The Alamannenmuseum, dedicated to the Alemanni of the early Middle Ages, displays remarkable funerary finds.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

places.name: Weissenhofsiedlung

visits.text: “Arab village”: that was how the Nazis mocked the Weissenhofsiedlung and its flat roofs. Built in 1927 for the Werkbund’s “Die Wohnung” exhibition under the direction of Mies van der Rohe, it brought together 17 architects from five countries. The duplex by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016, houses the Weissenhofmuseum: one half tells the story of the project, while the other recreates the 1927 interior. Admission is €6.50; the museum opens at 11 a.m. on weekdays and is closed Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

map_keywords: Weissenhofmuseum im Haus Le Corbusier Stuttgart

visits.text: The Weißenstädter See, 50 hectares of water ringed by forest, is surprisingly peaceful. No motors allowed: all you hear are windsurfing boards and grebes. The 4-km paved loop around the lake is equally suitable for strollers and roller skates.

The Felsenkeller carved into the granite near the cemetery look like the setting of a fantasy film. Overgrown with ivy and moss, these former cellars stored local beer. Photographers, come at dusk: the light between the vaults is striking.

activities.text: If the sun's out, lap the lake by SUP or pedal boat. The Siebenquell Therme, right on the shore, offers hot baths with views of the Schneeberg. Day pass around €20.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: Weißgerbergasse has Nuremberg’s largest collection of historic artisans’ houses: colorful half-timbered facades, oriel windows, and window boxes. The tanners who gave the street its name grew wealthy here during the Middle Ages, and many houses had their own well and garden. The tanneries have given way to cafés, stores, and workshops; stroll along the street at your own pace, then head to the Pegnitz via Maxplatz.

days_plan.itin_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO

visits.text: Weißwasser was long a glass capital, and the Glasmuseum Weißwasser tells this industrial and local story. You follow the glassmaking process and the daily lives of the glassworkers who built the town. The nearby Waldeisenbahn once transported raw materials to the glassworks, hence the tight connection between the two. Plan an hour, and combine the visit with a ride on the train for coherence.

activities.text: Board the Waldeisenbahn Muskau, the last forest railway of its kind preserved in Germany, with its tiny 600-millimeter gauge. Steam and diesel locomotives from the 1950s take you toward Kromlau or Bad Muskau, departing from Weißwasser's Teichstraße station. It runs mainly April through October, on weekends and public holidays. Buy your ticket at the station or directly from the conductor.

If you're traveling with children, Tierpark Weißwasser breaks the museum pace without breaking the budget. This small zoo stays human-scale, ideal for an hour or two between stops. It complements the town's glass-and-train day nicely. Check the opening hours on-site before going—they vary by season.

days_plan.itin_title: Upper Lusatia: Bad Muskau, Sorbian Country & Bautzen in 6 Days

visits.text: Contemplate the impressive half-timbered Town Hall of Wernigerode, one of the most photographed in Germany with its pointed turrets and medieval sculptures. This pearl of the Harz captivates with its ensemble of perfectly preserved half-timbered houses, including the town's smallest house that attracts the curious. The neo-Gothic castle enthroned on its hill offers a fairytale silhouette overlooking the colorful rooftops of the old town.

Visit Wernigerode Castle, residence of the Counts of Stolberg-Wernigerode transformed into a museum tracing 19th-century aristocratic life. The sumptuous apartments and decorative art collections testify to the refinement of German nobility. The panoramic view from the terraces embraces the Harz forests and surrounding peaks.

Discover the Steinerne Renne, a spectacular gorge of the Holtemme River where water cascades between huge moss-covered granite boulders. This natural wonder on the outskirts of Wernigerode offers a refreshing hike through preserved ancient woodland. At the Baumkuchenhaus, this traditional spit-baked cake keeps an old pastry-making craft alive.

activities.text: Excursion to the Schierke district, home of the Schierker Feuerstein herbal liqueur, about twenty minutes' drive from Wernigerode
Visit Pullman City Harz theme park in Hasselfelde, Germany's largest western town, about forty minutes' drive from Wernigerode

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns
Phantom Harz - 7 Days from Hamelin to the Brocken

visits.text: Burg Wertheim is worth the climb to understand the confluence rather than to find a furnished castle. The ruins overlook the meeting of the Main and Tauber, with the town’s rooftops below. Save this visit for a day with good visibility. Check access and wear shoes suitable for steps and uneven ground.

Reflections, bottles, and delicate decorations: the Glasmuseum Wertheim tells the story of glass in many different forms. Its collections range from decorative uses to everyday objects, in the heart of the old town. A glassblower’s presence can enhance the visit, but is not guaranteed. Check opening hours and ask whether a demonstration is scheduled for your chosen day.

The Grafschaftsmuseum Wertheim goes beyond a simple gallery of local memorabilia: its collections also explore floods, navigation, and trades. It occupies several historic buildings in the old town. Choose a few themes instead of trying to cover every room before leaving. Check opening hours and choose this museum over the Glasmuseum if urban history interests you more.

Two rivers, but just one town center to explore: Wertheim’s old town connects Marktplatz, Stiftskirche, and Spitzer Turm within a compact area. These landmarks help you find your way without requiring three additional admission tickets. Follow an outdoor loop from the square. Save interior visits for places that are open and fit the time you have left.

activities.text: Walk to the banks of the Main and Tauber in Wertheim to finish the route near their confluence. After the castles and half-timbered buildings, this break puts the town back in its geographic context. Choose a public path that is accessible given river conditions. Then check the route to the train station if you are returning the car before departing.

days_plan.itin_title: Neckar and Odenwald: 4 Days of Castles and Half-Timbered Buildings

visits.text: Built between 1906 and 1908 on an artificial mound four metres above the flats, the Leuchtturm Westerheversand stands 40 metres tall and its beam carries 39 kilometres — as far as Helgoland on a clear day. Since the 1970s it has appeared on Jever Beer bottles, earning it a fame its solitary setting would never suggest.

Sheep graze around the red-and-white tower in complete indifference — an absurd and entirely real scene. The Salzwiesen salt marshes at the foot of the lighthouse are a protected biotope within the Schleswig-Holsteinisches Wattenmeer National Park.

activities.text: Climb the 157 steps to survey the Eiderstedt peninsula from the platform at 37 metres: on a clear day you can count twenty church spires across the peninsula, along with the halligen islands to the north. The tower is only accessible on a guided tour, Wednesday to Monday, 11am–4pm, from Easter to late October.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Westerland is not pretty — it is functional: Sylt's “capital” concentrates hotels, shops and the Hindenburgdamm rail terminal. It is a logistical base, not a destination in itself. The Weststrand that stretches for kilometres north and south, however, is genuine wilderness: wind, waves, and few crowds outside high season.

The Hindenburgdamm, the 11 km railway causeway linking Sylt to the mainland since 1927, is the island's only land connection. Cars are loaded onto flat wagons — the car shuttle train. Watching one pass from Morsum beach gives a sense of Sylt's deliberate isolation.

St. Severin in Keitum is the real Romanesque church of Sylt — built in the 12th century in local sandstone, flanked by a mariners' churchyard with granite crosses. Keitum is also the best-preserved village on the island, with its thatched houses. It is 5 km east of Westerland by bike or bus line 1.

activities.text: Cycle the Weststrand from Westerland towards Wenningstedt or Kampen — the cycling paths follow either the Wattenmeer on the east side or the sea on the west. Hire a bike in town: €15–20 a day. The eastern route through the Braderup heath is less known and wilder.

The North Frisian wind snatches words from your mouth and makes flags snap — a constant on Sylt. Take the opportunity to watch kitesurfing at the Brandenburger Strand: the conditions are consistent and the riders spectacular.

Book a car-train ticket on the Hindenburgdamm to cross to Niebüll on the mainland — a 40-minute passage at rail level with the dunes and the Wattenmeer, perfect at sunset. Online booking is mandatory via DB Sylt Shuttle, especially at weekends in season.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Wetzlar Cathedral is famous for what it isn't: finished. The second Gothic tower never rose beyond its base, for lack of money after plague and 15th-century wars. The result is a strange asymmetric façade mixing Romanesque and Gothic. Free admission.

In 1772, young Goethe arrived in Wetzlar for an internship at the Reichskammergericht. He fell for Charlotte Buff, engaged to another. The Lottehaus on Pfaffengasse tells this story that became “The Sorrows of Young Werther.” Charming small museum, 30-minute visit.

Walk down to the Lahn via Pfaffengasse and Kornmarkt. Goethe lived at Kornmarkt during his stay. The half-timbered houses, small squares, and walls of the former imperial city can be covered in an hour. Six museums cluster in the old town.

activities.text: At Leitz-Park, the Leica world displays photography history since the invention of the Leica I in 1925. Galleries, workshops, boutique. The contemporary building contrasts with the Fachwerk downtown. Bus from Domplatz or 15 min by car.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: A spectacular castle hidden in a wooded valley: Burg Eltz does not overlook the Moselle from its riverbank. The interior can be visited on a guided tour; the ticket also includes the courtyard and Treasury. In 2026, some buildings are covered in scaffolding. Arrive at opening time and check the visiting season, which is scheduled to run through November 1, 2026.

activities.text: To see Burg Eltz emerge between the trees, walk to it from the Wierschem parking lot. The site offers access along the road and a trail passing the viewpoint depicted on the 500 deutsche mark banknote. Allow for the climb back up; bring cash for parking or the shuttle if you prefer to take it.

days_plan.itin_title: Moselle Valley Road Trip: 4 Days from Koblenz to Trier

visits.text: The Kurhaus of Wiesbaden is the city's emblem. Inaugurated in 1907 at the instigation of Wilhelm II—who made Wiesbaden his residence each spring and actively contributed to its development—this neoclassical building with its colonnade houses a casino (one of Germany's oldest, said to have inspired Dostoevsky's novel The Gambler), twelve reception rooms, and a large concert hall. It opens onto the Kurpark, landscaped in the 19th century in English style with a lake and fountains.

The Hessisches Staatstheater of Wiesbaden, inaugurated in 1894 in neo-Baroque style, is considered one of Germany's most beautiful theaters. It hosts opera, ballet, and drama. The Maifestspiele festival—founded in 1896 for Wilhelm II's visits—attracts internationally renowned opera productions each year.

Ascend to the summit of the Neroberg (245 m) via the Nerobergbahn, a water-powered funicular inaugurated in 1888—one of the oldest still operating in Germany. At the summit, the Russian Orthodox Church of Saint Elizabeth is hidden among the trees with its five golden onion domes. It was built in 1855 by Duke Adolf of Nassau in memory of his wife Elisabeth Romanova, daughter of Grand Duke Michael of Russia, who died in childbirth at age 19 on January 27, 1845. The princess's coffin still rests there. The view from the Monopteros—a temple-shaped belvedere—extends across the entire city and Rhine valley.

The Museum Wiesbaden, founded in 1819, brings together a collection of modern and contemporary art under one roof—including one of the world's most important collections of works by Alexej von Jawlensky, the Expressionist painter who lived in Wiesbaden—along with natural history collections featuring pieces from the Duchy of Nassau.

The Rheingau vineyards stretch across approximately 3,100 hectares between the Taunus and the Rhine's northern bank, around Rüdesheim am Rhein (35 km west of Wiesbaden). Riesling has been cultivated here since the Middle Ages—the first Johannisberg vineyard dates to 817. The south-facing slopes overlooking the Rhine and the thermal shadow of the Taunus create an exceptional microclimate. In Rüdesheim, the Niederwald cable car leads to the Germania statue, erected in 1883 to commemorate the founding of the German Empire.

The Upper Middle Rhine Valley, between Bingen (opposite Rüdesheim) and Koblenz, has been a World Heritage Site since 2002 for its cultural landscapes of vineyards, castles, and villages. Along 65 km, the river corridor is dotted with rocky outcrops, medieval ruins, and terraced slopes—a classic route that can be explored on foot, by bicycle, or by boat.

activities.text: Rheingau wine tasting at one of the wine shops in Wiesbaden's center—the city itself lies within the appellation. Riesling represents 80% of production; Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) occupies most of the remaining plots.

The Rheingauer Weinwoche (Rheingau Wine Week) takes place every year in early August on Wiesbaden's Schlossplatz. Over 100 winemakers present their wines on the castle forecourt. It's one of Hesse's oldest and most popular wine festivals.

visits.text: From outside, a simple country church with pastel walls set in a meadow. Inside, the Wieskirche is a rococo explosion: stucco, gilding, ceiling frescoes in shades of pink and blue. A UNESCO site since 1983, it draws visitors from around the world. Free entry.

In 1738, a peasant woman claimed to have seen tears flowing from the eyes of a statue of Christ. This “miracle of tears” triggered a pilgrimage, and the Zimmermann brothers built the Wieskirche between 1745 and 1754. Dominikus Zimmermann loved his work so much that he moved next door and stayed there until his death.

activities.text: Take the time to sit for ten minutes on a bench in the Wieskirche. The light streaming through the windows changes with the hour. Early morning, before the tour groups, the silence is total. On-site parking (paid).

visits.text: More than 530 burial mounds across 30 hectares of heathland: the Pestruper Gräberfeld is the largest Bronze Age necropolis in north-central Europe. The funerary urns date from approximately 800 to 200 BC. The site has free access, parking on the K248.

Continue to the Alexanderkirche in Wildeshausen's historic center, the only basilica in the Oldenburger Land. The medieval Stadtwall that surrounds it can be walked in twenty minutes. Have a look at the Gothic-gabled Rathaus while you're passing by.

activities.text: If you come between mid-August and early September, the flowering heather transforms the Gräberfeld into a purple carpet. In the morning, fog clings to dew-covered cobwebs: guaranteed spectacle for photographers.

days_plan.itin_title: Bremen to Münster: Peat Bogs, Canals and Castles

visits.text: Wilhelma began as a royal whim: William I wanted a Moorish-style country house, which Karl Ludwig von Zanth built between 1842 and 1846. Its pavilions, greenhouses, and Moorish garden now form Germany’s only combined zoological and botanical garden, home to around 8,500 plant species. In the pool, a single giant water lily leaf can support up to 70 kg. Arrive when it opens at 8:15 a.m., and keep in mind that the magnolias bloom in March and April.

activities.text: Next, move from the greenhouses to the animals: Wilhelma brings together around 1,200 species across roughly 30 hectares. The great ape house, opened in 2013, gives gorillas and bonobos some 4,500 m², thirteen times their former space, while the Amazonienhaus has recreated a tropical rainforest since 2000. In cold weather, save these heated houses for late morning: they become the park’s best refuge.

days_plan.itin_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque

visits.text: The locals simply call it 'the summit' — at 169 metres, Wilseder Berg is the highest point on the north-west German plain. On a clear day, Hamburg is visible 40 km away. You arrive on foot from Niederhaverbeck (about 4.5 km) or from Wilsede: cars are banned throughout the nature reserve.

Wilsede, a car-free village off-limits to tour coaches, looks like a fairy-tale set: half-timbered houses, sandstone walls, chickens roaming freely on cobbled paths. The Heidemuseum Dat ole Huus preserves 19th-century moorland peasant life — the attached Milchhalle serves a decent buckwheat cake.

activities.text: Walk the marked heathland trails around Wilseder Berg along the Heidschnuckenweg, the long-distance path that crosses the entire reserve. The curly-fleeced Heidschnucken sheep have been the moorland's gardeners for centuries: without them, the heather would revert to forest. Best time: August, when everything turns violet.

days_plan.itin_title: Schleswig-Holstein: Heathland, North Frisia and Sylt

visits.text: Ski resort in winter, heath trail in summer: Winterberg changes face with the seasons. The Kahler Asten, at 841 meters, is North Rhine-Westphalia's second-highest summit. An Astenturm with weather station has crowned the peak since 1895. The 36-hectare Hochheide surrounding it is a protected peat bog remnant dating from 1965.

activities.text: Climb the Kahler Asten via the Rothaarsteig from Winterberg (5.5 km, 1h30 walk). The trail cuts through spruce forest before emerging onto the bare summit heath. Parking at the summit if you prefer to drive.

In clear weather, from the Astenturm, the gaze extends to the Wasserkuppe in the Rhön and the Großer Feldberg in the Taunus. In winter, snow holds an average of 120 days per year. The Berggasthof at the summit serves regional dishes.

visits.text: The Wasserkunst stands in the center of Wismar's Marktplatz like a Dutch pavilion dropped there by mistake. This Renaissance bronze pavilion was built between 1579 and 1602 by Philipp Brandin and supplied the city with drinking water until 1897. Wismarians make it their emblem. The Marktplatz is one of northern Germany's largest, bordered by the Alter Schwede dating from around 1380.

St.-Nikolai-Kirche, consecrated in 1459, impresses with its central nave 37 m high. Built starting in 1381 to honor sailors and fishermen, it survived World War II almost intact, making it one of the region's best-preserved medieval buildings. Free entry.

The Alter Schwede leans slightly—it's intended, or rather time intended it. This Gothic brick facade dates from around 1380, and the name (the 'Old Swede') comes from a 19th-century tavern installed there in memory of Swedish occupation. Wismar was under Swedish rule from 1648 to 1803, a period of which the Zeughaus (Karl XII's baroque arsenal) bears witness.

activities.text: Walk along the Grube, a medieval canal dug in the 13th century to supply the city with fresh water, for its two kilometers through the old town. This canal is the last inner medieval moat preserved in a northern German old town. The walk passes former mills and brick facades.

If you have a stomach for smoked fish, try the Bückling—whole hot-smoked herring—in one of the Old Port stalls. Wismar's port has been active since the Middle Ages and still hosts reconstructed Kogge vessels. The Poeler Kogge Wissemara offers sailing excursions in summer.

visits.text: Autostadt is a 28-hectare theme park opened in 2000, built along the Mittelland Canal for the Hanover World Expo. It showcases the Volkswagen Group's brands in carefully designed pavilions. Its most spectacular attraction is a pair of fully automated, 48-meter-high glass towers that store up to 800 new vehicles and are connected to the factory by a 700-meter tunnel. Nearly 175,000 customers come here each year to collect their cars. The ZeitHaus museum traces automotive history from the Ford Model T to the Beetle.
The Kunstmuseum Wolfsburg, inaugurated in 1994, is one of northern Germany's most active contemporary art museums, featuring major temporary exhibitions in a building designed by Peter Schweger.

Wolfsburg Castle was first mentioned in 1302—a moated castle and former residence of the noble Bartensleben family. When the British renamed the town in May 1945, they chose this Weser Renaissance castle to erase the name “Stadt des KdF-Wagens” imposed by Hitler in 1938.

activities.text: Walk along the Mittelland Canal with an overview of the Volkswagen facilities: the chimneys of the factory founded in 1938 and the two glass delivery towers form a recognizable industrial skyline.

visits.text: Marvel at Wörlitz Park, one of Germany's most beautiful landscape gardens and jewel of the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This 18th-century gardening masterpiece spans 112 hectares of canals, artificial islands, and romantic vistas. Neoclassical pavilions, picturesque bridges, and Greek temples create an idealized landscape inspired by Prince Leopold III's travels to Italy and England.

Visit Wörlitz Palace, Germany's first neoclassical building, whose refined interiors house remarkable art and antiquities collections. St. Peter's Church, harmoniously integrated into the park landscape, completes this architectural ensemble of exceptional aesthetic coherence. Gondolas gliding along the canals offer a unique perspective on this earthly paradise designed according to Enlightenment ideals.

activities.text: Boat ride along the park canals for a romantic perspective

days_plan.itin_title: Saxony-Anhalt Road Trip: UNESCO Heritage Route and Medieval Towns

visits.text: Less famous than Speyer Cathedral, St. Peter’s Cathedral in Worms has more flair: Balthasar Neumann’s Baroque high altar, with gilded wood and colored marble, blazes in a Romanesque nave consecrated in 1181. The Song of the Nibelungs places the quarrel between Kriemhild and Brünhild here, before a north portal destroyed in 1689. Admission is free Monday through Saturday until 5:45 p.m.; head down to the crypt, where relatives of Emperor Conrad II are buried.

A deep silence hangs over the courtyard of the Worms synagogue. Destroyed during the pogrom of 1938, it reopened in 1961, modeled on the columned hall of 1174–1175 that inspired those in Regensburg, Vienna, Prague, and Kraków. Its Frauenschul, an annex reserved for women built in 1212–1213, is the earliest known in Europe. Admission is free daily; men must cover their heads—a cap is sufficient.

You’ll better understand what UNESCO inscribed in 2021 with a visit to the Jüdisches Museum in the Raschi-Haus on Hintere Judengasse. The building rests on medieval walls from the former community house, and the exhibition traces Jewish life in SchUM, the Hebrew acronym for Speyer, Worms, and Mainz, from the Middle Ages to the present. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with admission of €2.50; get the audio guide.

More than 2,000 gravestones still stand at Heiliger Sand, in use as early as the 11th century and described by the city as Europe’s oldest surviving Jewish cemetery. It shares World Heritage status with the synagogue, just beyond Willy-Brandt-Ring. The cemetery welcomes visitors Sunday through Friday, never on Saturdays or Jewish holidays; men must cover their heads.

A rebellious monk turned into a 3.5 m statue: on the Lutherdenkmal, unveiled in 1868, Luther towers over his forerunners Peter Waldo, Wycliffe, Jan Hus, and Savonarola. The ensemble rivals Geneva’s for the title of largest Reformation monument. Then head to the Heylshof garden, which marks the site of the Diet of 1521, where Luther refused to recant. The garden is free to enter, even when the museum is closed.

visits.text: A farming village turned artists' colony in 1889: Worpswede owes everything to Fritz Mackensen, captivated by the light of the Teufelsmoor. In 2026, the four museums celebrate Paula Modersohn-Becker's 150th birthday with interconnected exhibitions. Plan on spending the morning.

The low light of the Teufelsmoor filters through the windows of the Barkenhoff, a former farmhouse transformed into a Gesamtkunstwerk by Heinrich Vogeler as early as 1895. The Art Nouveau garden is the most photographed spot in the village. The Heinrich Vogeler Museum occupies the interior.

Hoetger's Niedersachsenstein divides visitors: an expressionist brick sculpture perched on the Weyerberg, some find it brilliant, others hideous. Climb up for the view over the peat bogs. Free access, five minutes' walk from the center.

activities.text: Rent a bike and pedal through the Teufelsmoor on dirt paths between drainage canals. The flat, misty landscape explains why the painters stayed. Count on 90 minutes for the classic loop.

visits.text: Founded in 1907, the Fichtelgebirgsmuseum occupies nine buildings around the Spitalhof, a medieval hospice bequeathed by the wealthy tinsmith Sigmund Wann in 1451. With its 3,100 m² of exhibition space, it's Bavaria's largest regional museum. The mineral collection alone is worth the trip. Closed Mondays.

The neoclassical alleyways around the Koppetentor smell of fresh bread and malt beer. Wunsiedel is the birthplace of Jean Paul, a cult writer in Germany, virtually unknown elsewhere. His bust greets you in the main square. Cross the town on foot in 20 minutes.

activities.text: Take advantage of summer to catch the Luisenburg-Festspiele, Germany's oldest open-air theater festival. The stage is literally wedged between the rocks. Book ahead: seats sell out fast in July and August.

days_plan.itin_title: Fichtelgebirge and Oberpfalz: Granite, Beer and Castles

visits.text: You're floating twelve meters above the Wupper, swaying gently as you glide. The Schwebebahn, a suspended monorail inaugurated in 1901, runs 13.3 km through the city across 20 stations. Several stations preserve their original Jugendstil architecture. The full round trip takes about an hour. Grab a window seat for photos as you pass over the zoo.

Founded in 1902 in the former Elberfeld town hall, the Von der Heydt Museum houses Monet, Picasso, Kirchner, and Dix. The collection comprises around 3,000 paintings and 30,000 graphic works. On the first Thursday of the month, the permanent collection is free from 5pm to 8pm. Allow a good two hours.

Take the Nordbahntrasse, a former railway line converted into a 22-km pedestrian and cycling path. It threads through tunnels and viaducts above the rooftops. A 3-km stretch between Mirke and Loh is enough to capture the reclaimed industrial vibe. Free access, wheelchair accessible.

activities.text: Wuppertal Zoo surprises with its hilly topography spread across 24 hectares. Lions and penguins share terraced woodland slopes. Founded in 1881, it's one of Germany's oldest zoos. Arrive at opening time to avoid weekend crowds.

If you arrive on a Thursday evening, the Von der Heydt Museum opens its doors free for the permanent collection. Otherwise, the cafés along Friedrich-Ebert-Straße offer ideal terraces to watch the Schwebebahn glide overhead.

days_plan.itin_title: From the Bergisches Land to the Lahn: an 11-day road trip

visits.text: The Würzburg Residence, built between 1720 and 1744 under the patronage of the Schönborn prince-bishops, is Europe's most stylistically unified Baroque palace according to UNESCO, which inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1981. Architect Balthasar Neumann, then 33 years old, oversaw the work with the help of specialists from Vienna, Paris, Italy, and Flanders. The grand staircase houses the world's largest fresco painted as a single continuous work (32 × 19 meters), created by the Venetian artist Tiepolo in just 210 days between 1752 and 1753: it depicts the four continents known at the time paying homage to the prince-bishop. The prince-bishop had initially hired a Milanese artist, but he painted so poorly that the prince-bishop decided to bring in Tiepolo, promising him 10,000 florins—three times his Venetian salary.

Step through the doors of the Hofkirche, the Residence chapel tucked into the southwest wing. Despite its modest dimensions, it's considered one of the most perfect achievements of 18th-century sacred architecture. Five oval domes rise in succession above twisted pink marble columns crowned with gilded Corinthian capitals. Tiepolo painted the altarpieces here, while Antonio Bossi crafted the stuccowork. After the chapel, stroll through the Court Gardens (Hofgarten), laid out in terraces between 1765 and 1780, adorned with sculptures, putti, and symmetrical flower beds—they too are part of the UNESCO listing.

The Alte Mainbrücke, Würzburg's oldest bridge, has connected the city to Marienberg Fortress since the 15th century. An earlier stone bridge existed as early as 1133, but floods in 1342 and 1442 destroyed it. The current bridge, 185 meters long and comprising eight limestone arches, was rebuilt between 1476 and 1703. Since the 1720s, twelve 4.5-meter-tall Baroque sandstone statues have adorned its pillars, including Saint Kilian, the city's patron saint, who was martyred in 689, and Charlemagne. Until 1886, it was the only way to cross the Main in Würzburg. Now pedestrianized, the bridge keeps a local tradition alive: residents gather there at the end of the day for a glass of Franconian Silvaner, the region's signature grape, served in the distinctive flattened Bocksbeutel bottles.

St. Kilian's Cathedral (Dom), Germany's fourth-largest Romanesque church, has dominated the cityscape since the 11th century. It is named after the city's patron saint, an Irish missionary who was martyred in 689 alongside his companions Colman and Totnan. Inside, works by the sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider stand alongside Ottoman elements from the early 11th century and Gothic additions. The Schönborn family's funerary chapel, designed by Balthasar Neumann in 1736, can be visited in the transept.

Marienberg Fortress, perched on the left bank of the Main, served as the residence of Würzburg's prince-bishops for five centuries before the Residence was built. Its origins date back to 706, when the first church was built on the site—one of the oldest in Germany. The present enclosure combines medieval fortifications with Renaissance bastions. Inside, the Main Franconian Museum (Mainfränkisches Museum) houses the world's largest collection of sculptures by Tilman Riemenschneider, a master of the late Gothic period who worked in Würzburg between 1483 and 1531 and whose limewood faces are strikingly expressive.

Climb the 247 steps along the Way of the Cross leading to the Käppele, the pilgrimage church of the Visitation, built by Balthasar Neumann between 1748 and 1750 on the Nikolausberg hill. It all began in 1640, when a fisherman from the Main placed a Pietà in his vineyard during the Thirty Years' War; miraculous healings were reported there a few years later, drawing pilgrims. The Way of the Cross, the largest in Germany, is marked by 14 chapels housing 77 life-size statues sculpted by Johann Peter Wagner. The church miraculously survived the bombing of March 16, 1945, which destroyed 90% of the city—a German soldier is said to have pretended to be out of ammunition to avoid shelling it.

The Juliusspital, a hospital founded in 1576 by Prince-Bishop Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn "for the indigent and the sick," remains operational today. It derives its income from about a hundred hectares of vineyards it has owned since the 16th century, making it one of Würzburg's three great historic wine estates alongside the Bürgerspital (founded by wealthy burghers). The arcaded inner courtyard, the 17th-century buildings restored after the war, and the bistro where you can taste Würzburger Stein are worth a stop.

On the market square, the Marienkapelle (St. Mary's Chapel) is a Gothic church recognizable by its white and red sandstone façade. Across from it, the Falkenhaus, with its magnificent yellow and white Rococo façade adorned with stucco, houses the tourist office. Franconia's first Baroque collegiate church, St. John im Haug (1670), designed by Italian architect Antonio Petrini, stands out with its two towers flanking a tall façade and an imposing dome—a Crucifixion by Tintoretto (1583) surmounts the high altar.

activities.text: Settle on the Alte Mainbrücke in the late afternoon to enjoy a glass of Franconian Silvaner as the sun sets over the Marienberg fortress and the vineyard-covered hills.

Descend into the vaulted cellars of the Bürgerspital or Juliusspital for a tasting of Franconian wines. Franconia, one of Germany's 13 wine regions, is known for its dry white wines—Silvaner, Bacchus, and Müller-Thurgau—served in flattened Bocksbeutel bottles. The terraced vineyards lining the Main and overlooking the city are an integral part of the landscape.

places.name: Zell

visits.text: A single cat tells the story of this place’s identity: the Zeller Schwarze Katz Brunnen gives Zell its most evocative landmark. The fountain on the Marktplatz celebrates the name of the local vineyard, which has become the town’s emblem. Make a brief stop around the square; the wine museum is an alternative if you would like to explore further.

activities.text: If you enjoy little clues on the ground, follow a section of the Zeller Schwarze Katz Themenwanderweg. Cat paw prints mark this route devoted to wine and Zell’s history. Information panels add substance to a simple walk. Limit yourself to a section near the center and retrace your steps to keep the day on track.

activities.text: Continue around Dutzendteich lake, following the German- and English-language signs leading from the Kongresshalle to the Zeppelintribüne. Designed by Albert Speer and built from 1935 to 1937, this 360 m grandstand overlooked grounds that could hold some 320,000 people; the swastika that crowned it was blown up on April 20, 1945. Today, the stone is crumbling, and a long-term conservation program is underway. Walking through stations 1 to 9 of the route takes about 1 hour 30 minutes.

visits.text: Zingst is the last link in the Fischland-Darß-Zingst peninsula. Its pier and the Max Hünten Haus (photography center) bring the seafront to life. In autumn, common cranes gather by the thousands on the Bodden lagoons before migration.

visits.text: Push open the Zwiefalten Minster door and brace yourself for impact: gilded stucco, Franz Joseph Spiegler frescoes covering the entire ceiling length, monumental high altar. The Benedictine abbey, founded in 1089, was secularized in 1803. The austere exterior betrays nothing.

activities.text: Stop at the Lautertal overlook on the road from Beuron: the view looks down into the steep-sided valley. Quiet forest roads with no traffic cross the Alb plateau.

days_plan.itin_title: Castles and the Baroque in Swabia in 8 Days

visits.text: Waldmuseum Zwiesel gives meaning to the landscapes you have traveled through: the forest, its inhabitants, and glassmakers share the same story. The galleries bring together wildlife, plants, local history, and glassmaking, with interactive displays. The miniature glassmakers’ village helps you visualize how the work was organized. Allow one hour for a selection of galleries; the museum is closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, except during Bavarian school vacations.

Stacking 93,665 drinking glasses without glue: Zwiesel’s Glaspyramide turns a tableware item into a structure. The glasses rest in stacked layers, protected by a transparent enclosure. After the collections in Frauenau, this stop reveals the industrial side of local glassmaking. Look for the installation at Schott-Arkaden and allow fifteen minutes.
